text:
神農本草經序

記曰醫不三世不服其藥鄭康成曰慎物齊也孔沖遠引僑說云三世者一曰黃帝鍼灸二曰神農本草三曰素女脈訣康成周禮注亦曰五藥草木蟲石穀也其治合之齊則存乎神農子儀之術是禮記注所謂慎物齊者窑言治合之齊指本草諸書而言也沖遠既治合說復疑其非鄉義過矣漢書引本草方術始載神農本草經三卷蔡邕志本草七卷今俱不而藪文志闕載賈公彥中經簿有子儀本草經一卷不言出於神農至隋經籍志始載神農本草經三卷又據陸元朗經典釋文所引則名又據今分上中下三品者相合當屬漢以來售本隋志又載雷公本草集注四卷蔡邕本草七卷今俱不傳自別錄以後累有損益升降隨時條記或傳合本文不相別白據陸元朗經典釋文所引則名正神農本經三卷又據醫所附益者合併為一其來售矣孫君伯淵借其從子因大觀本草黑白字書蓋定為後人竄入釋本太平御覽引經為最古散見於諸書徵引者定為本文其有預章朱崑常山奉高郡縣名系以考證非濫雅之倫草者以吳普本為最古散見於諸書徵引者定為本文其有預章才沈鬱之思未易為此也凡大夫含聲負氣以倒生勞達蠛飛蠛動之倫胃盡其性遇物能以生之具儒者宜致思焉淮南王書曰地黃主屬骨而甘草主生肉之藥也又曰大戟去水亭歷愈張用之不節乃反為病論衡曰治風用風治熱用熱治邊用蜜丹潛夫論曰治疾當眞人參反得支羅服當得麥門冬反蒸橫麥已而不識眞合而服之病以浸劇斯神農之緒音

神農本草經序
translation:
Preface to the Shennong Bencao Jing (Classic of the Divine Husbandman's Materia Medica)

The Record of Rites states: "One should not take medicines from a physician whose family has not practiced medicine for three generations." Zheng Kangcheng explained: "This means being careful about the preparation of medicinal compounds." Kong Chongyuan, citing an outside commentary, explains that "three generations" refers to: first, the Yellow Emperor's acupuncture and moxibustion; second, Shennong's materia medica; and third, the Plain Woman's treatise on pulse diagnosis. Kangcheng's Commentary on the Rites of Zhou also states that the five medicines are: herbs, wood, insects, minerals, and grains. The art of combining these into medicinal preparations belongs to the tradition of Shennong and Ziyi. Thus what the Commentary on the Rites of Zhou means by "being careful about compounds" refers specifically to the materia medica texts and their teachings. Kong Chongyuan, having accepted the theory of combination, then doubted its orthodox interpretation — this was going too far. The History of the Han Dynasty cites the Bencao Fangzhu as the first text to record the Shennong Bencao Jing in three volumes. Cai Yong's bibliography lists a materia medica in seven volumes, but both are now lost. The Bibliographic Treatise omits any record; Jia Gongyan's Zhongjing Bibliography lists a Bencao Jing attributed to Ziyi in one volume, without attributing it to Shennong. It was not until the Sui Dynasty's Bibliographic Treatise that the Shennong Bencao Jing in three volumes was recorded. According to citations in Lu Yuanlang's Jingdian Shiwen, the title is indeed the Shennong Bencao Jing in three volumes. The present division into upper, middle, and lower grades of medicinal substances corresponds with this, suggesting the text circulated in this form since the Han dynasty. The Sui bibliography also records Lei Gong's Bencao Jizhu in four volumes and Cai Yong's Bencao in seven volumes, but both are now lost. From the Bielu onward, there were successive additions and deletions, rises and reductions in classification, recorded as circumstances arose, or transmitted together with the original text without distinction. Sun Boyan borrowed his nephew's copy and, using the Daguan Bencao where texts are distinguished in black and white characters, determined that certain passages were later interpolations. The Taiping Yulan cites the classic most extensively from the oldest scattered sources found in various books; entries so cited were established as the original text. Place names such as Yuzhang, Zhukun, Changshan, and Fenggao counties were used as evidence — this was no arbitrary elegance. As for Wu Pu's version of the materia medica, it is the oldest text, and passages cited scattered in various books were established as the original text. Such an undertaking required deep and sustained thought — it was no easy task. All creatures — the great officers who breathe and bear vital energy, those born upside down, those who labor and wriggle, the gnats that fly and swarm — each has its nature fully realized in response to things, giving them life. The learned should give this careful thought. The Huainanzi states: "Rehmannia (dihuang) governs the bones, and licorice (gancao) governs the regeneration of flesh." It also states: "Euphorbia (daji) expels water retention, and woad seeds (tingli) relieve swelling; if used without proper measure, they will instead cause illness." The Lunheng states: "Wind ailments are treated with wind-related herbs; heat ailments are treated with heat-related herbs; borderland ailments are treated with honey and cinnabar." The Qianfu Lun states: "When treating illness, one must use genuine ginseng; conversely, if one obtains Zhiluo as a substitute, or Ophiopogon in place of something else, and the substitute is used without recognizing the genuine article, combining and taking them — the illness will only grow worse." This is the gist of Shennong's legacy.

text:
出版說明

神農本草經是中國最古的一部藥物文獻，相傳為神農所作，實係後人假託據歷代的考證，可能是東漢末的作品，經過魏吳普的輯述始成專書。後來比較完全的本草，如唐蘇敬等修本草、宋唐慎微的經史證類備用本草，和明時珍的本草綱目，都是以神農本草經為基礎而加以擴充的。

吳普輯據述的本草，又博采藝文類聚、初學記、後漢書注事類賦諸書，多有引據清嘉慶年間孫星衍根據太平御覽證類本草又博采藝文類聚、初學記、後漢書注事類賦諸書，多有引據清嘉慶年間孫星衍根據太平御覽證類本草又博采而輯本草，又經散佚，歷代各書，多有引據清嘉慶年間孫星衍根據太平御覽證類本草并附考異一卷。

各書的引文，附列每條之後，成為比較完善的單行本。明盧復從本草綱目中輯出神農本草經文，並將光也輯有神農本草經，收入武陵山人遺著祈輯錄本。

農本草經，收入漢學堂叢書；入清周海刊神農本草經三卷并附考異一卷。本書酌改個別字句日人森立之輯有叢書集成。我們重印本書的主要目的，是供給讀者以研究中國藥物的古代文獻讀過本草經，可以了解中國古代藥物逐步發展擴大的過程。孫本雖還存在着若干脫誤，但是本輯錄考證，比較詳備這次是利用舊版重印，並經過校勘本書有些脫誤，另在所附「校刊後記」中說明。

商務印書館
一九五五年三月
translation:
Publisher's Note

The Shennong Bencao Jing (Classic of the Divine Farmer's Materia Medica) is China's oldest pharmaceutical document. Traditionally attributed to the Divine Farmer (Shennong), it was in fact composed by later hands under his name. According to successive generations of scholarly verification, it is likely a work from the late Eastern Han period, and took shape as a dedicated text through the compilation and commentary of Wu Pu of the Wei state. Later, more comprehensive materia medica works — such as the Tang dynasty's Bencao (revised by Su Jing and others), the Song dynasty's Jingshi Zhenglei Beiyong Bencao by Tang Shenwei, and the Ming dynasty's Bencao Gangmu by Li Shizhen — all took the Shennong Bencao Jing as their foundation and expanded upon it.

Wu Pu's compilation drew widely from sources such as the Yiwen Leiju, the Chuxue Ji, and commentary on the Hou Han Shu, among other works, and contains many citations. During the Jiaqing reign of the Qing dynasty, Sun Xingyan, drawing on the Taiping Yulan and the Zhenglei Bencao and other widely gathered sources, compiled a recension of the Bencao, appending one additional volume of textual variants. Each cited passage from various books was appended after its relevant entry, making this a relatively thorough standalone edition. Ming scholar Lu Fu extracted the Shennong Bencao Jing text from the Bencao Gangmu and compiled it separately. There was also a compilation included in the Wuling Shanren Yizhu Qi collection. The Bencao Jing was incorporated into the Hanxue Tang Congshu; and in the Qing, Zhou Hai published the Shennong Bencao Jing in three volumes with one appended volume of variants. This book makes selective corrections to individual characters and sentences. Sun's recension, though it still contains certain errors and omissions, is nonetheless relatively thorough and well-documented in its collation and commentary. This reprint uses the old printing blocks; textual problems identified during proofreading are explained in the appended "Note on Collation."

The Commercial Press
March 1955

text:
神農本草經序

儒者不必以醫名而知醫之理則莫過於儒者。奉秋時。而實儒也世之言醫者必首推神農非與太乙遊。則其傳于醫者也。其通周易。辨皿蟲之義。醫也。其識不廣非以土地所生萬千類驗其能治與否則其業不神傳不正識不廣業不神雖巡五岳四瀆。取玉石草木禽獸蟲魚米穀之屬歷試之親嘗之亦僅與商買市販等耳。於醫乎何與吾攷日神農千古之大儒也。考崇文總目載食品一卷五臟論一卷皆繫之神農。本草經而亦無專本唐木審元真輯之書錄解題之大觀本草讀志謂之證類本草久不廣後繼者希雍有疏盧頤有乘皆以本經為主。然或參以隱說或以衍斷解愈紛義愈晦。未有考核精審卓然有所發明者則證古文難。古而折衷于至是為尤難孫淵如以觀察僧從子鳳卿輯神農本草經三卷于吳善名醫外則說古文。雅廣雅淮南子抱樸子諸書。不列古方非徒證脈而古聖殷農殷治世之意燦然如列眉孔子曰多識諸人也。獸草木之名又曰致知在格物。則是書也固宜或以本草之名始見漢書平帝紀。楼護傳幾有疑于本草經者。然神農始嘗百草始有醫藥見于三卷宗之至郡縣本屬後人所附。經但云生山谷生川澤耳。洪範

皇紀奏因三百六十五種盂祀復加簽定寫本草又宗之至郡縣本屬後人所附經廣為二十卷。始有醫藥見于唐本草宗之増一百十四種神農始嘗百草。始有醫藥。注釋為七卷見于陶隱居別錄矣増一百四種廣為二十卷。始唐本草宗之増

一百三十三種盂祀復加簽定寫本草又宗之至郡縣本屬後人所附。経但云生山谷生川澤耳洪範
translation:
Preface to the Shennong Bencao Jing (Divine Farmer's Classic of Materia Medica)

A Confucian scholar need not be famous as a physician in order to understand the principles of medicine — yet no one has surpassed the Confucians in this understanding. In the time of the Spring and Autumn period, those who were truly Confucians were the ones the world first praised as physicians, placing Shennong above all, not as one who wandered with the immortal Taiyi, but as one whose teachings were transmitted to physicians. He mastered the Zhou Yi and understood the significance of creatures and vessels. He was a physician in that sense. Without broad knowledge, without knowing the tens of thousands of plants, minerals, and creatures produced across the land — without testing and personally tasting them to determine whether they can heal — one's practice will lack spiritual depth and will not be properly transmitted. Even if one were to travel the Five Sacred Mountains and Four Great Rivers collecting jades, stones, herbs, trees, birds, beasts, insects, fish, grains, and cereals, and test them all, one would amount to no more than a merchant or market vendor. What would that have to do with medicine? I have considered that Shennong was one of the greatest Confucian scholars of all antiquity. The Chongwen Zongmu records works attributed to Shennong including a volume on food items and a volume on the five visceral organs. The Bencao Jing too has no single authoritative original text; from the Tang dynasty onward it was reviewed and compiled. The Daguanbencao, as the Zhulei Bencao notes, ceased to be widely transmitted for a long time, and those who followed — such as Xi Yong with his commentary and Lu Yi with his additions — all based themselves on the original classic, yet either incorporated hidden sayings or elaborated interpretations, so that meanings became ever more fragmented and obscure. No one had yet produced a refined, careful, and illuminating critical text, making it difficult to verify the ancient writing, and even more difficult to reach a balanced judgment. Sun Yuanru, through his connections as a commissioner and the work of his nephew Fengqing, compiled the Shennong Bencao Jing in three volumes, drawing on the Wushan, Erya, Guangya, Huainanzi, and Baopuzi and other texts, without listing ancient prescriptions — not merely to demonstrate the pulse tradition, but so that the intentions of the ancient sages, Shennong's healing of the world, would shine forth as clearly as one's eyebrows. Confucius said, "Broadly acquaint yourself with the names of birds, beasts, plants, and trees," and also, "The extension of knowledge lies in the investigation of things." Thus this book is entirely appropriate. Some have doubted the Bencao Jing because the name "bencao" (materia medica) first appears in the Han Shu under the record of Emperor Ping and in the biography of Lou Hu. Yet Shennong first tasted the hundred herbs and first established medicine and pharmacy, as seen in three volumes, which later editors appended by county and district. The original classic only says "grows in mountain valleys" or "grows in river marshes." The Hongfan...

The imperial annals record that because of the 365 types, sacrificial offerings were made, and further annotations were added, fixing the text of the Bencao; later compilers expanded it to twenty volumes, adding 114 types. Shennong first tasted the hundred herbs and established medicine; Tang dynasty scholars of the classic added 133 types; sacrificial editions were further annotated and fixed, and the Bencao was again compiled, with county and district information appended by later people. The classic itself only says "grows in mountain valleys" or "grows in river marshes." Hongfan...

出版記主

神農本草經序

惟其膽涉者博故引類比方．悉符藥論．後儒或忽為方技家言．漁獵所及．又是未師而非往古甚至經典所載鳥獸草木亦輾轉而昧其名不已償乎後漢書華陀傳吳普從陀學依準陀療多所全濟院以五禽之戲別傳．又載魏明帝使普為禽戲普以其法語諸醫疑其方術相傳別有奇文異數今觀普所釋本草．由於稽考之勤比則神農黃帝岐伯雷公桐君醫和．扁鵲以及後代名醫之說靡不賅載．則其多所全濟．由於稽考之勤比驗之密而非必別有其奇文異數信乎非讀三世書者不可服其藥也．世俗所傳黃帝神農扁鵲之書多為後人窺易．余願得夫閎覽博物者為之正也因孫君伯仲校定本草而發其端至其書考證精審則讀者宜自得之餘姚邵晉涵序
translation:
Publication Preface

Preface to the Shennong Bencao Jing

Because those who delved deeply into this subject were broadly learned, they drew analogies and comparisons across categories, all in accord with pharmaceutical discourse. Later Confucians sometimes dismissed this as mere talk of technical arts and crafts, lumping it together with hunting and fishing lore. Moreover, those who had not studied under a master and who departed from antiquity went so far as to obscure the names of birds, beasts, grasses, and trees recorded in the canonical texts, passing errors along until the original meanings were lost. Already in the biography of Hua Tuo in the History of the Later Han, it is recorded that Wu Pu studied under Hua Tuo, followed Tuo's methods of treatment, and cured many patients, using the Five-Animal Exercises as a separate transmission. It is also recorded that Emperor Ming of Wei had Pu compile the exercises for birds and beasts. Pu conveyed the methods to various physicians; some doubted that his techniques had been transmitted separately with esoteric texts and unusual formulas. Yet when one examines Pu's commentary on the Bencao today, one sees that it draws upon the sayings of the Yellow Emperor, Shennong, Qibo, Lei Gong, Tong Jun, Yi He, and Bian Que, as well as later famous physicians, omitting nothing. That he was able to cure so many patients was due to the diligence of his scholarly inquiry and verification — not necessarily because he possessed some separate esoteric texts or unusual formulas. It is truly said that one who has not read the books of three generations of physicians should not administer medicines. The texts of the Yellow Emperor, Shennong, and Bian Que that circulate in common society have largely been tampered with by later hands. I have long wished that men of broad learning and wide knowledge would set them right. Now, as Master Sun Bochang has collated and established the text of the Bencao and brought this matter to light, readers who wish to go further in examining its careful scholarship and precise annotations should seek that out for themselves.

Written by Shao Jinhan of Yuyao

text:
校定神農本草經序

神農本草經三卷所傳白字書見大觀本草。按嘉祐補注序云所謂神農本草經者。以朱字名醫因神農舊條而有增補者以墨字間於朱字開寶重定序云。舊據此三卷所流傳黑名醫別錄互為編纂至梁貞白先生而有增補乃以別錄參其本經。朱墨雜書實時謂明白據此則世所流傳名醫別錄陶弘景乃以別錄參其本經。以前神農黃帝岐伯雷公扁鵲之文各有成書。吳普見之故其說藥性主治各家殊異。後人纂為一書自然猶本草之以是不亂舊說。本經之文以是不胤漢書平紀及樓護傳。按載文志猶有勞注。或朱墨字之別。本經之文以是不亂吳普書之名僅見漢書

神農黃帝食藥七卷今本謂為食禁買公彥禮醫師疏。引其文正作食藥。宋人不考遂疑本草非七略

中書買公彥引中經纂又有子儀本草經一卷疑亦此也。梁七錄有神農本草三卷其卷數不同者古今略

分合之異神農之主世書契未作。識者以此疑經。如皇甫謐言此書四卷成於陶弘景云。其卷數不同已前文是日載文志良是癥。

字未傳藥性所主。當以識諸家。因至於桐乃著在於本傳。此書當與素問同類。其言良是大古書今見存有神

兵五行雜占。經書達以三填為三皇之書神農預其列。史記言秦始皇不去醫藥卜筮之書則此經幸與

農經易並存。顏之推家訓乃云。本草神農所述而有豫章。朱崖趙國常山奉高真定臨淄馮翊等郡縣名出

周易春秋傳注買家訓乃云三境為三皇農書神農預列史記言秦始皇不去醫藥下筮之書則此經幸與

諸藥物皆由後人所屬。非本文陶弘景亦云所出郡縣乃後漢時制。疑仲景元化等所記按群綜注張衡

校定神農本草經序
translation:
Preface to the Collated Shennong Bencao Jing (Classic of Materia Medica of Shennong)

The three-volume Shennong Bencao Jing has been transmitted in white-character editions. As seen in the Daguan Bencao, the preface to the Jiayou Supplementary Commentary states: what is called the Shennong Bencao Jing uses red characters, while the additions made by later physicians building on Shennong's original entries use black characters interspersed among the red. The preface to the Kaibao revised edition states: the old text, based on these three transmitted volumes, had the black-character Mingyi Bielu (Supplementary Records of Famous Physicians) edited and compiled together with it by Tao Hongjing up to the time of the Elder of Huayang (Tao Hongjing), who added supplementary entries and incorporated the Bielu alongside the original classic, mixing red and black in the writing. This was considered a clear and evident arrangement. Thus the Mingyi Bielu that has been transmitted in the world was compiled by Tao Hongjing, who interwove the Bielu with the original classic. The earlier texts attributed to Shennong, the Yellow Emperor, Qibo, Lei Gong, and Bian Que each existed as separate writings. Wu Pu saw them all, and that is why his account of the properties and indications of drugs varies among different schools. Later people compiled them into a single text, yet naturally the order of the Bencao remained undisturbed, so that the original classic's text was not confused with old explanations, nor was the original text mixed with such sources as the Hanshu Pingji (Annals of Emperor Ping) and the biography of Lou Hu. According to entries in the bibliographic treatise, there are still marginal notes and distinctions between red and black characters. Thus the text of the original classic is not confused with Wu Pu's writings, which are mentioned only briefly in the Hanshu.

The seven-volume Shennong Huangdi Shiyao (Shennong and Yellow Emperor's Drug-Eating [text]) is today referred to in some editions as Shijin (Food Prohibitions). Jia Gongyan's commentary on the Rites physician passage cites its text and correctly writes Shiyao (Drug-Eating). Song scholars, not examining this carefully, doubted that the Bencao was among the Seven Summaries.

The Zhongjing (Central Classic catalogue) cites a one-volume Ziyi Bencao Jing by Jia Gongyan, which is probably the same work. The Liang Qilu (Seven Records of the Liang dynasty) lists a three-volume Shennong Bencao; the discrepancy in the number of volumes is a matter of how texts were divided and combined in different periods.

The divergences in combining and dividing: the world's books were not yet written when Shennong and the Divine Farmer flourished, and knowledgeable people have therefore doubted the classic on this account. Huangfu Mi, for instance, said this work consists of four volumes compiled by Tao Hongjing; his statement about the varying volume count has already been addressed earlier. The bibliographic treatise's statement is well founded.

The characters not yet transmitted concerning medicinal properties and indications should be identified by reference to the various scholars. Eventually, in Tong, this work was recorded in the transmission. This text should be grouped with the Suwen (Plain Questions) and similar works.

Among works on military affairs, the Five Phases, and miscellaneous divination, the classic is counted as a book of the Three Sovereigns, with Shennong among them. The Shiji states that the First Emperor of Qin did not destroy books of medicine, pharmacology, and divination, and so this classic was fortunate to survive alongside those.

The Yijing and the Chunqiu with their commentaries are also preserved. Yan Zhitui's Jiaxun (Family Instructions) says that the Bencao was composed by Shennong, yet it contains the names of commanderies and counties such as Yuzhang, Zhuya, Zhaoguo, Changshan, Fenggao, Zhending, Linzi, and Fengyi.

All these drug entries with place-names were assigned by later people and are not part of the original text. Tao Hongjing also says that the commandery and county names of provenance are from the Later Han period, and he suspects they were added in the records of Zhang Ji (Zhongjing), Hua Tuo (Yuanhua), and others. According to collated commentaries, Zhang Heng [also touches on this matter].

出版說一

神農本草經序

以康寧為福，頤稱壽考萬年，又何疑于久服輕身延年為後世方士之說哉。大抵儒者之嗜學如醫然，開繹學以鴻儒名海內求其著淵源其脈也。覆審其診視也。辨邪正定是非則溫寒平熱之介也。觀察方以嘉慶四年太歲在己未冬十月望日宣城張炯謹於瞻園之灌花莊。

述者如金膏水碧之珍，鳳卵好博，開研丹吮墨，日以儒為事，則上溯之羲皇以前數千年如一日，非嗜之專且久，而能然耶。吾獨怪是編中無所謂治書癖者，安得起神農而一問之。
translation:
Publication Note, Part One

Preface to the Shennong Bencao Jing (Divine Farmer's Classic of Materia Medica)

To regard health and peace as blessings, and to speak of longevity and a life of ten thousand years — why should one doubt that long-term use of medicines to lighten the body and extend life is merely the talk of later-age Daoist practitioners? In general, a scholar's devotion to learning is like that of a physician: one opens and unravels learning, and seeks out the writings of great Confucians renowned throughout the land, tracing the origins and veins of their thought; examining and reviewing their diagnoses; distinguishing the upright from the deviant, settling right from wrong, and discerning the line between warmth and cold, balance and heat in the consideration of remedies. Written at Guanhua Villa in Zhanyuan Garden, on the fifteenth day of the tenth lunar month of the year jiwei, the fourth year of the Jiaqing reign, by Zhang Jiong of Xuancheng, recorded with reverence.

Those who write such works are like treasures of golden paste and jade-green water, like phoenix eggs of broad learning, who grind cinnabar and sip ink, devoting each day to scholarship as their sole endeavor — reaching back through thousands of years to the age of Fu Xi as if it were but a single day. How could this be possible without a devotion that is both singular and long-sustained? I alone find it strange that within this compilation there is said to be no remedy for the ailment of book-obsession. How I wish one could rouse Shennong himself and put the question to him.

translation:
The upper volume of the Classic of Herbs notes in its commentary: the origins of the nature of medicines, discussions of the names and manifestations of diseases. The middle volume says: jade, stones, herbs, and trees in three grades. The lower volume says: insects, animals, fruits, vegetables, grains, and combinations in three grades. These names were altered by later physicians. I now follow the ancient ordering. Furthermore, the Emperors' World Annals and Tao Hongjing's preface refer to four volumes; Zhang Yuxii says that according to the old text it also had four volumes; Han Baosheng likewise says that the Shennong Bencao comprised upper, middle, and lower volumes plus a table of contents, making four volumes in all. If that is so, the discrepancy between three and four volumes arises from the presence of the table of contents. Works such as Ge Hong's Essentials of Nurturing Life and the Taiping Imperial览 that cite the Shennong Classic sometimes say "according to Taiyi zi" or "Taiyi zi says" — all of which are absent from the received Classic, or may have been in the table of contents and cut by later editors. As for the text of the Classic itself: where 釋 has been written for 燧, 創 for 瘀, 淡 for 痰, 注 for 蛙, 沙 for 砂, 免 for 菟, and so on — these all arose from errors in transmission. I have collated against ancient sources and corrected them; one should not be alarmed at departing from common usage. In analyzing the classification of substances and citing various texts, the foundations lie in the Mao Odes, the Erya, Shuowen, Fangyan, Guangya, and the various philosophers and miscellaneous writers; Feng Luan contributed greatly to the supplementation. Written by Sun Xingyuan of Yanghu.

translation:
Preface to the Collated Shennong Bencao Jing (Classic of the Divine Farmer's Materia Medica)

The Taiping Yulan (Imperial览) cites the Bencao Jing entry on Taiyi Yuyuliang, whose alternate name is Shinao (Stone Brain), said to grow in mountain valleys. This reflects the original text, which contained no names of commanderies or counties — those were additions by later physicians. Today's Daguan edition places these names in black characters, or combines them into the text, noting "such-and-such mountain valley, such-and-such commandery, river or marsh." This is likely a copyist's error; the original text was not like this.

After the time of Zhang Zhongjing and Hua Tuo, Wu Pu composed a Bencao (Materia Medica) based on Shennong's, comprising 441 substances. The Sui Jingji Zhi (bibliographic treatise) records that Wu Pu studied under Hua Tuo. The Liang bibliographic records note that Wu Pu's Bencao ran to six scrolls; the Jiayou Bencao states that Wu Pu's book was already lost by his own time, and only scattered quotations survive. Today the full text no longer exists; it survives only through citations in compendia such as Chuxuji, Beitang Shuchao, annotations to the Hou Han Shu, Shilei Fu, and other works. The Taiping Yulan cites it most extensively. These sources supplement what is lacking in the Daguan edition. The present work therefore draws on Wu Pu's text and appends it to the main classic as a rough supplement. Where Wu Pu's explanations are cited, they derive from the main classic; the Daguan edition sometimes misrepresents these as black-character entries.

The total number of drugs appearing to exceed 365 is due to later persons arbitrarily splitting or combining entries; it is difficult to determine what is original. Some entries were clearly added by later hands, whether through oral transmission corrupting old names, or through other means.

Regarding the use of wine macerations: some argue that wine did not exist in Shennong's time. But the Bencao Yanyi has already addressed this by citing the Suwen. Similarly, attributing the text to the time of the Yellow Emperor need not be doubted from the outset. The Wenxuan commentary and the Bowu Zhi both record that Du Kang invented wine, and a letter ending a friendship with Du Kang mentions that at the time of the Yellow Emperor people could not yet obtain it from afar; one should not neglect to consult medical and pharmacological texts.

Scholars who slavishly follow vulgar editions without examining old versions, not checking for discrepancies in drug properties, have been misled. Li Shizhen of the Ming dynasty compiled the Bencao Gangmu; yet by his time names had become corrupted, and he merely took the Daguan edition, fragmenting the old text. He made arbitrary additions and emendations that have confused later students.

This present work was compiled together to complement and complete the classic and to enlighten those who study the arts of healing. The original preface by Tao Hongjing (written in red) states that the Upper Classic contains the upper-grade drugs, the Middle Classic the middle-grade drugs, and the Lower Classic the lower-grade drugs — the ancients divided the work into scrolls by category (minerals, plants, trees, etc., upper, middle, and lower grades), with a separate scroll for the general catalogue.

translation:
The chapter on Immortal Medicines states: Jade can be dissolved in crow-rice wine or di-yu wine to become water. It can also be dissolved with scallion juice to become powder, or sweetened into pills, or burned into powder. If taken for one year or more, one will not be wetted by water, not scorched by fire, not cut by blades, and no poison can harm. However, jade already fashioned into vessels should not be used — it benefits nothing and harms people. One must obtain unworked raw jade. The white jade from the kingdom of Khotan is the best; next is the jade from the border region of Xu-shan Pavilion in Nanyang; and also jade found in the waters of Lurong in Rinan — all are good.

Stalactite (Zhong Ru /钟乳石): flavor sweet, warm. It governs coughing with rising qi, brightens the eyes, benefits essence, calms the five viscera, opens the hundred joints, benefits the nine orifices, and promotes the flow of breast milk. The Imperial Encyclopaedia cites an alternate name: Gong Ru (Public Milk). The character "Gong Ru." Produced in mountain valleys.

Wu Pu states: Stalactite is also known as Xu Zhong (Hollow Center). According to Shennong: acrid. According to Tong Jun and the Yellow Emperor: harmonizing, sweet. According to Bian Que: sweet, non-toxic. The Imperial Encyclopaedia notes: greatly cold. Li [says]: produced in mountain valleys — the Imperial Encyclopaedia cites Taishan mountain valleys, in shaded places.

It forms from dripping juice along cliff faces. The juice gathers and drips; it looks like milk — yellow-white in color, hollow inside with connected passages. Collected in the second and third months, dried in the shade.

The Mingyi says: it is also called Gong Ru (Public Milk). The white kind is superior. Commentary notes: cited from the Imperially Reviewed Collectanea. Various texts such as the Lie Xian Zhuan state that pressing and consuming the stone marrow is called stalactite. Stalactite is described in the Han Shuo Wen.

Annex: Fan Zi Ji Ran states: stalactite is produced in Wudu. [Yellow...]

Increases years of life. Also named Yu Peng. Produced in mountain valleys. The Shan Hai Jing records this as "Zhong" with a substitute phonetic gloss; it is based on the local place-name graph. Stone Pu. Note. Flavor sour, cold. Governs cold and heat, diarrhea, white discharge, erosive sores, eye pain; strengthens sinews, bones, and teeth. Refined and taken as a food supplement, it lightens the body and prevents aging.

Lei Stone (泪石): mentioned in the Shan Hai Jing under the name "Xiang Stone." Stone cites: "the juice of milk-stone." The Shan Hai Jing Xiang commentary says: Yu Yan.

Wu Pu states: Yi Shi (藝石) is also called Yu Yan, also called Yu Ze. According to Shennong and Qi Bo: sour. According to Bian Que: salty. According to Lei Gong: sour, non-toxic. Produced in He Xi, or Long Xi, or Wudu. At Shi Men [cliff face], clusters [of it] without [end].

Qi Bo states: prolonged use harms the bones. The Imperial Encyclopaedia gives the alternate name Yu Yan. According to Shennong and Qi Bo: sour. Imperial Encyclopaedia.

text:
神農本草經 卷一

能作水澗鍊丹，與滑石服之按金石之藥，古人云久服輕身延年者謂當避穀絕人道，或服數十年乃
效耳，令人和肉食服之逐多相反，以成疾，不可疑古書之虛誑。
雲母，味甘平，主身皮死肌，中風寒熱，如在車船上，除邪氣，安五藏，益子精，明目，久服輕身延年，一名雲珠，
一名雲華，一名雲英，一名雲液，一名雲沙，一名磷石，生山谷。
案醫日生太山齊盧山及琅邪北定山石間，二月采，但此後錄人合之，者，無從別耳，卽是仲景元化，及普書所說也。
案列仙傳云，方回，鍊食雲母，抱朴子仙藥篇云，五色雲母具而多青者名雲英，宜以春服之，五色具而多赤者名雲珠，宜以夏服之，五色具而多黃者名雲沙，五色具而多白者名雲液，宜以秋服之，五色具而多黑者名雲英，宜以冬服之，晶鼻純白名磷石，可以四時長服之。
者名雲母，一名雲精，人地萬歲不朽，說文無磷字，御覽云，磷薄也，不也，雲母之別名。
也，李善文選注引異物志柔雲母，一名雲魄御覽，又引作長肌肉，益氣，久服耐寒暑，不飢渴，不老，神仙。
玉泉，味甘平，主五藏百病，柔筋強骨，安魂魄，長肌肉，益氣，久服耐寒暑，不飢渴，不老，神仙，一名玉札。
人臨死服五斤，死三年色不變，一名玉杧，御覽，覺覺引云，玉濃，初服學記引云，長生不死，玉，桃，若不服之，長生不得早服之，臨死御仙。
矸日，服則疑常作桃，天地，不，生山谷。
首翁體如白，吳普曰玉泉，一名玉屑，神農岐伯雷公，甘平，李氏平，畏冬華，惡青竹，御覽，白玉杧如白頭公，賦同上引云，專白類。
案周禮玉府，王齋則供食玉，鄭云，玉是陽精之純者，食之以禦水氣，鄭司農云，王齋，當食玉屑，抱朴子。
translation:
Shennong Bencao Jing, Volume One

The method of refining cinnabar at a mountain spring, taken together with talc as a mineral medicine — the ancients said that long-term use lightens the body and prolongs life, meaning one should give up grain and abstain from human intercourse, or take it for several decades before
the effects appear. When taken together with meat and food it tends to conflict and cause illness, so one should not doubt the truth of the ancient texts.

Mica (Yunmu): flavor sweet, balanced. Mainly treats dead skin on the body surface, wind-cold-heat [conditions], the feeling of being on a cart or boat, expels evil qi, calms the five viscera, benefits vital essence, brightens the eyes. Long-term use lightens the body and prolongs life. Also named Yunzhu, Yunhua, Yunying, Yunye, Yunsha, Linshi. Grows in mountain valleys.

According to medical records, it is found on Mt. Tai, Mt. Lushan in Qi, and among the rocks at Langya and Beiding mountains, and is gathered in the second month. Later records note that people combined them, so there is no way to distinguish them separately — these are the same as what is described in the writings of Zhang Zhongjing, Hua Tuo, and Pu's texts.

According to the Liexian Zhuan, Fang Hui refined and ate mica. Baopuzi's chapter on immortality medicines states: five-colored mica with predominantly blue-green is called Yunying and should be taken in spring; five-colored with predominantly red is called Yunzhu and should be taken in summer; five-colored with predominantly yellow is called Yunsha; five-colored with predominantly white is called Yunye and should be taken in autumn; five-colored with predominantly black is called Yunying and should be taken in winter. Pure crystal-white is called Linshi and may be taken throughout all four seasons.

What is called Yunmu — also named Yunjing — buried in the earth for ten thousand years will not decay. The Shuowen has no character for "lin"; the Yulan states lin means thin. This is another name for Yunmu.

Li Shan's commentary on the Wenxuan cites the Yiwu Zhi: soft mica is also named Yunpo (spirit of clouds); the Yulan also quotes: it lengthens muscle, benefits qi; long-term use enables tolerance of cold and heat, freedom from hunger and thirst, and immortality as a divine immortal.

Jade Spring (Yuquan): flavor sweet, balanced. Mainly treats the hundred diseases of the five viscera, softens sinews, strengthens bones, calms the hun and po spirits, lengthens muscle, benefits qi. Long-term use enables tolerance of cold and heat, freedom from hunger and thirst, and immortality as a divine immortal. Also named Yuzha.

If a dying person takes five jin of it, after death the body will not change color for three years. Also named Yumang. The Yulan notes: if one does not take it one will not attain long life; if taken early, one will not die.

Sun [Simo] says: taking it leads one to doubt — heaven and earth — not dying — growing in mountain valleys.

Shou Weng's body resembled white [jade]. Wu Pu says Yuquan is also named Yuxie; Shennong, Qibo, and Leigong rate it as sweet and balanced; Mr. Li rates it as balanced; it fears Donghua [winter flower], and dislikes green bamboo. Yulan: white Yumang resembles a white-headed duke, as the fu says in the same passage: it is entirely white and fine.

According to the Rites of Zhou, the Jade Steward section states that when the king fasts he is supplied with jade to eat. Zheng Xuan says jade is the pure essence of yang, and eating it wards off water qi. Zheng Siqing says that when the king fasts he should eat powdered jade. Baopuzi [also discusses this].

神農本草經 卷一

七

名醫曰。一名液石。一名共石。一名脫石。一名番石。生赭陽。及太山之陰。或掖北。白山。或卷山。采無時。
案范子計然云。滑石白滑者善。南越志云。嶺城縣生營石。即滑石也。石淋寒熱崩中下血。諸邪毒氣令人有子。鍊餌服之。
吳普曰。石膽味酸寒。主明目。目痛。金創。諸癇痙。女子陰蝕痛。石淋寒熱崩中下血。諸邪毒氣令人有子。鍊餌服之。
不老久服增壽。神仙能化鐵為銅。成金銀。御覽引作。
吳普曰。石膽酸小寒。李氏大寒。桐君辛有毒。扁鵲苦無毒。御覽引道或云。一名黑石。二月庚子辛丑。暫山。御覽道或句。暫山二月庚子辛丑。

名醫曰。一名黑石。一名基石。一名銅勒。生羌道。羌里句。青山。二月庚子辛丑采。
案范子計然云。石膽出隴西羌道。陶宏景云。仙經。一名立制石。周禮癰醫。凡療癰以五毒攻之。鄭云。今

醫方有五毒之藥。作之合黃整石。其中燒之三日三夜。其煙上著。以雞羽掃取之。
取之以注創。惡肉破骨則盡出。圖經曰。故翰林學士楊億嘗筆記。直史館楊嶠。有癰生於頰。人語之依。

鄭法合燒藥成。注之瘡中。遂愈。明目利九竅通血脈養精神。人服輕身延年。不老能化銅鐵鉛錫作金生山谷。

吳味甘寒。主管農甘。一經酸久服有神仙女來時使人志高。御覽。

名醫曰。生益州及越巂山有銅處。銅精熏則生空青。其膜中空。三月中旬采赤無時。
案西山經云。皇人之山其下多青雘。璞云。空青眥青之屬。范子計然云。空青出巴郡司馬相如賦云。丹
translation:
Shennong Bencao Jing, Volume One

[Page 7]

The Mingyi [Famous Physicians' Records] says: [Talc (huashi)] is also called Yeshi, Gongshi, Tuoshi, and Fanshi. It grows in Zhaoyang and on the north slope of Mount Tai, or at Beishan, Baishan, or Juanshan. It may be collected at any time of year.

The Anfan Ziji ran [Fanzi Jiran] says: Talc that is white and smooth is best. The Nanyue zhi says: Lingcheng County produces Yingshi, which is the same as talc. [It treats] stone strangury, cold and heat, uterine flooding and spotting, and various evil toxic qi; it enables women to conceive. Refined and taken as a dietary supplement, it promotes longevity; long-term use increases lifespan. The immortal adepts can use it to transform iron into copper and produce gold and silver. [Imperial Readings cites a variant.]

Wu Pu says: Sidan [Chalcanthite, blue vitriol] has a sour, cold flavor. Its main uses are: brightening the eyes, eye pain, metal-wound injuries, various epilepsies and spasms, female genital erosion pain, stone strangury, cold and heat, uterine flooding and spotting, and various evil toxic qi; it enables women to conceive. Refined and taken as a supplement, it prevents aging. Long-term use increases lifespan; immortal adepts can use it to transform iron into copper, producing gold and silver. [Imperial Readings citation.]

Wu Pu says: Sidan is sour and slightly cold. Li's [Materia Medica] says greatly cold. Tong Jun says pungent and toxic. Bian Que says bitter and non-toxic. [Imperial Readings] cites: also called Heishi. Collected in the second month on gengzi and xinzhou days. At Mount Zan. [Variant note in Imperial Readings.]

The Mingyi says: [Sidan] is also called Heishi, Jishi, and Tongle. It grows at Qiangdao in Qiangli. On Qingshan. Collected in the second month on gengzi and xinzhou days.

The Anfan Ziji ran says: Sidan comes from Longxi and Qiangdao. Tao Hongjing says: The immortal scriptures call it Lizhishi. The Zhouli [Rites of Zhou], in the section on physicians for swellings, states: for treating all carbuncles, attack with the Five Poisons. Zheng [Xuan] comments: Today's

physicians prepare the Five Poisons medicine by combining it with yellow alum and stone, burning the mixture inside a vessel for three days and three nights. The smoke rises and deposits on the surface; it is collected with a chicken feather.

It is then injected into wounds. Dead flesh and damaged bone will all be expelled. The Tujing [Illustrated Classic] says: The late Hanlin scholar Yang Yi once recorded in his notes that the Historiographer Yang Qiao had a carbuncle growing on his cheek. Someone told him to follow

Zheng's method of combining and burning the medicine and injecting it into the sore; it was soon cured. [Sidan] brightens the eyes, opens the nine orifices, circulates the blood vessels, and nourishes the spirit. Those who take it experience a lighter body and prolonged years; they do not grow old and can transform copper, iron, lead, and tin into gold. [Found] in mountain valleys.

Wu [Pu] says [of Kongqing, malachite/azurite]: flavor sweet and cold; its principal [use is in] agriculture… One classic says sour; long-term use brings divine immortal women who come and make the person's will lofty. [Imperial Readings.]

The Mingyi says: It grows in Yizhou and in the Yuexi mountains wherever copper is found. The essence of copper, when smoked, produces Kongqing [hollow azure]. Its membrane is hollow inside. Collected in mid-third month, or at any time, whichever is red.

The Anshan jing [Western Mountains Classic] says: Below the Mountain of the Huang Ren there is much green cinnabar. [Guo] Pu comments: Kongqing belongs to the category of azurite. The Fanzi Jiran says: Kongqing comes from Bajun. Sima Xiangru in his rhapsody says: Dan [cinnabar]…

神農本草經卷一

字作消

消
名醫曰。一名羽澤。生河西及隴西武都。石門朵無時。
案說文無礬字。玉篇云礬石也。碌礬石也。西山經云。女林之山。其陰多泥石。郭璞云即礬石也。楚人名為泥石秦名為羽泥。舊泥石作礬石。亦名日泥石也。本草經亦名日泥石非。
高誘云泥礬石名為羽泥。舊泥石作礬石非。
石味苦寒。主五藏積熱胃張閉。滌去蓄結飲食。推陳致新除邪氣。鍊之如膏。久服輕身。御覧引云一名大觀本

芒消
・黒
吳普日消石神農苦扁鵲甘。凡出寬着掌。再不錫答所引。・亦見
名醫曰一名芒消生盆州。及五都隴西西羌朵無時。

消異文。
消味苦寒。

朴
名醫曰。一名消石朴生益州有鹽水之陽朵耳舊作碩俗字。
吳普曰朴消主百病除寒熱邪氣逐六府積聚結固留癖能化七十二種石鍊餌服之。輕身神仙生山谷。

滑石
味甘寒。主身熱泄澼。女子乳難癃閉。利小便蕩胃中積聚寒熱。益精氣。久服輕身。耐飢長年。生山谷。
案說文云朴木皮也。此蓋消石朴生益州有鹽水之陽朵耳舊作碩俗字。

六
translation:
Shennong Bencao Jing, Volume One

[The character is written as Xiao (消)]

Xiao (Saltpeter/Niter)
The Mingyi [Famous Physicians' Record] says: Another name is Yuze. It is produced in Hexi and Longxi, Wudu, Shimen; the flowering season is unspecified.
According to the Shuowen [dictionary], there is no character for "fan" (alum). The Yupian says: fanshi is also called lüfan (green vitriol). The Xishan Jing says: at the mountain called Nülin, its shaded side has much nishi (mud-stone). Guo Pu says this is fanshi (alum). The people of Chu call it nishi; the people of Qin call it yuní (feathered mud). The old text writes nishi as fanshi; it is also named nishi. The Bencao Jing also calls it nishi, which is not the same.
Gao You says: nifanshi is named yuní. The old text writes nishi as fanshi, which is incorrect.
The stone has a bitter and cold flavor. It governs the accumulation of heat in the five viscera, distension and obstruction of the stomach. It flushes out accumulated and bound food and drink. It expels the old and brings in the new, and removes pathogenic qi. When refined it becomes like paste. Long-term use lightens the body. [Citation from Yulan and Daguan editions follows.]

Mangxiao (Mirabilite/Glauber's Salt)
[Noted in black:] Wu Pu says: Xiaoshi — Shennong [classifies it as] bitter; Bianque [classifies it as] sweet. [Note: this passage is cited in various editions including the Xiting edition, also seen elsewhere.]
The Mingyi says: Another name is Mangxiao. Produced in Penzhou and the five prefectures of Longxi, Xijiang; the harvesting season is unspecified.
Zi Fanzi Jiran says: Mangxiao stone comes from the Longdao area. According to the Mingyi it is also called Mangxiao. It is separately listed under the Mangxiao entry. It is not [the substance mentioned in] the Beishan Jing, which says: at Jingshan, on its shaded side there are primordial ore deposits, possibly mineral [of uncertain identity].

[On variant forms of the character Xiao:]
Xiaoshi has a bitter and cold flavor.
Wu Pu says: Puxiao — according to Shennong, Qibo, and Leigong, it is non-toxic; produced in Yizhou, or on the shaded side of mountains. When it enters the earth for a thousand years it does not change; when refined it cannot be formed into a preparation and cannot be taken. [Imperial encyclopaedia citation.]

Puxiao (Crude saltpeter)
The Mingyi says: Another name is Xiaoshipu. Produced in Yizhou, in areas of salty water exposed to sunlight. The old text writes [a variant character] as a common form.
Wu Pu says: Puxiao governs the hundred diseases, eliminates cold-heat pathogenic qi, expels accumulations and gatherings bound in the six bowels, dissolves fixed and lodged masses, and can transform seventy-two kinds of stones. When refined and taken as a preparation it lightens the body and [grants the powers of] a mountain immortal. Produced in mountain valleys.

Huashi (Talc/Soapstone)
Flavor: sweet, cold. Governs heat in the body and diarrhea with painful urination. In women: difficult lactation and urinary obstruction. Promotes urination, flushes out accumulations of cold and heat in the stomach, and benefits the essence-qi. Long-term use lightens the body, resists hunger, and prolongs life. Produced in mountain valleys.
According to the Shuowen: "Pu" means tree bark. This is because Xiaoshipu is produced in Yizhou, in areas of salty water exposed to sunlight. The old text writes [a variant character] as a common form.
The Mingyi says: Another name is Xiaoshipu.

案醫曰生薑及太山。
吳普曰。味如賦有白附。蘇林云白附。白石英也。司馬貞云。出魯陽山。

紫石英。味甘溫。主心腹欬逆御寬引作嗢逆。邪氣補不足女子風寒在子宮絕孕。十年無子。久服溫中輕身延年生山谷。
吳普曰紫石英神農扁鵲味甘平李氏大寒雷公大溫歧伯甘無毒生太山或會稽朵無時欲令如削。

紫色蓬頭如樗蒲者。
又曰達青石英形如白石英青端赤後者是赤石英形如白石英赤端白後者是赤澤有光味苦補心氣。
黃石英形如白石英黃色如金赤端者是黑石英形如白石英黑澤有光引此御寬擊再錫節文。
名醫曰生太山朵無時。
神農本草經卷一

九
translation:
The Baopu zi, "Gold Elixir" chapter, states: The Scripture of the Numinous Elixir uses cinnabar, realgar, orpiment, sulfur, azurite, alum, arsenolite, halite, and Taiyi-yuliang. It also uses the six-one clay.
After combining in the sacred chamber with ritual offerings for thirty-six days, the preparation is complete. White quartz (bai shi ying): flavor sweet, slightly warming. Main uses: relieves wasting-thirst, impotence, and deficiency; stops coughing and counterflow [variant reading: "hiccup"]; opens the chest; clears long-standing blockage; benefits the qi; eliminates wind-damp impediment [variant reading: "treats"]. Long-term use lightens the body [variant: "strengthens the body"]. Prolongs life. Grows in mountain valleys.
Wu Pu says: White quartz — Shennong [rates it] sweet; Qibo and the Yellow Emperor and Lei Gong and Bian Que [say it is] nontoxic. Grows on Mount Tai. Its shape resembles purple quartz; the white and lustrous ones are two to three inches long; harvested at no fixed season. [Variant citation follows.]
Long-term use frees the flow throughout the body.

The case physician states: It grows on ginger [terrain] and on Mount Tai.
Wu Pu says its flavor is like that of the white aconite appendage. Su Lin says "white aconite" means white quartz. Sima Zhen says it is produced at Luoyang Mountain.

Purple quartz (zi shi ying): flavor sweet, warming. Main uses: heart and abdominal coughing and counterflow [variant: hiccup and counterflow]; pathogenic qi; supplements insufficiency; treats cold wind lodged in the uterus causing infertility; used for women who have gone ten years without conceiving. Long-term use warms the interior, lightens the body, and prolongs life. Grows in mountain valleys.
Wu Pu says: Purple quartz — Shennong and Bian Que [rate it] sweet and balanced; Master Li [rates it] greatly cold; Lei Gong greatly warming; Qibo sweet and nontoxic. Grows on Mount Tai or in Kuaiji. Harvested at no fixed season; the ideal specimens appear as if freshly cut.

Those of purple color with a tufted top resembling draughts-pieces.
He further says: Azure quartz resembles white quartz but with a blue tip and red base. Red quartz resembles white quartz but with a red tip and white base; it is glossy with luster; flavor bitter; supplements heart qi.
Yellow quartz resembles white quartz; its color is golden with a reddish tip. Black quartz resembles white quartz; it is black, lustrous, and shining. [Variant citations and textual notes follow.]
The case physician says: Grows on Mount Tai; harvested at no fixed season.

Shennong Bencao Jing, Volume One

[Eight]

Qing [Azurite]: Master Yan Shigu says: "Qing" refers to the blue-green pigment, which today is called "danqing" (cinnabar blue).

Zeng Qing [Malachite]: Flavor: sour; slightly cold. Principal uses: eye pain, stopping tearing, wind impediment (feng bi), benefiting the joints and opening the nine orifices, breaking up concretions, hard accumulations and gatherings. Long-term use lightens the body, prevents aging, and can transform gold and copper. Grows in mountain valleys.

The Mingyi [Famous Physicians] record: It is produced in Shu (Sichuan) and Yuexi; harvested at no fixed season.

Commentary: The Guanzi, "Jidu" chapter, states that Qin Ming Mountain has zengqing. Yang Jing's annotation states: zengqing is the essence of copper. Fan Zi's Jiran states: qing comes from Hong; zengqing, copper's essence. Fan Zi's Jiran states: qing emerges after eight hundred years. Zeng Gao's Youyun states: qingzeng is stone.

Yuyu Liang [禹餘糧, Limonite]: Flavor: sweet; cold. Principal uses: coughing and counterflow, cold and heat, vexing fullness, diarrhea with red and white discharge, blood closure, concretions and conglomerations, great heat. Refined and taken as a food supplement, it prevents hunger, lightens the body, and prolongs life. Found in ponds, marshes, and on islands.

The Mingyi record: Another name is "white yuyu liang." Produced on the Eastern Sea and in ponds and marshes.

Commentary: Fan Zi's Jiran states: Yuyu liang comes from Hedong. Liexian zhuan states: Chifu went up Huashan and gathered yuyu liang. Bowu zhi states: tradition says that in ancient times when Yu controlled the floods, he left behind medicine remnants which he cast into the rivers, and these became medicinal substances. According to the Shennong Jing, "Yu" here does not refer to the Xia dynasty's Yu; or perhaps its original name was "white yuyu liang," and later physicians changed its name.

Another name: Shi Nao [Stone Brain]. Grows in mountain valleys.

Tai Yi Yuyu Liang [太一餘糧]: Flavor: sweet; balanced. Principal uses: coughing and counterflow, ascending qi, concretions and conglomerations, blood closure, persistent uterine discharge, and residual pathogenic qi. Long-term use builds tolerance to cold and heat, prevents hunger, lightens the body, allows one to travel a thousand li, and leads to immortality. [Referenced in the Yulan citing Shexian.]

Wu Pu states: Tai Yi Yuyu Liang, also named Yu Ai. According to Shennong, Qibo, and Leigong it is sweet and balanced; according to Master Li it is slightly cold; according to Bianque it is sweet and non-toxic. It grows on Mt. Tai; it has a shell, and inside the shell there is white matter.

The Mingyi record: It grows on Mt. Tai; within the white there is yellow like egg yolk. Harvested in the ninth month, or at no fixed season.

名醫曰。生朱崖武都朱提。采無時。
案范子計然云扁青出宏農豫章。
右玉石上品一十八種舊同。
昌蒲味辛溫。主風寒濕痹。欬逆。上氣開心孔。補五藏。通九竅。明耳目。出聲音。久服輕身。不忘不迷。或延年。一名堯韭。本引云。無生石生上石三上文字。聚有一寸九節者九節者良。身云云作黑字。大生池澤。

名醫曰。生上洛及蜀郡嚴道。五月十二日采根。陰乾。
吳普曰昌蒲。一名堯韭。一名昌陽。本鄭云昌本昌蒲根。切
案說文生云。苕昌蒲也。盆州生葀苕也。廣雅云。邛昌陽也。昌本鄭云昌。
之四寸為蓆。奉秋左傳云。變昌歜。杜云。預云。昌羊去蚤蛆而來蛤蟆高誘云。春秋云冬至後五旬七日昌始生。昌蒲列仙傳云商邱子胥。
百草之先。於是始耕。淮南子說山訓云。昌羊去蚤。蚤蛆而來蛤蟆高誘云。春秋云冬至後五旬七日昌始生。昌蒲列仙傳云商邱子胥。
鞠華味苦平。主風頭眩腫痛。目欲脫。淚出。皮膚死肌。惡風濕痹。久服利血氣輕身耐老延年。一名節華。生
食昌蒲根。務光服蒲非。根離騷草木疏云。沈存中云。所謂蘭蓀。即今昌蒲是也。
川澤及田野。
吳普曰菊華。一名白華。初學記。一名女華。一名女華。一名女蔓。一名更生。一名周盈。一名傅延年。一名陰成。生雍州。
名醫曰。一名精。一名女節。一名女華。一名女莖。
神農本草經卷一
二
translation:
The Mingyi (Eminent Physicians) record states: It grows in Zhuyai, Wudu, and Zhuti. Harvested at any time.
According to the Fan Zi Jiran text: Flat green stone (biān qīng) comes from Hongnong and Yuzhang.
The above are eighteen items in the upper grade of Jade and Stone category, in accordance with the old classification.

Calamus (Changpu): Flavor is acrid, warm. It governs wind-cold-damp impediment, coughing with counterflow and upward qi, opens the heart orifices, supplements the five viscera, penetrates the nine orifices, brightens hearing and vision, brings out the voice. Long-term use lightens the body; one does not forget, does not become confused, or may extend one's years. Another name is Yao Jiu (Yao's leek). According to commentary, it grows on rocks above water and on stones. Those with nine nodes per inch are considered the best. Grows in pools and marshes.

The Mingyi record states: It grows in Shangluo and Shu commandery's Yandao. The root is harvested on the twelfth day of the fifth month and dried in the shade.
Wu Pu states: Changpu, also named Yao Jiu, also named Changyang. According to Zheng, the root of Changpu, cut.
According to the Shuowen: "Tiao — it is Changpu." In Bin province it produces Guo Tiao. The Guangya states it is called Qiong Changyang. According to Zheng, Chang is the same as Chang.
The four-inch variety was used as a mat. In Zuo's Commentary to the Spring and Autumn Annals it says "Chang Chuo." Du notes: Changyang drives away fleas. Fleas and maggots bring frogs, according to Gao You's commentary. The Spring and Autumn record says that fifty-seven days after the winter solstice, Chang begins to grow. The Liexian Zhuan (Biographies of Immortals) mentions Shangqiu Zihu.
Among the hundred herbs it is first. From this, cultivation began. The Huainan Zi (Shanjun xun chapter) says Changyang drives away fleas; fleas and maggots attract frogs, per Gao You. After the winter solstice, fifty-seven days pass and Chang begins to grow. The Liexian Zhuan mentions Shangqiu Zihu,
who ate Changpu root. Wu Guang consumed cattail (pu). The "離騷" (Li Sao) in the Cao Mu Shu section: Shen Cunzhong says what is called Lan Sun is the Changpu of today.
[It grows in] rivers, marshes, and open fields.
Wu Pu states: Ju Hua (chrysanthemum). Also named Bai Hua. According to the Chuxue Ji (Beginners' Record), also named Nü Hua, also named Nü Hua, also named Nü Man, also named Gengsheng, also named Zhouying, also named Fuyan Nian, also named Yincheng. Grows in Yongzhou.
The Mingyi record states: Also named Jing, also named Nü Jie, also named Nü Hua, also named Nü Jing.

Shennong Bencao Jing, Volume One

神農本草經 卷一

青石、赤石黄石白石黒石脂等味甘平。主黄疸、洩利腸癖、膿血陰蝕、下血赤白邪氣癰腫疽痔惡創頭瘍。擠久服補髓益氣肥健不飢輕身延年五石脂各随五色補五藏生山各中。
吴普曰。五色石脂。一名青赤黄白黒符神農雷公甘黄帝扁鵲無毒神農雷公酸無毒桐君辛無毒。李氏小寒。生南山或海。
涯乞無時赤符神農雷公甘無毒李氏小寒或生少室或生太山。色絳滑如脂黄符李氏小寒桐君甘無毒。
扁鵲辛或生少室當山色如猪腦腸罐乞無時白符一名随髓岐伯雷公酸無毒生洛西山空地。
名醫曰。生南山之陽。一本作南陽又云黒石脂一名石泥桐君甘無毒生洛西山空地。一名石墨一名石涅一名范子計然云赤石脂出河東色赤者善列仙。
傳云吴普引神農云甘五石脂各有條後世合為一條也范子計然云。赤石脂出河東色赤者善列仙。
白青味甘平主明目利九竅耳聾心下邪氣令人吐殺諸毒三蟲久服通神明輕身延年不老生山谷。
吴普曰神農甘平雷公酸無毒生豫章可消而為銅。御覧。
名醫曰神農章采雷公酸無毒生豫章無時。
案范子計然云白青出巴郡。
扁青味甘平主目痛明目折跌癰腫金創不瘳破積聚解毒氣辟毒。御覧引作利精神。久服輕身不老生山谷。
吴普曰扁青神農甘平雷公小寒或生少室生蜀郡治丈夫内絶令人有子風濟。御覧引云久服輕身治癃脾。
translation:
Shennong Bencao Jing, Volume One

Five-Colored Stone Lipids (Green, Red, Yellow, White, and Black Stone Fat): Flavor sweet, balanced. Primarily treats jaundice, diarrhea, intestinal dysentery, pus and blood in stools, genital erosion, bloody discharge (red and white), evil qi, abscesses, swellings, carbuncles, hemorrhoids, malignant sores, and head ulcers. Long-term use supplements marrow, boosts qi, enriches and strengthens the body, prevents hunger, lightens the body, and prolongs life. Each of the five stone lipids corresponds to one of the five colors and supplements one of the five viscera; they grow in various mountains.

Wu Pu says: Five-colored stone lipids — also known as the Green, Red, Yellow, White, and Black Talismans. According to Shennong and Lei Gong: sweet; Huangdi and Bianque: non-toxic. Shennong and Lei Gong say the red type is sour and non-toxic; Tong Jun says it is acrid and non-toxic; Li Shi says it is slightly cold. It grows in the Southern Mountains or by the sea.

The red talisman: according to Shennong and Lei Gong, sweet, non-toxic; Li Shi says slightly cold; grows in Shaoshi or on Taishan; its color is deep red and smooth like fat. The yellow type: Li Shi says slightly cold; Tong Jun says sweet and non-toxic. The white type, also called Suiyi: Qibo and Lei Gong say sour and non-toxic; grows in open ground on the western mountains of Luo. Also called Stone Ink, Stone Mud, or Fan Zi. Ji Ran says: Red stone fat comes from Hedong; those of red color are best — this is recorded in the Liexian (Traditions of Immortals).

Chuan Yun quotes Wu Pu citing Shennong: sweet. Each of the five stone lipids has its own entry, but later generations combined them into one.

White Cyan (Bai Qing): Flavor sweet, balanced. Primarily brightens the eyes, benefits the nine orifices, treats ear deafness, evil qi below the heart, and causes vomiting to expel various toxins and kills the three worms. Long-term use penetrates the spirit and intelligence, lightens the body, prolongs life, and prevents aging. Grows in mountain valleys.
Wu Pu says: Shennong — sweet, balanced; Lei Gong — sour, non-toxic. Grows in Yuzhang; can be smelted into copper. (From Taiping Yulan.)
The Mingyi says: From Yuzhang; harvested without seasonal restriction.
The Fan Zi record says: White Cyan comes from Bajun.

Flat Cyan (Bian Qing): Flavor sweet, balanced. Primarily treats eye pain, brightens the eyes, heals injuries from falls and fractures, abscesses, swellings, and wounds that will not heal; breaks up accumulations and masses, resolves toxic qi, and repels poisons. (Taiping Yulan quotes: benefits the vital spirit.) Long-term use lightens the body and prevents aging. Grows in mountain valleys.
Wu Pu says: Shennong — sweet, balanced; Lei Gong — slightly cold. Grows in Shaoshi or in Shujun. Treats internal severance in men and enables men to have children. (From Yulan.) Long-term use lightens the body and treats urinary blockage and spleen disorders.

translation:
The Classic of Materia Medica (Shennong Bencao Jing), Chapter 2

Commentary citing Shuowen: The character "men" (虋) — men lu (虋廬) means asparagus (mén dōng). The Zhongshan Jing says: on the mountains of Tiaogu, the grass is mostly mén dōng. The Erya says: men lu and men dong. The Liexian Zhuan says: Chixuzi ate tian men dong (Asparagus cochinchinensis). Baopuzi's chapter on immortality herbs says: tian men dong is also called di men dong, yan men dong, dian ji, yin yang shi, or guan song. One source calls it men; another calls it mei.

Licorice (Gancao)
[Note: the character "dang" appears as a variant in the text tradition]

Taste: sweet, neutral. It governs the five viscera and six bowels, treats cold and heat, evil qi, strengthens sinews and bones, grows muscle and flesh, doubles strength, heals metal wounds and swellings, and detoxifies. Long-term use lightens the body and extends life.

Commentary: Shuowen notes the character. Guo Pu says: today's gancao is a creeping vine with leaves resembling lotus, yellow-green stems with reddish-yellow color, jointed with branches at each joint. Some call it lei, resembling di huang. This text uses the abbreviated character for "sweet." Other names recorded by physicians: one name is mi gan, one name is mei cao, one name is lu huo. It grows in the sandy mountains of Hexi and Shangjun. Roots are gathered on the second month, eighth day, on an "除" day and sun-dried.

Guo Pu notes that today's gancao vine spreads out; the Mao Shi (Book of Odes) says "in the wetlands there is ku (bitter herb)"; the commentary says ku means da ku (great bitter herb). The Erya says: tu means da ku. The Erya also says: cha means da ku. The Guangya says: mei cao is gancao.

Dried Rehmannia (Gan Di Huang)
Taste: sweet, cold. It governs fractures, severed sinews, internal injury; it drives out blood stagnation, fills the marrow, grows muscle and flesh. Prepared as a decoction it eliminates cold, heat, and accumulations, and removes impediment. Fresh rehmannia is especially good. Long-term use lightens the body and prevents aging. Also named di sui (earth marrow). It grows in rivers and marshes.

Commentary: Shuowen records the character "hu" (芐). The Liexian Zhuan says Lü Shang took di sui. The Liji mentions cut-grass for oxen and hu for sheep. The Guangya says di sui and di huang are the same. The Erya says hu is di huang. Guo Pu says it is also called di sui. In Jiangdong they call it hu. The Liexian Zhuan says Lü Shang ate di sui.

Atractylodes (Zhu)
Taste: bitter, warm. It governs wind-cold, damp impediment, dead flesh, itching sores; it stops sweating, eliminates heat, and aids digestion. Prepared as a decoction or confection, long-term use lightens the body, extends life, and prevents hunger. Also named shan ji. It grows in mountain valleys.

text:
神農本草經　卷一

正月采根，三月采葉五月采莖，九月采花，十一月采實皆陰乾。
案說文云，蘞治齲也，蘞日精也，似秋華或省作歛，爾雅云蘞治齲，郭璞云今之秋華菊，則蘞、蘞、歛、皆秋
華。字惟今作菊，說文以為大菊，蘧麥假音用之也。
人參味甘微寒，主補五藏安精神，定魂魄，止驚悸，除邪氣，明目開心益智，久服輕身延年。一名人銜，一名
鬼蓋，生山谷。

吳普曰人參一名土精，一名神草，一名黃參，一名血參，一名人微，一名玉精，神農甘小寒，桐君雷公苦。
岐伯黃帝甘無毒，扁鵲有毒，生邯鄲三月生葉小兒核黑蓋有毛，三月九月采根，根有頭足手面目如人。

探根，竹刀刮暴乾無令見風。
案說文云薻人薻，一名土藥草，精生上黨者佳，人形皆具能作兒啼，范子計然云，人參出上黨，狀類人者善，劉敬叔異
苑云人參出上黨，狀類人者善，劉敬叔異
苑云人參出上黨，狀顯然，人參出上黨，状類人者善。
天門冬味苦平，主諸暴風濕偏痹，強骨髓，殺三蟲，去伏尸，久服輕身益氣延年，一名顛勒，門冬一名滿冬。
文。今無生山谷。

translation:
Shennong Bencao Jing (Divine Farmer's Classic of Materia Medica), Volume One

Roots are collected in the first month, leaves in the third month, stems in the fifth month, flowers in the ninth month, and fruits in the eleventh month; all are dried in the shade.
According to the Shuowen, "lian" treats dental decay; "riping" resembles the autumn flower, or is written as "lian." The Erya says lian treats dental decay; Guo Pu says it is the present-day autumn chrysanthemum. Thus lian, lian, and lian all refer to the autumn flower. The character now written as "ju" (chrysanthemum) was regarded in the Shuowen as the great chrysanthemum, with Qu Mai used by borrowed pronunciation.

Renshen (ginseng): flavor sweet, slightly cold. It mainly supplements the five viscera, calms the spirit, stabilizes the ethereal and corporeal souls, stops fright palpitations, eliminates pathogenic qi, brightens the eyes, opens the heart, and increases wisdom. Long-term use lightens the body and prolongs life. Also called Renhan, also called Guigai. Grows in mountain valleys.

Wu Pu says: Renshen is also called Tujing, also called Shencao, also called Huangshen, also called Xueshen, also called Renwei, also called Yujing. According to Shennong it is sweet and slightly cold; according to Tongjun and Leigong it is bitter. According to Qibo and the Yellow Emperor it is sweet and non-toxic; according to Bianque it is toxic. It grows in Handan. In the third month its leaves emerge, small, with black-covered cores and hairs. Roots are collected in the third and ninth months; the roots have a head, feet, hands, a face and eyes resembling a human figure.

[Imperial Survey citation:]
The Mingyi (Celebrated Physicians) says: it is also called Shencao, also called Renwei, also called Tujing, also called Xueshen. Those shaped like a human form have spiritual power. It grows in Shangdang and Liaodong. Roots are dug in the second, fourth, and eighth months during the first ten days of the month. Scrape with a bamboo knife and dry in the sun without exposing to wind.

According to the Shuowen, the character "shen" [ginseng]: one name is Tuyaocao; the finest grows in Shangdang, and those with a complete human form can cry like an infant. Fan Zi Jiran says ginseng from Shangdang that resembles a human form is the best. Liu Jingshu's Yiyuan also says ginseng from Shangdang that clearly resembles a human form is the best.

Tianmendong (asparagus root): flavor bitter, balanced. It mainly treats all sudden wind-damp impediment conditions, strengthens the bone marrow, kills the three worms, removes hidden corpse pathogens. Long-term use lightens the body, benefits qi, and prolongs life. Also called Dianlü; Mendong is also called Mandong.
Note: no longer found growing wild in mountain valleys.
The Mingyi says it grows on Mount Fenggao; roots are collected in the second, seventh, and eighth months and dried in the sun.

神農本草經卷一
一五
translation:
[The Old/御覽edition gives the name] "Baibeisheng" — growing in valleys. 

Wu Pu says: Niu Jue (ox knee). Shennong: sweet. One classic says: sour. Huangdi and Bian Que: sweet. Master Li: warm. Lei Gong: sour, non-toxic. Grows in Henei or Linqiong. Leaves resemble summer indigo; the stem is reddish. Collected in the second and eighth months.

The Mingyi record says: Grows in Henei and Linxiong. Collected in the second, eighth, and tenth months. Collect the root and dry it in shade.

According to the Guangya: "Niu jing" is Niu Xi (ox-knee). Tao Hongjing says: Its stem has nodes resembling knees, hence the name. "Knee" should be understood as "joint."

Chongwei Zi (Leonurus fruit): flavor acrid, slightly warm. Principal uses — brightening the eyes, replenishing vital essence, eliminating water qi. Long-term use lightens the body. The stem treats skin rashes and itching; can be used in a bath decoction. Alternate names: Penmu, Penming, Dazha.

Grows in ponds and marshes.

The Mingyi record says: Also called Zhengwei. Grows along the seashore. Collected in the fifth month.

The Shuowen says: "Jiao" means a type of wild plant. Guangya says: Jiao ya, Penmu, Chongwei — these are the same. The Mao Shi says: "In the valley there is Yui" — the commentary says Yui is a plant. Han Shi and Sancang both say Penmu, so He Zi saw Penmu and was moved [to record it]. 

Lu Ji says: The old account and the account of Wei Scholar Ji Yin Zhou Yuanming both say it is Julü. Han Shi and Sancang both say Penmu, so He Zi upon seeing Penmu was moved.

[Qin] says: [The character] ya means foul stench; "foul stench" refers to Chongwei. The old text writes it as Ju, which is incorrect.

Nüwei (female fern / Polygonatum odoratum type): flavor sweet, neutral. Principal uses — wind stroke with sudden fever, inability to move the limbs, sinew contraction, muscle knotting, various deficiencies. Long-term use removes dark blemishes from the face, improves complexion, moistens the skin, lightens the body, and prevents aging. Grows in mountain valleys.

Wu Pu says: Nüwei — also called Zangji, Yuma, Dijie, Chongchan, Wuwei, Ying, and Yuzhu. Shennong: bitter; one classic says sweet. [Associated with] tong tree.

Lord Lei and [Bing]: long-term use lightens the body and helps one endure old age — same [as above]. Huangdi says: acrid. Grows in the valleys of Mount Tai. Leaves are blue-green and yellow alternating like ginger. Collected in the second and seventh months. Treats wind stroke with sudden fever. Long-term use lightens the body. [御覽edition] — one [entry].

Shennong Bencao Jing, Volume One

一四
translation:
Shennong Bencao Jing, Volume One

Wu Pu says of Yu [Atractylodes/thistle-type herb]: it is also called Shan Lian, Shan Jie, Tian Su, and Shan Jiang.
The Mingyi [Supplementary Physicians' Records] says: it is also called Shan Jiang, and Lian Sheng. It grows in Zheng, in the Hanzhong region, and in South Zheng. The root is harvested in the second, third, eighth, and ninth months and dried in the sun.
Commentary: The Shuowen [dictionary] says: Yuan is a mountain thistle. The Guangya [dictionary] says: it is Shan Jiang; it also grows in the Zhongshan wilderness as Bai Yu Mudan; the Zhongshan Jing says: Shou Mountain has much of this plant. Guo Pu says: Yuan is a mountain thistle. The Erya says: Yu-mountain thistle. Guo Pu says: today Yu resembles the thistle and grows on mountains. Fan Zi Ji Ran says: Yu comes from the Three Adjunct Regions [around the capital]; the white-colored variety is the best. The Liexian Zhuan [Biographies of Immortals] says: Juanzi liked to eat Yu and Embraced Simplicity [Baopu].

Dodder [Tusizi]
The Immortal Medicines chapter says: Yu is also called Shan Ji and Shan Jing. The Sacred Medicine Classic says: if you truly wish to attain long life, take Shan Jing continuously.

Dodder seeds: flavor acrid, balanced [neutral]. Main [uses]: restores severed tendons and sinews, supplements insufficiency, replenishes qi and strength, fattens and invigorates. The juice removes facial blemishes. Long-term use brightens the eyes, lightens the body, and extends the years. Another name is Tu Lu. It grows in rivers and marshes.
Wu Pu says: Dodder is also called Yu Nü [Jade Maiden], Song Luo, Niao Luo, Ya Luo, Fu Shi, and Chi Wang. It grows in the fields and wilderness of Chaozhou, climbing over grass and trees; its color is yellow and fine, forming [what is called] Chi Wang [Red Net]. It grows ascending hillside valleys. [Imperial note/poetic reference]
The Mingyi says: it is also called Mian Si, Yu Wu, Tang Meng, Song Luo, Niao Luo, Ya Luo, Fu Shi, and Chi Wang. It grows in the fields of Chaozhou and in mountain valleys. Chi Wang is pale in color and large; the seeds ripen in the ninth month and are dried in the sun. [Poetic reference]
The Shuowen says: it is a creeping vine. The Guangya says: Mian Qiu means dodder. It is the female vine [nü luo]. The commentary says: Song Luo is pine-moss. The Erya says: female vine is dodder; it is also called Meng Yu Nü. Tang Meng is female vine. Lu Ji says: today's dodder twines and creeps over plants, growing yellow-red [stems] like—
[The text continues:] "Gathering Tang in that place" — the female commentary says Tang Meng Rong is also called Niao, with pine-moss growing above and below, having branches of pure green, differing from dodder. The Chuci [Songs of Chu] says: covered with creeping vines and girdled with female vine. Wang Yi's commentary says: female vine—
The current pharmaceutical preparation uses dodder seeds; it is not pine-moss. The Huainanzi says: below a thousand-year-old pine there is poria; above it grows dodder. Gao You's commentary says: poria is the resin of a thousand-year-old pine; dodder grows above it without roots.

[Note:] "Luo" written as "Tu" is incorrect. The Huainanzi says: the thousand-year pine [passage].
Formerly written as Tu: flavor bitter, sour, acrid [imperial variant reading]. Ling [version] reads: [its] main [use is for] cold damage, cold injury [imperial/Ling variant]. Clears epidemic impediment disease, four-limb contracture and spasm, stubborn pain with inability to flex or extend, drives out blood-qi injury heat, fire sores, promotes abortion [expels fetus]. Long-term use lightens the body and increases endurance.

神農本草經卷一
一七
translation:
The Bowuzhi (Record of Diverse Matters) states: The leaves of the yun-hao plant resemble those of the xie-hao herb. In spring and autumn it produces white clusters of growth, four to five cun in length, fragrant, pleasant in flavor, and good to eat. It is found both in Chang'an and in Henei. The Xia Xiao Zheng (Lesser Annuary of the Xia) says: In the first month the yun is gathered. The Yueling (Monthly Ordinances) says: In mid-spring the yun begins to grow. The Lüshi Chunqiu (Annals of Lü Buwei) says: Among the finest of herbs, the yun of Huayang is most prized — all of these refer to the same yun plant. Yan Shigu's commentary says this is what is now called wan-zu. Thus the hu-ye (foreign leaf) and this yun are one and the same. The Mingyi Bie Lu (Supplementary Records of Famous Physicians), in the section on qian-hu, and Tao Hongjing's commentary note that the Bencao Jing's upper-grade category includes this hu but not this yun. The Jijiu Pian (Primer of Urgent Terms) does include it.

The physicians of later times used it accordingly.

Maidong (Ophiopogon japonicus): Flavor sweet, nature balanced. It governs binding qi in the chest and abdomen, internal injury, injury from overeating, obstruction of the stomach's network vessels, wasting and emaciation, and shortness of breath. Long-term use lightens the body, prevents aging, prevents hunger. It grows in river valleys and on embankments. One alternate name is yang-jiu (sheep leek). [Imperial览] citation says: Also called sui-zhi; the Taiyi name is pu-lei; also called ren-dong; also called bu-si-yao (medicine of immortality). According to Shennong and Qibo its flavor is sweet and its nature balanced; according to Huangdi and Tong Jun it is sweet and non-toxic; according to Master Li it is sweet and mild.

[Various sources record] the alternate names: ma-jiu (horse leek), yu-jiu (Yu's leek), yu-yu-liang (Yu's surplus grain), yang-xu-jiu (sheep-beard leek), ren-ling, yang (sheep), ren-dong (winter-enduring), yu-liang (surplus grain).

Wu Pu states: One name is ma-jiu, one name is yu-jiu, one name is juan-dong, one name is yue, one name is ren-dong, one name is yang-xu-jiu.

Warm; according to Bian Que, non-toxic. It grows in fertile valley soil. Its leaves are like leek; it grows lush in moist ground in clumps. It fruits at no fixed season; the fruit is bluish-yellow. Also called yu-ge, also called yu-yu-liang; leaves like leek, evergreen through winter and summer, growing in valley grain fields.

The Mingyi states: In Qin it is called yang-jiu; in Qi it is called juan-jiu; in Chu it is called ma-jiu; in Yue it is called yang-xu. Another name is yu-yu-liang. Shennong and Huangdi [say it grows] among rocks and stones in long-abandoned places; it is gathered in the second month, third month, eighth month, and tenth month, and dried in shade.

Commentary: The Shuowen (Analytical Dictionary of Characters) says: its roots, like green pearls, resemble those of the mai (barley) herb. The Zhongshan Jing says the mountain of mai-men-dong has many pu-lei plants. According to Wu Pu's account this is indeed mai-men-dong. The word ren-hui is phonetically identical to man, as Tao Hongjing notes.

The fruit is like green pearls; the roots resemble those of layered barley — hence the name mai-men-dong (barley gate winter).

Duhuo (Angelica pubescens): Flavor bitter, nature balanced. It governs injuries from wind-cold, metal-wound pain, ben-tun (surging-pig) syndrome, epileptic spasms, and women's shan-jia (hernial masses). Long-term use lightens the body and increases longevity. One name is qiang-huo, one name is qiang-qing, one name is hu-qiang.

The alternate name "Envoy" — it grows in river valleys.

Wu Pu states: Duhuo is also called hu-wang-shi-zhe (envoy of the barbarian king). According to Shennong and Huangdi it is bitter and non-toxic. It is gathered in the eighth month. This herb has flowers: when there is wind the flowers do not move; when there is no wind the plant sways on its own. [Imperial citation ends here]

Shennong Bencao Jing, Volume One

Eminent physicians say: It is also called Ying, also called Dijie, also called Yuzhu, also called Mahun. It grows on Mount Tai and in hills and mounds. Gather after the Start of Spring; dry in the shade.
The Erya states: "Ying is Weiwei." Guo Pu notes: it is a medicinal herb whose leaves resemble bamboo but are longer, white on the upper surface, green underneath, with roots as large as a finger and one to two feet long.
Tao Hongjing says: The core text of the Classic has "Nüwei" but not "Weirui"; the Bielu has "Weirui," yet their uses are identical, so it is suspected that Nüwei is in fact Weirui, differing only in name. Chen Cangqi says: The biography of Hua Tuo in the Weizhi mentions "Qingzhan," also called Huangzhi, also called Dijie — this is precisely Weirui, also known as Xianren Shi. Large specimens resemble bamboo shoots, with nodes, and have narrow, elongated leaves.

Fangkui: flavor acrid, cold. It governs wasting and blockage, intestinal diarrhea, heat accumulation in the bladder causing inability to urinate, cough with counterflow, warm-type malaria, epilepsy, fright and madness, and mania. Long-term use consolidates the bones and marrow, replenishes qi, and lightens the body. Another name is Ligai. Grows in river valleys.

Wu Pu says: Fangkui is also called Ligai, Jueli, Fangyuan, Chencao, Liru, and Fanggai. According to Shennong: acrid, slightly cold. According to Tong Jun and Bian Que: non-toxic. According to Wu, Qibo, Leigong, and Huangdi: bitter, non-toxic. The stem and leaves resemble mallow; the upper part is dark yellow. The root emerges in the second month; the root is as large as a balloon-flower root, red and white inside. Flowers are white in the sixth month; fruit forms in the seventh and eighth months. Roots are gathered on the third day of the third month. (Imperial览)

Eminent physicians say: Also called Fangci, Jueli, Nongguo, Liran, and Fanggai. It grows in Linzi and on Mount Song, Mount Tai, and Shaoshi. Roots are gathered on the third day of the third month. Dry in the sun.

The Bowu Zhi (Treatise on Natural Phenomena) notes: Fangkui and wolfsbane (Langdu) resemble each other.

This Hu: flavor bitter, balanced (ping). It governs qi stagnation in the chest and abdomen, eliminates accumulation of food and drink in the intestines and stomach, and dispels cold-heat and evil qi, promoting the new by expelling the old. Long-term use lightens the body, brightens the eyes, and replenishes essence. Another name is Diхun.
Wu Pu says: This sprout is also called Shanrong and Rucao. According to Shennong, Qibo, and Leigong: bitter, non-toxic. It grows in Hongnong and Yuanju. Roots are gathered in the second and eighth months and dried in the sun.
Eminent physicians say: Also called Shanrong, Rucao Ye, and Yunhao — acrid and fragrant, edible. Grows in Hongnong and Yuanju. Roots are gathered in the second and eighth months and dried in the sun.

translation:
Prolonging life. One name is Mountain Yam (shanyù). It grows in mountain valleys.

Wu Pu says: Shǔyù, one name is Zhūshǔ (the Imperially Reviewed edition writes shǔ). One name is Shǔyù (also written as Zhūshǔ). In Qi and Yue it is called Mountain Yam. One name is Xiūcuì. One name is Ércǎo. The Imperially Reviewed edition quotes: In Qi and Yue it is named Ruòruò.

Mountain Yam, one name is Jùnyuè. The extended name is Shān. According to Shennong, it is sweet, slightly warm. Tong Jun and Lei Gong say sweet; the Imperially Reviewed edition gives the taste as bitter.

The fruit is greenish-yellow. It ripens in the eighth month; the root interior is white with yellow skin, resembling taro. The Imperially Reviewed edition notes: harvest the root in the second and eighth months. It is sweet and non-toxic. It can grow in the area of Linxiong and Zhenshan. The young plant has red vines and fine tendrils. It flowers white in the fifth month.

The Mingyi says: In Qin and Chu it is called Yùyán; in Zheng and Yue it is called Tǔzhǔ. It grows on Mount Song (Gāo). The root is harvested in the second and eighth months and dried in the sun.

Commentary from the Guangya: Yùyán and all its names (zhūyù) are the same plant, also called yùqì. The Northen Mountains Classic says: On Jingshan Mountain the herb zhūyù grows abundantly. Guo Pu notes that the root resembles sheep's-hoof (Rumex) and is edible. In Jiangnan today, people simply call it zhǔ, saying it with varying tones.

Fan Zi's Ji Ran says: Zhūyù mainly comes from the three auxiliary capitals (San Fu) around the capital; the white-colored ones are the best. The Bencao Yanyi says: The first character of the name Shānyào (Mountain Medicine) was a taboo name of Emperor Yingzong of the Song (whose given name was Shǔ), and the second character was zhǔ; Tang dynasty usage had it as a name taboo for Emperor Daizong, whose personal name was Yù, so the second character was changed to yào (medicine).

Job's Tears (yì yǐ rén). Flavor: sweet, slightly cold. It governs: tension and cramping of the sinews with inability to flex or extend; wind-damp impediment (bi) conditions; it descends qi. Long-term use lightens the body and augments qi. The root expels three types of worms. One name: Jiělǐ. It grows in level marshes and in fields.

The Mingyi says: Another name is Wūtǎn; another name is Qǐshí; another name is Gàn. It grows in Zhending. The fruit is harvested in the eighth month; the root is gathered at any season.

Commentary from the Shuowen: Yìyǐ, also called Qiángyīng and Xiāng, also called Yìyǐ. The Guangya says it is also called Qiáng, Qǐshí, and Zōu. The Wu-Yue Chunqiu records that the woman named Nǚxǐ of the Yǒushēn clan was of marrying age but not yet wed. While playing at the Dǐ Mountain she obtained a Job's Tears seed and swallowed it, and felt as if stirred by a divine force, and so became pregnant. The Hou Hanshu biography of Ma Yuan says that while stationed in Jiaozhi he regularly consumed Job's Tears (yìyǐ). They are effective for lightening the body and reducing desire and for overcoming miasmic illness. The popular written form is also yìyǐ.

Alisma (zéxiè). Flavor: sweet, cold. It governs: wind-cold damp impediment; difficult lactation; disperses water; nourishes the five viscera; augments qi and vital force; enriches and strengthens. Long-term use sharpens hearing and vision; prevents hunger; prolongs life; lightens the body; makes the face radiant; enables the body to move like water.

Shennong Bencao Jing, Volume One
