The Physicians' Record states: it is also called Hu Wang Shi Zhe (Envoy of the Barbarian King), and also called Du Yao Cao (Plant That Sways Alone). This plant does not sway when there is wind, yet moves on its own when there is no wind. It grows in Yong Prefecture, or in Longxi, Nan'an. The root is gathered in the second and eighth months, then sun-dried.

Examination: The Traditions of the Immortals records that Shan Tu took Qiang Huo and Du Huo; these two names both seem to refer to the same thing. "Hu Wang" and "Hu Qiang" all carry the character Qiang (meaning the Qiang people), just as "Zhuan Zhu" was also called "Zhuan She Zhu," and "Yu Gong Cha" was also called "Yu Gong." There is no other special significance to these names.

Che Qian Zi (Plantain seed): flavor sweet, cold, non-toxic. It governs urinary blockage, stops pain, promotes the flow of water passages and urination, eliminates dampness-impediment. Long-term use lightens the body, increases endurance against aging. Another name is Dang Dao.
The Imperial Survey notes: another name is Niu Yi (Cow's Trace), [marked in black characters].

It grows in flat marshy areas.

The Physicians' Record states: another name is Fu Yi, another name is Ha Ma Yi (Toad's Coat), another name is Niu Yi (Cow's Trace), another name is Sheng Ma.

Examination: The Shuowen says Fu, alternatively called Fu Yi... Another name is Ma Xi (Horse's Sandal), or Ma Che Qian. Guo Pu says it is what is now called Che Qian Cao (Plantain herb), with large leaves and long spikes, fond of growing beside roads; in Jiangdong it is called Ha Ma Yi (Toad's Coat), and also hides in cow dung. Sun Yan says it is called Dang Dao (Road-center), also called Ma Niao. The Erya says Dang Dao is Ma Niao. [Various sources concur.]

Another name is Niu Fen Mao. The Odes says "gather, gather the Fu Yi." The commentary says it is Che Qian. The bird called Ma Niao has another name, Che Qian; another name, Dang Dao. It is fond of being in cattle hoofprints. It is named Che Qian and Dang Dao because it grows in the middle of where vehicles pass and cattle tread. Today's medicinal Che Qian Zi is precisely this. People in You Prefecture call it Niu She Cao (Ox-tongue Herb). [Noted in black characters.] Long-term use prevents dreaming of demons and nightmares [reference to Imperially Reviewed sources]. It also says: lightens the body. Another name [follows].

[Regarding the entry for] Shu Yu (Chinese yam):

The Physicians' Record formerly written as Shu Xu. Another name: Ling. Grows in Yongchang. Another name in the Physicians' Record: Shen Shu. It is this. Grows in mountain valleys. Flavor sweet, warm. Governs injury to the center, supplements vacuity and emaciation, eliminates cold-heat evil qi, supplements the center, increases qi and strength, builds up muscle and flesh. Long-term use makes hearing and vision acute, lightens the body, and prevents hunger.

The Eminent Physicians say: It grows in Huayin. The root is collected in the second and eighth months and dried in the shade.

Shihu [Dendrobium]: flavor sweet, nature balanced. Its main functions are: healing injury to the interior, dispelling impediment, directing qi downward, supplementing the five viscera for deficiency-taxation and emaciation, strengthening yin; taken over a long time, it thickens the intestines and stomach, lightens the body, and prolongs life. Wu Pu says: Shihu — Shennong [classifies it as] sweet and balanced; Bianque [classifies it as] sour; Li's [canon classifies it as] cold. [Imperial citation.]

A note from Fan Zi's Jiran says: Shihu comes from Liu'an.

Bajitian [Morinda officinalis]: flavor acrid, slightly warm. Its main functions are: the great wind evil qi, yin flaccidity and failure to rise, strengthening sinews and bones, calming the five viscera, supplementing the center, increasing resolve, and boosting qi. Grows in mountain valleys.
The Eminent Physicians say: It grows in Ba Commandery and Xiapi. Root is collected in the second and eighth months and dried in the shade.

Baiying [Solanum lyratum]: flavor sweet, cold. Its main functions are: cold-heat, the eight kinds of obstruction sores, dispelling thirst, supplementing the center, boosting qi; taken over a long time, it lightens the body and prolongs life. Also known as Gu Cai. [The original text has an error here.] Grows in mountain valleys.
A note from the Erya says: Another name is Baicao. Guo Pu notes: In Jiangdong today there is the Guimu grass; its stem resembles kudzu, its leaves are round and hairy, its seeds are like ear-jewels. They grow in red clusters. The Tang commentary on Baiying says: this is the Guimu grass.

Baihao [Artemisia]: flavor sweet, balanced. Its main functions are: evil qi of the five viscera, wind-cold damp impediment, supplementing the center, boosting qi, growing hair and causing it to turn black, treating a suspended sensation in the heart, scant eating and constant hunger; taken over a long time, it lightens the body, sharpens hearing and vision, and prevents aging.

Shennong Bencao Jing, Volume One

The Mingyi records: grows on Zhongshan, harvested in the second month.

Examination: The Shuowen says "fan" means white wormwood (bai hao); "ai" means bing tai. The Guangya says fan-mu means lao-na. The Erya says ai means bing tai; Guo Pu says today's ai (mugwort) is bai hao. The Xia Xiao Zheng says the second month.

The Er'er zhuan says: fan comes from the hu, from hu means fan-mu, fan-mu means lao-bo. The Erya says fan-pang-hao; Guo Pu says bai hao, also fan from hu, Guo Pu says uncertain.

The Maoshi says: "to gather fan," the commentary says pang-hao. Also "fan-qi-qi," the commentary says fan is bai hao. Lu Ji says all ai of white color is pang-hao. The Chuci commentary by Wang Yi says ai is bai hao. According to this, pang and ai are similar in sound and meaning; ai is named in the Bencao Jing; those without it are bai hao. The Mingyi lists ai separately, which is not correct.

Chi Jian (Gastrodia elata): flavor pungent, warm. Main uses: kills ghost essences and malevolent things, eliminates gu-poison and evil qi. Long-term use increases qi and strength, nourishes yin, fattens and strengthens the body, and increases longevity. Also named Li Mu; also named Gui Du You. Grows in valleys.

Wu Pu says: grows in Chencang, Yongzhou, and Taishan Shaoshi; roots are harvested in the third, fourth, and eighth months and sun-dried.

Yuzhi (imperial encyclopedia): dried, treats swelling.

The Mingyi says: grows in Chencang, Yongzhou, and Taishan Shaoshi; roots harvested in the third, fourth, and eighth months. Sun-dry daily.

Also named Du Yao, also named Li Mu. The reason it is called He Li Mu: a separate account says the tian ma used by physicians today is this chi jian root, which has twelve lateral tubers encircling it, extending several chi from the main tuber.

The Baopuzi says: the immortal formulas include a plant called He Li Cao.

Although the parts depend on each other, they are not actually connected, but are linked through their qi. A separate account says: when this plant forms its underground root like a taro corm — that is this chi jian root — it has twelve lateral tubers circling it, several chi from the main tuber.

Yan Lü zi: noted also as yan na, yu lü.

[Formula for] not aging, growing in valleys.

Wu Pu says: Yan Lü — Shennong, Leigong, Tongjun, and Qibo all say it is bitter, slightly warm, non-toxic; Li's [classification] says warm. Or grows in Shangdang. The leaves are blue-green and thick, matched in pairs. Flowers are white in the seventh month; fruit is black in the ninth month.

二五
translation:
Wu Pu says: Juanbai (Selaginella): Shennong classifies it as acrid; Tongjun and Leigong classify it as sweet. The Yulan encyclopedia cites: one name is Shenzhi; also called Shangugo. One name is [from another source].
The Mingyi (Noted Physicians) says: One name is Baozu (leopard foot); one name is Qiugu; one name is Jiaoshi. It grows on Changshan. Collected in the fifth and seventh months; dried in the shade.

Lanshi (Isatis/indigo fruit): Fan Zijiran says: Juanbai comes from Sanfu. One name is Biedu.
The Mingyi says: Its stems and leaves can be used to dye blue-green. It kills ghost-toxins from mosquito bites. Long-term use keeps the hair from turning white and lightens the body. It grows in flat marshes.
Commentary: Shuowen says "jue" is horse-indigo; indigo is a blue-dyeing herb. Erya says jue is horse-indigo. Guo Pu says: today this is the large-leafed winter indigo. The Rites of Zhou mentions dyeing herbs; Zheng notes that the dyeing herb is indigo. The Xiazhengzheng (Summer Ordinances) says: in the fifth month, the indigo begins to pour forth. The Book of Odes says "gathering indigo all morning long"; the commentary says indigo is a dyeing herb.

Hao (Artemisia/wormwood):
[The Xiao Zheng passage on indigo is repeated here in the original.]
Wu Pu says: Cuhao (Artemisia) is acrid and warm in flavor; it governs wind stroke entering the brain, headache, cold impediment, cramping of sinews, critical wounds, and blockage of blood in women causing infertility. It grows in river valleys.
Commentary: Shuowen says: Shennong, the Yellow Emperor, Qibo, and Leigong classify it as acrid and non-toxic; Bianque classifies it as sour and non-toxic; Master Li says it is warm when fresh, cold when processed, or it grows on the shady side of Hutao Mountain.
Or [it grows on] Taishan ridge. The Yulan encyclopedia, or alternatively the Xiangguo source, says: leaves are fragrant, fine, blue-black in pattern, reddish like the drug-base plant; it grows in clumps through winter and summer; it flowers red in the fifth month; fruit turns black in the seventh month; two leaves at the tip of the hao stalk; collected in the third month.
The root has joints resembling a horse's bit in shape.
The Mingyi says: One name is Xiangguo. Its leaves are named Yaomai. It grows in Wugong, in the Xiegu valley west of the ridge. Root is collected in the third and fourth months and dried in the sun.
Shuowen says: One name is Huhao; it is a fragrant herb. Sima Xiangru [mentions it in his rhapsody]. The Zuo Zhuan (Spring and Autumn Annals commentary) says: "there is mountain juhao." Du Yu says juhao is used to resist dampness to the west.
Yaoshuo says: It is also called Shanying or Yingxiang herb. Sima Xiangru's account, or written with the "bow" radical.
The Classic of Mountains and Seas says: Xiong (Ligusticum) – this plant is found in abundance as xiong-hao. Guo Pu says: Xionghao, one name is Jiangli. Fan Zijiran says xionghao grows without ever drying up; its quality is good. [Cited in] Sima Xiangru's rhapsody.
There is xionghao: Sima Zhen cites Sima Peng saying xionghao resembles the drug-base plant. Guo Pu says: today in Liyang it is called Jiangli.

二四
translation:
Red Zhi (Ganoderma): flavor bitter, nature balanced. Governs chest constriction. Benefits heart qi. Supplements the center. Increases wisdom and intelligence. Prevents forgetfulness. Long-term consumption lightens the body, prevents aging, and extends life to the level of an immortal. Also called Dan Zhi.

Black Zhi: flavor salty, nature balanced. Governs abscesses. Benefits the water passages. Supplements kidney qi. Opens the nine orifices. Sharpens hearing and vision. Long-term consumption lightens the body, prevents aging, and extends life to the level of an immortal. Also called Yuan Zhi.

Green Zhi: flavor sour, nature balanced. Governs vision. Supplements liver qi. Calms the ethereal soul. Promotes benevolence and forbearance. Long-term consumption lightens the body, prevents aging, and extends life to the level of an immortal. Also called Long Zhi.

White Zhi: flavor acrid, nature balanced. Governs coughing and counterflow of qi. Benefits lung qi. Opens and benefits the mouth and nose. Strengthens the will. Promotes courage and fortitude. Settles the corporeal soul. Long-term consumption lightens the body, prevents aging, and extends life to the level of an immortal. Also called Yu Zhi.

Yellow Zhi: flavor sweet, nature balanced. Governs the five evils of the heart and abdomen. Benefits spleen qi. Calms the spirit. Fosters loyalty, trustworthiness, and contentment. Long-term consumption lightens the body, prevents aging, and extends life. Also called Mu Zhi.

Purple Zhi: flavor sweet, nature warm. Governs deafness. Benefits the joints. Protects the spirit. Supplements essential qi. Strengthens sinews and bones. Improves complexion. Long-term consumption lightens the body, prevents aging, and extends life to the level of an immortal. Also called Mu Zhi. [Note: the six types are also called Jin Zhi.]

Wu Pu says: Purple Zhi is also called Mu Zhi.

The Mingyi says: Red Zhi grows on Huo Mountain; Black Zhi grows on Heng Mountain; Green Zhi grows on Tai Mountain; White Zhi grows on Hua Mountain; Yellow Zhi grows on Song Mountain; Purple Zhi grows on high summer ground, is purple in color, and shaped like...

The Sanguan Yuji notes: all six Zhi are non-toxic. They are harvested in the sixth and eighth months.

The Chuci says: "Gather the triple-flowering herb on the mountain clearing." Wang Yi explains: "The triple-flowering herb refers to the Zhi plant." Guo Pu says the Zhi flowers three times in one year. The Liji, Nei Ze chapter, mentions Zhi. The Hou Han Shu, biography of Hua Tuo, mentions a lacquer-leaf and green-sticky powder. The commentary cites Tuo's biography: Zhi is a woody plant, also called Mei. Lu Zhi's commentary says the green-sticky variety is also called Di Jie.

One type called Yellow Zhi governs and regulates the five viscera and supplements essential qi. The character "jun" (mushroom) does not appear in older character dictionaries. It is traditionally said that Jin Nu Lian, as listed in the Liexian Zhuan, states that Lü Shang consumed Ze Zhi. The Bao Pu Zi, Xianyao chapter, states:

The red ones resemble coral; the white ones resemble cut fat; the black ones resemble the lacquer plant; the green ones resemble kingfisher feathers; the yellow ones resemble purple gold — all are luminous and translucent like solid ice. Also called Wan Sui (Ten-thousand Years). Grows in mountain valleys.

Juanbai (Selaginella): flavor acrid, nature warm. Grows in mountain valleys. Governs evil qi of the five viscera. Treats cold-heat pain in women's genitalia. Treats abdominal masses, blood obstruction, and inability to conceive. Long-term consumption lightens the body and improves complexion. Also called Wan Sui. Grows in mountain valleys.

二七
translation:
Collected in the first month of the new year.

A note from the Classic of Mountains and Seas (Shan Hai Jing) states: "The mountain of Shang Shen is rich in resonant stones," suggesting this is the same substance. Guo Pu's commentary says: "Qing stone, a large rock, not quite right." The Tang dynasty commentary notes: "Its popular name is Nai Dong; people in the south of the mountains call it thus."

Ji Li Zi (Tribulus terrestris fruit): Flavor bitter, warm. Governs malign blood, breaking up concretions and accumulations, throat obstruction, and difficulty with lactation. Long-term use strengthens the muscles, brightens the eyes, and lightens the body. Also called Pang Tong, Qu Ren, Zhi Xing.

Luo Shi (Trachelospermum jasminoides): Named because it wraps around rocks and trees to grow. The Bie Lu calls it Shi Long Teng. Those growing on rocks are best.

Also named Ji Li, and Ci. Grows in flat marshes or roadsides. Harvest the fruit in the seventh and eighth months and dry in the sun.

A physician's note: "Also named Ji Ci, and Ci, grows at Feng Shuo; fruit collected in the seventh and eighth months and dried in the sun." [No text in the Jun version or Da Guan edition.]

A note from Shuo Wen says: Shou means Ji Li. The Book of Odes says: "The wall has Ci." Using Ci to mean Mao Man is incorrect. The Er Ya says: Ci is Ji Li. Guo Pu says: spreads along the ground, with fine leaves, the fruit has three corners and pricks people. Mao Shi says: the wall has inflammation, the commentary says inflammation means Ji Li. Old texts writing it as Ji Li are incorrect.

Huang Qi (Astragalus): Flavor sweet, slightly warm. Governs abscesses and festering sores, chronic wounds, draining pus, stopping pain, severe wind and leprosy conditions, five types of hemorrhoids, and rat fistulas. Supplements deficiency and treats all children's diseases. Also named Dai San. Grows in mountain valleys.

A physician's note: Also named Dai Shen, Du Shen, Shu Zhi, Bai Ben. Grows in Shu Commandery, Bai Shui, and Han Zhong. Collected in the second and tenth months and dried in shade.

Rou Cong Rong (Cistanche deserticola): Flavor sweet, slightly warm. Governs the five strains and seven injuries, supplements the middle, eliminates cold and heat pain in the stem, nourishes the five viscera, strengthens yin and benefits essence and qi, increases fertility, and treats women's concretions and accumulations. Long-term use lightens the body. Grows in mountain valleys.

A physician's note: Also written Rou Sui Rong or Rou Song Rong. According to Shennong and the Yellow Emperor it is salty; according to Lei Gong it is acidic and slightly warm; Li says it grows in Hexi and He Dong regions. Yu Kuan notes it grows in Shanyin, three to four inches long, in clumps. Also found in Dai Commandery and Yanmen. Collected from the second to eighth month and dried in shade.

Wu Pu says: Rou Sui Rong, also called Rou Song Rong. Shennong and Yellow Emperor say salty; Lei Gong says acidic and slightly warm; Li says grows in Hexi and Dai Commandery, Yanmen region. Collected second through eighth month, dried in shade.

A physician's note: Grows in Hexi and Dai Commandery, Yanmen. Collected on the fifth day and dried in shade.

Shennong Bencao Jing, Volume One

神農本草經卷一

蘭蕉味辛溫。主欬逆定驚氣辟邪惡除蠱毒鬼注去三蟲。久服通神。一名薇蕉。生川澤。

吳普曰。一名芫蕎。一名芎藭苗也。生雍州及冤句四月五月朵葉暴乾。

名醫曰。一名茳蕎寬御

案說文云。廲廱蕉也。廲蕎莊蕎離蕭爾雅云。薪蒿叢蕉郭璞云香草葉小如委狀淮南子云似蛇牀山海

經云臭如廲廱蕉司馬相如賦有江離廲廱蕉司馬貞引樊光云藥本一名廲廱蕉根名薪芷。

黃連味苦寒。主熱氣目痛皆傷泣出明目。御大覧引本無。主蟲傷腸游腹痛下利婦人陰中腫痛。久服令人

不忘。一名王連生川谷

吳普曰黃連神農岐伯雷公苦無毒李氏小寒或生蜀郡太山之陽寬御

名醫曰生巫陽及蜀郡范子計然云黃連出蜀郡肥堅者善。

寒廣雅云。王連黃連也太山二月八月采。

絡石味苦溫。主風熱死肌癰傷口乾舌焦癰腫不消喉舌腫水漿不下久服輕身明目潤澤好顏色不老

延年。一名石鯪生川谷

吳普曰落石一名鱗石。一名明石。一名縣石。一名雲華。一名雲英。一名雲丹神農苦小溫雷

公茍無毒扁鵲桐君甘無毒李氏大寒云藥中君采無時寬御

名醫曰一名石蹉一名略石一名明石一名領石一名縣石生太山或石山之陰或高山巖石上或生

二六
translation:
Shennong Bencao Jing, Volume One

Lan Jiao: flavor pungent, warm. It governs cough and counterflow, calms fright qi, repels evil and malignant influences, eliminates gu toxin and ghost-infixation, expels the three worms. Long-term consumption opens spiritual awareness. Another name: Wei Jiao. Grows in river marshes and pools.

Wu Pu says: also called Yuan Qiao; also called Xiong Qiong seedling. Grows in Yong Prefecture and Yuanju; collect leaves in the fourth and fifth months and dry in the sun.

The Mingyi records: another name is Jiang Qiao. [Imperial citation note]

According to the Shuowen: Li Yong Jiao is another name. The plant resembles Qiong; Zhuang Qiao, Li Xiao — the Erya says: Xin Hao, Cong Jiao; Guo Pu says it is a fragrant herb with small leaves resemblingWei; Huainanzi says it resembles snake-bed; the Classic of Mountains and Seas says its smell is like Li Yong Jiao; Sima Xiangru's rhapsody mentions Jiang Li and Li Yong Jiao; Sima Zhen cites Fan Guang, who says in the pharmacopeia it is also called Li Yong Jiao root, with the alternate name Xin Zhi.

Huang Lian (Coptis): flavor bitter, cold. It governs heat qi, eye pain, all eye injuries with tearing, and brightens the eyes. [Imperial citation note: the version cited in Taiping Yulan lacks the following:] governs insect wounds, intestinal wandering, abdominal pain, diarrhea, swelling and pain in women's genital area. Long-term consumption prevents forgetfulness. Another name: Wang Lian. Grows in mountain valleys.

Wu Pu says: Huang Lian — Shennong, Qibo, and Leigong [classify it as] bitter, non-toxic; Master Li [says] slightly cold. Grows in Shu Commandery or on the sunny side of Taishan. [Imperial citation note]

The Mingyi records: grows in Wu Yang and Shu Commandery. Fan Ziiran says: Huang Lian from Shu Commandery — the firm and fat ones are best.

The Guangya says: Wang Lian is Huang Lian. On Taishan, collect in the second and eighth months.

Luo Shi (Trachelospermum): flavor bitter, warm. It governs wind-heat, dead flesh, abscesses and wounds, dry mouth, scorched tongue, swelling and abscesses that will not disperse, swelling of the throat and tongue, inability to swallow liquid. Long-term consumption lightens the body, brightens the eyes, moistens and nourishes the complexion, prevents aging, and prolongs years. Another name: Shi Ling. Grows in mountain valleys.

Wu Pu says: Luo Shi — also called Lin Shi, Ming Shi, Xian Shi, Yun Hua, Yun Ying, Yun Dan. Shennong [classifies it as] bitter, slightly warm; Leigong [classifies it as] non-toxic; Pian Que and Tong Jun [classify it as] sweet, non-toxic; Master Li [says] greatly cold. According to pharmacists, it is a sovereign herb; collect at any time. [Imperial citation note]

The Mingyi records: also called Shi Cuo, Lüe Shi, Ming Shi, Ling Shi, Xian Shi. Grows on Taishan, or on the shaded side of rocky mountains, or on cliff rocks of high mountains, or grows [text continues on next page]

二九
translation:
Wu Pu says: Also called Sui Stone, also called Xiang Pu (fragrant cattail). According to Shennong and Leigong, it is sweet in flavor. It grows in the South Sea, in ponds and marshes.

According to the Shuowen, the character "pu" means a fragrant herb; the Pian (Yupian) says it is the same as "ju" (a type of marsh plant). Another reading gives the pronunciation "pu." The Bencao Tujing says the young shoots of Xiang Pu, before they emerge from the water, are reddish-white.
The Mingyi says: Another name is Su; it grows in the South Sea.

Xuduan (Dipsacus): flavor bitter, slightly warm. Main uses: treating cold-damage disorders; supplementing deficiency; gold-wound (sword-wound) abscesses and injuries; fractures and falls; knitting sinews and bone; difficulties in childbirth and in nursing. Long-term use increases vital energy.

Also called Longdou, also called Shuzhe; grows in mountain valleys.

The Mingyi says: Also called Jiegu (bone-joiner), also called Nancao, also called Huai. It grows on Changshan. Harvest in the seventh and eighth months; dry in the shade.

According to the Guangya: also called Bao Duan. The Fanzi Jiran says Xuduan comes from Sanfu. The Tongjun Yaolu says Xuduan grows as a trailing vine; the leaves are fine and trailing like perilla; the root is large, yellowish-white inside, and contains juice. Harvest the root in the seventh and eighth months.

Loulu: flavor bitter and salty, cold. Main uses: malignant sores; heat-type scrofula; goiter; scrofulous lumps; promotes milk secretion. Long-term use lightens the body, increases vital energy, sharpens hearing and eyesight, prevents aging, and extends years. Also called Yelan (wild orchid); grows in mountain valleys.

The Mingyi says: [text notes names and origins]

According to the Guangya: also called Feilian and Pianlu. Harvest the root in the eighth month; dry in the shade. Tao Hongjing says that in common usage the root is taken and called Luli.

Rong Shi (Rosa fruit): flavor sour, warm. Main uses: abscesses and malignant sores; hardening of flesh from injuries; dissipating pathological heat; erosion of the yin parts that will not heal. Also indicated for benefiting the joints. Also called Qiangwei (climbing rose), also called Qiangma, also called Niuji. Grows in river valleys.

Wu Pu says: Also called Qiangwei, also called Niule, also called Qiangmi, also called Shanjie. Grows in Lingling and Shujun. Harvest in the eighth and ninth months; dry in the shade.

Shennong Bencao Jing, Volume One

神農本草經卷一

二八

案吳普云。一名肉松蓉當是古本蓉即容字俗寫蓯蓉非正字也陶宏景云。是野馬精落地所生時似肉舊作肉蓯蓉非

防風味甘温無毒主大風頭眩痛惡風風邪目盲無所見風行周身骨節疼痹御寬作煩滿久服輕身。

名銅芸御寬作生川澤。

吳普曰防風一名迴雲。一名回草。一名百枝。一名蘭根。一名百韭。一名百種神農黃帝岐伯桐君雷公甘無毒李氏小寒或生邯鄲上蔡正月生葉細圓青黑白五月花黃六月實黑三月十月采根。

扁鵲甘無毒。李氏小寒。或生邯鄲上蔡正月生葉細圓青黑白五月花黃六月實黑三月十月采根。

名琅邪者良御寬

暴乾。

名醫曰。琅邪者。良御寬

案范子計然云防風出三輔白者善。

名醫曰生河東四月采。

蒲黃味甘平主心腹旁光寒熱利小便止血消瘀血久服輕身益氣力延年神仙生池澤。

案玉篇云蒿謂今蒲頭有臺臺上有重臺中出黃即蒲黃陶宏景云。此即蒲鸁花上黃粉也仙經亦用

此考爾雅蒿離謂其上蒿荷離與蒲鸁聲相近疑即此。

香蒲味甘平主五藏心下邪氣口中爛臭堅齒明目聰耳久服輕身耐老能老御寬作一名雌唯御寬云生池澤。
translation:
Shennong Bencao Jing, Volume One

[Page 28]

Editor's note: Wu Pu states: another name is "Rou Songrong" (Cistanche). This must be the original form of the character "rong," which in popular writing became "Cong Rong" — a non-standard character. Tao Hongjing says: it grows where the semen of wild horses has fallen to the ground, hence it resembles flesh. The old text wrote it as "rou cong rong," which is incorrect.

Fangfeng [Saposhnikovia divaricata]: flavor sweet, warm, non-toxic. It mainly treats great wind, dizziness and headache, aversion to wind, wind evil, blindness and loss of vision, wind moving through the body, painful obstruction of the joints. [御寬 commentary reads: "fullness and vexation."] Long-term consumption lightens the body.

Other name: Tong Yun [御寬 commentary reads: "grows in rivers and marshes"].

Wu Pu says: Fangfeng — another name Hui Yun, another name Hui Cao, another name Bai Zhi, another name Lan Gen, another name Bai Jiu, another name Bai Zhong. According to Shennong, Huangdi, Qibo, Tong Jun, and Lei Gong: sweet, non-toxic. According to Master Li: slightly cold. May grow in Handan and Shangcai. In the first month the leaves emerge, fine, round, greenish-black and white; in the fifth month the flowers are yellow; in the sixth month the fruit is black. Roots collected in the third and tenth months.

Bianque [says it is] sweet, non-toxic. Master Li [says it is] slightly cold. May grow in Handan and Shangcai. In the first month leaves emerge, fine and round, greenish-black and white; fifth month yellow flowers; sixth month black fruit; roots collected in the third and tenth months.

The Langye variety is the best. [御寬 note]

Dried by exposure to sun.

The Physician's Record states: the Langye variety is best. [御寬 note]

According to Fan Zi Jiran: Fangfeng from the three auxiliary regions [Sanfu], the white variety is good.

The Physician's Record states: grows in Hedong; collected in the fourth month.

Puhuang [Typha pollen]: flavor sweet, balanced. It mainly treats pain in the abdomen beside the bladder, cold and heat, promotes urination, stops bleeding, disperses stagnant blood. Long-term consumption lightens the body, augments energy, prolongs life to that of an immortal. Grows in ponds and marshes.

According to the Pian Yu [dictionary]: the term "gao" refers to what is now the head of the cattail plant, which has a platform, and above the platform there is a double platform, from which the yellow [pollen] emerges — this is Puhuang. Tao Hongjing says: this is the yellow powder on the flowers of the cattail. It is also used in the immortality classics.

Further examination of the Erya [dictionary]: the term "gao" is said to refer to "Pulu" [cattail]. The pronunciations of "gao" and "Pulu" are similar, suggesting they may be the same thing.

Xiangpu [Typha orientalis, fragrant cattail]: flavor sweet, balanced. It mainly treats evil qi in the five viscera below the heart, decay and foulness in the mouth, strengthens the teeth, brightens the eyes, sharpens the ears. Long-term consumption lightens the body and enables one to resist aging. [御寬 commentary reads: "able to grow old."] Another name: Ci Wei [雌唯]. [御寬 note says: "grows in ponds and marshes."]

案廣雅云卻蟬丹參也。
茜根味苦寒主寒濕風痹黃疸補中生川谷。
名醫曰可以染絳一名地血一名茹蘆一名茅蒐一名蒨生喬山二月三月采根暴乾。
案說文云茜蒨也可以染絳茹蘆也蒨草茹蘆也茹蘆人所生在阪傳云从草从鬼廣雅云地血茹蘆也爾雅云茹蘆齊人謂之蒨徐州人謂之牛蔓徐廣注史記云茜一名紅藍其花染絳赤黃也接名醫別出紅藍條非。

飛廉味苦平主骨節熱脹酸疼久服令人身輕一名飛輕一名木禾生河內正月采根七月八月采花陰乾生川澤。
名醫曰一名伏兔一名飛雉一名木禾生河內正月采根七月八月采花陰乾生川澤。
案廣雅云伏豬木禾也飛廉扁蘆也陶宏景云今既別有漏蘆則非此別名耳。作一名會及生山谷。

五味子味酸溫主益氣欬逆上氣勞傷羸瘦補不足強陰益男子精。御覽作大觀引本云此別名。

吳普曰五味五味子味酸溫主益氣元及御覽。
名醫曰一名會及一名元及生齊山及代郡八月采實陰乾。
案韭也廣雅云會及五味也蔓生子叢在蔓頭抱樸子仙藥篇云五味。
名醫曰一名會及及五味也廣雅云珎云五味也蔓生子叢在蔓頭抱樸子仙藥篇云五味。

旋華味甘溫主益氣去面黯。覽作黑色媚好色悅澤。令人其根味辛主腹中寒熱邪氣利小便久服不。
著五行之精其子有五味移門子服五味子十六年色如玉女入水不溺入火不灼也。仙藥篇云五味。

神農本草經卷一
三一
translation:
The Guangya (dictionary) says: "Que Chan" is the same as Dan Shen (Salvia).

Qian Gen (Madder root, Rubia cordifolia): flavor bitter, cold; governs cold-damp wind impediment, jaundice; supplements the center; grows in mountain valleys and streams.
The Mingyi (Famous Physicians) says: it can be used to dye crimson; another name is Di Xue (earth blood); another name is Ru Lu; another name is Mao Sou; another name is Qian. Grows on Qiao Mountain. The root is gathered in the second and third months and dried in the sun.
Commentary: The Shuowen (dictionary) says "Qian" means Qian-herb, used to dye crimson; Ru Lu is the same herb. Ru Lu grows on slopes. The character is composed of "grass" and "ghost" radicals. The Guangya says Di Xue is Ru Lu. The Erya says Ru Lu is what the people of Qi call Qian; the people of Xuzhou call it Niu Man. Xu Guang's notes to the Shiji say: Qian is also called Hong Lan; its flowers dye crimson-red-yellow. The entry for Hong Lan in the Mingyi is a separate herb, not the same thing.

Fei Lian (Carlina/Carline thistle, Carduus): flavor bitter, balanced; governs heat and swelling in the joints, sour pain; long-term use makes the body light. Another name is Fei Qing; another name is Mu He. Grows in Henei. The root is gathered in the first month; the flower is gathered in the seventh and eighth months and dried in the shade. Grows in river marshes.
The Mingyi says: another name is Fu Tu; another name is Fei Zhi; another name is Mu He. Grows in Henei. Root gathered in the first month; flower gathered in the seventh and eighth months, dried in the shade. Grows in river marshes.
Commentary: The Guangya says Fu Zhu is Mu He; Fei Lian is Bian Lu. Tao Hongjing says: since there is now a separate herb Lou Lu, this is a different name. [Note:] One name is Hui Ji; also "grows in mountain valleys."

Wu Wei Zi (Five-Flavor Berry, Schisandra): flavor sour, warm; governs replenishing qi, cough with counterflow qi, taxation damage and emaciation; supplements insufficiency; strengthens yin and increases male essence.

Wu Pu says: Wu Wei Zi — five flavors; flavor sour, warm; governs replenishing qi; also recorded in the Yulan (encyclopedia).
The Mingyi says: another name is Hui Ji; another name is Yuan Ji. Grows in the mountains of Qi and in Daijun. Gathered in the eighth month; dried in the shade.
Commentary: The Guangya says Hui Ji is Wu Wei Zi. The vine grows with berries clustered at the tips of the branches. The Baopuzi, chapter on immortal drugs, records five flavors.

Xuan Hua (Field bindweed, Calystegia): flavor sweet, warm; governs replenishing qi, removing facial dark spots [darkened complexion]. Makes the person's face beautiful and lustrous. Its root: flavor acrid; governs cold and heat evil qi in the abdomen, promotes urination. Long-term use does not [text continues on next page].
[Note:] It concentrates the essence of the five phases; its seeds have five flavors. If one takes it for sixteen years, the complexion becomes like jade; women who enter water do not sink; entering fire they are not burned.

Shennong Bencao Jing, Volume One
31

text:
神農本草經 卷一

三〇

案陶宏景云．即是牆薇子．
天名精味甘寒主瘀血血瘕欲死．下血．止血．利小便．久服輕身耐老．一名麥句薑．一名蝦蟆藍．一名家首．
生川澤．
名醫曰．一名天門精．一名玉門精．一名彘顱．一名蟲蛤蘭．一名觀生．平原．五月采．
案說文云．蠿冢首也．爾雅云．芍藭冢首也．郭璞云．今江東呼為地松掌再錫云陳藏器別立地菘條後人不嘗
猶葛唐本云鹿活草是也別錄一名天蔓菁南人呼為地松掌再錫云陳藏器別立地菘條後人不嘗
仍其謬．
決明子味鹹平．主青盲目淫膚赤白膜．眼赤痛淚出．久服益精光．太平理．御寬引作理．目球．輕身．生川澤．
吳普曰決明子．一名草決明．一名羊明御覽．
名醫曰．生龍門石決明．生豫章．十月朔．陰乾百日．
案廣雅云形似馬蹄蘑英光也．又決明羊明也．爾雅云蘚莒英光．郭璞云明．也葉黃銳．赤華實如山茱萸．

丹
參味苦微寒主心腹邪氣腸鳴幽幽如走水寒熱積聚破癥除瘕止煩滿益氣．一名郤蟬草生川谷．
陶宏景云．形似馬蹄蘑英光決明．
吳普曰．丹參．一名赤參．一名木羊乳如茯小方如茬毛根赤四月華紫五月采根陰乾治心腹痛御．
生桐柏或生太山山陵陰蒸華小方如茬毛根赤四月華紫五月采根暴乾．
名醫曰．一名赤參．一名木羊乳．一名郤蟬草．神農桐君黃帝雷公扁鵲苦無毒．李氏大寒岐伯戢．
translation:
Shennong Bencao Jing, Volume One

[Page 30]

Commentary: Tao Hongjing says: This is exactly the Qiangwei (rose) seed.

Tianming Jing [Carpesium]: Flavor sweet, cold. Governs stagnant blood, blood masses with near-fatal symptoms, bleeding below; stops bleeding; promotes urination. Long-term use lightens the body and promotes longevity. Also named Maijujiang, also named Hamalan, also named Jiashou.
Grows in rivers and marshes.

Physicians say: Also named Tianmen Jing, also named Yumen Jing, also named Zhilu, also named Chongge Lan, also named Guansheng. Found on level plains. Harvested in the fifth month.

Commentary from the Shuowen: "Zhan" means "Zhong Shou." The Erya says: "Shao Qiong" means "Zhong Shou." Guo Pu says: In Jiangdong it is called Disong zhang; Zaxi says that Chen Cangqi separately established the entry "Disong," and later people no longer recognized it —
— just as with Ge; the Tang ben says it is the same as Luhuo grass. The Bieludeng also names it Tianmanjing; southern people call it Disong; Zaxi says Chen Cangqi separately created the entry Disong, and later people no longer recognized it —
— and perpetuated the error.

Juemingzi [Cassia seed]: Flavor salty, neutral. Governs blindness, eye infections, skin redness, white films on the eye, red and painful eyes with tearing. Long-term use benefits the essence-light [vision]. [Reference to Taiping御 and other editions]. Lightens the body. Grows in rivers and marshes.

Wu Pu says: Juemingzi, also named Caojueming, also named Yangming [per the Yulanjuan].

Physicians say: Grows at Longmen as Shijueming; also grows in Yuzhang. Harvested on the first day of the tenth month. Dried in the shade for one hundred days.

Commentary: The Guangya says it resembles a horse's hoof mushroom; the Yingguang. Also, Jueming is also called Yangming. The Erya says Xian Ju Yingguang. Guo Pu says it is bright, with yellow pointed leaves, red flowers, and fruit resembling Cornus officinalis.

Danshen [Salvia miltiorrhiza]:
Flavor bitter, slightly cold. Governs evil qi in the heart and abdomen, intestinal rumbling like rushing water, cold and heat, accumulations, breaks up conglomerations and removes masses, stops vexation and fullness, benefits qi. Also named Qichan Cao. Grows in valleys.

Tao Hongjing says: Its form resembles the horse's hoof mushroom Yingguang Jueming.

Wu Pu says: Danshen, also named Chishen, also named Muyangruruxiaofang, leaves like a mat, red root, flowers purple in the fourth month, root harvested in the fifth month, dried in the shade, treats heart and abdominal pain [per the Yulanjuan].

Grows at Tongbai or on Taishan mountain ridges, shaded slopes, small fragrant flowers, red roots, purple flowers in the fourth month, roots harvested in the fifth month, sun-dried.

Physicians say: Also named Chishen, also named Muyangru, also named Qichan Cao. Shennong, Tongjun, Huangdi, Leigong, and Bianque [all say] bitter, non-toxic. Li's [text says] greatly cold; Qibo [says] restrained.

translation:
Kochia scoparia (Di Fu Zi): Flavor bitter, cold. Governs bladder heat, promotes urination, supplements the center, and benefits essential qi. Long-term use brightens the ears and eyes, lightens the body, and resists aging. One name is Di Kui. The imperial commentary cites: also called Di Mai; also called Da Di.
[Note:] The character Mai in some editions is written without the Shen radical; various black-inked characters note: grows in marshes and open fields.
According to the Guangya: also called Di Mai; grows in Jingzhou; the fruit is gathered in the eighth and tenth months and dried in the shade. The Liexian Zhuan says Wen Bin took Di Fu; local commentary says Di Fu is also called Luo Dai, and also called Di Sao; the Erya calls it Mang Madai — this is the same plant.
Ancient physicians say: one name Di Kui; Di Fu is the same plant.
People today also use it as a broom.
The Guangya says: flavor bitter and balanced; governs great heat, fire sores, bodily fever, vexation, evil and perverse qi; governs women's flooding and spotting with red and white discharge; lightens the body and brightens the eyes. One name Jie Huo; one name Shen Huo. The imperial commentary cites: also called Shui Yun.
[Note on Jing commentary]: grows in river valleys.
The Mingyi says: one name Huo Mu; one name Shu Huo; one name Liao Huo; grows on Mount Tai; gathered on the fourth day of the fourth month and the seventh day of the seventh month; dried in the shade.
Tao Hongjing says: people today all store it on rooftops, saying it wards off fire. Flavor bitter and balanced; governs wind-damp cold-heat evil qi; heat bind and jaundice; acrid and non-toxic. Long-term use lightens the body, benefits qi, and resists aging. Imperial commentary notes: grows on hillsides and riverbanks.
Wu Pu says: according to Shennong, Qibo, and Leigong — bitter, non-toxic; according to Huangdi — acrid, non-toxic. Grows in fields; leaves resemble indigo; gathered in the eleventh month.
The Mingyi says: white rabbits eat it and become immortal; grows on Mount Tai; gathered in the fifth month and at the Beginning of Autumn; dried in the shade.
The Guangya says: Yin Lu and Ma Xian are the same. Tao Hongjing says: the immortal scriptures say white artemisia — white rabbits eat it and become immortal. But today Yin Chen is said to be this, which is probably not correct. Chen Cangqi says: Yin Chen.
It does not die over winter; it grows from the old stalks, hence the name Yin Chen Hao; the character Hao was added later. From this we know the old name was written as Yin Chen without Hao. Also, by the Guangya, Ma Xian is probably the same as Ma Xin Hao.
It belongs to the category of white artemisia.

Shennong Bencao Jing, Volume One

Investigation: The physicians say it grows in Yuzhou; harvested in the fifth month and dried in shade. (Da Guan edition.)

Investigation: Tao Hongjing says people in the east call it Shanjiang ("mountain ginger"); people in the south call it Meicao ("beautiful herb"). The Bencao Yanyi says it is also called in the world Guzihua ("morning glory").

Lancao [Eupatorium/orchid herb]: Flavor is acrid, balanced. Mainly benefits the waterways, kills gu-poison toxins, wards off inauspicious influences; long-term use benefits the qi, lightens the body, prevents aging, and penetrates the spirit-clarity. Another name is Shuixiang ("water fragrance"); grows in ponds and marshes.

The physicians say: grows in greater Wu; harvested in the fourth and fifth months.

Investigation: The Shuo Wen says "lan." The physicians say it is also called lan; it is a fragrant herb. The Guangya says lan is also an herb. The Yi [Classic] says its scent is like lan. Xiang [commentary] says lan is a fragrant herb. The Xiazheng (Summer Ordinances) says: in the fifth month, hao-lan [flourishes]. The Mao Shi (Odes) says: "fragrant jian."

The commentary says: lan is lan. Lu Ji says lan is namely the fragrant herb; its stem and leaves resemble the medicinal herb Zhelan. The Fanzi Jiran says: Greater Lan comes from Hanzhong; the three auxiliary [commanderies'] lan comes from Hedong. Hong [says:]...

Nong: In Bailiang County to the west, Yuan Yangxian's commentary on Li Bai's poetry, citing the Bencao, says: Lancao has green leaves and purple stems; Zhelan — these two things share the name "lancao," one also called Shuixiang ("water fragrance"). The Shuijing (Water Classic) [mentions] Lingling...

In Duliang County, on a small hill to the west, there is lancao growing as Zhelan. Throughout it, lancao grows with green leaves and purple stems; Zhelan resembles mint, lightly fragrant. In Jing, Xiang, and the Ling'nan mountain regions, families cultivate many kinds of it, along with lan.

Generally they are similar in type; Yan Shigu regarded lancao as Zhelan — this is incorrect.

Shechuangzi [Cnidium seed]: Flavor is bitter, balanced. Mainly treats swelling and pain in women's vaginal area, and flaccidity and damp itching of men's genitals; eliminates painful obstruction of the qi, benefits the joints, [treats] epilepsy and malign sores; long-term use lightens the body. Another name is Shemi ("snake rice"); grows in valleys and fields.

Wu Pu says: Shechuang, another name Shezhu ("snake pearl"). Yuguan [edition].

The physicians say: another name Shexiao ("snake millet"), another name Huichuang, another name Siyan ("longing salt"), another name Shengdu ("rope poison"), another name Zaoji ("jujube-thorn"), another name Qiangmi; grows in Linzi; harvested in the fifth month, the fruit dried in shade.

Investigation: The Guangya says: Shexiao, Machuang, Huichuang — these are all the same. The Erya says: Hanchuang, Chuang, Chuang. The Huainanzi, "Fanlun Training" chapter says: what confuses people is Shechuang mistaken for Limei [a fragrant herb].

Note: Tao Hongjing says: I have never heard of anyone who has identified this plant. He suspects it may resemble kudzu. The Tang commentary notes: This herb grows abundantly in the mountain valleys of Jing and Xiang regions, where people commonly call it "white kudzu."

Xu Changqing: Flavor is acrid and warm. It governs ghost-objects, the hundred essences, gu-toxins, epidemic diseases, malevolent and evil qi, warm malaria. Long-term use strengthens and toughens the body and lightens the frame. One name is Gui Du You (Ghost Postal Courier). It grows in mountain valleys.

Wu Pu records: Xu Changqing, also named Shi Xia Chang Qing (Below-the-Stone Long-Green). According to Shennong and Lei Gong: acrid; some say it grows in Longxi and is harvested in the third month.

According to the Guangya: It grows on Tai Mountain and in Longxi, harvested in the third month.

The Mingyi records: It grows on Tai Mountain and in Longxi, harvested in the third month.

Commentary from the Guangya: The names for Xu Changqing and Gui Du You are numerous. The Xu Changqing used commonly today has a root exactly like that of xi xin (Asarum) but shorter and flatter, and the aroma is also similar.

Shi Long Chu: Flavor is bitter and slightly cold. It governs evil qi in the heart and abdomen, difficult urination, strangury and urinary blockage, wind-damp, ghost-possession and malevolent toxins. Long-term use supplements vacuity and emaciation, lightens the body, sharpens hearing and vision, and extends years. Also named Long Xu (Dragon Whisker), Cao Xu Duan (Herb Xu Duan), Long Zhu (Dragon Pearl). Grows in mountain valleys.

Wu Pu records: Dragon [herb] is bitter and non-toxic; Bian Que says acrid and non-toxic; grows in Liangzhou; harvested on the seventh day of the seventh month; applied topically. [This entry is appended under Xu Duan in the Yulan.]

Commentary from the Guangya: It is Long Xu. The Classic of Mountains and Seas states: The Mountain of Mai Chao has an abundance of Long Xiu. Guo Pu comments: It is Long Xu; resembles Wan-rush but more slender; grows among rocks and caves in the mountains; listed in various categories.

Wei Heng: Flavor is bitter and balanced. It governs wind-damp impediment, pain in all the joints, fright epilepsy with protruding tongue, palpitations, thieving wind, rat-fistula, and abscesses. Also named Fei Heng. Grows in rivers and marshes.

Shennong Bencao Jing, Volume One

Du Ruo (Pollia japonica). Flavor: pungent, slightly warm. Governs: counterflow qi in the chest and flanks, warming the center; wind entering the brain-gate causing head swelling and pain, excessive discharge of mucus and tears. Long-term use benefits the essence and qi. One other name [given in the Cang Wen Lei Ju citation]. It grows in rivers and marshes. Brightens the eyes and lightens the body. Also called [one further name].

The Mingyi (Supplementary Physicians) say: also called Du Lian, Bai Qin, Ruo Zhi; grows in Wuling and Yuanqiu. Roots are gathered in the second and eighth months and dried in the sun.

Commentary: The Shuowen says "Ruo Du Ruo is a fragrant herb." The Guangya says it is Chu Heng and also Du Heng. The Western Mountains Classic says: "Above the Emperor of Heaven there is a plant shaped like mallow, smelling like Mi [an aromatic herb], called Du Heng." The Erya says Du Shi Ruo is a fragrant herb; Guo Pu comments it is Du Heng, a fragrant plant. The Chu Ci mentions fragrant Du Ruo growing in Nanjun and Hanzhong. Shen Kuo in the Supplementary Brush Talks says Du Ruo is what is now called Galangal (Gaoliangjiang); later people did not recognize it and separately listed Galangal as a distinct entry. According to the Classic, Du Heng is another name for it, so the Supplementary Physicians' separate entry for Du Heng is incorrect. "Heng" is the standard character; the vulgar form adds the grass radical. Long-term use benefits the person. Also called Zhi Mu. Grows in valleys and gorges.

Sha Shen (Adenophora/Ladybell root). Flavor: bitter, slightly cold. Governs: blood accumulation, fright qi, elimination of cold and heat, supplementing the center and benefiting lung qi. Long-term use benefits the person. Also called Zhi Mu. Grows in valleys and gorges.

Wu Pu says: White Sha Shen is also called Ku Xin, Shi Mei, Hu Xu, Wen Xi; grows in the river valleys of Henei or around the Banyang hills; in the third month it produces mallow-like leaves and white fruit; the root is large and white like a turnip; harvested in the third month. Also called Wen Hu. According to Shennong and the Yellow Emperor, Bian Que: non-toxic. According to Qi Bo: greatly cold. Grows in the river valleys of Henei or around the Banyang hills. In the third month it produces mallow-like leaves, with white fruit; root large and white like a turnip; harvested in the third month. Also called Zhi Qu, Bai Shen, Shi Mei, Wen Xi; grows in Henei and Yuanqiu, Banyang, and the surrounding mountains; harvested in the second month.

The Mingyi say: Also called Ku Xin, Zhi Qu, Hu Xu, Bai Shen, Shi Mei, Wen Xi; grows in Henei and Yuanqiu, Banyang, and surrounding mountains; roots gathered in the second and eighth months and sun-dried.

Commentary: The Guangya says "Ku Shen-xin Sha Shen" — its green husk; Fan Zi Ji Ran says: White Sha Shen from Luoyang is best when white.

Bai Tu Huo (White Hare藿, Marsdenia). Flavor: bitter, balanced. Governs: bites of snakes, vipers, bees, scorpions; dog bites; fox; vegetables; flesh; gu-toxin and parasitic poisoning. Also called Bai Ge. Grows in mountain valleys.

Wu Pu says: Bai Tu Huo is also called Bai Ge Mi Kuan.

名醫曰。生河東。

味苦主胸脅下痛邪氣腹開寒熱陰痿久服輕身益氣耐老益能作補。生川澤無毒。蕭在唐本逕。今增。中

淮木
味苦平主久欬上氣腸中盧蟲女子陰蝕漏下赤白沃。一名百歲城中木。生山谷。無毒。蕭在唐本逕。今增。中

神農本草經 卷一
三七
translation:
Qing Rang (Green Sesame Seedling)
Flavor: sweet, cold. It governs evil qi of the five viscera, wind-cold-damp impediment, benefits qi, supplements brain marrow, strengthens sinews and bones. Long-term use makes the ears and eyes keen and bright, prevents hunger, prevents aging, and extends life. It is the seedling of the giant sesame plant. Grows in river valleys.

Wu Pu says: Qing Rang, also called Dream [Herb]. Shennong [rates it as] bitter; Lei Gong [rates it as] sweet.

The Mingyi says: It grows in the Central Plains.

According to the Baopuzi, chapter on Immortal Medicines: The Filial Piety Classic's援神契states that giant sesame extends the years. It also says giant sesame is another name for sesame (huma). Taking it as food prevents aging, increases tolerance of wind and damp, and supplements debilitation and old age.

Gu Huo: Flavor sweet, warm. Governs severe wind evil qi, damp-impediment cold pain. Long-term use lightens the body, benefits longevity, and increases tolerance of old age. Another name is Dong Kui Zi.

The Mingyi says: It grows in Hedong.

Bieqi: The active pill is in fact wild kudzu. Another name; also called Dong Kui Zi — it is not the winter mallow seed. It treats the body differently [from mallow]. Tao Hongjing says: Prescriptions also have no use for this; something called Gu [active] does exist, however.

The Mingyi says: Also named Biezhi, also named Bieji, also named Luan Lantian. Harvested in the second and eighth months. Tao Hongjing says: Physicians occasionally found uses for it, but in common practice it has now completely fallen out of use. Grows in river marshes; non-toxic.

Qu Cao (Bent Herb)
Flavor: bitter. Governs pain in the chest and flanks, evil qi, abdominal distention, alternating cold and heat, and impotence. Long-term use lightens the body, benefits qi, and increases tolerance of aging. Also able to serve as a supplement. Grows in river marshes; non-toxic.

The Mingyi says: Grows in Hanzhong. Harvested in the fifth month.

According to Tao Hongjing: This herb is no longer used in prescriptions, and no one in common practice recognizes it.

Huai Mu (Locust Tree Wood)
Flavor: bitter, balanced. Governs prolonged coughing with counterflow of qi, intestinal parasites (lu chong), vaginal erosion in women, and flooding-downward discharge of red and white fluid. Another name: Wood from a Hundred-Year-Old City Tree. Grows in mountain valleys; non-toxic.

Shennong Bencao Jing, Volume One

神農本草經
卷一

吳普曰薇銜。一名糜銜。一名承膏。一名無顛。一名承肌。一名無心。覽御
名醫曰。一名承膏。一名無心。一名無顛。
雲實味辛溫主洩利腸癖殺蟲蠱毒去邪惡結氣止痛除熱華主見鬼精物多食令人狂走。
久服輕身通神明生川谷。
吳普曰雲實一名員實。神農辛小溫黃帝鹹。雷公苦葉如廕兩兩相值高四五尺大莖空中。
六月花八月九月實十月采覽御
名醫曰。一名員實。一名天豆。神農生河間。十月采暴乾。
吳普曰王不留行。王不留行。王不留行王主金創止血逐痛出刺除風痹內寒久服輕身耐老能御覽御。作增蓄生山谷。
案鄭樵王不留行。主解宮花日剪百金花葉似花實作房。甘三月八月采。神農苦平歧伯雷公甘。
升廉麻邪氣味甘辛。覺蟲蠱毒。觀本大觀本甘御。一名周升廉。主解百毒殺百蟲老物殃鬼辟溫疾障邪毒蠱久服不天。百觀大觀本物主解鬼。百辟瘧。瘲殺
此癢麻邪氣味用御覺文蟲蠱毒作大觀本甘御。
吳普曰。生益州。二月八月采根日乾。
名醫曰。生廕州神農甘覧。一名周升廉。作大觀本。生山谷甘。＊則本經當有此。有云。今增入。神農本物主鬼解。百辟瘧瘲殺
案廣雅云周廕升廉也。御覽據吳普。有此覧。

三六
translation:
Shennong Bencao Jing (Divine Farmer's Classic of Materia Medica)
Volume One

Wu Pu states: Wei Xian (Viscum/catchfly herb). Also called Mi Xian, Cheng Gao, Wu Dian, Cheng Ji, and Wu Xin. [Referenced in the Imperial览 (encyclopedia).]
The Mingyi (Supplementary Physicians' Records) states: Also called Cheng Gao, Wu Xin, and Wu Dian.

Yun Shi (Cloud Seed / Caesalpinia): Flavor acrid, warm. It governs diarrhea and intestinal flux, kills worms and gu-parasites, expels evil and malign binding qi, stops pain, and eliminates heat. The flowers cause one to see ghost-spirits and, if eaten in excess, cause a person to run about madly.
Long-term use lightens the body and penetrates the spirit-brightness. Grows in river valleys.

Wu Pu states: Yun Shi — also called Yuan Shi. Shennong classifies it as acrid and slightly warm; the Yellow Emperor classifies it as salty; Lei Gong classifies it as bitter. The leaves resemble shade-plants, growing in opposite pairs, the plant reaching four to five feet in height, with a large hollow stem. Flowers in the sixth month; fruit in the eighth and ninth months; harvested in the tenth month. [Imperial encyclopedia reference.] The Mingyi states: Also called Yuan Shi and Tian Dou. According to Shennong it grows in the Hejian region. Harvested in the tenth month and sun-dried.

Wu Pu states: Wang Bu Liu Xing (Vaccaria segetalis / cow soapwort). Wang Bu Liu Xing. The king's [herb that] does not stop for rank. Governs as chief herb for metal-weapon wounds, stops bleeding, drives out pain, expels thorns and splinters, dispels wind-impediment and internal cold. Long-term use lightens the body, builds endurance in old age. [Imperial encyclopedia reference.] Also recorded as Zhu Xu; grows in mountain valleys.

An investigation: Zheng Qiao's [account of] Wang Bu Liu Xing states it governs and resolves palace flower; harvested in the third month; flowers like hundred-gold petals, leaves resembling flowers, fruit forms pods. Sweet; harvested in the third and eighth months. Shennong: bitter, neutral. Qibo and Lei Gong: sweet.

Sheng Lian (Siegesbeckia / St. Paul's wort): The qi of the evil influence, flavor sweet and acrid. Awakens [against] gu-worm toxin. [According to the Da Guan Ben] sweet, [per the] imperial [encyclopedia]. Also called Zhou Sheng Lian. Governs resolving the hundred poisons, killing the hundred worms, destroying old malignant gui-sprites, warding off epidemic illness, impediment disorders, evil toxin and gu-poison; long-term use prevents early death. [Various textual variants noted from the Da Guan Ben editions regarding the main actions against gui, dispelling malaria and convulsions, and killing.]

[Variant notes on the evil-influence qi, sweet and acrid flavor, gu-worm toxin.]

Wu Pu states: Grows in Yizhou. Root harvested in the second and eighth months and sun-dried.
The Mingyi states: Grows in Yinzhou. Shennong: sweet. [Imperial encyclopedia reference.] Also called Zhou Sheng Lian. [Da Guan Ben variant noted.] Grows in mountain valleys, sweet. This passage should properly appear in the Bencao Jing. There is a note: now added. Shennong's [classification]: governs gui, resolves the hundred [poisons], wards off malaria and convulsions, and kills.

An investigation: The Guangya dictionary says: Zhou Yin (廕) — that is, Sheng Lian. The Imperial Encyclopedia draws on Wu Pu. This reference appears there.

神農本草經卷一

三九
translation:
Grain. Pine resin (松脂): flavor bitter, warm; governs festering sores, malignant wounds, head ulcers, white scalp disease, scabies and skin lumps, wind-qi; calms the five viscera; removes heat; long-term use lightens the body, prevents aging, and extends years. Another name: pine paste (松膏); another name: pine fat (松肪). Grows in mountains.

Sophora fruit (槐實): flavor bitter, cold; governs internal evil qi and heat, stops drooling and excess saliva, supplements exhaustion and injury, the five kinds of hemorrhoids, fire wounds, breast lumps in women, and acute pain of the uterus. Grows in level marshes.
Commentary: The Shuowen says: huai (槐) is a tree; sometimes written as jù (窶). Fan Zi Jiran says: pine resin comes from Longxi; pine gum is best.
The Mingyi says: grows on Taishan mountain; harvested in the sixth month.

Commentary: The Shuowen says: huai wood (槐木); also called 橽huai; large-leaved and dark. Guo Pu says: the huai tree with large dark-colored leaves is called 橽; and the Shou-gong huai has leaves that open by day and close at night.
The Mingyi says: grows in Henan.
Ji (璣) says: the huai whose leaves open by day and close at night is called Shou-gong huai (守宮槐).

Wolfberry (枸杞): flavor bitter, cold; governs evil qi and heat in the five viscera, heat in the middle, wasting-thirst, and generalized painful obstruction (bi); long-term use strengthens sinews and bones, lightens the body, prevents aging, and is enduring. Also called: qi root (杞根), earth bone (地骨), gou-ji (枸忌).

Another name: earth supplement (地輔); grows in level marshes.
Wu Pu says: wolfberry is also called lamb's milk (羊乳), dispel-summer (卻暑), immortal's staff (仙人杖), and Queen Mother of the West's staff (西王母杖); grows at Changshan and various hills, slopes and banks; roots collected in winter, leaves in spring and summer.
The Mingyi says: also called lamb's milk (羊乳), dispel-summer (卻暑), immortal's staff (仙人杖), Queen Mother of the West's staff (西王母杖); grows at Changshan and various hills, slopes and banks; roots collected in winter, leaves in spring and summer, and in autumn

the vine-fruit (蔓實) is collected and dried in the shade.
Commentary: The Shuowen says: gou (枸) and ju (橺) are both forms of qi (杞). Lu Ji says: bitter qi, ripens red in autumn; taking it lightens the body and benefits qi. Traditions of Immortals (列仙傳) says: Lu Tong ate the fruit of the lou-lu tree. Bao Pu Zi, chapter on immortal medicines:
The Zhuanzhuan says: ji (杞) is gou-ju (枸橺). Lu Ji says: gou-qi (枸杞). Guangya says: di-jin (地筋) is gou-qi (枸杞). Erya says: gou (枸) is ju (橺). Guo Pu says: this is today's gou-qi (枸杞). Shijing (Mao text) says: the tian-zhi-tu (隼子菟)…

Shennong Bencao Jing, Volume One

神農本草經 卷一

吳普曰淮木神農雷公無毒生晉平陽河東平澤治久欬上氣傷中贏虛補中盆氣寵御

名醫曰一名炭木生太山采無時

案李當之云是樟樹上寄生樹大銜枝在肌肉今人皆以胡桃皮當之非也桐君云生上洛是木皮狀如厚朴色似桂白其理一縱一橫今市人皆削乃以厚朴而無正縱橫理不知此復是何物莫測真假

何者為是也

右草上品七十三種舊七十二種考六芝當為一升廕當白字米穀部誤入青囊唐本退六種姑活屈

草淮木皆當入此

牡桂味辛溫主上氣欬逆結氣喉痹吐吸利關節補中盆氣久服通神輕身不老生山谷

名醫曰生南海

案說文云桂江南木百藥之長桂也南山經云招搖之山多桂郭璞云郭璞云桂葉似枇杷長二尺餘廣數寸今人呼桂皮厚者為木桂及單名桂者是也白花叢生山峯冬夏常青開無雜木爾雅云楥木桂

桂味辛溫主百病養精神和顏色為諸藥先聘通使久服輕身不老面生光華媚好常如童子生山谷

菌桂味辛溫主百病養精神和顏色為諸藥先聘通使久服輕身不老面生光華媚好常如童子生山谷

案楚詞云雜申椒與菌桂兮王逸云荣桂皆香木列仙傳云范蠡好服桂
translation:
Shennong Bencao Jing (Divine Farmer's Classic of Materia Medica), Volume One

Wu Pu says: Huaimu — according to Shennong and Leigong, it is non-toxic; grows in Jinping, Yanghe, and Hedong in level marshes; treats chronic cough, counterflow qi, internal injury, emaciation and deficiency; supplements the center and augments qi. [Imperial notation]

The Mingyi (Renowned Physicians) Record says: also named Tanmu; grows on Taishan; harvested at no fixed season.

According to Li Dangzhi: this is the camphor tree (zhang shu), a parasitic tree growing on it; large branches embed in the flesh. People today all use walnut bark as a substitute, which is wrong. Tong Jun says it grows in Shangluo and resembles tree bark in form like Magnolia bark (houpo), its grain running one vertical and one horizontal. Today's market vendors shave it and use thick Magnolia bark, which lacks the proper vertical-horizontal grain pattern. It is unknown what this substance truly is — its authenticity remains uncertain.

As to which is correct, that remains to be determined.

The above are 73 herbs of the Upper Grade among the Grasses; formerly listed as 72 — examination shows the Six Zhi (mushrooms) should count as one, rising into the Shade category (yin). The "white character" items from the Grain section were mistakenly placed in Qingnang; the Tang edition withdrew six items including Guhuo and Ququ.

Both Huaimu and all grasses above should be entered here.

Mugui (male cinnamon): flavor pungent, warm; governs counterflow qi and cough, binding qi, throat obstruction, difficult breathing, benefits the joints, supplements the center and augments qi; long-term use penetrates the spirit, lightens the body, and prevents aging; grows in mountain valleys.

The Mingyi Record says: grows in Nanhai.

According to the Shuowen: "Gui is a tree of the Jiangnan region, the chief of all medicines." The Nanshan Jing says: "Mount Zhaoyao has much gui." Guo Pu says: "Gui leaves resemble loquat leaves, over two feet long and several cun wide; people today call thick-barked specimens Mugui or simply Gui — this is that plant." It has white flowers growing in clusters on mountain peaks, evergreen in winter and summer, with no mixed trees nearby. The Erya says: "Yuan is Mugui."

Gui (cinnamon): flavor pungent, warm; governs the hundred diseases, nourishes essence and spirit, harmonizes complexion, acts as a herald leading all medicines, promotes circulation; long-term use lightens the body, prevents aging, makes the face glow with radiance and beauty, keeping one like a child; grows in mountain valleys.

Jungui (tube cinnamon): flavor pungent, warm; governs the hundred diseases, nourishes essence and spirit, harmonizes complexion, acts as a herald leading all medicines, promotes circulation; long-term use lightens the body, prevents aging, makes the face glow with radiance and beauty, keeping one like a child; grows in mountain valleys.

According to the Chuci: "Mixed with Shenjiao pepper and Jungui cinnamon" — Wang Yi comments: Rong and Gui are both fragrant trees. The Liexian Zhuan says: Fan Li loved taking cinnamon.

text: 蘯萏郭璞云今云刺榆毛詩云東門之枌傳云枌白榆也又山有蕤傳云樞榛也陸璣云其鍼刺如柘其葉如榆瀹為茹美滑如白榆之類有十種葉皆相似皮及木理異矣酸棗味酸平主心腹寒熱邪結氣聚四肢酸疼濕痹久服安五藏輕身延年生川澤案說文云河東八月采實陰乾四十日成名醫曰生漢中及永昌壁木味苦寒主五藏腸胃中結熱黃疸腸痔止泄利女子漏下赤白陰陽蝕創一名檀桓生山谷是也案說文云棘酸棗也爾雅云棘小棗所謂酸棗郭璞云味小實酢孟子云養其棘棘趙岐云棘小棘乾漆味辛溫無毒主絕傷補中續筋骨填髓腦安五藏五緩六急風寒濕痹生漆去長蟲久服輕身耐老案說文云棗棘之屬也案醫曰生漢中及永昌名醫曰生漢中生川谷案說文云榤棄木也司馬相如賦有蕖張揖云蕖木可染者顏師古云蕖黃蔆也五加皮味辛溫主心腹疝氣腹痛益氣療躄小兒不能行疽創陰蝕一名豺漆漆林為泰林杜子春云當為漆林案說文云泰木汁可以鬆物象形泰如水滴而下以漆為漆水字周禮載師云漆林之征鄉元云故書神農本草經卷一四一
translation:
Dang Ling: Guo Pu says that what is now called ci yu (thorny elm) is what the Ode "East Gate" calls fen, and the commentary explains that fen is the white elm. Also, the "Mountains have rui" commentary says that the shu is a hazel. Lu Ji says its thorns are like those of the zhe tree, its leaves resemble elm, and when boiled as a vegetable it is smooth and pleasant like white elm. There are about ten varieties, all with similar leaves, but differing in bark and grain of wood.

Sour Jujube (Ziziphus spinosa): flavor sour, nature balanced. It governs cold and heat in the chest and abdomen, pathogenic binding of qi, accumulation in the four limbs, aching and soreness, and damp bi-obstruction. Taken long-term, it calms the five viscera, lightens the body, and extends one's years. It grows in river marshes. Commentary from the Shuowen: "In Hedong it is harvested in the eighth month, dried in the shade for forty days." The Mingyi says it grows in Hanzhong and Yongchang.

Wall-wood (Bi mu): flavor bitter, nature cold. It governs heat binding in the five viscera and intestines and stomach, jaundice, intestinal hemorrhoids; it stops diarrhea, and women's flooding downward with red or white discharge, and erosive sores of the yin parts. Another name: tan huan. Grows in mountain valleys. Commentary: the Shuowen says棘 is the sour jujube. The Erya says棘 is the small jujube, which is what is called sour jujube. Guo Pu says the fruit is small and tart. Mencius says "nurture its棘"; Zhao Qi explains棘as the small jujube.

Dried Lacquer (Gan qi): flavor acrid, warm, non-toxic. It governs severed injuries, tonifies the center, reconnects sinews and bones, fills marrow and brain, calms the five viscera, addresses the five slackenings and six urgencies, and wind-cold-damp bi-obstruction. Fresh lacquer eliminates long worms. Taken long-term it lightens the body and resists aging. Commentary from the Shuowen: the zao and ji belong to the same category. The Mingyi says it grows in Hanzhong. It grows in river valleys. Commentary from the Shuowen: jie is a wood used to make arrows. Sima Xiangru's rhapsody mentions qu; Zhang Yi explains qu as a wood used for dyeing; Yan Shigu says qu is the yellow ling plant.

Five-Bark Spurge-Olive (Wu jia pi): flavor acrid, warm. It governs shan qi and abdominal pain in the chest and abdomen, boosts qi, treats paralysis and inability of children to walk, abscesses, sores, and erosion of the yin parts. Another name: chai qi. Lacquer-forest is called tai-forest; Du Zichun says it should be written "lacquer-forest." The Shuowen says: the juice of the tai tree can be used to coat objects; its character is pictographic, showing the juice dripping down; the character for lacquer uses this as the water signifier. The Rites of Zhou, chapter on the Land Overseer, mentions the tax on lacquer groves; Yuan (Zheng Zhong) says the older text reads thus.

Shennong Bencao Jing, Volume One — page 41

text:
神農本草經卷一

柏實味甘平。主驚悸安五藏盆氣除濕痹久服令人悅澤美色耳目聰明不飢不老輕身延年生山谷。
云象柴。一名托盧是也。或名仙人杖。或云西王母杖。或名天門精。或名卻老。或名地骨。或名枸杞也。
案說文云。柏鶉也廣雅云栝柏葉尤良田四時各依方面朵陰乾。礼記曰以栩范子計然云柏脂出三輔上。
名醫曰生太山柏葉尤良田四時各依方面朵陰乾。

伏苓味甘平。主胸脅逆氣憂恚驚邪恐悸心下結痛寒熱煩滿欬逆口焦舌乾利小便久服安魂養神。不飢延年。一名伏菟。御覽寬氣御覽作。憂志驚邪。伏神伏案。元本云黑字。其有生山谷。
吴普曰茯苓通神桐君甘無毒或生茂州大松根下入地三丈一尺二月七日采御覽寬御。
名醫曰其有抱根者名茯神生太山大松下二月八月采陰乾。
案廣雅云茯苓也范子計然云茯苓出嵩高三輔列仙傳云昌容采茯苓餌而食之史記褚先生。
云傳曰淮南子說林訓云伏苓掘兔絲死所謂舊作茯靈者在兔絲之下狀似飛鳥之形伏靈者千歲松根也食之不死。

榆皮味甘平。主大小便不通利水道除邪氣久服輕身不飢。其實尤良一名零榆生山谷。
名醫曰生穎川三月采皮取白暴乾八月采實。

translation:
Shennong Bencao Jing, Volume One

Cypress Seed (Bai Shi): Flavor sweet, nature balanced. Governs fright palpitations; calms the five viscera; supplements qi; eliminates dampness-impediment. Long-term use makes a person radiant with beautiful complexion, keen of ear and eye, free from hunger, resistant to aging, with a light body and prolonged years. Grows in mountain valleys.
[Commentary]: It resembles the appearance of firewood. One name is "Tuolu" — that is this herb. Also called "Immortal's Staff," or "Queen Mother of the West's Staff," or "Heavenly Gate Essence," or "Repel-Old," or "Earth Bone," or "Wolfberry."
The Shuowen says: bai is the quail. The Guangya says: "kuo-bai." The Bai leaves are especially good; harvest at all four seasons according to the cardinal directions, dry in shade. The Liji refers to xu. Fan Zi Jiran says cypress resin comes from the Three Adjuncts (Sanfu) region.
The Mingyi says: grows on Mount Tai; the cypress leaves are especially good; harvest at all four seasons according to the cardinal directions, dry in shade.

Poria (Fu Ling): Flavor sweet, nature balanced. Governs counterflow qi in the chest and flanks; anxiety, fright, and malign influences; fearful palpitations; binding pain below the heart; alternating cold and heat; vexation and fullness; coughing with counterflow; parched mouth and dry tongue; promotes urination. Long-term use calms the ethereal soul, nourishes the spirit, eliminates hunger, and prolongs years. Another name is "Fu Tu."
Wu Pu says: Poria calms the spirit. Tong Jun says: sweet, non-toxic; or grows at Mao Prefecture, from under large pine roots going three zhang one chi into the ground; harvested on the seventh day of the second month.
The Mingyi says: the kind that clasps the root is called Fu Shen; grows on Mount Tai under large pines; harvested in the second and eighth months; dried in shade.
The Guangya says: it is Fu Ling. Fan Zi Jiran says poria comes from Songgao in the Three Adjuncts region. The Liexian Zhuan says Chang Rong gathered poria and ate it. The Shiji (Chu Sheng commentary) and the Huainanzi Shulin Xun say: poria forms where dodder withers and dies; what was called "Fu Ling" lies beneath the dodder, shaped like a flying bird; "Fu Ling" is a thousand-year-old pine root; eating it prevents death.

Elm Bark (Yu Pi): Flavor sweet, nature balanced. Governs obstruction of urination and defecation; promotes water pathways; eliminates evil qi. Long-term use lightens the body and eliminates hunger. Its fruit is especially good. Another name is "Zero Elm." Grows in mountain valleys.
The Mingyi says: grows in Yingchuan; bark harvested in the third month, the white part taken and sun-dried; fruit harvested in the eighth month.
The Shuowen says: "yu" refers to the white-powder elm. The Guangya says: kuo elm and geng elm. The Erya says: elm, white-powder. Guo Pu says: the powder elm first grows leaves, then bears pods; the bark is white in color; also…

夏常青末嘗凋落若有節攝故以名焉陳藏器云冬青也。枇其樹如栲槳器。藥說文云槇劂木也東山經云太山上多槇木郭璞云女槇也葉冬不凋毛詩云南山有杞陸璣云木。一名狗骨理白滑其子為木蚤子可合藥司馬相如賦有女貞師古日女貞樹冬。

女貞實味苦平生武陵立多采。名醫曰生武陵立多采。

藥廣雅云杜仲曼榆也博物志云杜仲皮中有絲折之則見。名醫曰杜仲。一名思仲。一名木棉生上黨漢中。二月五月六月九月采皮。

吳普曰杜仲。一名思仲。一名木棉。一名思仙。御覽。

杜仲味辛平主要脊痛補中益精氣堅筋骨強志除陰下痒澼小便餘澼久服輕身耐老。一名思仙生山谷。

名醫曰。一名鳶。寄宏農桑樹上三月三日采葉陰乾。藥說文云鳶寄生也詩曰鳶與女蘿或作橘廣雅云宛童寄生也。又寄屏寄生也中山經云龍山上多寫木宛童子郭璞云寄生樹。一名蔦毛詩云鳶與女蘿傳云鳶寄生也陸。璣云寫木寄生也寓木郭璞云寓童也如覆盆子赤黑甜美。

Magnolia bark: flavor bitter, cold. Governs great heat in the body when it is in the skin; removes facial heat, red pimples, rosacea from wine, malign wind, epilepsy, itching below the genitals, and clears the ears and eyes. One name: Lin Lan. Grows in river valleys.

It stays green throughout summer and has never been known to wither and fall; it appears to have joints and sections, hence its name. Chen Cangqi says it is the winter-green. The loquat tree resembles the kào [a type of oak]; used for vessels. The Shuowen says zhēn is a kind of tree; the Eastern Mountain Classic says that Mount Tai has many zhēn trees; Guo Pu says it is the female zhēn, whose leaves do not fall in winter; the Mao Odes say the southern mountains have Qi; Lu Ji says it is a tree. One name: Dog Bone — the grain is white and smooth; its seeds are like wooden fleas and can be combined into medicine. Sima Xiangru's rhapsody mentions the female zhēn; Gu says the female zhēn tree in winter [continues similarly].

Female Zhēn fruit: flavor bitter, balanced. Grows in Wuling; gather abundantly.
The Mingyi ji says: grows in Wuling; gather abundantly.

The Guangya says Du Zhong is also called Màn Yú; the Bowu Zhi says the bark of Du Zhong has silk-like threads inside that become visible when broken.
The Mingyi ji says: Du Zhong. One name: Si Zhong. One name: Mu Mian. Grows in Shangdang and Hanzhong. Gather the bark in the second, fifth, sixth, and ninth months.

Wu Pu says: Du Zhong. One name: Si Zhong. One name: Mu Mian. One name: Si Xian. [Source: Yulan.]

Du Zhong: flavor acrid, balanced. Governs pain in the lumbar spine; supplements the center; augments essence and qi; strengthens sinews and bones; fortifies the will; eliminates itching below the genitals, dribbling urination, and urinary residue. Long-term use lightens the body and resists aging. One name: Si Xian. Grows in mountain valleys.

The Mingyi ji says: one name Yuan [kite]. A parasite growing on mulberry trees in Hongnong; gather leaves on the third day of the third month and dry in the shade. The Shuowen says Yuan is a parasitic plant; the Odes say Yuan and female luo [lichen], or written as Jú; the Guangya says Wǎn Tóng is a parasitic plant. Also: Ji Ping and Ji Sheng [both meaning "parasitic growth"]. The Central Mountain Classic says the Dragon Mountain has many Xiě trees and Wǎn Tóng children; Guo Pu says it is the tree parasite, one name Niǎo; the Mao Odes say Yuan and female luo; the tradition says Yuan is a parasitic plant; Lu Ji says Xiě wood is a parasitic plant; also Yù Mù [lodging wood]; Guo Pu says Yù Tóng; it resembles the raspberry — red, black, sweet, and delicious.

translation:
Shennong Bencao Jing, Volume One

The Mingyi (Supplementary Physicians' Records) states: It is also known as Mujie (Stem Knot). It grows in Hanzhong and Wanju. The flowers are gathered in the fifth and tenth months; the roots are gathered in the tenth month and dried in the shade.

Examining the Daguan Bencao, it quotes the Donghuan Zhenren Yuan Shi Jing (Scripture of the Immortal Yuan Shi of East Florescence), which says: "I have climbed Mount Puwu and, tired of the fragrant herbs of gold and jade, I have rested in the correct way — this is the Five-加 (wu jia) plant." Lu Ding Gong's mother took Five-加 wine alone and thereby avoided death.

Manjing Shi (Vitex fruit): flavor bitter, slightly cold. It governs cold-heat painful obstruction in the spaces between sinews and bones, brightens the eyes, strengthens the teeth, benefits the nine orifices, expels white worms. Long-term use lightens the body and makes one resistant to aging. The fruit of small Vitex is equivalent. It grows in mountain valleys.

The Mingyi states: It grows on the southern slopes of Yangku in Henan, or around the high banks of Ping Shou Township, and in open fields. The fruit is gathered in the eighth and ninth months and dried in the shade.

Examining the Guangya: it says Mujing (male Vitex) and Manjing (trailing Vitex) are the same. The Guangzhi says: the Chu region calls it Jing; Mujing and Manjing are the same. Because the pronunciations of mu (牡) and man (蔓) are close, the Bencao Jing does not separately list the provenance of Manjing but incorporates it under Mujing, noting that it governs the five viscera, bodily cold-wind, head and brain pain, and beautifies the face; taken internally it descends qi, lightens the body, brightens the eyes, and increases longevity and resistance to aging. Another name is Xin Ke (per imperial citation, written as Kuan); another name is Hou Tao.

Xinyi (Magnolia bud): flavor acrid, warm. It governs the five viscera, bodily cold-wind, head and brain pain, and beautifies the face. Taken internally it descends qi, lightens the body, brightens the eyes, and increases longevity and resistance to aging. Another name is Xin Shen; another name is Hou Tao. It grows in river valleys.

Another name is Fang Mu. It grows in river valleys.

Examining the Han Shu: Yang Xiong's rhapsody says "listing Xinxiong among the thickets"; Shi Gu's commentary says Xinxiong is Xinyi. Tao Hongjing says: when young the bud is acrid and fragrant, which is what離駒 called Xinyi; Chen Cangqi records this.

Ma Xiang's commentary on Yang Xiong's rhapsody says "listing Xinxiong to flow as Yi"; the Han Shu commentary says Liuyi is the same as Xinyi (new-fresh); Xinxiong is Xinyi. Tao Hongjing says: when young its qi is acrid and fragrant, which is what 離駒 called Xinyi; Chen Cangqi records this.

It is said: when it first sprouts it resembles a writing brush; its flowers come earliest of all. Southerners call it Yingchun (Welcoming Spring); Tang people named it Yurui (Jade Pistil) and also Yulan (Jade Orchid).

Sang Shang Ji Sheng (Loranthus / Mistletoe on Mulberry): flavor bitter, balanced. It governs lumbar pain, stiffness of the back in children, carbuncles and swellings; it stabilizes the fetus, fills out the skin and flesh, strengthens the hair and teeth, promotes growth of beard and eyebrows. Its fruit brightens the eyes, lightens the body, and opens the spirit. Another name is Ji Xie; another name is Yu Mu; another name is Wan Tong. It grows in river valleys.

案說文云。髮根也。髲髢也。髢鬄也。或作髢毛詩云。不屑髢也。鬠云。髮鬄也。儀禮云。主婦被錫。注云。被錫。
讀為髲髢。古者或剃賤者刑者之髮。或童男髮。本經不忍取人髮用之。故用剃餘也。方家至用天靈蓋害及枯骨卒不
能治病。古人所無矣。
髮髮當是剃刑人髮。或童男髮据漢人說。是童男髮。李當之云。為飾。因名髲髢為。

右人一種舊同。

龍骨味甘平。主心腹鬼注精物老魅逆洩利膿血。女子漏下。癥瘕堅結。小兒熱氣驚癇。主小兒大人
驚癇疾狂走。心下結氣不能喘息。諸癰殺精物。久服輕身通神明延年生山谷。
吳普曰。龍骨生晉地山谷陰大水所過處。是龍死骨也。青白者善。十二月采或無時。龍骨畏乾漆蜀椒。
理石龍齒神農李氏大寒治驚癇。久服輕身。御節大觀本節文。
名醫曰。龍齒生晉地及太山巖水岸土穴中死龍處。采無時。
案范子計然云。龍骨生河東。
廚香味辛溫。然云主碎惡氣殺鬼精物。溫瘧盅毒。癇痓去三蟲。久服除邪不夢寤厭寐生川谷。
名醫曰。生中臺及盆州雍州山中春風取之生者益良。

牛黃味苦平。主驚癇寒熱熱盛狂痓。除邪逐鬼。生平澤。

translation:
The Shuowen Jiezi says: "Fa" means the root of hair; "bi" means a hairpiece; "di" and "ti" are the same; or written as "di." The Book of Odes says: "Not worth wearing a hairpiece." Guan says: "Fa-ti is a hairpiece." The Book of Etiquette and Ceremony says: "The mistress of the house wears a xi (hairpiece)." The commentary says: "Being given a xi" is read as "bi-di" (a hairpiece). In ancient times, the hair of condemned criminals or those subjected to punishment was shaved off, or the hair of young boys was used. This Classic (Bencao Jing) would not tolerate using people's hair directly, so it used the trimmings left over from shaving. Some physicians have gone so far as to use the tianling gai (skull cap) to harmful effect, and even dried bones — none of this was done by the ancients.
Bi-fa (hairpiece) should be the shaved hair of a punished criminal, or the hair of a young boy according to Han dynasty scholars. It is the hair of a young boy. Li Dangzhi says it was used as an adornment, hence the name bi-di.

The above is one kind, same as the old classification.

Dragon Bone: flavor sweet, neutral. Primarily treats abdominal ghost-infestations, spirit possession, old demon influences, diarrhea, pus and blood in stool, vaginal discharge in women, hardened concretions and accumulations, and childhood heat with convulsions. Also treats convulsions and mania in both children and adults, qi binding below the heart causing inability to breathe, various abscesses, and kills spirit entities. Long-term use lightens the body, opens the spirit-mind, and extends life. Found in mountain valleys.
Wu Pu says: Dragon Bone is found in Jinди in mountain valleys near large rivers where water flows past. It is the bone of a dead dragon. The blue-white ones are best. Collected in the twelfth month or at any time. Dragon Bone fears dried lacquer and Sichuan pepper.
Lishi and Dragon Tooth: According to Shennong and Li's classification, greatly cold, treats convulsions and epilepsy; long-term use lightens the body. [See Imperial Daguan edition, this section.]
The Mingyi says: Dragon Tooth is found in Jindi and in the rocky waterside caves of Taishan where dragons have died. Collected at any time.
Note: The Fanzi Jiran says Dragon Bone comes from Hedong.

Musk (Chuixiang): flavor pungent, warm. Said to primarily break up foul qi, kill ghost-spirit entities, treat warm-malaria, gu-toxin (parasitic venom), epilepsy and tetanic spasm, and expel three worms. Long-term use eliminates evil influences and prevents oppressive nightmares. Found in mountain valleys.
The Mingyi says: Grows in Zhongtai and in Pengzhou and Yongzhou mountain regions; collected in spring when alive; the living substance is best.
Note: The Shuowen says: Musk deer resembles a small roe deer, with fragrant glands at the navel; it is a black-colored musk deer. The Erya quotes: "Chui" — the father is "chui," the feet are "chui." Guo Pu says: the feet resemble a musk deer and it has fragrance.

Cattle Gallstone (Niuhuang): flavor bitter, neutral. Primarily treats convulsions with chills and fever, high fever with mania and tetanic spasm. Eliminates evil and expels ghosts. Found in marshy lowlands.

名醫曰。一名杜蘭皮似桂而香生零陵及太山。十二月采皮陰乾。

案廣雅云木欄桂欄也劉逵注蜀都賦云木蘭大樹也葉似長生冬夏榮常以冬華其實如小柿甘美。

名醫曰生函谷及巴西。

草作熬今椒核是也。

橘柚味辛溫主胸中痰熱逆氣利水穀久服去臭下氣通神。一名橘皮生川谷。鼸非。果部

案說文云橘果出江南。柚子似橙而酢爾雅云吳楚之國有木焉其名為櫾碧樹而冬生實丹而味酸食其皮汁。偶

孔大曰橘小曰柚條問篇云吳楚之國有木為欒。似橙實酢。生江南禹貢云厥包橘柚。

translation:
Shennong Bencao Jing, Volume One

The Physicians' Records state: It is also called Du Lan; its bark resembles cinnamon and is fragrant; it grows in Lingling and Mount Tai. The bark is harvested in the twelfth month and dried in the shade.

Examining the Guangya: Mulan and Guilan are the same. Liu Kui's commentary on the Rhapsody of Shu Capital states that Mulan is a large tree whose leaves resemble those of evergreens; it blooms in winter and its fruit is like a small persimmon, sweet and delicious.

Southern people use it as plum; its bark can be eaten. Yan Shigu's commentary on the Han History states: the bark resembles roots in appearance and is fragrant, and can be used as a cosmetic preparation.

Huike: Flavor sweet, warm. Governs evil qi in the heart and abdomen, brightens the eyes, relieves red painful eyes with tearing. Long-term use lightens the body and augments qi so one does not feel hunger. Grows in river valleys. Long-term use prevents hunger.

Wu Pu states: Boke, also named Tu Shen. According to Shennong and Lei Gong: sweet, balanced, non-toxic. Grows in ponds and marshes; harvested in the eighth month. Supplements the center, strengthens the will, brightens the eyes. Grows in river valleys.

The Physicians' Records state: grows in Hangu and Baxi.

Examining the Shuowen: Jiao refers to white pepper; the Erya states jiao is a small shrub growing in clusters, with thorns; its fruit resembles an eardrop, purple-red, and can be spat out. The Yiqie Jing Yinyi states: the herbal classic renders it as ao; today's pepper seeds are precisely this.

Ju You (Citrus/Pomelo): Flavor acrid, warm. Governs phlegm-heat in the chest, counterflow qi; promotes movement of water and grain. Long-term use eliminates foul odors, descends qi, and opens the spirit. Also named Ju Pi (orange peel). Grows in river valleys. [Note: belongs to the Fruit category.]

Examining the Shuowen: Ju is a fruit from south of the Yangtze. You resembles the orange but is sour. The Erya states: in the states of Wu and Chu there is a tree called Yuan, with green bark, bearing fruit in winter; the fruit is red and the flavor is sour; one eats the skin and juice.

Kong [commentary]: the large is called Ju, the small is called You. The Tiaowenpian states that in Wu and Chu there is a tree called Luan, resembling the orange, sour-fruited, growing in Jiangnan. The Yugong states: their tribute included oranges and pomelos.

Those already accustomed to it lose their aversion to the illness. Sima Xiangru's rhapsody mentions oranges and pomelos. Zhang Yi states: You is the same as the orange (cheng), resembling the Ju but larger, sour in flavor, with thick skin.

The above Wood Upper-Grade items number twenty, of which nineteen are counted; the Ju You of the Fruit section should be included here.

Hair and Whiskers: Flavor bitter, warm. Governs the five types of urinary blockage, blockage of the passages, promotes urination and water pathways. Treats convulsions in children and tetanic stiffness in adults; spontaneously returns to and transforms through the spirit.

丹雄雞。味甘微溫。主女人崩中漏下。赤白沃。補虛溫中。止血通神。殺毒辟不祥。頭主殺鬼。東門上者尤良。
肋主耳聾。腸主遺溺胜裹黃皮主溲利尿。白蠱肥脂。黑雌雞。主風寒濕痹五緩六急安胎。翮
羽主下血閉。雌子主作瑯御。除熱火瘡癰疽可作虎魄神物。雞白蠱肥脂生平澤。

雁
肋味甘平。主風攣拘急偏枯氣不通利。久服益氣不飢輕身耐老。一名鶩肪。生池澤。

據說文云。今江東呼鵝又舒鳧也。鳧方言云雁自關而東謂之鴿鵝南楚之外謂之鵁或謂之倉鴈。禮記曰出如舒鵝。
鷲肋條又別有白鴨鵝條反疑此為鴻雁字無鵝字。鵝字即雁之急音此雁肋即鵝鴨脂也當作鶩字名醫不曉別出
