四七
translation:
Red Rooster: Flavor sweet, slightly warm. Governs women's flooding and spotting, red and white vaginal discharge. Supplements deficiency, warms the center, stops bleeding, connects the spirit, kills toxins, and wards off inauspiciousness. The head governs killing demons. Those from the east gate are especially good.
The ribs govern deafness. The intestines govern enuresis. The crop lining governs diuresis. The white fat of the black hen governs wind-cold-damp impediment, the five slackenings and six urgencies, and stabilizes the fetus. The wing feathers govern stopping bleeding and blockage. The hen governs making amber-like objects. Removes heat, fire sores, and carbuncles; can be made into amber-like spirit objects. The white fat of the chicken grows in level marshes.

Wu Pu says: The red hen's egg can be made into amber-like objects.
The Mingyi says: It is produced in Joseon (Korea).
Regarding the Shuowen: "A domestic animal that knows the time." The character in the Jing is written as 雞. The ribs, intestines, large and small intestines, thigh flesh, the bird's gizzard, its droppings, its feathers and long feathers are all noted.

Wild Goose (Yan):
The fat, flavor sweet, balanced. Governs wind-induced contracture, clenching and acute one-sided withering, qi obstruction and poor circulation. Long-term use benefits qi, prevents hunger, lightens the body, and promotes longevity. Another name is Mu Fang (duck fat). Grows in pools and marshes.
Wu Pu says: Mu Fang — Shennong, Qibo, and Leigong say flavor sweet, non-toxic. Current editions should have the two characters "Mu Fang."
The Mingyi says: Produced in Jiangnan. Harvested at no fixed season.
Chong's Shuowen commentary says: Mu (鶩) is the Jiangnan goose. Guangya says: Goose is Mu; also called Jiaojing. Guo Pu says: Goose is also called Cang Yan.
According to the Shuowen: Today in Jiangdong, the domestic goose is also called Shu Fu (domesticated wild duck). The Fangyan says: East of the passes, geese are called Ge-e; in the outer regions of southern Chu, they are called Jiao or Cang Yan. The Liji says they come out like domesticated geese.
The entry for Jiu's fat also separately lists white duck and goose entries, which raises doubts that this refers to the wild goose. The character e (鵝) has no duck character; the character yan used for goose is the hurried pronunciation of yan. Therefore this goose fat entry is duck and goose fat, and should be written with the character Mu (鶩); the Mingyi did not understand this and listed it separately.

The above are two kinds of birds in the superior category, same as the old edition.

Shennong Bencao Jing, Volume 1

四六
translation:
Shennong Bencao Jing, Volume One

Wu Pu says: Ox Gallstone (Niu Huang) is bitter in flavor and non-toxic. When an ox is entering or leaving [a place] and moaning (the Yulan edition writes "those who have it"), at night it emits light (the Yulan edition writes "at night one can see its light"), and the ox runs about. The character "yu" is present. Inside the horn the ox dies; it enters the gallbladder, resembling a chicken egg yolk. [This is referenced in] the Hou Han Shu, in the biography of Yan Du, as a method.

The Mingyi says: It is produced in Jin region; it is obtained from oxen. Dry it in the shade for one hundred days; do not let it be exposed to sunlight or moonlight when processing.

Bear Fat (Xiong Zhi) is sweet and slightly cold in flavor. It governs wind impediment with loss of sensation, muscle spasms, accumulations and gatherings in the five viscera and abdomen, cold and heat, emaciation, head sores, white baldness, facial blotches and pustules. Long-term use strengthens the will, prevents hunger, lightens the body. It grows in mountain valleys.

The Mingyi says: It is produced in Yong Prefecture; collected in the eleventh month.

Commentary: Shuowen says that the bear is a beast resembling a pig that lives in the mountains and hibernates in winter.

White Glue (Bai Jiao) is sweet and balanced in flavor. It governs internal injury, extreme fatigue, pain in the lumbar region, emaciation, supplements the middle and boosts qi, closes the blood in women with no children, stops pain, calms the fetus. Long-term use lightens the body and prolongs life. Another name is Deer Antler Glue (Lu Jiao Jiao).

The Mingyi says: It is produced in Yun Zhong. Yun refers to the offering; it uses the hide or the antler.

Commentary: Shuowen says the glue from the courtyard is blue-white; ox glue when heated turns red. Zheng says: the so-called offering uses either the hide or the antler.

Glue

Donkey-hide Glue (E Jiao) is sweet and balanced in flavor. It governs collapse within the heart and abdomen, extreme fatigue with shivering as in malaria, pain in the lumbar and abdomen, aching of the four limbs, and bleeding in women. It calms the fetus. Long-term use lightens the body and boosts qi. Another name is Fu Zhi.

The Mingyi says: It is produced in Dongping Prefecture, made from the hide of the Lou ox, and comes from Dong'a.

Commentary: The two glues are not listed separately in the Bencao Jing as to their origins. It is suspected that the original Bencao Jing simply recorded "Glue," and that the Mingyi added the characters "White" and "E (Donkey-hide)" to separate them into two entries.

The above are six items from the upper grade of the Beasts category, same as the old edition.

四九
translation:
The Eminent Physicians say: It grows in Wudu, in beehives among wood and stones.
A note from the Xijing Zaji (Miscellanies of the Western Capital) states that the King of Nanyue presented Emperor Gaozu with two hundred pieces of beeswax. The Yupian (Jade Chapters dictionary) says: "Wax is beeswax." Tao Hongjing says: White wax is produced within honey, hence it is called beeswax. The Shuowen (Explaining Writing) has no character for "la" (wax). Zhang You notes that "wei" is a separate character from "la," and that the original form was not "fen"; it has been amended here to "la" following that authority.

Oyster (Muli). Flavor: salty, balanced. Main uses: cold damage with alternating chills and fever, malarial shivers, fright, rage and anger; removes muscle stiffness and flaccidity, scrofulous sores; women's vaginal discharge, red and white. Long-term use strengthens the bones and joints, eliminates pathogenic qi, and prolongs life.
Named Muli; grows in ponds and marshes.

A note from the Shuowen: The li is a type of clam, resembling the li but somewhat larger, produced in the sea; people today eat them. Some sources say it is one of three kinds all born in the sea, belonging to the clam family, formed from thousand-year-old clams. The Qin [dynasty sources also mention this].
The Eminent Physicians say: Also called Muha (male clam); grows in the Eastern Sea; harvested at any season.

Tortoise Shell (Guijia). Flavor: salty, balanced. Main uses: flooding discharge of red and white fluids, breaking up masses and concretions, scabies and sores, the five hemorrhoids, genital erosion, damp impediment, heaviness and weakness of the four limbs, unclosed fontanelle in infants. Long-term use lightens the body and prevents hunger. Also called Divine House (Shenwu).
Grows in ponds and marshes.
The Eminent Physicians say: Grows in the Southern Sea and in lake waters; harvested at any season.
A note from the Guangya (Expanded Elegantiae): "Jie gui" means tortoise. Gao You's annotation to the Huainan [zi] says: "Gui ke" and "gui jia" are both terms for the tortoise shell.

Mantis Egg-case (Sangpiaoxiao). Flavor: salty, balanced. Main uses: internal injury, hernia and concretions, genital flaccidity, benefits essence and enables conception in women, blood occlusion, pain in the waist, the five urinary stranguries, promotes urination. Also called Shipi; grows on mulberry branches.
[Pertaining to the swallow section.]
Wu Pu says: The entry for Sangpiaoxiao — a second name is missing here — Shipi is omitted. Also called Haijiao. Also called Zhishen. According to Shennong: salty, non-toxic. [Verified from the Lan and Yu collections.]

Shennong Bencao Jing, Volume One

石蜜味甘平主心腹邪氣諸驚癇痓安五藏諸不足益氣補中止痛解毒除衆病和百藥久服強志輕身。
不飢不老一名石飴生山谷

吳普曰石蜜神農雷公甘氣平生河源或河梁生御覽又一引云武都山谷。
案醫曰生武都河源及諸山石中色白如膏者良。
案說文云蠲甘飴也一曰蜎子或作蜜中山經云平逢之山多沙石實惟蜂蜜之廬郭璞云蜜赤蜂。
名西京雜記云南越王獻高帝石蜜五斛玉篇云蠲蠢甘飴也蘇恭云當去石字。

氣蜂子味甘平主癰腫風頭除蠱毒補虛羸傷中久服令人光澤好顏色不老大黃蜂子主心腹復滿痛輕身益。
名士蜂子一名蛅蟖生山谷。
案醫曰生武都。
案說文云蠭飛蟲螫人者古文作蠦廣雅云蠭。
士蠮螉也又上蠭蠮螉也爾雅云士蠭郭璞云今江南。

大蠮在地中作房者為士蠮喙咬其子禮記郎馬蠮今荊巴聞呼為蠣又木蠮郭璞云似士蠮而小在樹上作孔燕趙之間謂之蠮螉其小。
房江東亦呼為木蠮方言云蠮燕趙之間謂之蠭冠鄭云范則為蠮也又木蠮郭璞云今黑蠮穿竹木作孔亦有蜜者或呼笛師按蠮。

蜜蟻味甘徵溫主下利膿血補中續絕傷金創益氣不飢耐老生山谷。
名為范者聲相近者司馬相如賦以泥為楓左傳郭璞云今汎汎郎汎汎也名謂之蠻蜢或謂之蚼蚁其大而蜜謂之壼蠮郭璞云范則冠鄭云范則為蠮也。
translation:
Stone Honey (Shi Mi): Flavor sweet, nature balanced. Governs evil qi in the abdomen, all manner of fright and epileptic convulsions, calms the five viscera, replenishes all deficiencies, supplements qi, tonifies the center, relieves pain, resolves toxins, eliminates the hundred diseases, harmonizes all medicines. Long-term use strengthens the will and lightens the body.
One does not suffer hunger or age. Another name is Stone Malt Sugar (Shi Yi). Grows in mountain valleys.

Wu Pu says: Stone Honey — according to Shennong and Lei Gong, its qi is sweet and balanced, produced from river sources or river embankments; born [according to] Yulan, also citing one source, in the mountain valleys of Wudu.
The medical commentaries say: produced in the river sources of Wudu, among mountain rocks, white in color like paste — of excellent quality.
The Shuowen says: juan means sweet malt sugar; also called yuan-zi or written mi. The Classic of Mountains and Seas says: At Pingfeng Mountain there are many sandy rocks with beehives. Guo Pu says: the honey is from red bees.
The Xijing Zaji records: The King of Nanyue presented Emperor Gao with five hu of stone honey. The Pian says: juan and chong both mean sweet malt sugar. Su Gong says the character "stone" should be removed.

Bee Larva (Feng Zi): Flavor sweet, nature balanced. Governs swellings, wind in the head, eliminates gu toxins, supplements deficiency and emaciation, and damage to the center. Long-term use makes the skin luminous, complexion beautiful, and prevents aging. Large yellow bee larvae govern fullness and pain in the abdomen, and lighten the body with benefit.
Another name is Mason Bee Larva (Shi Feng Zi), also called Zhan Si. Grows in mountain valleys.
The medical commentaries say: produced in Wudu.
The Shuowen says: feng (蠭) is a flying insect that stings people. The old written form is written as lu. The Guangya says: feng...

The large ground-nesting wasp builds its chamber in the earth and is called the Earth Wasp (Shi Yao Weng). It stings and bites with its rostrum. The Liji refers to it as lang-ma-yao. Today in Jing and Ba regions it is called xian. Also the wood wasp — Guo Pu says it resembles the earth wasp but is smaller, nests in holes in trees, and in the Yan-Zhao region it is called yao-weng; the small ones...
In the Jiangdong region it is also called the wood wasp. Fangyan says: in the Yan-Zhao region the wasp is called feng. Zheng's commentary says fan is another term for yao. Also the wood wasp — Guo Pu says today the black wasp bores holes in bamboo and wood; some of these also have honey, and they are sometimes called di-shi (flute master). See yao...

Honey Ant (Mi Yi): Flavor sweet, slightly warm. Governs dysentery with pus and blood, supplements the center, continues severed injuries, heals metal wounds, supplements qi; one does not suffer hunger or age. Grows in mountain valleys.
The name fan is phonetically close; Sima Xiangru's Rhapsody uses ni for feng (maple). Zuo Zhuan — Guo Pu says today... The large ones with honey are called hu-yao; Guo Pu says fan is another form for yao. Zheng's commentary says fan is yao.

text:
也。据說文云鱧。鱧也。與鱧不同。而毛莨郭璞以鯇釋鱧。與許不合。然初學記引此亦作鱧。蓋二字音同。以致譌舛不可得詳。廣雅又作鱺。亦音之譌。又廣志云豚魚一名鯇覽御。更異解也。又陸璣云鱧即鮐魚道家以為頭有星為厭。据此文頭以為鱧。廣雅以本草衍義以為黑鯉魚。若作鯉字。說文又以為鱧。廣志以本草衍義日鱧魚。今人謂之黑鯉。黑鯉魚。諸說若作鱧字。今京東人猶呼醍魚。又作鱺。亦音之譌。又廣志云豚魚一名鯇覽御。

鯉魚膃。名醫曰。味苦寒。主目熱赤痛青盲目久服強志氣生池澤。

案說文云。鯉也。鱸也。衛雅云。鯉鱸。舍人云鯉。一名鱸。郭璞注鯉云。今赤鯉魚注鱸云。大魚似鱧毛。詩云鱸鮦發傳云。鱸鯿鯉也。据此知郭璞別為二。非今古注云兗州人呼赤鯉為赤驪謂青鯉為青。馬黑鯉為元駒。白鯉為白驊。黃鯉為黃雄。

右蠱魚上品一十種舊同。名醫曰。一名遷。生汝南八月采。

案說文云。郭璞云遷謂房也。又其根藕。茹夫渠蓬爾雅云荷芙渠。郭璞云別名芙蓉。江東呼荷又其蓬茹。

神農本草經 卷一

五一
translation:
According to the Shuowen, it is written as "li" (鱧). The character "li" (鱧) is different from "li" (鱧), yet Mao Chang and Guo Pu used "huan" (鯇) to gloss "li" (鱧), which does not accord with Xu Shen. However, the Chuxue Ji quotes this passage also writing it as "li" (鱧). These two characters share the same pronunciation, which has led to errors and corruptions making it impossible to determine the details precisely. The Guangya also writes it as "li" (鱺), which is likewise a phonetic corruption. The Guangzhi says: "Tunyu has another name, huanlan yu." This is yet another divergent explanation. Lu Ji says: "Li (鱧) is the puffer fish (tai yu); Daoist practitioners consider it inauspicious because its head has star-like markings." Based on this, using "head" in the text as "li" (鱧) — the Guangya and the Bencao Yanyi take it to be black carp (hei li yu). If written with the character "li" (鯉), the Shuowen further takes it as "li" (鱧). The Guangzhi and the Bencao Yanyi say: li fish — people today call it black carp (hei li). Various explanations, if written with the character "li" (鱧), indicate that people in the eastern capital region still call it "ti yu." Also written as "li" (鱺), which is likewise a phonetic corruption.

Li Yu (Carp) Lard. The Mingyi says: flavor bitter, cold. It governs hot, red, painful eyes, blue-green blindness, and prolonged visual dimness. Long-term use strengthens the will and vital energy. It lives in ponds and marshes.

Commentary: The Shuowen says: li (鯉), also lú (鱸). The Erya says: li lú. The commentator Sheren says: li, another name lú. Guo Pu's note on li says: today this is the red carp (chi li yu); his note on lú says: a large fish resembling the li with bristles. The Shijing says "lú tong fa," the commentary says lú biǎn lǐ. From this we know Guo Pu distinguished them as two different fish. People in Yanzhou of today call red carp "chi li," call them "chi lü," call green carp "qing," call black carp "yuan ju," call white carp "bai hua," and call yellow carp "huang xiong."

The above are the superior-grade scaled fish, ten varieties in all, same as the old edition.

The Mingyi says: another name is Qian. It grows in Runan; harvested in the eighth month.

Commentary: The Shuowen says: Guo Pu says Qian means the root-stalk (fang, i.e., lotus rhizome). Also, its root is the lotus root (ou). The herb is called fuqu; the Erya says: he, furong (lotus). Guo Pu says its other name is furong; in Jiangdong people call it he, and also its seed-pod is called peng-ru.

Shennong Bencao Jing, Volume One

51

text:
神農本草經 卷一

五〇

名醫曰螳螂子也二月三月采火炙。
案說文云蟲蟲蛸也或作蜱蛸。爾雅云蛑蟷烏洩冒焦螲蛸也爾雅云不過螳螂其子蜱蛸郭璞云一名螺焦螳螂卵也范子計然云螲蛸出三輔上價三百舊作螵聲相近字之誤也玉篇云。

案說文云金屈海者。百歲燕所化魁。一名復靈老服翼所化爾雅云魁陸郭璞云本草云魁狀。
名醫曰生南海神農苦岐伯甘扁鵲鹹大節頭有文如磨齒采無時。
吳普曰海蛤神農苦岐伯甘扁鵲鹹大節頭有文如磨齒采無時。
海蛤味苦平。主欬逆上氣喘息煩滿胸痛寒熱。一名魁蛤。
同螺。

如海蛤圓而厚朴有理縱橫即今名蚶也周禮饔人供饔鄭司農云廩蛤也杜子春云廩蟀也周書王。

50

The Physicians record: The egg of the mantis is collected in the second and third months and roasted over fire.
Commentary: The Shuowen [Jiezi] says it is the egg-case of the mantis, also written as "pi shao." The Erya says: "wu xie mao jiao" — the mantis egg case. The Erya also says it is not to be confused with the mantis itself; its young are called pi shao. Guo Pu says: another name is luojiao, being the egg of the mantis. Fan Zi Jiran says: pi shao comes from the three districts around the capital and fetches three hundred [cash] at the old price. The character "piao" has a similar sound and is an error. The Yupian says...

Commentary: The Shuowen says the jinjuhai [gold-curved sea shell] is what a hundred-year-old swallow transforms into, also called fu ling, transformed from an aged bat. The Erya calls it kui lu. Guo Pu says the Bencao describes its shape.
The Physicians record: It is produced in the South Sea. Shennong [classifies its taste as] bitter; Qibo [classifies it as] sweet; Bianque [classifies it as] salty. The large joints of the shell have markings like grinding teeth. It is collected at any season.
Wu Pu says: The sea clam — Shennong [classifies it as] bitter; Qibo sweet; Bianque salty. The large joints have markings like grinding teeth. Collected at any season.
The sea clam is bitter in flavor and balanced in nature. It governs coughing with counterflow of qi, panting, vexation and fullness, chest pain, and alternating cold and heat. Another name is kui ge.
[Same as luo (螺).]

The sea clam is round and thick with natural markings running lengthwise and crosswise — this is what is now called the cockle (han). The Rites of Zhou mentions the palace cook providing ge; Zheng Situ-Agriculture says this refers to lin ge [granary clam]; Du Zichun says lin shuai; the Zhou Shu [Book of Zhou states]...
One account says: the eastern sea clam has a hollow at the hole. The Yulan [encyclopedia] says: when pressing the clam, it is called han; it is listed separately under the sea clam entry, also named kui lu, also named huo dong fei.
The wen clam (wen ge) governs malignant sores, erosion, and genital erosion. According to the Yulan, it also removes the five hemorrhoidal conditions. [Note: the large characters below in the Yulan text with the note about holes and bleeding are in smaller script.]

The Physicians record: It is produced on the eastern coast. The shell is patterned. Collected at any season. [It treats] wasting emaciation, puffiness of the face and eyes, and discharges great quantities of water.
Li fish (snakehead): The Physicians record — the Chuxue Ji cites "yu" (魚) as "li yu" (鱧魚). Flavor: sweet, cold. Governs wasting emaciation, puffiness of the face and eyes, and discharges great quantities of water. Another name: tong fish. Found in ponds and marshes.

Commentary: The Shuowen says li is the same as tong (鮦). The Erya says: li. Guo Pu says: it is the tong. The Odes of Mao mention fang and li; the commentary says li is tong.

translation:
The root of wild vine (Rubus): It is said this is what people commonly eat as berries. Tao Hongjing says: "Penglei is the root name; Fupen (覆盆) is the fruit name."

Eagle's-beak fruit (Euryale ferox): Flavor sweet, balanced. It mainly treats dampness-impediment, back and spine pain, supplements the center, eliminates sudden illness, benefits essence-qi, strengthens the will, sharpens hearing and vision. Long-term use lightens the body, staves off hunger, promotes longevity like an immortal. Another name: [one name follows].

Chicken-head fruit (Euryale ferox): Flavor sweet, balanced. Mainly treats dampness-impediment, back and spine pain, supplements the center, eliminates sudden illness, benefits essence-qi, strengthens will, sharpens hearing and vision. Long-term use lightens the body, staves off hunger, promotes longevity like an immortal. Another name: [one name follows].

The medical records say: Another name is Qian (芡); it grows at Leize and is harvested in the eighth month.

The Shuowen says: Qian is the chicken-head plant. The Guangya says it is called Hongtou. The Zhouli says border peoples use it as a food; Zheng Xuan says Qian is the chicken-head plant. Regional speech calls it Ling-Qian or chicken-head; in some places it is called wild-goose head or crow's head. In Huainan it is said that the northern Yan region calls it Ci; in the Qing-Xu-Huai-Si area it is called Qian; in southern Chu along the Jiang and Xiang rivers it is called Yantou (wild-goose head). Ancient and modern notes say: its leaves resemble lotus but are large; the surface of the leaves is glossy and wrinkled as if boiling, with thorny spines.

In mountain streams the grains can relieve hunger and now serve as the fruit. Inside is what is called the chicken-head; Gao You says it grows in water. The Youzhou region calls it Yantou (wild-goose head).

Summary of upper-grade fruits: Five kinds. The old text listed six kinds; now Juzi (tangerine) and You (pomelo) are placed under "wood." The Yulan edition reads [variant].

Sesame (Sesamum indicum): Flavor sweet, balanced. Another name: Fang Jin. The Divine Farmer's text says: non-toxic. Another name: Goushi (dog-louse). Harvested at the Beginning of Autumn. Benefits qi, builds muscle and flesh, fills marrow and brain. Long-term use lightens the body and prevents aging. Another name: Jusheng; its leaves are called Qingrang. Grows in river marshes.

Wu Pu says: Sesame is also called Goushi, also called Fangzheng, also called Hongzang. It grows in Shangdang.

The medical records say: Another name is Goushi; Jusheng; another name Fangzheng. The Classic of Filial Piety's援神契says: "Jusheng prolongs life." Song Jun says: "The world takes Jusheng to be wolfberry seeds." Tao Hongjing says in the original text:

The Guangya says: Goushi and Jusheng, another name Fangzheng. The Classic of Filial Piety's援神契says: "Jusheng prolongs life." Song Jun says: "The world takes Jusheng to be wolfberry seeds." Tao Hongjing says: It originated in Dayuan (Ferghana), hence the name Huma (foreign hemp). According to the original Classic it already contained this; Tao's statement is incorrect. Furthermore, it is listed alongside hemp in the category of "foreign" things — the word "hu" means "great," or alternatively it is named so because its leaves are larger than those of hemp.

translation:
Jujube (Da Zao)
Flavor: sweet, neutral. Governs heart and abdominal evil qi, calms the middle, nourishes the spleen, benefits the twelve channels, balances stomach qi, opens the nine orifices, supplements deficient qi and body fluids, addresses insufficiency in the body, great fright, and heaviness of the four limbs, and harmonizes the hundred medicines. Long-term use lightens the body and extends years. The leaves, when spread over Ephedra, can induce sweating. Grows in level marshes.

Wu Pu says: Jujube governs regulating the middle and benefiting spleen qi, makes the complexion good and the will and spirit flourishing. Cited in Wu's Materia Medica.

The Mingyi says: one name is Gan Zao (dried jujube), one name is Mei Zao (fine jujube). Harvested in the eighth month, sun-dried. Grows in Hedong.

Guo Pu says: the common small round purple-black one is now popularly called Yangshi Zao (sheep-dung jujube), also called Liang Zao. Harvested in the eighth month, sun-dried, grows in Hedong. Guo Pu says: today in Yishi County of Hedong the large jujubes are produced, their fruit the size of a chicken egg.

Commentary from Shuowen: jujube — also the sheep jujube. Erya says: Zun is the sheep jujube.

Grape (Pu Tao)
Flavor: sweet, neutral. Governs sinew and bone dampness impediment, supplements qi, doubles strength, strengthens the will, makes people fat and healthy, able to endure hunger and tolerate wind and cold. Long-term consumption lightens the body, prevents aging, and extends years. Can be made into wine. Grows in mountain valleys.

The Mingyi says: grows in Longxi, Wuyuan, and Dunhuang.

Commentary: The Records of the Grand Historian, in the Account of Dayuan, states that Dayuan and surrounding areas make wine from grapes; Han envoys brought back seeds, and thereupon the Son of Heaven first cultivated them. The soil of Mǔ in regions with grapes is fertile and rich. Some doubt whether this plant was not already in ancient China and was only added by the Mingyi, which would make it a black-ink entry. Yet the Rites of Zhou, in the section on Garden Stewards, lists it among rare fruits and vegetables. Zheng Xuan glosses the rare items as grapes and loquats. This shows ancient China already had and cultivated this plant. The old orthography writes it as 葡; according to the Shiji the form is 蒲.

Rubus (Lou / Fu Pen)
Flavor: sour, neutral. Governs calming the five viscera, supplementing and governing essence qi, growing yin, making it firm and strong, doubling strength and will, producing offspring. Long-term use lightens the body and prevents aging. One name: Ma Liu; one name: Lu Jing Shang; one name: Fu Pen (overturned basin). Grows in level marshes.

Wu Pu says: one name Que Pen, one name Yin Yao; Ying grows on Jing Mountain and in Kuanju.

The Mingyi says: one name Jue Pen, Kuanju. Master Yu's Materia Medica calls it Fu Pen.

Commentary: Shuowen says: Luo is a woody plant; Ying is Que Pen. Guangya says: Wu is Que Pen. Guo Pu says: it is Fu Pen; the fruit resembles raspberry but smaller and also edible. The Shijing says: the kudzu and Luo vines growing on the mounds. Lu Ji says: one name Giant Gourd, resembles wild grape, also with trailing vines, leaves like mugwort, white in color, fruit red and edible. Traditions of Immortals says: Chang Rong ate Peng (fleabane/rushes)...

Amaranth Seed (Xian Shi): The Mingyi (Famous Physicians' Record) lists separately an entry for "Luo Kui" (Malabar spinach). The name "Fan Lu" (Abundant Dew) is also given, but this is not correct. Tao Hongjing considered it a plant that produces seeds from late winter through spring, calling it "Winter Mallow," which is quite mistaken.
The Mingyi states: flavor sweet, cold; governs blue-green blindness of the eyes, expels pathogenic qi, promotes urination and defecation, eliminates cold and heat; long-term use benefits qi, prevents hunger, lightens the body. Another name: Horse Amaranth (Ma Xian).
Commentary from the Shuowen: it is the "Mo Xian." The Erya states that the Ji red amaranth has red stems; Li Dangzhi says Xian Shi should be today's White Kudzu; the Tang Ben annotation states:
The Mingyi says: another name is Mo Shi; grows in Huaiyang and in fields; leaves resemble indigo; harvest in the eleventh month.

Red Amaranth (Chi Xian): Another name is Lan. Today called Mo Shi — the character is a scribal error.

Melon Stalk (Gua Di): Flavor bitter, cold. Governs great water-swelling of the body, face, and four limbs; drains water; kills gu toxins; treats counterflow ascent of qi and eating of various fruits causing illness in the chest and abdomen — all such conditions are treated by inducing vomiting or purging downward. Grows in marshy flatlands.
The Mingyi says: another name is Tu Zhi; grows in Songao; harvest on the seventh day of the seventh month; dry in the shade.
Commentary from the Shuowen: gua (melon) means die (small melon). The Guangya says: water芝 is melon. Tao Hongjing says: it is the stalk of the sweet melon. The Yilan edition reads "grows in marshy flatlands."

Melon Seed (Gua Zi): Flavor sweet, balanced. Governs making people's skin lustrous, complexion beautiful, benefits qi, prevents hunger; long-term use lightens the body and promotes longevity. Another name: Water芝 (Shui Zhi).
The Mingyi says: another name is White Melon Seed (Bai Gua Zi); another name is Melon Flesh (Bian); the Guangya states that winter melon seed is called rang.
Wu Pu says: Melon Seed, another name Bian; harvest on the seventh day of the seventh month; it is the kernel of the winter melon; also harvested in the eighth month.
Commentary from the Shuowen: bian means the flesh inside the melon. The Guangya says: winter melon produces dié; its seeds are called rang. Tao Hongjing says: "white" should be "sweet"; the old text had the character "white," but according to the Mingyi, another name is "White—"

Bitter Vegetable (Ku Cai): The Mingyi says: another name is You Dong (Endures Winter); grows in Yizhou, on hillsides along roads; does not die in winter; harvest on the third day of the third month; dry in the shade.
Flavor bitter, cold. Governs pathogenic qi of the five viscera, aversion to grain, and stomach impediment. Long-term use calms the heart, benefits qi, sharpens hearing and sight, reduces need for sleep, lightens the body, and promotes longevity. Another name: Cha Cao (Tea Herb); another name: Xuan. Grows in mountain valleys.

translation:
Hemp seed (廡蕡): flavor acrid, balanced. Governs the five taxations and seven injuries; benefits the five viscera; disperses blood; [treats] cold qi. Eating too much causes a person to see ghosts and run about wildly. Long-term use penetrates the spirit and lightens the body. Also named:廡勃, 廡子; flavor sweet.
Balanced. Governs supplementing the center, boosting qi, fattening and strengthening, preventing aging, and becoming an immortal. Grows in river valleys.

Wu Pu says: The kernel of 廡子— according to Shennong and Qibo, it is acrid; according to Leigong, it is sweet. The male hemp (牡廡) and 白薇: what is stored first in the ground, if eaten, kills a person. 廡藍, also named 廡蕡, also named 花; Leigong says acrid, non-toxic.

The Mingyi records say: 廡勃is the pollen on the hemp flower, the floating powder appearing in the seventh month; gather on the seventh day of the seventh month. Good. The seeds are gathered in the ninth month. Grows on Mount Tai.

Also named Qing Ge (青葛). Shennong: acrid. Qibo: toxic. Leigong: sweet, non-toxic. Do not use with 牡廡 and 白薇; the leaves are toxic; eating them kills a person. 廡勃, also named 花; Leigong: acrid, non-toxic.

Case note: The Shuowen says 廡is the same as 林—the place where people take shelter under a roof; it is what is meant by ancestral hall (宗廡). Guo Pu says there are two other names; also 芋廡 (each); using 蕡 as aromatic herb (雞香草); the Erya [records this].
廡 means the ancestral hall's fruit; 廡孫 means its seed. Guo Pu gives two alternate names; also called 芋廡每; 蕡 is used as a fragrant herb for chickens; the Erya [confirms this].
The true 廡: based on this, 廡Hongjing says it is the fruit. Zheng notes that the agricultural officer says 廡日廡; the Huainanzi, "Common Customs" chapter, says: when the Hu people see the full 廡seeds, they use them in the Zhou rites at the Biao ceremony as decoration; its 廡...
Hongjing says it is 廡fruit; Zheng says 廡fruit. Since now there is no fruit, the Tang edition considers this to be 廡fruit—that is correct.

The above are two kinds of grains, upper grade: [they treat] cold and heat, emaciation, the five types of urinary blockage; promote urination. Long-term use strengthens the bones, builds muscle and flesh, lightens the body, and extends the years.

Mallow seed (冬葵子): flavor sweet, cold. Governs the cold and heat [conditions] of the five viscera and six bowels, emaciation, the five types of urinary blockage; promotes urination. Long-term use strengthens the bones, builds muscle and flesh, lightens the body, and extends the years.

The Mingyi records say: Grows on Mount Shaoshi. Gather in the twelfth month.

Case note: The Shuowen says 早 is the ancient form of 終葵 (winter mallow), a type of vegetable. The Guangya says it is 蔠葵. An examination of variant forms shows it is close in form to 終葵, which should be the same as the Erya entry 終葵. The Erya says: 菘葵 is also 繁露. Guo Pu says: it is also called 承露 (dew-receiver). It has a large stalk and small leaves; the flowers are purple-yellow. The Bencao Tujing says: people in Wu call it 繁露; the common name is 胡燕支; its seeds can be used by women as a facial cosmetic and for making lip rouge. According to [this]...

案說文云茶苦荼也廣雅云游冬苦菜也爾雅云茶苦菜又檟苦荼郭璞云樹小如梔子冬生葉可煮作羹今呼早採者為荼晚取者為茗一名荈蜀人名之苦荼陶宏景云此即是今茗茗一名茶又令人不眠亦凌冬不凋而兼其止生益州唐本注廢之非矣選與荈音相近右榮上品五種舊同
translation:

Commentary: The Shuowen [Jiezi] says: "tu (荼) is bitter tu (苦荼)." The Guangya says: "youdong (游冬) is bitter vegetable (苦菜)." The Erya says: "tu (荼) is bitter vegetable; also called jia (檟), bitter tu (苦荼)." Guo Pu says: "The tree is small, like the gardenia; its leaves grow through winter and can be boiled to make a soup." Today, leaves picked early are called tu (荼); those taken late are called ming (茗). Another name is chuan (荈). The people of Shu call it bitter tu (苦荼). Tao Hongjing says: "This is precisely what is now called ming (茗); ming is also called cha (茶). It also prevents sleep and endures through winter without withering." The Tang [dynasty official] commentary abolished [this entry], which was wrong. The selection [of this name] is phonetically close to chuan (荈). The above Rong category, upper-grade, five varieties, follows the old [arrangement].

translation:
Realgar (Xiong Huang): Flavor bitter, nature balanced and cold. It governs cold and heat disorders, scrofula sores, malignant sores, carbuncles, hemorrhoids, dead flesh; kills spirit entities, evil ghosts, evil qi, and the toxins of a hundred insects; overcomes five weapons. Refined and eaten, it lightens the body and makes one an immortal. Another name is Huang (Yellow). Found growing at Stone Mountain valleys.

Shennong's Classic of the Materia Medica

Realgar: Flavor bitter, nature balanced and cold. It governs cold and heat disorders, scrofula, malignant sores, carbuncles, hemorrhoids, dead flesh; kills spirit entities, evil ghosts, evil qi; overcomes the toxins of a hundred insects and five weapons. Refined, it lightens the body and makes one an immortal. Another name is Huang (Yellow Stone). It grows on mountain slopes.

Wu Pu states: Realgar — according to Shennong it is bitter. The shaded side of mountains has cinnabar-colored realgar; the sunny side of mountains produces realgar. Hence it is called "male" (xiong). It is the male of cinnabar, which is why it is named Realgar.

According to the physicians: It grows in Wudu and Dunhuang on the sunny sides of mountains; collected at any time.

According to the Western Mountain Classic: On High Mountain, below it there is much realgar. Guo Pu states: In former times, in the third year of Taihe, in the territory of Gaoping Commandery, a mountain collapsed, and from within it several thousand jin of realgar emerged. Ge Hong's Baopuzi states: Realgar must be the type produced from the mountains of Wudu — pure and unmixed, its red like a rooster's comb, brilliantly bright — only then can it be used. What is merely pure yellow, resembling realgar in color but without [the red brilliance], cannot be used.

The Pharmaceutical Chapters state: Realgar, when obtained from the mountains of Wudu — pure and unmixed, red like a rooster's comb, brilliantly luminous — only then can it be used. What is merely pure yellow, resembling realgar but without [those qualities]—

Sulphur (Stone Flowing Yellow): [Flowing yellow,] the red-glowing type produced from flowing streams — it is not suitable for use in immortality medicines, but can be compounded to treat women's vaginal erosion sores, hemorrhoidal carbuncles, evil blood, and sinew and bone collapse; removes head baldness; and can transform gold, silver, copper, and iron. A marvelous substance. Imperial览quotes: Stone flowing blue-green...

Sulphur (flowing yellow from white stone, red color): It grows [in mountain valleys]. Wu Pu states: Sulphur — another name is Stone Flowing Yellow. According to Shennong and the Yellow Emperor and Lei Gong: salty and toxic. According to Yi He and Bian Que: bitter and non-toxic. It is produced either in Yiyang, or from west of the river, or is jade-colored yellow — this is the liquid of the stone Pan Water. The ancient character is huang (磺). Burn it until it has a purple flame. Collected in the eighth and ninth months. Treats blood stagnation in women. Imperial览states it can combine gold and silver; treats women with complete yin deficiency.

According to the physicians: It grows at Donghai, Muyang Mountain, and Taishan; also from the stone liquid of mountains west of the river.

Fan's Ziran states: Water sulphur comes from Hanzhong. Also states: Liu Feng ingested sulphur and aged more slowly. Liu Kui's annotation to the Wudu Fu states: Flowing sulphur is the essence of earth.

Orpiment (Ci Huang): Flavor acrid, nature balanced. It governs malignant sores, head baldness, scabs and mange; kills poisonous insects and lice; body itching, evil qi, and all toxins. Refined and taken over a long time, it lightens the body, increases years, and prevents aging. Found in mountain valleys.

Shennong's Classic of the Materia Medica, Volume One

translation:
The Mingyi (Famous Physicians) say: Also called Cold Water Stone, also called Ling Water Stone. It is the essence of salt. It grows in Changshan, and also in Zhongshui County and Handan.

Note: Fan Zi Jiran says Condensed Water Stone comes from Hedong; those with good luster are best. It governs崩中 (uterine flooding), leakage downward, breaking up accumulations in the uterus, blood concretions and masses in the viscera, bound qi, chills and fever, abdominal pain, infertility, and impotence that fails to arise. [Editorial note on sources disagrees; serves to supplement deficiency.]

Yangqi Stone (Actinolite)
Second entry. Alternate name: White Stone. Found in mountain valleys.

Wu Pu says: Yangqi Stone — according to Shennong and Bian Que: sour, non-toxic; according to Tong Jun, Lei Gong, and Qi Bo: salty, non-toxic; according to Master Li: slightly cold. It grows on Tai Shan. The Imperial Encyclopedia citation says it also grows on Yangqi Mountain. Collect at any season.

The Mingyi say: Also called Sheng Stone; also called Yangqi Stone. It is the root of mica (yunmu). Grows in Qi Mountain and Langya, or according to some, on Yangqi Mountain. Collect at any season.

Kong Gong Nie (Stalactite offshoot)
The Mingyi say: Flavor pungent, warm. Governs failure to digest food, bound qi, evil malign sores, pox-itching, hemorrhoids; promotes flow through the nine orifices and brings down breast milk. The Imperial Encyclopedia cites the main text giving an alternate name of Bi Stone. Found in mountain valleys.

Wu Pu says: Kong Gong Nie — according to Shennong, pungent; according to Qi Bo, salty, non-toxic; color is blue-yellow.

The Mingyi say: Also called Tong Stone; it is the root of Ban Nie. Blue-yellow in color. Found in Liang Mountain.

Ban Nie (Stalactite drip)
The Mingyi say: Flavor pungent, warm. Governs ulcerous injuries, bleeding dysentery, chills and fever, scrofula, concretions and bound qi. Also called Jiang Stone. Found in mountain valleys. [Editorial note: this entry should be combined with the Kong Gong entry above.]

Jing Tie (Well Iron)
The Mingyi say: It is the root of Zhongrǔ (stalactite); found in the Zhao region, also in Liang Mountain and the South Sea; collect at any season. The Mingyi say: Zhong Luo, also called Iron Liquid. Can be used to dye black. Grows at Muyang and Qi City or Xi City; collect at any season. Properties: balanced, neutral. Governs brightening the eyes and dissolving copper and iron. Flavor pungent, neutral. Governs wind-heat, malign sores and ulcerations, pox sores, itching eruptions, and qi in the skin. Iron governs hardening the muscles, increasing endurance against pain. Found in level marshes. [Note: formerly divided into three separate entries, now combined.]

Note: The Shuowen (dictionary) says: Tie (iron) is a black metal. Sometimes abbreviated, ancient script writes it as 銕.

Quicksilver (Mercury). The Celebrated Physicians say: It is produced in Wudu in the same mountains as realgar. It grows on the shaded side of mountains where gold is found. When the essence of gold is fumigated, cinnabar-yellow (orpiment) is produced; it is gathered at any time. Flavor: acrid, cold. It mainly treats scabies, itching, crusted sores, white baldness, and kills worms in the skin. It causes miscarriage, eliminates heat, and neutralizes the toxicity of gold, silver, copper, and tin. When smelted and refined it reverts to cinnabar. Long-term use confers immortality.
It grows in level ground.

Commentary from the Shuowen: Dian's cinnabar transforms into quicksilver. The Guangya says quicksilver is called gong. The Huainanzi, "Dixing" chapter says: White alum (baiyu), after nine hundred years, produces white mercury (baihong). White mercury, after nine hundred years...
Celebrated Physicians say: Another name is gong. It is produced at Fuling and comes from cinnabar.

Gypsum (Shigao). Flavor: acrid, slightly cold. It mainly treats wind-cold with fever, counterflow qi below the heart, fright and wheezing, dry and scorched mouth, inability to catch one's breath, hardness and pain in the abdomen, and eliminates evil demons. It promotes childbirth and heals metal wounds. It grows in mountain valleys.
It reaches one hundred years and produces white gold; Gao You says baiong is quicksilver.

Celebrated Physicians say: Another name is xishi. It grows on Qi Mountain and on Qilu Mountain and Lumeng Mountain. It is gathered at any time.

Lodestone (Cishi). Flavor: acrid, cold. It mainly treats generalized painful obstruction (zhou bi), wind-damp, pain in the joints and limbs that prevents one from holding objects, washing sensations of soreness, eliminates great heat, vexing fullness, and deafness. Another name is yuanshi. It grows in mountain valleys.
Wu Pu says: Cishi is also called cishi (磁石).

Celebrated Physicians say: Another name is chushi. It grows on Mt. Tai and on the shaded side of Mt. Ci Mountain where iron is present; it grows on the sunny side. It is gathered at any time.
The Classic of Mountains and Seas (Northern Mountains section) says cishi looks like chushi, and says the mountains contain much magnetite. Guo Pu says it can attract iron. The Guanzi, "Dishu" chapter says: Mountains with lodestone above must have copper below. The Lüshi...

Wu Pu says: Shennong: acrid; Qibo, Yi He, and Bian Que: sweet, non-toxic; Li's: greatly cold. Or it grows in Handan; it is gathered at any time. It resembles mica in color. It is also called Yuhan Shuishi. A note says: Baishuishi grows in mountain valleys; another name is Hanshuishi. A further note on the stone says...

Congealing Water Stone (Ningshuishi). Flavor: acrid, cold. It mainly treats fever in the body, accumulations and gatherings of pathogenic qi in the abdomen, skin that feels as if burning, vexing fullness; drinking it with water. Long-term use eliminates hunger. Another name is Baishuishi. It grows in mountain valleys.

The Chunqiu Jingtong chapter says: Lodestone summons iron, or attracts it. The Huainanzi, "Shuoshan" chapter says: Lodestone can attract iron; only use the term "ci" (慈); the old form "ci" (磁) is incorrect. The Celebrated Physicians separately list yuanshi as an entry, which is also incorrect.

Lishi (理石): Flavor acrid, cold. Mainly treats body heat; benefits the stomach, relieves vexation, augments essence, brightens the eyes, breaks up accumulations and gatherings, eliminates the three worms. Another name is Lizhishi (立制石). Grows in mountain valleys.
The Mingyi says: Another name is Jishi (飢石). Treats body heat with cold limbs, promotes urination, unblocks the blood vessels; fine-textured. Grows in Hanzhong and Lushan; collected at any time.

Changshi (長石): Flavor acrid, cold. Mainly treats body heat, cold in the four limbs, promotes urination, unblocks blood vessels, brightens the eyes, removes cloudiness, expels the three worms, kills gu toxins; long-term use prevents hunger. Another name is Fangshi (方石). Grows in mountain valleys.
Wu Pu says: Changshi is also called Fangshi, Zhishi, and Shengzhangzi; found in mountain valleys; resembles horse teeth; moist and lustrous, jade-colored; long-term use prevents hunger and thirst.
The Mingyi says: Also called Tushi (土石) and Zhishi (直石); its texture resembles horse teeth, square and lustrous, jade-colored; grows in Zhangzi Mountain and Taishan; collected in Linzi at any time.

Fuqing (膚青): Flavor acrid, balanced. Mainly treats gu toxins, snake-plant flesh poisons, and various toxic sores and malignant wounds. Another name is Tuiqing (推青), another name is Tuishi (推石). Grows in Yizhou, in river valleys.
Case note: Tao Hongjing says that common formulas and immortal classics alike make no use of this substance, and it has become generally unrecognized.

The above jade and mineral middle-grade items number fourteen kinds; formerly sixteen kinds — upon examination, iron filings (鐵落) and iron essence (鐵精) are counted as one.

Ganjiang (乾薑, Dried Ginger): Flavor acrid, warm. Mainly treats fullness in the chest, coughing and counterflow qi, warms the interior, stops bleeding, promotes sweating, expels wind, relieves damp impediment, and treats intestinal dysentery with downward flux. Fresh ginger is especially good; long-term use removes foul qi, opens the spirit and brightens the mind. Grows in river valleys.
The Mingyi says: Grows in Jianjian, Jingzhou, and Yangzhou; collected in the ninth month.
Case note: Shuowen says ginger is a vegetable that repels dampness. Guangya says: "chu" and "lian" are types of ginger. The Lüshi Chunqiu, "Ben Wei" chapter says: among the finest seasonings is the ginger of Yangpu; Gao You's commentary notes that Yangpu is a place name — located in Shu commandery, as Sima Xiangru's "Shanglin Fu" mentions this ginger.

Quaner Shi (泉耳實, Cocklebur fruit): Flavor sweet, warm. Mainly treats wind headache with cold pain, wind-damp impediment, pain and contracture of the four limbs, malignant flesh and dead skin; long-term use benefits the qi, sharpens hearing and vision, strengthens the will, and lightens the body. Another name is Huxi (胡枲).

Sophora root (Ku Shen). Flavor: bitter; nature: cold. Governs binding qi in the heart and abdomen, concretions and accumulations, jaundice, dribbling urination with residual fluid, expels water, eliminates abscesses and swellings, supplements the center, brightens the eyes, stops tearing. Alternative names: Water Sophora (Shui Huai), Bitter Burdock (Ku Zhi). Grows in mountain valleys and in open fields. The Mingyi says: also called Ground Sophora (Di Huai), Rabbit Sophora (Tu Huai), Proud Sophora (Jiao Huai), White Stem (Bai Jing), Tiger Hemp (Hu Ma), Ridge Stem (Cen Jing), Lu Yue, Mound Youth (Ling Lang). Grows in Runan. Roots collected in the third, eighth, and tenth months and dried in the sun.

Dang Gui (Chinese Angelica). Flavor: sweet; nature: warm. Governs coughing with counterflow and rising qi, warm malaria, alternating cold and heat washing through the skin, uterine bleeding with inability to conceive, all manner of malign sores, ulcers, and metal-wound injuries — decoct and drink. Alternative name:
[phonetic gloss: xi, large sound; guàn; variant text]

Dried Gui grows in river valleys.

Wu Pu says: Dang Gui — Shennong, Huangdi, Tong Jun, and Bian Que classify it as sweet and non-toxic; Qi Bo and Lei Gong classify it as acrid and non-toxic; Li's classification is slightly warm. It grows spontaneously in Qiang and Hu territories.

The Mingyi says: Shan Qi from the west — roots collected in the second and eighth months and dried in the shade. The Guangya case-note says "Xue-shan-qi." Guo Pu says it resembles Qi but is coarser and larger; also "Bai Qi." Guo Pu says this is the upland Qi. Fan Zi Ji Ran records this.

Ma Huang (Ephedra). Flavor: bitter; nature: warm. Governs wind stroke and cold damage with headache, warm malaria; releases the exterior and promotes sweating; eliminates pathogenic heat qi; stops coughing with counterflow and rising qi; eliminates alternating cold and heat; breaks up firm concretions and accumulations. Alternative name: Dragon Sand (Long Sha).
Wu Pu says: Ma Huang, alternative name Bi Xiang, also called Bi Yan. Grows in Jin territory. Shennong and Gong Jun classify it as bitter and non-toxic; Bian Que as sour and non-toxic; Li's classification is neutral (ping). It may also grow in Hedong. Collected at the Beginning of Autumn in the fourth month. [Imperial览reference]

The Mingyi says: alternative name Dog Bone (Gou Gu). Grows in Jin territory and Hedong. Collected at the Beginning of Autumn, steamed, and dried in the shade until green.

Case note from Guangya: "Long Sha — this is Ma Huang." Ma Huang, Ma Zheng, Dog Bone — these are all the same. Fan Zi Ji Ran says Ma Huang comes from Hanzhong and the Three Auxiliary Regions.

Qin Yi: flavor bitter, nature balanced; governs cold-heat, pathogenic qi, cold astringency, wind impediment, pain in the limbs and joints; drains water and promotes urination. Grows in mountain valleys.
Mingyi (Famous Physicians) states: grows on Flying Crow Mountain; roots are collected in the second and eighth months and sun-dried.
Commentary: The Shuo Wen classifies it as a grass with related forms; the Yu Pian writes it as "fu." Zang Feng notes that the Bencao originally called it Qin Gua, so the present name in the Bencao may also be a later emendation by physicians.

Wu Pu states: Bai He (Lily) is also named Zhong Da, also named Mo Luo, also named Zhong Ting; grows wide-chested in Jing Mountain.
Bai He: flavor sweet, nature balanced; governs pathogenic qi, abdominal distension, heart pain; benefits urination and defecation; supplements the middle and augments qi. Grows in river valleys.
Mingyi states: also named Zhong Xiang, also named Li Luo, also named Zhong Ting; grows in Jing Mountain; roots collected in the second and eighth months and sun-dried.
Commentary: The Yu Pian states: She captures Bai He and garlic together.

Zhi Mu: flavor bitter, cold; governs wasting-thirst, internal heat; eliminates pathogenic qi, limb swelling; drains water; supplements deficiency and augments qi. Also named Di Mu, also named Lian Mu, also named Ye Liao, also named Di Shen.
Wu Pu states: Zhi Mu, also named Shennong Tong Jun Wu Du, also named Huo Mu, also named Di Mu; grows in river valleys.御覧 cites it as Ti Mu.
Mingyi states: also named Nü Lei, also named Nü Li, also named Er Cao, also named Lu Lie, also named Jiu Feng, also named Er Zhong Cao, also named Dong Gen, also named Shui Xu, also named Shen.
Also named Qiang; grows in He Nei; roots collected in the second and eighth months and sun-dried.
Commentary: The Shuo Wen states: Wang is the mother of Yi. Guang Ya states: Wang Xi Qiang. Guo Pu states: grows on mountaintops.

Shennong Bencao Jing, Volume Two
Page 67

text:
神農本草經 卷二

吳普曰蟲實一名劇草一名三堅一名劇荔電御一名澤藍一名豕首神農黃帝甘辛無毒生宛句五月采上同

名醫曰一名荔實生河東五月采實陰乾

案說文云荔草也似蒲而小根可作啟廣雅云馬薢也月令云仲冬之月荔挺出鄭云荔挺馬薤也高誘注淮南子云荔馬草也通俗交云一名馬蘭顏之推云此物河北平澤率生之江東頗多種于

釐麥味苦寒主關格諸癃結小便不通出刺決癰腫明目去翳破胎墮子下閉血一名巨句麥生川谷

名醫曰一名大菊一名大蘭生大山立秋采實陰乾

案說文云遽遽麥也案陶宏景云子頗似菊故名蟄麥廣雅云此威陵若遽麥也爾雅云大菊遽麥郭璞云一名麥句薑即

元參味苦微寒主腹中寒熱積聚女子産乳餘疾補腎氣令人目明一名重臺一名鹿腹一名正馬一名元臺神農桐君黃帝雷公扁鵲苦

吳普曰元參一名鬼藏一名正馬一名重臺一名鹿腹一名端生川谷

無毒岐伯鹹或生冤胸山陽二月生葉如梅毛四四相值似與藥黑塗方高四五尺華赤生枝

開四月實黑寔御

名醫曰一名元臺一名鹿腸一名正馬一名減一名端生河間及冤句三月四月采根暴乾
translation:
Shennong Bencao Jing, Volume Two

Wu Pu says: "Chong Shi" (Kochia fruit) — also named Ju Cao, also named San Jian, also named Ju Li. According to the Emperor Huang Di and Shennong: sweet, acrid, non-toxic; grows in Wanju; harvest in the fifth month. [Same as above entry.]

The Mingyi says: Also named Li Shi; grows in Hedong; harvest the fruit in the fifth month and dry in the shade.

Examining the Shuowen: Li is a grass resembling cattail but with small roots that can be used for mats. The Guangya says it is also called Ma Xie. The Yueling says: "In the middle month of winter, the li shoots emerge." Zheng [Xuan] comments: "Li shoots are Ma Xie." Gao You's annotation to the Huainanzi says: "Li is a horse-grass." The common saying calls it Ma Lan. Yan Zhitui says: "This plant grows abundantly on the flatlands and marshes of Hebei; in the Jiangdong region many varieties are grown."

Qu Mai (Dianthus/fringed pink): Flavor bitter, cold. It governs blockage and obstruction of the passages, all forms of urinary retention, inability to urinate, expels thorns, lances abscesses and swellings, brightens the eyes, removes cataracts, breaks up fetal obstructions, expels the fetus, clears stagnant blood. Also named Ju Ju Mai. Grows in valley regions.

The Mingyi says: Also named Da Ju; also named Da Lan. Grows on great mountains; harvest the fruit at the onset of autumn and dry in the shade.

Examining: The Shuowen says "ju" is a type of grain. Tao Hongjing says: "The seeds rather resemble chrysanthemum, hence the name Zhe Mai." The Guangya says: "This is Weiling Ruo, also called Ju Mai." The Erya says: "Da Ju is Ju Mai." Guo Pu comments: "Also called Mai Ju Jiang," which is the same plant.

Xuan Shen (Scrophularia): Flavor bitter, slightly cold. It governs cold and heat in the abdomen, accumulations and gatherings, women's lingering ailments after childbirth, tonifies kidney qi, brightens the eyes. Also named Chong Tai; also named Lu Fu; also named Zheng Ma; also named Yuan Tai. [According to] Shennong, Tong Jun, Huang Di, Lei Gong, Bian Que: bitter.

Wu Pu says: Xuan Shen — also named Gui Zang; also named Zheng Ma; also named Chong Tai; also named Lu Fu; also named Duan. Grows in valley regions.

Non-toxic. Qi Bo [says]: salty. Or grows in Yuanxiong, Shanyang. In the second month the leaves emerge, resembling plum leaves, arranged in groups of four facing each other, similar in appearance to the black-smeared medicinal. Grows to four or five chi tall, with reddish flowers on branches.

Blooms in the fourth month; fruit is black and solid.

The Mingyi says: Also named Yuan Tai; also named Lu Chang; also named Zheng Ma; also named Jian; also named Duan. Grows in Hejian and Wanju. Harvest the root in the third and fourth months and dry in the sun.

涇
羊蓍味辛寒。主陰痿絕傷。蓋中痛。利小便。益氣力強志。一名剛前。生山谷。
吳普曰涇羊蓍神農雷公辛。李氏小寒堅骨。御

黃
吳岑味苦黃芩。一名黃文。一名經本。一名妒婦。一名虹勝。一名經本。一名印頭。一名內虛神農桐君黃帝雷公扁鵲
苦無毒李氏小溫。二月生赤黃葉兩兩四四相值。莖空中或方員高三四尺。四月花紫紅赤。五月實黑

脊味苦平。主腰背強關機緩急周痹寒溼邪鄔痛頗利老人。一名百枝生川谷。

六九
translation:
Jing (涇)

Yangshu (Sheep's Plantain): Flavor pungent, cold. Governs impotence due to injury, pain in the genitals, promotes urination, boosts vital energy and strengthens the will. Also called Gangqian. Grows in mountain valleys.

Wu Pu states: Yangshu — Shennong and Leigong classify it as pungent; Li's text says slightly cold, strengthens bone. [Imperial note]

According to the Mingyi: Grows at Shangjun Yangshan. Governs various heat conditions, jaundice, intestinal dysentery, diarrhea, expels water, opens blood blockages, treats malignant sores, ulcers, and fire-sores. Also called Fuchang. Grows in river valleys.

Huangqin (Scutellaria/Chinese Skullcap)

Wu Cen: Flavor bitter, Huangqin. Also called Huangwen, Jingben, Dufu, Hongsheng, Jingben, Yintou, Neixu. Shennong, Tongjun, Huangdi, Leigong, Bianque [classify it as]: bitter, non-toxic; Li's text says slightly warm. In the second month the leaves grow in pairs, reddish-yellow, arranged in fours, the stem is hollow or square, growing three to four feet high. In the fourth month the flowers are purple-red, in the fifth month the seeds are black.

Wu Pu states: Governs various heat conditions, jaundice, intestinal dysentery, diarrhea, expels water, opens blood blockages, treats malignant sores, ulcers, and fire-sores. Also called Fuchang. Grows in river valleys.

The root is yellow; harvest from the second to ninth month. [Imperial note]

According to the Mingyi: Also called Kongchang, Neixu, Huangwen, Jingben, Dufu. Grows in Gui and Yuanju. Harvested root on the third day of the third month and dried in shade.

Case notes: Shuowen says "gai" means yellow gai. Guangya says Zhemei, Huangwen, Neixu, and Huangqin are the same. Fanzi Jiran says Huangqin from Sanfu, the yellow ones are best.

Gouji (Cibotium/Dog's Backbone Fern)

Flavor bitter, neutral. Governs stiffness of the lower back and spine, loosens joints, relieves acute pain, expels wind-damp painful obstruction (bi), greatly benefits the elderly. Also called Baizhi. Grows in river valleys.

Wu Pu states: Gouji, also called Gouqing, also called Chigen Bai. Resembles bamboo root, with thorny hairs. Qibo says: Huangdi, Leigong, Bianque classify it as sweet, non-toxic. Li's text says slightly warm. Resembles Bixie in its nodes. Greenish-red skin, white interior with red veins.

The bamboo-like plant has thorny leaves, round red root that is yellow-white inside. Also resembles bamboo root, with thorny hairs. Qibo says: Huangdi, Bianque classify it as sweet, non-toxic. Li's text says slightly warm. Resembles Bixie in its nodes. Greenish-red skin, white interior with red veins.

According to the Mingyi: Also called Qianglü, Fugai, Fujin. Grows at Changshan. Harvest leaves in the second and eighth months and dry in sun. The ends are round, the skin is greenish-red with white interior and red veins.

Case notes: Guangya says Bajie is the same as Gouji. Yupian says Bajie is the root of Gouji. The Mingyi lists Bajie as a separate entry — this is incorrect.

Shilongrui (Ranunculus sceleratus/Cursed Crowfoot)

Flavor bitter, neutral. Governs wind-cold-damp painful obstruction, evil qi in the chest and abdomen, benefits the joints, stops vexation and fullness. Long-term use lightens the body, brightens the eyes, and prevents aging. Also called Luguo Neng. [Imperial note: the word "neng" is written as "guo" in one edition.] Also called Di[long]...

Shennong Bencao Jing, Volume 2
Page 69

text:
神農本草經 卷二

貝母
葉如韭．一曰蝱母．出三輔．黄白者善．玉篇作莔母．
名醫曰．一名藥實．一名苦花．一名苦菜．一名商草．一名勤母生晉地十月采根暴乾．
案說文云菡貝母也廣雅云貝母苦菜也爾雅云菡貝母郭璞云根如小貝圓而白華葉似韭毛詩云言采其蝱傳云蝱貝母也陸璣云其葉如括樓而細小其子在根下如芋子正白四方連累相著有分

白茹
解也．
吳普曰白芷一名白臒．
名醫曰．一名芳香生川谷．
朶根暴乾．一名白茹一名臒一名澤芬一名薦蕪可作湯生河東下澤二月八月．一名澤芬葉一名薦蕪可作浴湯生河東下澤二月八月．
白茹味辛温主女人漏下赤白閉陰腫寒熱風頭侵目泪出長肌膚潤澤可作面脂．一名芳香生川谷．一名臒御

案說文云蕀鷺也楚謂之蘺齊謂之茝廣雅云白芷其葉謂之藥西山經云號山其草多薬王逸注
薊藿郭璞云薊薊也鷺楚詞謂之鷺香草也淮南子修務訓云身苦秋藥被風高誘云薊白芷香草也

楚詞云白蒲一名符蘺楚謂之莞豊蒲與茸相似而名醫誤合為一平或說文別有臒夫蘺也蘺上也是
非一草舍人云白芷按名醫一名莞云似即爾雅修莞訓云身苦秋藥被風高誘云薊白芷其上南而說文別有臒夫蘺也蘺上也是楚謂之蘺即

夫蘺也未可得詳舊作芷非
translation:
Shennong Bencao Jing (Divine Husbandman's Classic of Materia Medica), Volume 2

Fritillaria (Beimu)
Its leaves resemble chives. It is also called Mangmu. It is produced in the three auxiliary regions around the capital. The yellow-white variety is best. The Pian (character dictionary) writes it as Mengmu.
The Mingyi (Renowned Physicians' Record) states: It is also called Yaoshi, also called Kuhua, also called Kucai, also called Shangcao, also called Qinmu. It grows in Jin territory; roots are gathered in the tenth month and dried in the sun.
According to the Shuowen (dictionary), "Han" refers to beimu. The Guangya says beimu is kucai. The Erya says:郭璞 (Guo Pu) notes that the root is like a small cowrie shell, round and white; the flowers and leaves resemble chives. The Mao Ode says "we gather the mang"; the commentary explains mang is beimu. Lu Ji notes the leaves resemble those of trichosanthes but are smaller and finer; the seeds are found below the root, like taro tubers, pure white, clustered on four sides together in sections.

Baizhi (Angelica dahurica)
It resolves.
Wu Pu states: Baizhi is also called Bai'e.
The Mingyi states: It is also called Fangxiang; it grows in river valleys. The roots are dug and dried in the sun. It is also called Baifu, also called E, also called Zefen, also called Jianwu; it can be made into a decoction; it grows in the lowland marshes east of the He River and is gathered in the second and eighth months.
Baizhi: flavor is acrid and warm. It governs women's flooding and spotting with red and white discharge, closed and swollen vagina, cold and heat, wind in the head attacking the eyes with tearing, promotes growth of muscles and skin, moistens and nourishes; it can be made into a face cream. Also called Fangxiang, growing in river valleys. Also called E (imperial).

The Shuowen states: Ji is lu; what Chu people call "li," Qi people call "zhi." The Guangya says baizhi's leaves are called yao. The Western Mountains Classic says: at Mount Hao, its grasses include much yao. Wang Yi's commentary and Guo Pu's notes say ji and ji are the same; lu, which the Chuci calls lushanglucao (a fragrant herb). The Huainanzi, "Wuxun" chapter, says the body suffers from autumn herbs beaten by high winds; Gao You's commentary says ji is baizhi, a fragrant herb.

The Chuci mentions baipú, also called Fuli; Chu people call it Guan. Fengpu and rong are similar, and the Mingyi mistakenly merged them into one. Or, the Shuowen separately has the entry "E-fuli," meaning li is the superior form. These are not one single herb. Sheren (a commentator) says baizhi, according to the Mingyi also called Guan, seems to be what the Erya calls xiuguan. The Wuxun chapter says the body suffers in autumn herbs under high winds; Gao You says ji is baizhi. The Shuowen separately gives "E-fuli," meaning li is the superior — what Chu people call li, that is to say…

Fuli has not yet been fully clarified; the old text wrote it as "zhi," which is incorrect.

吳普曰．紫草節赤．二月花．窠御
名醫曰．生硭山及楚地三月采根陰乾．
案說文云．此草也．貌爾雅云．菤草也．此草也可以染留黃廣雅云．此蒀．此草也．山海經云．勞山多此草．郭璞云．

七一
translation:
Wu Pu says: Zicao (Lithospermum/gromwell) has purple-red nodes; it flowers in the second month, growing in clusters.

The Renowned Physicians say: It grows in Mang Mountain and in the Chu region; roots are gathered in the third month and dried in the shade.

According to the Shuowen, this plant is called "ci cao." The Erya describes its appearance. The Guangya calls it "yun" and notes it can be used to dye a留-yellow color. The Shanhaijing states that Lao Mountain has much of this plant. Guo Pu says...

Baijiang (Patrinia/败醬): flavor bitter, balanced. It governs sudden heat, fire sores, red-flush conditions, scabies and itching, abscesses and hemorrhoids, saddle sores, and heat qi. One alternate name is Luchang. Grows in river valleys.

The Renowned Physicians say: Also called Lushou, Macao, and Zebai. Grows in Jiangxia; roots are gathered in the eighth month and sun-dried.

According to Fan Zi's Jiran, Baijiang comes from the Sanfu region. Tao Hongjing says its smell resembles rotten sauce, hence the name.

Baixian (Dictamnus/白鮮): flavor bitter, cold. It governs wind in the head, jaundice, vomiting and dribbling urination, swelling and pain inside women's genitals, damp-obstruction causing dead flesh so that one cannot bend or extend limbs or walk. Grows in river valleys.

The Renowned Physicians say: It grows in Shanggu and Wanju; roots are gathered in the fourth and fifth months and dried in the shade.

According to Hongjing, it is commonly called "white sheep's fresh" or sometimes "white lian."

Suanjiang (Physalis/酸醬): flavor sour, balanced. It governs heat and vexed fullness, steadies the will, benefits qi, facilitates the water passages, and eases difficult labor; discarding the fruit alone can hasten delivery. One alternate name is Kujiang. Grows in river marshes.

Wu Pu says: It grows in Jingchu and in people's gardens; gathered in the fifth month and dried in the shade.

The Renowned Physicians say: It grows in Jingchu and in people's home gardens; gathered in the fifth month and dried in the shade. In Jiangdong it is called Kuzhao.

According to the Erya, Guo Pu notes that what is now called Suanjiang grass is called Kuzhao in Jiangdong.

Zishen (Salvia/紫參): flavor bitter, acrid, cold. It governs accumulations and gatherings in the heart and abdomen, cold-heat evil qi, opens the nine orifices, and promotes urination and defecation. One alternate name is Mumeng. Grows in mountain valleys.

Shennong Bencao Jing, Volume Two
71

神農本草經卷二
七〇
translation:
[Ranunculus/Stone Dragon Rui] grows along the banks of rivers, streams, and beside rocks.
Wu Pu says: Long Rui (Stone Dragon Rui) is also called Jiang Ku, also called Tian Dou; Shennong classifies it as bitter and balanced; Qibo says sour; Bian Que and Master Li say greatly cold; Lei Gong says salty and non-toxic. Harvested on the fifth day of the fifth month.
The Mingyi Lu says: it is also called Shi Neng, also called Peng Gen, also called Tian Dou; grows on Tai Mountain; the seeds are harvested on the fifth day of the fifth month; bark is harvested in the second and eighth months and dried in the shade.
According to Fan Zi Ji Ran: Stone Dragon Rui comes from the Three Adjuncts region; the yellow-colored specimens are the finest.

Mao Gen (Imperata/cogon grass root): flavor sweet, cold. Principally treats overwork injury, consumptive weakness; tonifies the center and augments qi; eliminates fatigue, blood obstruction, cold and heat; promotes urination. Its sprouts principally move water downward. Also called Lan Gen, also called Ru Gen. Grows in mountain valleys and open fields.
The Mingyi Lu says: also called Di Guan, also called Di Jin, also called Jian Du; grows in the Chu region; roots are harvested in the sixth month.
According to the Shuowen: Mao means Ying (a type of grass); Ying is Mao. The Guangya says: Jian is Mao. The Erya says: Bai Hua (white-flowered) is wild Jian; Guo Pu notes that Jian belongs to the Mao type. The Odes say: "White-flowered Jian, white Mao bound." The Mao Zhuan commentary says: Bai Hua is wild Jian; once warmed it becomes Ying.

Zi Wan (Aster tataricus): flavor bitter, warm. Principally treats coughing and counterflow of qi, fullness in the chest with cold and heat, bound qi; eliminates gu toxin; treats wilting and paralysis; calms the five viscera. Grows in mountain valleys.
Wu Pu says: Zi Wan is also called Qing Yuan. [Source: Imperial览]
The Mingyi Lu says: also called Zi Qian, also called Qing Yuan; grows in Fang Ling and in Zhen Ding and Han Dan; roots are harvested in the second and third months and dried in the shade.
According to the Shuowen: Wan — this Wan comes from Han Zhong in Fang Ling. Tao Hongjing says: the white variety is called Bai Wan. The Tang Ben annotation says: Bai Wan is the same as Nü Wan. The Imperial Lan quotes the text as: also called Di Xue (earth blood); grows...

Zi Cao (Lithospermum/gromwell): flavor bitter, cold. Principally treats evil qi in the heart and abdomen, the five types of jaundice; tonifies the center and augments qi; opens the nine orifices; frees the waterways. Also called Zi Dan, also called Zi Mie. [Imperial Lan quotes the text as: no text; earth blood; grows...] Grows in mountain valleys.

Shennong Bencao Jing, Volume Two
70

水萍
一類
名水萍。味辛寒。主暴熱身痒。作浴湯文。類聚此是。初學記。下水氣勝酒。長須髮。作烏薑類聚。消渴。久服輕身。一名水華。攷藏

名引云。水廉。生池澤。一名水蘇。一名水澤。水上葉員小。一莖。一葉根入水五月華白。三月采日乾。御覽

吳普曰。水萍。廣雅云。藻萍也。夏小蘋大萍也。廣雅云。藻萍也。暴乾。

案說文云。郭璞云。萍也。無根。水中浮萍。水而生者。萍也。褒大萍也。廣雅云。藻萍也。夏小蘋大萍也。范子計然曰水。

名醫曰。一名水白。一名水蘇。生雷澤。三月采乾。

萍出三輔。色青者善。淮南子原道訓云。萍樹根于水。高誘云于大蘋也。傳云小蘋大萍也。正云七月漫漫生萍而雅。

云萍萍。郭璞云。水中浮萍。江東謂之萍。又其大者蘋。毛詩云于以采蘋。傳云大蘋也。范子計然曰水。

王瓜味苦寒。主消渴。內痹血。月閉。寒熱酸疼益氣。俞聾。一名土瓜生平澤。

名醫曰。生魯地野及人家垣墻閉。三月采根陰乾。

案說文云。賣王賣也。廣雅云。廡菇瓤王瓜也。夏小郷元云。正云四月王賣秀爾雅云。鉤廡菇郭璞云。鉤瓤也。鄧王瓜也管子。

一名王瓜。實如瓤。正赤。味苦月令王瓜生。郷元云。五沙其種大黃細蒼白莖青秀以蔓本草圖經云。大賣孔穎達即王賣也。苾亦謂之土瓜。

地員篇剝土之次曰五沙。其種大黃細蒼白莖青秀以蔓本草圖經云。大賣孔穎達即王賣也。苾亦謂之土瓜。

自別是一物。

地榆味苦微寒。主婦人乳痓痛七傷帶下病。止痛除惡肉。止汗療金創。御覽引本草。主消酒作。又字云。明而目。

目無明。生山谷。

神農本草經 卷二

七三
translation:
Water Duckweed (Shui Ping)

Category: One name is Shui Ping (water duckweed). Flavor: acrid, cold. Governs: sudden fever, body itching; used in bath decoctions. Reduces water-qi, overcomes alcohol. Promotes growth of hair and beard. Also used for wasting-thirst. Long-term use lightens the body. Another name: Shui Hua (water flower). [Reference: Kao Cang]

Also named:引yun Shui Lian. Grows in ponds and marshes. Another name: Shui Su. Another name: Shui Ze. Leaves on water are round and small. Single stem, single leaf, roots enter water. Flowers white in the fifth month. Harvest in the third month, dry in the sun. [Imperial览]

Wu Pu says: Shui Ping. Guangya states: Zao Ping (algae-duckweed). Summer: small Ping; large: Da Ping. Guangya states: Zao Ping. Dry in the sun.

Commentary from Shuowen: Guo Pu says: Ping. Without roots. Floating duckweed in water. Those that grow on water: Ping. Large ones: Da Ping. Guangya: Zao Ping. Summer small Ping, large Da Ping. Fan Zi Ji Ran says: water [duckweed].

The physician's record says: Another name Shui Bai. Another name Shui Su. Grows at Leize. Harvest in the third month, dry.

Ping comes from Sanfu region. The green variety is best. Huainanzi, Yuandao chapter says: the Ping tree roots in water. Gao You notes: the large Ping. Commentary says small Ping and large Ping. Zheng Yun: in the seventh month duckweed grows abundantly on the water, as noted in the Erya.

Commentary: Guo Pu says: floating duckweed in water. People east of the Jiangnan call it Ping. The large ones are called Bin. The Mao Odes says: go gather the Bin. Commentary: large Bin. Fan Zi Ji Ran says: water [duckweed].

---

Wild Cucumber (Wang Gua)
Flavor: bitter, cold. Governs: wasting-thirst; internal impediment with blood; menstrual blockage; fever and chills with aching pain; benefits qi; deafness. Another name: Tu Gua. Grows in flat marshes.

The physician's record says: grows in the wilds of Lu region and along the walls of homes. Harvest roots in the third month, dry in the shade.

Commentary from Shuowen: Wang Gua. Guangya: it is also called Wang Gua. In summer the Xiao Zheng says: in the fourth month Wang Gua blooms. Erya says: Gou Lou, Guo Pu notes: Gou Rang. Also called Wang Gua. Pipe-master text [Guanzi].

One name: Wang Gua. Fruit like a gourd-shape, bright red. Flavor bitter. Monthly Ordinances: Wang Gua grows. In the fifth month, its variety has large yellow, fine pale, blue-green stems, spreading on vines. Bencao Tujing says: Da Mai, Kong Yingda notes it is Wang Mai. Also called Tu Gua.

The Di Yuan chapter on stripping soils says: fifth-grade sandy soil; its plant variety is large yellow, fine pale, blue-green stems, spreading on vines. Bencao Tujing says: Da Mai, Kong Yingda says it is Wang Mai. Also called Tu Gua.

Separately, this is a distinct item.

---

Burnet-Bloodwort (Di Yu)
Flavor: bitter, slightly cold. Governs: women's breast convulsions and pain, seven injuries, vaginal discharge disease. Stops pain, removes malignant flesh. Stops sweating. Treats metal-wound injuries. [Imperial览citation from Bencao.] Also governs dispelling alcohol intoxication. [Another character gloss]: clarifies the eyes.

Target [also noted]: no eye-brightening. Grows in mountain valleys.

Shennong Bencao Jing, Volume 2

Page 73

神農本草經 卷二

吳普曰伏蒙。一名紫參。一名泉戎。一名音腹。一名伏蒐。一名重傷。神農黄帝苦。李氏小寒。生河西山谷
或宛句商山圓聚生根黄赤有文皮黒中紫五月花紫赤實黒大如豆三月采根本。御覽。節交。大觀

名醫曰。一名衆戎。一名童腸。一名馬行。生河西及宛句三月采根。火炙使紫色

案范子計然云紫參出三輔赤青色者善

鑒本味辛温。主婦人疝瘕陰中寒腫痛腹中急除風頭痛。長肌膚說顔色。一名鬼卿。一名地新生山谷。

名醫曰。一名微蕈生崇山。正月二月采根暴乾三十日成。

案廣雅云。山莛蒿香蕈本也管子地員篇云五月根暴乾三十日成。蘭茸蕈本。漸于蜜醴。一佩

易之。樊光注爾雅云山莛蒿香蕈本一名糞蕪根名靳芷舊作蕪非。蔞根云臭嗜生蕈本茍子大略篇云蘭茸蕈本。漸于蜜醴。一佩

石韋味苦平。主勞熱邪氣五癃閉不通利小便水道。一名石鱉。生山谷石上。

名醫曰。一名石皮生華陰山谷不聞及人聲者良二月采葉陰乾

蔛韋味苦平。主腰背痛強骨節風寒溼周痹惡創不瘳熱氣生山谷

名醫曰。一名赤節生真定八月采根暴乾

案博物志云菝葜與草薢相亂身熱肢滿忽忽不知人。狂惑邪氣寒熱酸姑温瘧洗洗發作有時生川谷。

白薇味苦平。主暴中風身熱肢滿忽忽不知人。狂惑邪氣寒熱酸姑温瘧洗洗發作有時生川谷。

名醫曰。一名白幕。一名薇草。一名春草。一名骨美生平原三月三日采根陰乾
translation:
Shennong Bencao Jing (Divine Farmer's Classic of Materia Medica), Volume 2

Wu Pu says: Fu Meng — also called Zi Shen, Quan Rong, Yin Fu, Fu Sou, and Chong Shang. According to Shennong and the Yellow Emperor it is bitter; according to Master Li it is slightly cold. It grows in the mountain valleys of Hexi, or at Yuanju and Shangshan. It grows in clusters with yellow-red roots that have a patterned skin, dark purple inside. It flowers in the fifth month with purple-red flowers, and bears black fruit as large as beans. The roots are collected in the third month. [Cited in: Yu Lan, Jie Jiao, Da Guan.]

The Mingyi says: Also called Zhong Rong, Tong Chang, and Ma Xing. It grows in Hexi and Yuanju; collect roots in the third month and roast over fire until they turn purple.

According to Fan Zi Jiran: Zi Shen comes from Sanfu; specimens with red-blue color are the best.

Jian Ben: Taste is acrid, warm. It governs women's hernias and lumps, cold swellings and pain in the yin region, acute abdominal pain; it eliminates wind headache, enriches the skin and flesh, and improves complexion. Also named Gui Qing and Di Xin. Grows in mountain valleys.

The Mingyi says: Also called Wei Rong; grows at Chongshan. Collect roots in the first and second months, dry in the sun for thirty days until ready.

According to Guang Ya: Shan Ting hao, Xiang Rong, Ben — these are all one thing. The Guanzi "Di Yuan" chapter says: In the fifth month collect the roots and dry in the sun for thirty days. The orchid-rush plant, when soaked in honey-wine, becomes a single sachet.

Fan Guang, annotating the Erya, says: Shan Ting hao, Xiang Rong — also called Fen Wu root, or Jing Zhi; the old text wrote it as Wu incorrectly. Lou root: has a rank smell, grows with Rong; Master Xun's "Da Lue" chapter also says: The orchid-rush plant soaked in honey-wine makes a single sachet.

Shi Wei (Pyrrosia): taste bitter, neutral. It governs fatigue with pathogenic heat, the five types of urinary blockage, promotes urination and clears the water passages. Also called Shi Bie. Grows in mountain valleys on rocks.

The Mingyi says: Also called Shi Pi; grows in the mountain valleys of Huayin where human voices cannot be heard. Collect leaves in the second month and dry in the shade.

Hu Wei: taste bitter, neutral. It governs lumbar and back pain, strengthens the bones and joints, and treats wind-cold damp bi-obstruction, malignant sores that will not heal, and heat qi. Grows in mountain valleys.

The Mingyi says: Also called Chi Jie; grows at Zhending. Collect roots in the eighth month and dry in the sun.

According to Bowu Zhi: Baqia and Bi Xie are easily confused. [Symptoms include] fever, fullness in the limbs, stupor with loss of consciousness, manic confusion, pathogenic qi, alternating cold and heat with aching and sourness, warm malaria with chills that come in recurring bouts. Grows in river valleys.

Bai Wei (Cynanchum atratum): taste bitter, neutral. It governs sudden stroke with body fever, fullness in the limbs, stupor with loss of consciousness, manic confusion, pathogenic qi, alternating cold and heat with aching and sourness, warm malaria with chills that come in recurring bouts. Grows in river valleys.

The Mingyi says: Also called Bai Mu, Wei Cao, Chun Cao, and Gu Mei. Grows on the plains. Collect roots on the third day of the third month and dry in the shade.

名醫曰生漢中二月八月采根陰乾。
棠范子計然云防已出漢中旬陽。
款冬花味辛溫主欬逆上氣善喘瘠諸驚癎寒熱邪氣。一名覺吾石。御覽作一名顆凍。御覽冬作一名虎須。
款冬味辛溫主欬逆上氣善喘瘠諸驚癎寒熱邪氣。一名免奎生山谷。
吳普日一名氏冬生常山及上黨水傍。十一月采花黄白。聚文類
名醫曰一名款冬十二月花黄白。
棠廣雅云苦萃款凍也爾雅云寬笑顆凍郭璞云款冬也紫赤華生水中。西京雜記云款冬華于嚴冬。
傅咸款冬賦序曰仲冬之月。氷凌積雪凍郭璞款冬獨敷華豔。
牡丹味辛寒主寒熱中風痙瘈瘲邪氣除癥堅瘀血留舍腸胃安五臟療癰創。一名鹿韭一名鼠姑。
生山谷。
吳普日牡丹神農岐伯辛李氏小寒。雷公桐君苦無毒黄帝苦有毒藥如蓬相植根如柏黑中有核二。
月采八月采日乾人食之輕身益壽御覽。
名醫曰生巴郡及漢中二月八月采根陰乾。
棠廣雅云白渧牡丹也范子計然云牡丹出漢中河内赤色者亦善。
馬先蒿味平主寒熱鬼注中風澄痹女子帶下病無子。一名馬屎蒿生川澤。
神農本草經卷二
七五
translation:
The Eminent Physicians say: it grows in Hanzhong; roots are gathered in the second and eighth months and dried in the shade.
Fan Zi Jiran says: Fangji comes from Hanzhong, Xunyang.
Kuandong Flower: flavor acrid, warm. Governs cough with counterflow qi, wheezing, various fright epilepsies, cold-heat, and pathogenic qi. Another name is Juewushi [per Yulan]. Yulan gives "dong" as an alternative; another name is Keleng; another name is Huxu.
Kuandong: flavor acrid, warm. Governs cough with counterflow qi, wheezing, various fright epilepsies, cold-heat, and pathogenic qi. Another name is Miankui. Grows in mountain valleys.
Wu Pu says: another name is Shidong; grows in Changshan and Shangdang near water. Flowers in the eleventh month, yellow and white. [Source: Juwen Lei]
The Eminent Physicians say: another name is Kuandong; flowers in the twelfth month, yellow and white.
Guangya says: bitter stalks are frozen-kuandong; Erya says: Kuanxiao is Keleng; Guo Pu says: Kuandong, the purple-red flower grows in water. Xijing Zaji says: Kuandong flowers in the depths of winter.
Fu Xian's "Ode to Kuandong Flower" preface says: in the middle of winter, ice and snow pile up and freeze, yet Kuandong alone spreads its brilliant flowers.
Tree Peony (Mudan): flavor acrid, cold. Governs cold-heat, wind stroke, tetanic spasm, convulsions, pathogenic qi; eliminates abdominal masses, static blood lodged in the intestines and stomach; calms the five viscera; treats abscesses and wounds. Another name is Lujiu; another name is Shugu. Grows in mountain valleys.
Wu Pu says: Mudan — Shennong and Qibo say acrid; Li says slightly cold; Lei Gong and Tong Jun say bitter, non-toxic; Huangdi says bitter, toxic. The herb resembles artemisia; the root resembles cypress bark, black inside with two kernels. Gather in the second month and eighth month, dry in sunlight. People who eat it become light in body and prolong their lifespan. [per Yulan]
The Eminent Physicians say: grows in Bajun and Hanzhong; gather roots in the second and eighth months and dry in the shade.
Guangya says: Bai Di is Mudan. Fan Zi Jiran says: Mudan comes from Hanzhong and Henei; the red-colored ones are also good.
Maxianhao: flavor neutral. Governs cold-heat, ghost-injection [consumptive] disorders, wind stroke, impediment bi-syndrome, women's vaginal discharge, and infertility. Another name is Mashihao. Grows in streams and marshes.
Shennong Bencao Jing, Volume Two
75

神農本草經 卷二

名醫曰生桐柏及冤句二月八月采根暴乾花子紫黑色如鼓故名玉鼓一名落首生池澤

寒廣雅云菰除地榆也陶宏景云葉似榆而長初生布地而花子紫黑色如鼓故名玉鼓一名落首生池澤

澤漢味苦寒主癰瘤氣頸下核破散結氣癰腫瘡疽堅氣腹中上下鳴下十二水腫一名落首生池澤

案醫曰一名瀾生東海七月七日采暴乾

案說文云澤水草也或作藻廣雅云海藻也爾雅云齊東食之或曰澤葉似蘺而大生水底也亦可食

生海中本草云又澤石衣郭璞云水苔也一名石髮江東食之或曰澤葉似蘺而大生水底也亦可食

澤蘭一名龍棗一名水香神農黃帝岐伯桐君酸無毒李氏溫生下地水傍葉如蘭二月生香赤節四葉

虎蘭吳味苦徵溫主乳婦內衄御覽血作中風餘疾大腹水腫身面四肢浮腫骨節中水金創癰腫創膿一名

吳普曰澤蘭一名龍棗一名水香神農黃帝岐伯桐君酸無毒李氏溫生下地水傍葉如蘭二月生香赤節四葉

名醫曰虎蘭澤蘭也

案廣雅云虎蘭澤蘭也一名虎蒲生汝南三月三日采陰乾

防己

吳普曰木防已一名解離一名解燕神農辛黃帝岐伯桐君苦無毒李氏大寒如芬蒸蔓延如芃白根

案味辛平主風寒溫瘧熱氣諸癎除邪利大小便一名解離二月八月十月采根御覽作石解引云大觀本六字通瀹理生川谷
