translation:
Shennong Bencao Jing, Volume 2

[Entry: Yugu / Luoshou (Sargassum seaweed)]
According to physicians: grows at Tongbai and Yuanju; roots are gathered in the second and eighth months and sun-dried. The flowers and seeds are purple-black, like a drum, hence the name Yugu ("Jade Drum"); another name is Luoshou; grows in lakes and marshes.

[Entry: Haizao (Sargassum / sea algae)]
The Guangya says: "Gu" refers to removing [impurities]; Tao Hongjing says the leaves resemble elm leaves but are longer; the plant first grows spread along the ground; flowers and seeds are purple-black like a drum, hence "Yugu"; another name is Luoshou; grows in lakes and marshes.

Taste: bitter, cold. Governs: scrofula and tumors, lumps below the neck, breaks up and disperses accumulations, carbuncles and swellings, hard masses, rumbling above and below in the abdomen, and twelve kinds of water-swelling [edema]. Another name: Luoshou. Grows in lakes and marshes.

According to physicians: another name is Lan; grows in the Eastern Sea; harvested on the seventh day of the seventh month, sun-dried.

According to the Shuowen: ze (澤) is an aquatic plant; also written as zao (藻). The Guangya says it is sea algae (haizao). The Erya says people in Qi's east eat it; some call it ze; leaves resemble water-chestnuts but are larger; grows on the water bottom; also edible.

Grows in the sea. The Bencao says it is also called Ze Shiyi; Guo Pu says it is water-moss (shuitai); another name is Shifa; people in the Jiangdong region eat it; some call it ze; leaves resemble water-chestnuts but are larger; grows on the water bottom; also edible.

[Entry: Zelan (Lycopus lucidus, bugleweed)]
Another name: Longzao; another name: Shuixiang. Shennong, Huangdi, Qibo, and Tongjun all rate it as sour, non-toxic. Li's [pharmacopoeia] says: warm; grows in lowlands near water; leaves like orchid; sprouts in the second month with fragrant reddish nodes and four leaves.

[Entry: Hulan]
Wu Pu says: taste bitter, slightly warm. Governs: postpartum internal bleeding, wind ailments, residual disease, great abdominal water-swelling, swelling of the body, face and four limbs, water in the joints and bones, metal-wound carbuncles and swellings, and festering sores. Another name: [Hulan].

Wu Pu says: Zelan — another name Longzao, another name Shuixiang; Shennong, Huangdi, Qibo, Tongjun [rate it as] sour, non-toxic; Li's [pharmacopoeia] says warm; grows in low-lying ground near water; leaves like orchid; in the second month produces fragrant reddish nodes with four leaves.

[Where the branches and nodes meet, it opens.]

Physicians say: Hulan is the same as Zelan.

According to the Guangya: Hulan is Zelan; another name is Hupu; grows in Runan; harvested on the third day of the third month; dried in the shade.

[Entry: Fangji (Stephania tetrandra)]
Wu Pu says: Mu Fangji — another name Jieli; another name Jieyan. Shennong: acrid. Huangdi, Qibo, Tongjun: bitter, non-toxic. Li's [pharmacopoeia]: greatly cold; like fragrant vines spreading and extending, like lush white roots.

According to [another source]: taste acrid, balanced. Governs: wind-cold, warm malaria, heat-qi, all types of epilepsy; expels evil [pathogenic factors]; promotes urination and defecation. Another name: Jieli. Roots are gathered in the second, eighth, and tenth months. [The Yulan quotes from Daguanben with six characters, referencing "penetrating and regulating"; grows in river valleys.]

The exterior is yellow and resembles platycodon root; the interior is black and resembles the spokes of a carriage wheel. Roots gathered in the second and eighth months.

text:

The Mingyi [Supplementary Physicians' Records] states: The Wu name is Zigong grass; the Chu name is Wangsun; the Qi name is Changsun; also called Huangsun, Huanghun, Haisun, and Manyuan. It grows west of the sea and around the city walls of Runan.

Commentary: Tao Hongjing says that prescribers today all call it Wanghun, also called Zhuangmeng.

Shu Yangquan: Flavor bitter, slightly cold. Governs baldness of the head, malignant sores with heat qi, scabies, crusted sores, and worm-caused tooth decay. Grows in river valleys.

The Mingyi states: Also called Yangquan; also called Guan. Grows in Shujun.

Commentary from the Guangya: Qiugu, Aidan, Luhe, Zechi — also the Tang Ben annotation states: this herb is also called Qizhan.

Wei Zhuang: Flavor salty, cold. Governs lumbar and spinal pain with inability to lie flat, difficulty bending and straightening, removes heat; can be prepared as a decoction. Grows in river valleys and fields.

Wu Pu states: Jue Zhuang, also called Jue Luan. [Imperial览reference]

The Mingyi states: Grows in Hanzhong.

Commentary: A separate annotation states that people today call it Xiangsu (fragrant perilla).

Wu Pu states: Jiasu, also called Shushi, also called Jiangjie. [Imperial reference] Also called Jingjie; leaves resemble chenopodium but finer; grows in Shu; annotation from the Shu text, now moved.

The Mingyi states: Also called Jiangjie; grows in Hanzhong.

Jiasu: Flavor acrid, warm. Governs cold-heat conditions, scrofula, lymphatic nodules, fresh sores, breaking up accumulations of qi, dispersing static blood, and eliminating abscesses and swellings. Also called Shuming. Grows in river marshes. [Formerly in the Rong section, now moved.]

Commentary: Tao Hongjing says this is Jingjie. "Jiang" and "jing" sound similar — it was originally in the herbs section, and people eat it, so it was recorded in the vegetables section.

Qiaogen: Flavor sweet, cold, and plain [bitter, plain per the Imperial览version]. Governs dispelling heat qi below, replenishing yin essence, brightening the face and eyes; long-term use lightens the body and resists aging. Grows in level marshes. [Formerly in the Tang text, now moved and retired.]

Physicians say: It grows in Nanyang.
According to the Shuowen, "Wei" is the male mugwort (Artemisia). The Guangya says it is also called Luma xian. The Erya calls it "Wei, the male qiao." Guo Pu says: it bears no seeds. The Shijing says "not wrapped in wei"; the commentary says: wei, the male [plant].
According to the Shuowen, wei is male mugwort. The Guangya says it is also called Luma xian.
It is sour. Lu Ji says: it begins to grow in the third month; it flowers in the seventh month; the flowers resemble sesame but are purplish-red; in the eighth month it forms pods, the pods resemble small beans, pointed and long. One name is Maxinhao. Note: "xin" and "sheng" are phonetically close.

Jixuecao (Centella). Flavor: bitter, cold. Governs great heat, malignant sores, carbuncles and festering wounds, spreading sores, reddened and inflamed skin, bodily heat and fever. Grows in river valleys.
Physicians say: grows in Jingzhou.
Tao Hongjing says: people of Jing and Chu call it Diqiancao (ground-coin herb) because its leaves resemble coins. Xu Yi's Yaotu names it Lianqiancao (linked-coins herb). The Bencao Tujing says it is also found in Xianyang and Luoyang, and is sometimes called Hu[mint]...

Nüwan [and other entries follow with editorial notes on the source texts]
Wu Pu says: flavor pungent, warm; governs wind with shivering sensations, cholera, benefits the intestines, borborygmus moving up and down without fixed location, fright epilepsy, alternating chills and fever, and a hundred ailments. Grows in river valleys or on the sunny side of mountains.
Physicians say: another name is Baiwan; another name is Zhinüwan. [Source: Yulan]
According to the Guangya, Nücháng and Nüwan are the same.
Physicians say: one name is Baiwan, one name is Zhinüwan, one name is Mao. Grows in Hanzhong; harvested in the first and second months; dried in shade.

Wangsun. Flavor: bitter, balanced. Governs evil qi of the five viscera, cold-damp impediment, aching and sourness of the four limbs, stagnant cold pain. Grows in river valleys.
Wu Pu says: Huangsun, also called Wangsun, also called Manyan, also called Gongcao, also called Haisun. Shennong and Leigong [classify it as] bitter, non-toxic; Huangdi [classifies it as] sweet, non-toxic. Grows in the mountain valleys of the Western Sea and in Runan, spreading along city walls, with red-veined stems and leaves arranged in matching pairs. [Source: Yulan]

translation:
Shennong Bencao Jing, Volume 2

Wu Pu states: Qiao-gen (Forsythia root) — according to Shennong and Leigong, it is sweet and toxic. Gathered in the third and eighth months. Used to prepare steamed preparations and medicinal wine for patients with illness. [Good for] comfort.

The Mingyi (Eminent Physicians' Record) states: It grows in Songgao. Gathered in the second and eighth months.

Note: Tao Hongjing says that this drug is no longer used in prescriptions, and the common people do not recognize it. Among the right-hand section of the middle-grade items, there are forty-nine species, formerly forty-six. Examining the Rong section, Jiasu and the Tang Bencao retire it; Qiaogen should be placed here.

Mulberry root bark: Flavor sweet, cold. Mainly treats internal injury, the five labors, the six extreme deficiencies, emaciation and wasting, uterine bleeding with pulse exhaustion; supplements deficiency and augments qi. The leaves mainly eliminate cold and heat and promote sweating. Mulberry ear (fungus), the black variety, mainly treats female uterine discharge.

Red and white fluids, blood diseases, conglomerate accumulations; supplements yin, balances yin and yang, [treats] cold and heat, and childlessness. The five wood-ear fungi, called "rou," augment qi, prevent hunger, lighten the body, and strengthen the will. Grows in mountain valleys.

The Mingyi states: Mulberry ear is also called Sang Jun (mulberry mushroom) and Mu Mai (wood wheat). It grows on chickens [meaning unclear; likely refers to a specific environment]. Gather in the sixth month during periods of heavy rain and immediately dry in the sun.

Shuowen (Dictionary) notes: Mulberry is what silkworms eat. The mushroom is a wood ear. The chicken-mushroom — Erya says: gather in the sixth month during heavy rains and dry immediately. Sang Xun — Guo Pu says: nowadays commonly called the female mulberry tree, which is small with long branches. Also called pressed mountain mulberry — Guo Pu says it resembles mulberry wood.

Guo Pu says: [it] distinguishes the ox-half. Also, the female mulberry-willow-branch mulberry — Guo Pu says: supple and with drooping branches.

Used in making bows and also as wedges. Mulberry-sophora-stalk — Guo Pu says: nowadays people call the small mulberry tree with long branches the female mulberry; also pressed mountain mulberry — Guo Pu says it resembles mulberry wood.

Bamboo leaves: Flavor bitter, balanced. Mainly treats coughing with counterflow qi, overflowing sinews with urgency, malignant sores, and kills small parasites. The root, prepared as a decoction, augments qi, relieves thirst, and supplements the lower qi. The juice mainly treats wind-induced stiffness and convulsions. The flesh opens the spirit and brightens the mind, lightens the body and augments qi.

The Mingyi states: Grows in Penzhou.

Shuowen notes: Bamboo grows in winter; it is the commander of grasses. The form resembles drooping — the lower drooping parts are the joints.

Evodia fruit (Wu Zhu Yu): [Reference to Yulan encyclopedia citation] Flavor acrid, warm. Mainly warms the center, descends qi, stops pain, [treats] coughing with counterflow, cold and heat; eliminates stagnant blood and painful obstruction, expels wind pathogen, opens the interstices. Prepared as a decoction it is beneficial. The root kills [parasites/worms] — three [varieties/doses].

translation:
The Celebrated Physicians say: It is also called Qin Pi (Ash bark), also called Shi Tan. It grows in Lujiang and Yuanju. The bark is gathered in the second and eighth months and dried in the shade.
Investigating the Shuowen dictionary: the character "sha" refers to a blue-barked tree, also written as "zha." The Huainan Zi, chapter "Jia Zhen Xun," says: the sha tree and the bitter li tree grow in the mountains. One strips the bark and soaks it in water; the liquid turns green and is used to wash the eyes, curing cloudiness and film over the pupils. According to Wu Pu, the color of the sha bark gives its name "Qin Pi." The Classic writes it as Qin Pi; later people changed it to a common name, which became the current form.

Qin Pi (Ash Bark)

Zanthoxylum (Qin Zhu): flavor acrid, warm. Governs wind-evil qi, warms the center, eliminates cold impediment, strengthens the teeth, brightens the eyes. Long-term use lightens the body, improves complexion, promotes endurance into old age, and connects one to the spirit. Grows in river valleys.

Investigation of the Shuowen: grows on Mount Tai, the Qin range, or Langye. The spent ones resemble husks, the cooked ones resemble zhuyu. Gathered in the eighth and ninth months.
The Celebrated Physicians say: grows on Mount Tai, the Qin range, or Langye. The spent ones resemble husks, cooked ones resemble olive-zhuyu. Gathered in the eighth and ninth months.

Guo Pu says: the seeds resemble pepper but the leaves are finer, a grass-like plant. The Erya says: the large-fruited pepper tree is called "gan." Also, pickled pepper vegetables — Guo Pu says:
Investigating the Shuowen: the zhuyu clusters form pod-like structures. In Jiangdong it is also called zheng yu. It resembles zhuyu but is smaller, with red hairy clusters; the large-fruited variety is called "gan." The Classic of Mountains and Seas, Jing Shan entry, says there is much Qin pepper on Jing Shan.
Resembles zhuyu with needle-like thorns; the leaves are hard and smooth. Shu people make tea from it; Wu people make ming (tea); both blend and steep the leaves for fragrance. Fan Zi Ji Ran's Tradition says: pepper and liao... Lu Ji says: the pepper tree.
The fine-leafed variety is good. The Huainan Zi, chapter "Jian Xun," says Shen Jiao and Du Hao are what beautiful women carry at their waists. The old text writes "jiao," but checking the Classic of Mountains and Seas, which records Qin pepper growing in Jian Jing Shan, the identification is not certain.

Evodia (Qin Zhu): flavor sour, balanced. Governs evil qi below the heart, alternating cold and heat, warms the center, expels cold-damp impediment, eliminates three worms. Long-term use lightens the body. Also named Shu Zao (Sichuan date). Grows in valleys.

Wu Pu says: Cornus officinalis (Shan Zhu Yu). Also named Ba Shi, also named Shu Shi, also named Ji Zu. According to Shennong, Huangdi, Lei Gong, and Bian Que: sour, non-toxic. According to Qi Bo: acrid. One classic says sour. Or grows in Yuanju, Langye, or Donghai, Cheng County. Leaves resemble plum leaves with thorny hairs. Flowers in the second month like apricot blossoms. Fruit in the fourth month resembles sour dates; turns red. Fruit gathered in the fifth month. [Source: Imperial览]

Shennong Bencao Jing, Volume Two

Shennong Bencao Jing, Volume 2

Wu Gu (elm fungus): Its fruit — Guo Pu states: "Wu Gu is the elm mushroom (gu yu). It grows in the mountains; the leaves are round and thick. Peel the bark, steep it together. Its flavor is pungent and fragrant." This is what is called wu yi (fermented elm paste). Fan Zi Ji Ran states:

Wu Yi: When it grows in the ground with a red center, it is the best quality. It governs great wind lodged in the skin manifesting like hemp-seed or bean-sized painful itching. Removes cold-heat accumulation, stops dysentery. Builds muscle, benefits the five viscera, augments qi.

Zhi Shi (unripe bitter orange): Flavor bitter, cold. Governs great wind lodged in the skin like hemp-seeds or beans with bitter itching. Removes cold-heat accumulation, stops dysentery.

Wu Pu states: Zhi Shi — Lei Gong says: sour, non-toxic. Li's [Canon]: greatly cold. Harvested in the ninth and tenth months, dried in the shade.

Growing in river marshes.

The Mingyi states: Zhi Shi is bitter. Lei Gong says: sour, non-toxic. Li's [Canon]: greatly cold. Harvested ninth and tenth months, dried in the shade.

Commentary: Shuowen says: "Zhi is a tree resembling the orange." The Zhouli states: "When the orange crosses the Huai River it transforms into zhi." Shen Kuo's Mengxi Bitan states: "In the Six Dynasties period and before, medical prescriptions only used zhi shi; no one used zhi ke. Later people used the small, young fruit as zhi shi and the large as zhi ke."

Hou Po (magnolia bark): Flavor bitter, warm. Governs wind-stroke, cold damage, headache, alternating chills and fever, fright palpitations, qi and blood obstruction, dead muscle (anesthesia), eliminates three worms.

Wu Pu states: Hou Po — flavor bitter, warm, non-toxic. Li's [Canon]: slightly warm. Grows in Jiaozhi. Another name: hou po.

Mingyi states: Another name used by Shennong, Qi Bo, and Lei Gong — pu, non-toxic. The tree is called zhen. Guangya says: "Zhen bark is hou po." Also: "Double bark is hou po." Its seed is called zhu sheng. Fan Zi Ji Ran states: Hou Po comes from Hong Nong. By current popular usage, zhen is used as a vegetable; it is not clear whether this is correct.

Commentary: Shuowen says: "Pu is a tree." Zhen is a wood; the character is written with the wood radical.

Qin Pi (ash bark): Flavor bitter, slightly cold. Governs wind-cold marsh impediment, washing-washing chills, removes heat, blue-green nebula and white membrane in the eyes. Long-term use prevents the hair from turning white, lightens the body. Grows in valleys.

Wu Pu states: Qin Pi, also called Qin Pi. Astringent impediment, washing chills. Shennong, Lei Gong, Huangdi, Qi Bo: sour, non-toxic. Li's [Canon]: slightly cold. Or grows near water at Ku Ju. Harvested in the second and eighth months.

translation:
The seedling era: this is not truly the same thing. The Classic says: Tianmen Dong (Asparagus tuber) is also called Dian Le. Since "Le" and "Ji" are close in form, people today use this herb, which is not without reason.

Longan (Dragon Eye Fruit). Flavor: sweet, balanced. Main uses: treats evil qi of the five viscera, calms the mind, relieves poor appetite. Long-term use strengthens the hun-soul, sharpens hearing and eyesight, lightens the body, prevents aging, and opens the spirit. Also called Yi Zhi (Intelligence-boosting). Grows in mountain valleys.

Wu Pu says: Longan is also called Yi Zhi and Yao Shu, and also called Bi Mu. [Imperial citation]

The Famous Physicians say: the large ones resemble the Chinese hemp palm. They grow on pine trees in the South Sea region. Harvested in the fifth month and dried in shade.

Commentary from Guang Ya: Yi Zhi is longan. Liu Da's annotation to the Wu Du Fu says longan resembles lychee but is smaller and round like a pellet. Its flavor is sweeter than lychee. It is offered as tribute from the mountain valleys of Cangwu, Jiaozhi, and the South Sea.
People in the mountains also cultivate it.

The Famous Physicians say: flavor bitter and balanced. Main uses: treats anger and evil qi, stops night sweats and headache, and treats cold abscess conditions in women's yin region. Also called Nü Luo (Female Luo). Grows in mountain valleys.

Song Luo (Usnea lichen). Flavor: bitter, balanced. Main uses: treats anger and evil qi, stops night sweats and headache, treats cold abscess conditions in women's yin region. Also called Nü Luo. Grows in mountain valleys.

Commentary from Guang Ya: Nü Luo. The Mao Shi says: "Diao and Nü Luo together" — the commentary says Nü Luo is dodder. Lu Ji says: Song Luo twines up pine branches and is deep green, similar to dodder.

The Famous Physicians say: grows on Xiong'er Mountain.

Wei Mao (Euonymus alatus). Flavor: bitter, cold. Main uses: treats women's flooding and spotting with blood below the abdomen, treats fullness and sweating, dispels evil, kills ghost toxins and gu poison. Also called Gui Jian (Ghost Arrow). Grows in mountain valleys.

Wu Pu says: grows on Huo Mountain; harvested in the eighth month and dried in shade. Also called Wei Mao. Shennong, the Yellow Emperor, and Tong Jun all say: bitter, non-toxic; leaves resemble those of peach; shaped like feathers. Harvested in the first, second, and seventh months, dried in shade. Also grows in open fields. [Imperial citation]

The Famous Physicians say: Gui Jian is also called Shen Jian. Tao Hongjing says: its stems have three wing-like ridges shaped like arrow feathers.

Commentary from Guang Ya: Gui Jian is also called Shen Jian. Tao Hongjing says...

[Section on] Si (Dodder variants)

He Huan (Albizia, Silk Tree). Flavor: sweet, balanced. Main uses: calms the five viscera, benefits the heart and will. [The Imperial encyclopedia editions record it as harmonizing heart qi and the will and heart qi.] Makes people joyful and free from worry. Long-term use lightens the body, brightens the eyes, and fulfills one's wishes. Grows in mountain valleys.

Shennong Bencao Jing, Volume Two
Page 83

名醫曰。一名雞足。一名魁實。生漢中及琅邪兗句。東海承縣。九月十月采實。陰乾。
紫葳味酸鹹。御一覽作微寒。主婦人產乳餘疾崩中。癥瘕血閉寒熱羸瘦胎生川谷。
帝甘無毒。如麥根黑正月八月采。或生貞定。覽御一名武威。一名瞿麥。一名陵居腹。一名鬼目。一名茇華神農雷公酸岐伯辛扁鵲苦鹹黃。
吳普曰紫葳。
名醫曰。一名陵苕。一名麦華。生西海及山陽。
棠廣雅云。此葳陵苕遺麥也。爾雅云。苕陵苕。郭璞云。一名陵時。本草云。又黃華薰。白華茇。郭璞云。苕、華、
色異名亦不同。廣雅合而唐本注引術云之華傳云。苦陵苕也。爾雅四字謂即陵雷花出三輔。陵璣以為鼠尾疑皆非故不采之。李當之云。是瞿麥根據李說。
與廣雅合而唐本注引術有一名陵雷四字謂即陵雷花出三輔。陵璣以為鼠尾疑皆非故不采之。
猪
吳普曰。猪苓甘平主疥瘙解毒盡注蚣御寬注有作。一名祥利水道久服輕身耐老。能覽老。作一名猳豬屎生山谷。如伏苓八月采。可以治渴。
名醫曰。生衡山及濟陰兗句。馬彭注作宛囿句。一名猪鹼。生川谷。
棠莊子云家零司。山陰龐注作二月八月采陰乾。猪苓根似猪卵。
白棘味辛寒。主心腹痛癰腫潰膿止痛。一名棘鍼。生川谷。
名醫曰。一名棘刺。生雍州。
棠說文云。棘小棗叢生者爾雅云。髭顫棘采炎云。一名白棘。李當之云。此是酸棗樹鍼。今人用天門冬
translation:
Shennong Bencao Jing, Volume Two

The Mingyi [Supplementary Physicians' Records] states: Also called "Chicken's Foot" and "Kui Fruit." Grows in Hanzhong and Langye, Yanzhou district, Dongguo, and Chenxian county of Donghai. The fruit is harvested in the ninth and tenth months and dried in the shade.

Ziwei [Campsis grandiflora, Trumpet Creeper]: Taste is sour and salty (one edition records slightly cold). It governs women's postpartum residual ailments, uterine flooding, abdominal masses and accumulations, blood obstruction, alternating cold and heat, and emaciation. Grows in river valleys.

The emperor [note]: non-toxic. Resembles wheat-root and is black. Harvested in the first and eighth months, or found growing in Zhending. Also named Wuwei, Qumai, Lingjufu, Guimu, and Baihua. Shennong and Lei Gong classify it as sour; Qibo as acrid; Bian Que as bitter and salty; and [one note] yellow.

Wu Pu states: Ziwei.
Mingyi states: Also named Lingshao and Maihua. Grows in Xihai and Shanyang.

The Guang Ya [dictionary] says: This is the Weitiao Lingshao, also called Maiye. The Er Ya says: Shao is Lingshao. Guo Pu says: Also called Lingshi. The Bencao says it also has yellow flowers and fragrant white flowers. Guo Pu says: Shao has flowers. The names differ widely across sources.

Both the Guang Ya and the Tang Ben Zhu [Tang commentary] cite the term "Linglei" (a four-character phrase meaning Linglei Flower, produced in Sanfu). Lingji identifies it as mouse-tail grass, but this is probably wrong, so it has not been collected. Li Dangzhi says it is the root of Qumai, and according to Li's account it agrees with the Guang Ya.

Zhu Ling [Polyporus umbellatus, Pig Sclerotia]:
Wu Pu states: Zhu Ling is sweet and balanced in nature. It governs scabies and itching, resolves toxins, and eliminates [harmful influences]. Also named Xiangli. Taken long-term it lightens the body and prolongs the capacity for hard work in old age. Also called Jia Zhu Shi [pig dung]. Grows in mountain valleys. Resembles Fuling [Poria]. Harvested in the eighth month. Can treat thirst.

Mingyi states: Grows in Hengshan and Jiyinyan county. Also named Zhu Jian. Grows in river valleys.

The Zhuangzi and other texts say it is a type of zero-[fungus]. It grows in the mountain yin areas. Harvested in the second and eighth months; dried in the shade. The Zhuling root resembles a pig's testicle.

White Jujube Thorn [Bai Ji, Ziziphus spine]:
Taste is acrid and cold. Governs heart and abdominal pain, swellings and abscesses, rupture of pus, and relieves pain. Also named Ji Zhen [thorn needle]. Grows in river valleys.

Mingyi states: Also named Ji Ci [spine]. Grows in Yongzhou.

The Shuo Wen [dictionary] says: Ji is a small date that grows in thickets. The Er Ya says: Zi Zhan Ji [bristle jujube]. Some records say it is also called Bai Ji. Li Dangzhi says: This is the spine of the sour jujube tree. People today use Asparagus root [Tianmendong] instead.

八五
translation:
Antelope Horn (羊角): Flavor: salty, cold. Main uses: brightens the eyes, boosts qi, arouses yang, dispels bad blood and downward flooding, wards off gu toxins, evil ghosts, and inauspicious influences, calms the heart qi, prevents nightmares and oppressive sleep. Grows in river valleys.
The Mingyi [Supplementary Physicians' Records] states: It grows at Shicheng and Huayin Mountain. Collected at any time.

Commentary: The Shuowen says: "Li is a large sheep with slender horns." The Guangya says: "Beautiful hide, cool horns." The Erya says: "The ling is a large sheep." Guo Pu says: "The ling sheep resembles a sheep but with large, round, sharp horns, preferring to live on mountain cliffs." Tao Hongjing says: The Erya name is shan. The Guangya says beautiful hide and cool horns. The Erya says the ling is a large sheep. Guo Pu says the shan resembles the Wu-sheep but with large horns projecting outward.
In western regions it is called bi, the correct character in the Bencao Classic is ling, which is in fact the character li written in common form. This should properly be written li. Guo Pu's Erya commentary says: the shan resembles the Wu-sheep but with large horns projecting outward.

Rhinoceros Horn (犀):
The Mingyi states: Grows in Yongchang and Yizhou.
Flavor: bitter, cold. Main uses: counters the hundred toxins, worm infestations, evil ghost miasma qi, kills the poisons of gou-wen plant, zhen-feather poison, and snake venom; eliminates confusion, delusion, and oppressive dreams. Long-term use lightens the body. Grows in mountain valleys.

Commentary: The Shuowen says: "The rhinoceros is an ox from south of the frontier, with one horn on the nose and one horn on the top of the head, resembling a pig." The Erya says the rhinoceros resembles a domestic pig. Guo Pu says: It looks like a water buffalo with a pig's head, large belly, and short legs.
It has three hooves, is dark in color, and has three horns — one on the nose, one on the top of the head, one on the forehead; the one on the nose is the feeding horn, small and not projecting outward; it likes to eat thorns. There are also single-horned varieties. The Shanhai Jing says: On Gu Mountain there are many white rhinoceroses. Guo Pu says: These are all different species from the bi-cold, chu-nu, bi-chen, bi-shu, and other types of rhinoceros horns. Fan Zi Ji Ran says rhinoceros horn comes from Nanjun.
Top grade priced at eight thousand, middle grade at three thousand, lower grade at one thousand.

The above: seven items of medium-grade animal substances, same as the old [classification].

Xi (熙) Dung: Flavor: acrid, neutral. Main uses: treats gu toxins, ghost-possession ailments, expels inauspicious qi, breaks the five types of urinary obstruction, promotes urination. Grows in level valleys.
The Mingyi states: Grows on high mountains.
Commentary: The Shuowen says: The swallow (yan) is the primordial bird; it holds cloth in its mouth and distributes it to branch-ends; its tail is like the character for "elephant" (象); it builds nests and avoids the days wu and ji; it is the primordial bird; the people of Qi and Lu call it yi; the name comes from its own call; the character is shaped like the bird's form, also written as [alternate form].
Shennong Bencao Jing, Volume 2
Page 85

八四
translation:
Shennong Bencao Jing (Divine Farmer's Classic of Materia Medica), Volume 2

Physicians say it grows in Yizhou.
Annotation: The Tang Bencao commentary says: some say "He Hun" (closing at dusk) — "Mo" and "Hun" are similar in pronunciation — and Rihuazi calls it "Ye He" (night-closing).
Stone and Wood section, middle-grade products: seventeen entries, same as the old edition.
White Horse Penis: flavor salty, nature balanced. Governs injury to the center, severed pulse, inability of the yin organ to rise, strengthens the will, benefits qi, grows muscle and flesh, fattens and strengthens, produces offspring. Eyes govern fright and epilepsy, abdominal fullness, and festering sores; when slaughtered it is used medicinally. The beard and hooves govern [related conditions].
Egret [herb]: dispels evil qi, scrofula sores, difficult lactation, wards off injury, evil qi, ghost toxins, and gu-poison infestations and inauspicious influences. Grows in flat marshes.
Physicians say it grows in Yunzhong.
Velvet Deer Antler: flavor sweet, warm. Governs bleeding downward of bad blood, cold and heat, fright and epilepsy; benefits qi, strengthens the will, grows teeth, and prevents aging. The hardened antler governs malignant sores, carbuncles and swellings, drives out evil and malign qi, and stagnant blood in the yin region.
Physicians say: the velvet is taken in the fourth or fifth month when the antlers are shed, dried in the shade, and used when dry; the antlers are taken in the seventh month when they are in velvet.
Annotation from Shuowen: the eel antler ... closes downward blocking blood, treats blood accumulations, blood pain, women's vaginal discharge, and replenishes the marrow, fills the bone marrow; long-term use increases longevity and the fat can be used as a medicinal.
Ox Horn Core: flavor salty, warm. Governs blue-green blindness of the eyes, kills itch mites, stops cold diarrhea, wards off evil ghosts and fierce tigers and wolves, stops fright palpitations; long-term use calms the heart, benefits qi, lightens the body. Grows in river valleys.
Physicians say it grows in Hexi and is collected at any time.
Ram's Horn: flavor salty, warm. Governs blue-green blindness, kills itch mites, stops cold diarrhea, wards off evil ghosts, tigers, and wolves, stops fright palpitations; long-term use calms the heart, benefits qi, lightens the body. Grows in river valleys.
Annotation from Shuowen: "Gu" refers to a summer ram; the male is called "Gu." Erya says: the female sheep is called "Gu." Guo Pu says: nowadays people simply use "Zhu" and "Gu" as the names for black and white sheep.
Male Dog Penis: flavor salty, balanced. Governs injury to the center, yin flaccidity with inability to rise, enables strength and endurance, produces offspring, removes the twelve diseases of women's vaginal discharge. Another name is "Dog Essence Fat," which governs brightening the eyes.
Physicians say: collected on the first day of the Fufu period in the sixth month and dried in the shade for one hundred days.

蟹味鹹寒主胸中邪氣熱結痛喎僻面腫敗漆燒之致鼠生池澤。

案說文云蟬又名伏蟬桑蛓即桚字周禮考工記云俗則柞蟬鄭元云柞讀為咋咋然之咋聲大外也說文云諝大。
蟬音同柞今據作柞蟬也舊作蚍蟬別錄云蛀者鳴蟬也殼一名梧。
聲也詩云如蚧傳云蚧蟬即夏小蟬也。朱衡之閒謂之蚧蟬陳鄰之閒謂之蚧蟬泰昏之閒謂之蚧蛻。
之蟬海倡之閒謂之蚧蟬衡方言云楚謂之蚧蟬復育開背而出而玉篇云蛓蟬七月生陶宏景音蛓作笋云癮謂。
蟬毛詩云如蚧傳云蚧蟬即夏小蟬也。朱衡之閒謂之蚧蟬陳鄰之閒謂之蚧蟬泰昏之閒謂之蚧蛻。
蟬是為月令之寒蟬爾雅所云蚍夬唐本注非之也。
蠐螬味鹹微溫主惡血血瘀血療壅作癰氣破折血在脅下堅滿痛月閉目中淫膚青翳白膜一名蠹蟬生。
神農本草經卷二
八七
translation:
The Shuowen Jiezi says: the turtle-shell insect (gui jia chong).

Crab: flavor salty, cold. Governs evil qi and heat accumulation with pain in the chest, facial distortion and swelling. Burning [the shell] drives away mice. Grows in ponds and marshes.

The Shuowen says: found in the waters of the Yi and Luo rivers; collected at any time. The Mingyi says: produced in the Yi and Luo rivers; collected without a fixed season.

The Shuowen says: the clam (bang ge) has no fixed abode. The Erya says: the small clam is the luo (螺). Guo Pu says: it is also called the bie shao (鱉蛸); it resembles a crab but is smaller.

The Shuowen says: [the crab] has two large claws and eight legs, moves sideways, is not a snake or eel. The Erya says: crabs have six joints and two pincers.

Cicada shell: flavor salty, cold. Governs childhood fright epilepsy, night crying, epileptic disorders, and alternating cold and heat. Grows on willow trees.

The Shuowen says: in the fifth month the millet dries out [at the same time the cicada sings].

The Mingyi says: the cicada is the one that sings from exertion.

The Shuowen discusses the various names and pronunciations of the cicada, noting it is also called fu chan (伏蟬) and sang ci (桑蛓); the Zhou Rites Artificer's Record refers to "zuo chan," and Zheng Xuan reads zuo as the sound "zha zha," meaning a loud external sound. The Shuowen glosses it as meaning "great."

The cicada's pronunciation is the same as zuo; the old text wrote it as pi chan. The Bielu says: the singing one is the ming chan (鳴蟬); its shell is also called wu (梧).

Various regional dialects have different names for types of cicada (jie chan, etc.), as recorded in the Shiming, Fangyan, and other sources. The Bencao Jing's Tao Hongjing gives variant pronunciations.

The cicada referred to in the Monthly Ordinances as the "cold-cicada" is identified in the Erya as pi kuai (蚍夬); the Tang edition's note disputes this.

Maggot (qi cao): flavor salty, slightly warm. Governs bad blood, blood stasis, blood clots, swelling and abscesses, broken bones with blood accumulation below the ribs, hard fullness and pain, menstrual blockage, clouding of the eyes with superficial opacities and white membranes. Also called du chan (蠹蟬). Found growing [in the earth].

Shennong Bencao Jing, Volume Two

八六
translation:
Shennong Bencao Jing, Volume 2

[On the swallow:] The Erya calls the swallow "fu"; the Xiazheng says it arrives in the second month, descending — the swallow then gazes about. The commentary says the swallow is the "yi" [second Heavenly Stem]. In the ninth month it ascends; the "yuan bird" — the commentary says the yuan bird is the swallow.

Bat Droppings: Flavor acrid, cold. Mainly treats facial abscesses and swellings, skin that feels washed with pain, intestinal bleeding, breaks up accumulations of cold and heat, disperses fright palpitations. Also called "shuyuan," also called "shigan." Grows in mountain valleys.

The Mingyi says: produced at Hepu; harvested in the tenth and twelfth months.

According to Li Dangzhi: this is the same as the droppings of the flying squirrel. Li says that in the regional speech, the "tianrat" has one name: "liru."

According to the present text of the Fangyan: some call it "laoshu" — but "lao" should be "tian" (heaven); this is a scribal error.

The above are medium-grade items from the Birds category, two kinds, same as the old [classification].

Hedgehog Skin: Flavor bitter, balanced. Mainly treats the five hemorrhoids, genital erosion, bleeding of red and white and five-colored discharge that will not stop, swelling and pain of the genitals radiating to the back, killed by cooking in wine. Grows in river valleys.

The Mingyi says: grows in the hills and fields of Chu; harvested at any time.

According to the Shuowen and Erya: [the hedgehog] resembles the porcupine; sometimes written as "gua." The Guangya says it is the "tiger king hedgehog." The Erya says its fur has spines. Guo Pu says that today it is described as mouse-shaped. The Huainanzi's "Shunxun" chapter...

Wasp Nest: Flavor bitter, balanced. Mainly treats fright epilepsy and convulsions, cold and heat, evil qi, seizure disorders, possession by ghosts, gu poison, intestinal hemorrhoids; excellent for fire-heat conditions. Also called "fengchang." Grows in mountain valleys.

[Note:] Inside the gull's droppings there is a hedgehog.

The Mingyi says: also called "baichuan," also called "fengqiao." Grows on sheep-柯; harvested on the seventh day of the seventh month; dry in the shade.

According to the Huainanzi's Xunlun chapter: a wasp nest cannot contain eggs. Gao You's commentary says: the nest is a hive.

Basket [creature] innards: Flavor salty, balanced. Mainly treats concretions and conglomerations in the abdomen, hard accumulations, alternating cold and heat, removes masses, flesh polyps, genital erosions, hemorrhoids, and malignant flesh. Grows in marshes and ponds.

The Mingyi says: produced at Danyang; harvested at any time.

八九
translation:
The Physicians say: it is found in the Southern Sea, collected without a fixed season.
Commentary from the Shuowen: the horseshoe crab's skin is called "hao," and can be used to make drums. The water insect resembles a gecko and grows large quickly. Tao Hongjing says: the tuo is the shell of the lu.

Chujī (Ailanthus silkworm): bitter, neutral in nature. It governs heart and abdominal evil qi, impotence, and benefits the essence; strengthens the will, promotes fertility, improves complexion, supplements the center, and lightens the body. It grows in river valleys.

The Physicians say: it is found on ailanthus trees in Henei. Collected in the seventh month and sun-dried.

Commentary: the Guangya says the chujiu is the chujī. The Erya says: lun, the heavenly chicken—Guo Pu says it is a small insect with a black body and red head, also called shājī, or alternately chujī.

The Shijing says: in the sixth month the shājī beats its wings. Lu Ji says: the shājī resembles a butterfly but has spotted, multi-layered wings that are bright red; it is sometimes called the "heavenly chicken." In the sixth month it flies and beats its wings.

It makes a rustling sound. The people of Youzhou call it pucuo—this is the same creature.

Huó qūqiāo: salty, cold in nature. It governs bandit wind, retching, stiffness of the sinews, loss of liver function, fright impediment, and spasms and contracture. Another name is língtū; it lives in ponds and marshes.

The Physicians say: another name is shìqiāo; another name is fùqiāo, found on great mountains and in shaded, sandy embankments; collected in the eighth month.

Commentary from the Shuowen: qiāo is a type of snail creature. Ying is another name for the snail shell. The Guangya says: the liying and qiāo-ox and mou-qiāo. The Zhongshan Classic says: Mount Qingyao has many pú-qiāo; Guo Pu says: pú-qiāo is another name for the ox-snail. The Physicians list the snail-ox separately.

[The passage on the qiāo insect and snail references the Shuowen, the Zhouli, and the Erya regarding various names and rites, concluding that it is also called xīyì and lives in river valleys.]

Stone Dragon Lizard (Scincus): salty, cold in nature. It governs evil qi of the five viscera, breaks up stone-strangury, stops bleeding below, and promotes urination and water passages. Also called shǒugōng (wall gecko), also called shíyì (stone skink), also called shí lóngzǐ.

Wu Pu says: the stone dragon is also called mountain dragon-child, also called shǒugōng, also called stone skink. It is found in Pingyang and in the rocky hills of Jingshan. Collected in the fifth month, placed on stones, and dried.

Shennong Bencao Jing, Volume 2

八八
translation:
Shennong Bencao Jing, Volume Two

Physicians' note: Also named Panjì, also named Dūnjì. Found in the interior of He (Henei), taken from manure and compost heaps around human dwellings; those that move backward are the best.

Commentary citing the Shuowen: The character zào (竈) refers to dung beetles (qiānglàng). The Guangya says: wánhuí, cáo, and dung beetles are all the same creature; the qiānglàng and its variant names are noted in the Erya. The soil of dung heaps is where these creatures — called qiān and sāo and qiānglàng — are found, though in different localities different names are used. The Mao Shi (Odes) says: the cricket resembles the qiānglàng; the Commentary says it lives in wood; variant names from eastern dialects are given. The Liezi, "Tianrui" chapter, says the wūzú creature produces the qiānglàng; its shell in the Liang-Yi region is called chán; it moves on its back, swiftly on foot. The Shuowen has no character péng; the character dù is borrowed for it by phonetic resemblance; the character chí is a scribal error.

The root of the qiānglàng: the Bowuzhi (Records of Diverse Matters) states: it is used to treat vaginal bleeding, reddish-white discharge, stoppage of menstrual blood, swelling and pain in the lower yin region, fever and chills, boils and scrofula, infertility; found in pools and marshes.

Physicians' note: Found in the East Sea; gathered at any season.

Cuttlefish bone: flavor salty, mildly warm. Governs: palpitations, concretions and accumulations, persistent hard masses, alternating cold and heat, heavy uterine bleeding and five-colored vaginal discharge in women, pain drawing from the lower abdomen to the genitals, sores, scabies, dead flesh. Found in pools and marshes.

Commentary citing the Shuowen: jì — the cuttlefish — also written as lǐ; the Zuo Si rhapsody mentions the "ink fish." Liu Da's annotation says the cuttlefish has ink inside its belly. Tao Hongjing says this creature is a transformation of the seagull.

Physicians' note: Found in Yingchuan; gathered in the fourth month, taking only those that have died naturally.

White silkworm (dead and stiff): flavor salty. Governs: fright and epilepsy in children, night crying, expels the three worms, removes dark spots and blemishes, makes the complexion good; treats male genital sores. Found in flat marshes.

Note: The mated worm also produces offspring; after mating, the silkworm loses its eyebrows and eyes, is easily injured. Collected and processed; the Yupian writes it as cán zào. It should properly be written as jiāng (stiffened); the character yǒng (奮) is incorrect.

Commentary citing the Shuowen: zào means "producing silk." The Huainanzi, "Shuilin Xun" chapter states: the silkworm eats but does not drink; after twenty-two days it transforms. The Bowuzhi says the silkworm transforms three times; it conceives before mating and after mating does not [continue to eat — text breaks off].

Dried fish (bào yú) scales: flavor pungent, mildly warm. Governs: palpitations, concretions and accumulations, persistent hard masses, alternating cold and heat, heavy uterine bleeding and five-colored vaginal discharge in women, pain drawing from the lower abdomen to the genitals, sores, scabies, dead flesh. Found in pools and marshes.

神農本草經卷二　九一
translation:
Gu (Shennong Bencao Jing, Tang edition note): People in Hanzhong eat it to move qi downward. It is called Shican (stone silkworm), also known as Lufei, also known as Fupan. Formerly written as Lian; the Shu commentary cites this and writes it as Lian.

Wu Pu says: Flavor salty, cold. It governs cold and heat in the abdomen and chest, washing sensations, blood accumulation, concretions and conglomerations, breaks up hard masses, promotes the discharge of blood stasis, and facilitates childbirth. An excellent remedy. Also named Dibie (ground turtle). Grows in rivers and marshes.

The Mingyi (Supplementary Physicians) says: Also called Tubi. Found in Hedong and sandy places, under the walls of people's homes, in damp underground spots. Dried in the sun in the tenth month.

Examination: The Shuowen says it belongs to the Fei category of insects. The Guangya says it is also called Fufei. Guo Pu says it is the same as Changyang. The Mao Shi (Book of Odes) says: "The grass insects chirp" — the commentary says they resemble locusts in varying sizes, with a peculiar sound, greenish color, and like to live among taro plants.

Fuyi (bat): Flavor salty, balanced. It governs dim vision, enabling one to see clearly at night with keen eyesight. Long-term use makes people cheerful and free from worry. Also named Bianfu. Grows in river valleys. Formerly classified under the Birds section, now moved.

Wu Pu says: Fuyi sometimes lives in people's homes. After the Beginning of Summer (Lixia), dry it in the shade. Treats dim vision and enables people to see in the night with a luminous clarity. The Wen Lei classifies Bianfu as living in river valleys.

The Mingyi says: Found on Mount Tai and in people's houses. Harvest after the Beginning of Summer and dry in the shade.

Examination: The Shuowen says it is the Bianfu. The Guangya says Fuyi, Feishu (flying mouse), Xianshu (immortal mouse), and Yougong are all the same. The Erya says Bianfu is also called Fuyi. The Fangyan (Dictionary of Regional Expressions) says: west of the passes, in the Qin and Long regions, it is called Bianfu.

East of the passes: Li Dong's text says it is the Tianshu (sky mouse), also called Feishu or Xianshu. West of the passes, in the Qin and Long regions, it is called Bianfu.

The insect section refers to it as Fuyi, or as the insect Fuyi, also called Laoshu (old rat) or Xianshu (immortal mouse). The Erya classifies Bianfu as Fuyi. The Fangyan says north of the passes, the Yan region calls it Fei.

The above medium-grade entries in the Insects and Fish section total seventeen kinds; formerly sixteen kinds. Examination: the Fuyi from the Birds section should be moved here.

Meireal (plum fruit): Flavor sour, balanced. It governs descending qi, eliminating heat and vexing fullness, calming the mind, pain in the limbs, hemiplegia, loss of sensation, dead flesh; removes dark blemishes and treats malign diseases. Grows in river valleys.

Wu Pu says: Plum fruit — as recorded in the Daguan Bencao, it brightens the eyes and boosts qi. The Wu clan's Bencao and the Daguan Bencao cite it for removing dark blemishes and treating malign diseases. Grows in river valleys.

Shennong Bencao Jing, Volume 2 — 91

translation:
Shennong Bencao Jing, Volume 2

[Regarding various names:] The Shuowen [dictionary] says: "Qiuyin [earthworm], also called Yi; Yi is also called Zhi; Zhi is the gecko — it resembles [a certain] shape. The Zhi on a wall is called Zhi; the Zhi in grass is called Yi." It may also be written as "doctor-lizard" (yi/医), or Yuanrong, or Yuanshe. The Guangya [dictionary] says it is called Ge, Jie, Jiao, Yan, also called Erjia or Lunshen, or it may be called the "snake-doctor." It resembles a gecko but is greenish in color, as large as a finger, fearsome-looking. The Fangyan [dictionary] says it is the "house-guardian." The Book of Odes says "the hu-wei si-zhi is the house-guardian."
The commentary says: The newt, or "house-guardian," is also called Yuanying or Yunshen.
In the regions of Qin, Jin, and Western Xia, Lu Ji says: it may be called "house-guardian" or "snake-doctor"; those found in marshes are called "easy-to-resolve"; in the south of Chu it is called "snake-doctor" or "Rongyuan"; in the east of Qi and the Dai region it is called Rongyuan; in northern Yan it is called Zhuzhi; in the region of Guilin, the large ones that can call out are called "easy-to-resolve," with the alternate name Hunchang; it lives in rivers and marshes.

Wood Silkworm (Mu Can): Flavor bitter, balanced [in nature]. Governs: red and painful eyes, tearing [of the eyes], scabies, blood stagnation, blood closure, fever-and-chills, acid [belching], and infertility. Alternate name: Hunchang. Grows in rivers and marshes.
The Mingyi [Supplementary Physicians' Records] says: produced in Hanzhong; harvested in the fifth month.
The Shuowen says: "Can — a flying insect." The Guangya says: "Lu-can is an insect." This is an abbreviated form. The Huainanzi, chapter on "Equal Customs," says: "Water silkworms become Lu-cong." Gao You [the commentator] says: "This is the green clam." There is also another explanation.

Gu Chong [Mole Cricket?]: Flavor bitter, slightly cold. Governs: blood blockage, expels obstruction, breaks up accumulations in the abdomen, expels blood accumulations below [the abdomen], relieves hard masses, fever-and-chills; promotes circulation through blood vessels and the nine orifices. Grows in river valleys.
The Mingyi says: produced in Jiangxia; harvested in the fifth month; those with blood in the abdomen are best.

Gu Lian [a flying insect]: Flavor salty, cold. Governs: blood blockage, expels malign blood, concretions and conglomerations, fever-and-chills; breaks up accumulations, [relieves] throat blockage, internal cold, and infertility.
Wu Pu says: the Fei Lian insect mainly expels [pathogenic factors]. [Imperial note.]
The Mingyi says: produced in Jinyang and in human dwellings; harvested at the Beginning of Autumn.

Gu Chong [another flying insect]: Flavor bitter and salty, cold. Governs: blood blockage, expels malign blood, concretions and conglomerations, fever-and-chills; breaks up accumulations, [relieves] throat blockage, internal cold, and infertility. [Imperial note.]
The Shuowen says: "Gong — an insect." The Guangya says: "Fei Lu, Fei Lu." The Erya says: "Fei Lu [is the same as] Biao." Ji [璣] says: it is the Fufen, [which has a] foul smell.
The Shuowen says: "Gong Lu — a crab; it is a malodorous insect, [also called] Fuchan." The Guangya says: "Fei Lu, Fei Lu." The Erya says: "Fei Lu [is also] Biao." Ji says: it is the Fufen, [which has a] foul smell.

九三
translation:
The Shuowen commentary says: liang (millet/sorghum) is a fine-grain crop. Sun Yan's annotation to the Erya says: liang is also called liang. Today people in the Guanzhong region call small millet liang-rice.

Shu (glutinous millet) grain: flavor sweet, warm. Its main action is to supplement qi and replenish the center; it generates much heat and may cause irritability. [Note added by Wu Pu, with imperial editorial black characters.]

The Shuowen commentary says: shu — according to Shennong, it is sweet and non-toxic; harvested in the seventh month and dried in the shade. Supplements qi in the center.

Wu Pu says: shu belongs to the he (grain) family but is glutinous. It is planted at the Great Heat solar term. Confucius said shu can be used to make wine; it enters water. The Guangya says shu is like dao (rice) in its cluster form.

The Shuowen commentary says: nian (a non-glutinous type) belongs to the grain family but is not sticky. Planted at Great Heat; overall, it grows through the cyclical signs from chou and yin to mao. It is said this grain is born at si, reaches maturity at you, grows at xu, ages at hai, dies at chou, and dislikes the positions of bing and wu; it is inauspicious at certain times.

The above covers the medium-grade items of the grains section: three kinds as now counted, formerly two kinds. Glutinous millet is not included.

Ling shi (water caltrop fruit): flavor pungent, warm. Its main actions are to brighten the eyes, warm the center, resist wind and cold, drain water qi, and reduce facial and eye swelling; it purges and removes intestinal parasites, and lightens the body. It grows in rivers and marshes.

Wu Pu says: ling shi is also called tian ling, ye ling, and ze ling.

The medical authorities say: it grows at Leize.

Commentary: The Shuowen says ling is a pungent herb. The Erya says it is the dragon-beard water plant. The Guangya says it is the hu-meng ling. Guo Pu says it is commonly called hu-meng ling, the name having shifted from the older term. The Mao Shi (Classic of Poetry) says "in the lowlands there is the swimming dragon," the commentary explaining that long (dragon) refers to the red grass. Lu Ji explains that hu-meng ling is also called ma ling ye (horse-caltrop leaf).

The larger variety, according to Guo Pu, is commonly called hu-meng ling. The Guangya calls it long-xu ma ling (dragon-beard horse-caltrop). It grows in water, reaching over a zhang in height; its tender shoots can be used as tea. The commentary says ling is a water plant.

Ju shi (a fruit/seed): flavor pungent, warm. Its main actions are to heal metal wounds and festering sores, lighten the body, prevent hunger, and resist aging. It grows in flat marshes.

Ci shi (another fruit/seed): flavor pungent, warm. Its main actions are to heal metal wounds and festering sores, lighten the body, prevent hunger, and resist aging. It grows in flat marshes.

Shennong Bencao Jing, Volume Two

translation:
Shennong Bencao Jing, Volume 2

The Illustrious Physicians say: It grows in Hanzhong, is gathered in the fifth month, and dried over fire. According to the Shuowen, "xuan" refers to dried plum and related items, or written as "yao"; "mou" is a sour fruit, and the plum is called "xuan." The Erya says: "mei" and "xuan"; Guo Pu comments that it resembles an apricot and has a sour fruit, thus "mou" is glossed as "mei" (plum). The Liji states that people at the border offered food including large dried plum. The actual dried plum: Zheng says dried plum is "mei." There are also peach-plums and other plums; these are the dried ones. The Mao Shi commentary says plums were preserved as seasoned meat relish for consumption. Holding it in the mouth freshens the breath. Listed among the middle-grade fruits, one variety, same as the old text.

Soybean Yellow Sprouts (Da Dou Huang Juan): According to Shennong, Huangdi, and Lei Gong, it is non-toxic. Gathered at any time, removes dark patches from the face. Combined with Qianhu, Wuhui, Xingren (apricot kernel), Muli (oyster shell), Tianxiong, and mouse droppings mixed with honey — an excellent combination. Does not counteract crow-bean toxicity; should not be used together with Xuanshen or red adzuki bean. [Grows in] level marshlands.

Wu Pu says: Da Dou Huang Juan — according to Shennong, Huangdi, and Lei Gong, it is non-toxic. Gathered at any time, removes dark facial patches. Combined with Qianhu, Wuhui, Xingren, Muli, Tianxiong, and mouse droppings mixed with honey — excellent. Does not counteract crow-bean toxicity; should not be used with Xuanshen or red adzuki bean. Red Adzuki Bean — according to Shennong and Qibo, whether raw or cooked it is cold. Gathered in the ninth month; counteracts crow-bean toxicity; should not be combined with Xuanshen or red adzuki bean.

The Illustrious Physicians say: Grows in great mountains; gathered in the ninth month.
According to the Shuowen: "shu" means beans — the character resembles a bean plant growing. "Tai" means small beans. The Guangya says: large beans are "shu," small beans are "tai." The bean pod is called "jia," the leaves are called "huo." The Erya: Rong Shu. Sun Yan says large beans are also called "shu"; Rong Shu is the lesser variety. The Guangya says: large beans are "shu," small beans are "tai." Bean pods are called "jia," their leaves "huo."

Millet (Su Mi): Flavor salty, slightly cold. Principal use: nourishes kidney qi, removes stomach heat, and boosts qi. Aged millet — according to Shennong and Huangdi, bitter and non-toxic, treats spleen heat and thirst. Millet nourishes kidney qi. [Source: Imperial Compendium]

Wu Pu says: Aged millet — according to Shennong and Huangdi, bitter, non-toxic. Treats spleen heat, relieves thirst and polydipsia, promotes urination. [Note: the character in the Bencao, Wu Pu's text, added in black.]

translation:
Shennong Bencao Jing, Volume 3 (Part 1)

Lower Classic

The Lower Drugs, one hundred and twenty-five kinds, serve as subordinate agents. They mainly treat illness in response to the Earth. Most are toxic and cannot be taken over a long period. Those who wish to expel cold, heat, and evil qi, break up accumulations, and cure disease should look to this Lower Classic.

Shíhuī (lime). Báisù (foxtail millet). Fùzǐ (aconite). Yuānwěi (iris). Cǎohāo (artemisia). Shéhé (snake-joint herb). Qīngxiāngzǐ (feather cockscomb seed). Yīnchén (wormwood). Shānglù (pokeweed). Guǐjiù (may-apple). Wūxī (a moss herb).

Dōnghuī (winter ash). Wūtóu (aconite crown). Dàhuáng (rhubarb). Xuánfùhuā (elecampane flower). Héngshān (dichroa). Jiǎnjùn (a fungus). Guànzhòng (shield fern). Yángtí (sorrel). Yángtáo (a plant). Lùhuò (kudzu relative).

Róngzhǎn, dàyán, lǔyán (varieties of salt). Qiāndān (red lead). Qīngláng­gān (a mineral); varieties include jade, old stone, and refined tin, powdered tin, tin mirror — eight grades in all.

神農本草經 卷二

名醫曰，生魯山。

案說文云，虆荣也葉似韭廣雅云，韭，虆，蒿其華謂之菁爾雅云，虆，鴻蒼，郭璞云，即虆荣也又勁山虆，陶

宏景云，虆竈異物而今其條本經旣無韭以其同類故也。

水蘇味辛微溫主下氣辟口臭去毒辟惡久服通神明輕身耐老生池澤。

吴普曰，芥葅一名雞蘇，一名水蘇，一名勞祖，一名勞祖籠御。

名醫曰，一名雞蘇，一名水蘇，一名勞祖，一名芥葅，一名芥苴生九真七月采。

案說文云，蘇桂荏也廣雅云，蘇荏類故名桂荏方言云，蘇亦荏也。

關之東西或謂之蘇或謂之荏也爾雅云，蘇，桂荏，郭璞云蘇荏類故名桂荏方言云，蘇亦荏也。周之鄭之閑謂之公費，沅湘之南謂之擊其小者謂之蘭茝按蘭藥即香

爾也亦名香藥名醫別出香藥條非今紫蘇薄荷等皆蘇類也名醫俱別出之。

右荣中品三種舊四種考蔰實宜與竈同條今并假蘇宜入草部。
translation:
Shennong Bencao Jing, Volume 2

The Eminent Physicians record: it grows on Mount Lu.

The Shuowen [Jiezi] states: lei (虆) is a type of rong (荣); its leaves resemble chives. The Guangya states: chives (韭), lei (虆), and hao (蒿) — their flowers are called jing (菁). The Erya states: lei (虆) is hongsang (鴻蒼). Guo Pu says: this is what is called lei-rong; it also grows on steep mountains. Tao [Hongjing]...

Tao Hongjing says: lei and zao (竈) are different things, yet the present entries in the Classic do not include chives, because they belong to the same category.

Water Su (水蘇): flavor is acrid, slightly warm. It mainly descends qi, repels bad breath, removes toxins, dispels malign influences; taken over a long time it opens the spirit and mind, lightens the body, and makes one resistant to aging. It grows in ponds and marshes.

Wu Pu says: Jie-zu (芥葅) — also called Jisu (雞蘇), also called Shuisu (水蘇), also called Laozhu (勞祖), also called Laozhu-long (勞祖籠御).

The Eminent Physicians record: also named Jisu (雞蘇), Shuisu (水蘇), Laozhu (勞祖), Jiezu (芥葅), Jieju (芥苴); grows in Jiuzhen; harvested in the seventh month.

The Shuowen states: Su (蘇) is Guiren (桂荏). The Guangya states: Su and Ren are of the same type, hence the name Guiren. The Fangyan states: Su is also called Ren.

East and west of the Guan [pass], some call it Su, others call it Ren. The Erya says: Su is Guiren. Guo Pu says: Su and Ren are of the same type, hence the name Guiren. The Fangyan says: Su is also Ren. In the region of Zhou and Zheng it is called Gongfei; south of the Yuan and Xiang rivers it is called Ji; the smaller variety is called Lanzhi. Note: Lan-herb is the same as xiang (fragrant herb).

It is also called xiangcao (fragrant herb). The Eminent Physicians list xiangcao separately under its own entry. The items listed — purple su, peppermint, and similar plants — are all of the su type; the Eminent Physicians have listed each separately.

The above rong-plants: in the middle grade there are three types, formerly four. Examination shows that the su-shi (蔰實) entry should be combined with the zao (竈) entry. Jiasu (假蘇) is hereby moved to the herb section.

translation:
Supplementary text.

Limestone (石灰): Flavor is acrid, warm. It governs carbuncles, sores, scabies, itching with heat, malignant sores, epileptic disorders, dead flesh, falling eyebrows; kills hemorrhoid worms, removes black moles and polyps. An alternate name is "Malignant-disease [stone]." Found in mountain valleys.

Appended from Wu Pu's Bencao:

The Mingyi (Eminent Physicians) Record says: another name is Xihui; grows in Zhongshan.
Note: "Ehuì" is probably equivalent to "Mohui." The rush and slow forms for Xishi (inkstone).
This stone has an acrid flavor, great heat; governs cold-heat, scrofulous sores, corrosive lesions, dead flesh, wind impediment, abdominal hardness. Another name is Qingfenshi; another name is Lizhishi; another name is Guyangshi. Eliminates heat. The Yulan citation says: kills the hundred [pests].

[Beast/Léi section — text partially damaged or corrupt in source]

Wu Pu says: White Léi-stone. One name: Xiangnong; Qibo says: acrid, toxic; Tongjun says: toxic; Huangdi says: sweet, toxic; Li's record says: grows in Weixing or in Shaoshi, collected in the twelfth month. [Various alternate names follow in the source.]

The Mingyi Record says: another name is White Léi-stone; another name is Salt-food; grows in Hanzhong and Shaoshi; collected at no fixed time.
Commentary: The Shuowen says: léi is a poisonous stone. The Huainanzi "Dixing" chapter says: on Mount Tu there is white stone; Gao You's commentary says this is White Léi-stone. The Shuowen "Lin" chapter says people who eat Léi-stone [will suffer ill effects]. It grows in the western mountains of Hanzhong. The Xishan Jing says: on Mount Gaotu there is white stone called Léi, which can be used to poison rats. Fan Zi Jiran says: Léi-stone comes from Hanzhong; the white variety is best. Gao You says Léi-stone comes from Yinshan. One account says it can kill rats; the Xishan Jing's "poison rat" entry is thus about curing rat-fistulas. The Yulan citation says [it causes] vomiting and purging.

Dead magpies that eat it grow fat; Gao You says Léi-stone comes from Yinshan. One account says heaven produces white Léi after nine hundred years; Gao You says this is White Léi-stone. The Shuowen "Lin" chapter says people who eat Léi-stone [suffer ill effects].

Lead Minium (鉛丹): Flavor is acrid, slightly cold. It governs rebellious qi causing vomiting, epileptic convulsions; eliminates heat, descends qi; when refined and transformed it becomes Jiuguang [nine-radiance elixir]; long-term use penetrates the spirit-mind. One source says long-term use achieves immortality.

The Mingyi Record says: another name is Qianhua; grows in Shu Commandery. Found in level marshes.

translation:
White Chalk (Bai E)
White Chalk. Flavor: bitter, warm. Governs cold and heat accumulations (zheng jia) in women, closed eyes, and lumpy accumulations. Grows in mountain valleys.
Wu Pu says: White Chalk, another name is Bai Shan (White Goodness). [One classical source notes it has another name.]
The Bencao commentary says: The Shuowen [dictionary] records another name as Bai Tu (White Plaster). The Zhongshan Jing [Classic of Mountains] states that the Yusheng mountain has an abundance of White Chalk.
The Mingyi [Eminent Physicians] say: Another name is Bai Shan; grows in Handan; harvested at any time.

Winter Ash (Dong Hui)
Flavor: acrid, slightly warm. Governs dark spots on skin, removal of warts, polyps, blemishes, corrosive sores, and itching. Another name: Li Hui (goosefoot ash). Grows near rivers and marshes.
The Mingyi say: Grows in Fanggu.

Green Coral (Qing Lang Gan)
Flavor: acrid, balanced. Governs itching of the body, burns, abscesses, and injuries, fractures, dead flesh. Another name: Stone Pearl. Grows in level marshes.
The Mingyi say: Another name is Qing Zhu (Green Pearl); grows in Shu Commandery; harvested at any time.
Commentary: The Shuowen records that lang gan resembles pearls; in ancient script written as a variant character. The Tribute of Yu section of the Book of Documents records that Yong Province paid tribute of lang lin gan. Zheng [Xuan] says lang gan is a type of pearl.

The above nine items in the lower-grade Jade and Stone category — formerly listed as twelve — powder lead and refined lead are counted as two; salt from the Rong region, large salt, and brine salt are each counted as one, making three.

Aconite (Fu Zi)
Flavor: acrid, warm. Governs wind-cold, coughing and counterflow of qi, pathogenic influences, warming the middle, metal wounds, breaking up hard accumulations and lumpy masses, blood conglomerations, cold-damp paralysis, cramping and contractions of tendons and joints, and knee pain preventing walking.
The Da Guan edition notes: Aconite, another name Langdu. According to Shennong: acrid; Qibo and Lei Gong: sweet, toxic; Li Shi: bitter, very warm. May be grown in Guanghan. Harvested in the eighth month; skin is black, flesh white. [Noted as] the foremost of all medicines. Grows in mountain valleys.
Wu Pu says: Aconite, another name Langdu. Shennong says acrid; Qibo and Lei Gong say sweet, toxic; Li Shi says bitter, very warm. May grow in Guanghan. Eighth-month harvest, skin black, flesh white.
The Mingyi say: Grows in Jian Wei and Guanghan. Harvest in the eastern mountains in a certain month for Aconite (Fu Zi); harvest in spring for Monkshood (Wu Tou).
Commentary: Fan Zi Ji Ran records that aconite comes from Shu and Wudu; those that are white in color are best.

Shennong Bencao Jing, Volume 3

神農本草經卷三

案說文云。鉛青金也。陶宏景云。即今熟鉛所作黃丹也。
粉錫味辛寒。主伏尸毒螯殺三蟲。一名解錫錟鼻。主女子血閉癥瘕。伏腸絕孕。生山谷。舊作二種。今并一種。

案說文云。錫銀鉛之閉也。
名醫曰。生桂陽。

代赭味苦寒。主鬼注賊風。蠱毒殺精物惡鬼。腹中毒邪氣。女子赤沃漏下。一名須丸。生山谷。

名醫曰。一名血師。生齊國。赤紅青色如雞冠有澤染爪甲不渝者良。朱無時。

案說文云。赭土也。北山經云。少陽之山多美赭。管子地數篇云。山上有赭者其下有鐵范子計。今作黑膽字。結熱。鹵鹽味苦寒。主大熱消渴。

然云。石赭出齊郡。赤色者善蜀出蜀郡。其中和郡縣志云。少陽山在變城縣其地近代也。其下有鐵。

戎鹽主明目。目痛益氣堅肌骨。去毒蠱。大鹽令人吐。御覽引云。大鹽。名寒。覺引云。一名。今作三種。今作井三種。

名醫曰。戎鹽及下蠱毒柔肌膚。明目益氣。大鹽令人吐。御覽引云。大鹽。一名。蕃引云。今作并三種。

郢又謂河東鹵鹽。一名胡鹽。河東鹽生胡鹽山及西羌北地酒泉福祿城東南角北海青南海赤。十月采大鹽生邠。

名醫曰。戎鹽及下蠱毒柔肌膚御石覺明引云金氣一名寒今作并三種。

案說文云。鹽鹹也古者宿沙初作煮海鹽鹵西方鹹地也從西省象鹽形安定有鹵縣東方謂之斥西方謂之鹵。

方謂之鹵鹽。河東鹽池猗氏縣案在山西安邑運城。縣鹽池也今在河東猗氏縣案在山西安邑運城。

五十一里廣七里周百十六里北山經云景山南望鹽販之澤郭璞云即解縣鹽池也今在河東猗氏縣案在山西安邑運城。
translation:
Shennong Bencao Jing, Volume 3

The Shuowen commentary states: Lead (qian) is a blue-gray metal. Tao Hongjing says: This is what is now called yellow lead (minium), made from refined lead.

Powder of tin (fen xi): Flavor: acrid; nature: cold. Governs: hidden corpse toxins, venomous stings, kills the three worms. Also known as "dissolved tin." The nasal preparation governs: menstrual obstruction in women, abdominal masses and accumulations, intestinal stagnation, and infertility. Found in mountain valleys. Formerly listed as two entries, now combined into one.

The Shuowen commentary states: Tin (xi) is a closed form of silver and lead.
The Mingyi says: Found in Guiyang.

Ochre (dai zhe): Flavor: bitter; nature: cold. Governs: ghost infestation and bandit-wind illness, gu toxin, kills malevolent spirits and evil ghosts, abdominal toxin and pathogenic qi, red discharge and uterine flooding in women. Also named xu wan. Found in mountain valleys.

The Mingyi says: Also called xue shi (blood stone). Produced in the state of Qi. It is red-scarlet and blue in color like a rooster's comb, with a lustrous surface that stains the nails without fading — this is the good quality. Zhu: available at all times.

The Shuowen commentary states: Zhe is a red earth. The Northern Mountains Classic says: On the mountain of Shaoyang there is much fine ochre. Guanzi's chapter on Earth Quantities says: Where ochre appears on a mountain, iron ore lies below. Fan zi ji states [this too]. Now written with the character for "black bile." Clears heat.

Lu salt (halite, bitter salt): Flavor: bitter; nature: cold. Governs: intense heat and wasting thirst.

Commentary: Stone ochre comes from Qi commandery and is red in color. The Shu variety comes from Shu commandery. The Harmonious Commandery Gazetteer states: Shaoyang Mountain is in Biancheng county — this locality is from recent times. Below it there is iron.

Rong salt: Governs: brightening the eyes, relieving eye pain, boosting qi, firming muscles and bones, expelling poison and gu. Large salt causes vomiting. As cited in the Imperial览: large salt. A secondary name: Han. Another citation: one name. Current edition: three types combined.

The Mingyi says: Rong salt also expels gu toxin and softens the skin and muscles, brightens the eyes and boosts qi. Large salt causes vomiting. Imperial citation: large salt, one name. Fan citation: currently listed together as three types.

Ying also refers to Hedong lu salt. One name: hu salt. Hedong salt is produced in the Hu Salt Mountain, and also in the western Qiang northern territories, Jiuquan, Fulu city's southeast corner, the northern sea (blue), and the southern sea (red). Harvested in the tenth month. Large salt is produced in Bin.

The Mingyi says: Rong salt also expels gu toxin and softens the skin and muscles. [Imperial citation text] one name cold, current edition combined as three types.

The Shuowen commentary states: Salt is salty. In ancient times Susha first made salt by boiling sea water. Lu refers to the alkaline lands of the west. The character is derived from "west," shaped like the form of salt. Anding has a Lu county. In the east it is called chi; in the west it is called lu.

Western dialects call it lu salt. The Hedong salt lake is in Yi clan county — commentators place this in Yuncheng, Anyi, Shanxi.

The salt lake in Yi clan county (now in Yuncheng, Anyi, Shanxi): fifty-one li wide, seven li across, one hundred and sixteen li in circumference. The Northern Mountains Classic states that from Jing Mountain one looks south toward the Salt Merchant Marsh. Guo Pu says this is the salt lake of Jie county, presently located in Yi clan county, Hedong — identified by commentators as Yuncheng, Anyi, Shanxi.

translation:
The text discusses several medicinal herbs from the Shennong Bencao Jing (Classic of Materia Medica), Volume 3:

The entry on Tianxiong (Aconitum carmichaelii), Wuhui (crow's beak aconite): These are violently toxic drugs, yet skilled physicians use them to save lives.

Half-summer (Banxia, Pinellia ternata): Flavor: acrid, neutral. Main actions: treats cold-damage with alternating chills and fever, hardness below the heart, descends qi, treats throat and pharyngeal swelling and pain, dizziness, chest distension, coughing and counterflow, intestinal rumbling, and stops sweating. Also named "Diwen" and "Shuiyu." Grows in river valleys.
Wu Pu states: It grows alongside Gugu plants, with leaves in pairs of three. It begins growing in the second month, with white flowers. Harvested in the eighth month.
The Annals of Monthly Ordinances state that Banxia sprouts in mid-second month. According to Fan Zi Jiran, Banxia from the Sanfu region is white and of good quality. The biography of Chisongzi states he took Shuiyu to teach Shennong — this is probably an alternate name for Banxia.

Tiger's Palm (Tiannanxing, Arisaema): Flavor: bitter, warm. Main actions: treats heart pain, alternating chills and fever, bound qi, accumulations and gatherings, submerged beam, sinew damage, itching, cramping and limpness, and promotes urination. Grows in mountain valleys.
Wu Pu states: Shennong and Leigong classify it as bitter and non-toxic; Qibo and Tongjun classify it as acrid and toxic. Harvest in the ninth month at the start of autumn, at Taishan.
The Mingyi records: grows in Hanzhong and Yuanju; harvest second and eighth months, dry in shade.

Kite's Tail (Yuanwei, Iris): Flavor: bitter, neutral. Main actions: treats gu toxin, malign qi, ghost-inflicted disease, all toxins, breaks up concretions and accumulations, expels water, and kills the three worms. Grows in mountain valleys.
Wu Pu states: also named Wuyuan; grows at Jiuyi Mountain; harvested in the fifth month.
The Mingyi records: also named Wuyuan Pengsheganye — this refers to two different plants.
The Tang Materia Medica commentary notes: it is completely distinct from Shegan (Belamcanda).

Shennong Bencao Jing, Volume 3

text:

卷三

Shennong Bencao Jing (Divine Farmer's Classic of Materia Medica)
Volume Three

Wutou (Aconite main root): Flavor pungent, warm. Governs wind stroke, aversion to wind with shivering and sweating, eliminates cold-damp impediment, coughing with counterflow qi, breaks up accumulations and gatherings, cold and heat. Its juice, when decocted, is called Shewang and kills birds and beasts. Also named Xidu, Jizi, Wuhui. Grows in mountain valleys.

Wu Pu states: Wutou is also named Langdang, Qiandi, Dugong, Beifuguo [variant: Beiguo]. Another name is Gengzi. Shennong, Lei Gong, Tong Jun, and Huangdi: sweet, has toxicity. It begins growing in the first month; the leaves are thick, the stems grow in fours opposite each other, resembling artemisia. It resembles the head of a crow with two prongs joined together like a crow's beak, hence the name Wuhui. In the tenth month the fruit is reddish; Li's [classification]: greatly cold. In the eighth month it turns red; dry in the shade. This is the large-angled form of Fuzi (accessory root).

Also stated: Wuhui — Shennong, Lei Gong, Tong Jun, Huangdi: has toxicity. Li's [classification]: slightly cold. In the tenth month the shape resembles a crow's head with two prongs joined like a crow's beak, hence it is named Wuhui.

The counteractions and incompatibilities are the same as Wutou. One name is Jianzi, another is Langzi. Shennong and Qibo: greatly toxic. Li's [classification]: greatly cold. In the eighth month dry in the shade. This is the large-angled form of Fuzi.

The avoidances and counteractions are the same as Fuzi. [Original text and commentary follow.]

The Mingyi [Additional Physicians] record: grows on the north side, in the second month the fruit turns red. Dry in the shade. When it grows to three cun or more it becomes Tianxiong. Guo Pu says: it is the same as Wutou; in the east of the Yangtze it is called Langcao. Fan Zi Ji Ran says: Wutou comes from the Sanfu region; the white ones — according to Shuowen, grown in the north. Zhaozhou says it is the Langcao plant. Guo Pu says it is Wutou. Huainanzi Zhushu Xun says: nothing is more dangerous than chicken poison. Gao You's commentary says: chicken poison is Wutou. Note on chickens —

The Guoyu says: Li Ji placed aconite in the meat — "jun" refers to the seedling of this plant. Zhaozhou says it is the Langcao plant. The Mingyi list Cezu (lateral accessory root) as a separate entry, which is incorrect.

The toxicity: what is called "laughing toxin" is also the same as Qianzhuzi and Cezu. The Mingyi listing of Cezu as a separate entry is incorrect.

Tianxiong (Tall Aconite): Flavor pungent, warm. Governs major wind, cold-damp impediment, pain in all the joints, cramping and contracture, breaks up accumulations of evil qi, metal wounds; strengthens sinews and bones, lightens the body, makes one tireless in walking. Also named Baimu. Imperial commentary cites: "Grows yin qi."

Without fatigue, strengthens the will, causes people to increase in martial strength. [Variant of the black-text edition:] grown from strength.

The Mingyi state: grows at Shaoshi [mountain]. In the second month gather the roots, dry in the shade.

Note: The Guangya says: Quju, Tudu, and Fuzi — at one year it is Qianzhuzi; at two years it is Wuhui; at three years it is Fuzi; at four years it is Wutou; at five years it is Tianxiong. [As cited in] the Huainanzi Jing —

Shen Nong's Classic of Materia Medica, Volume 3

[On Jiegeng (balloon flower root):] The Shuowen says: Jiegeng is the name of a medicine. The Guangya says it resembles jiegeng. The Zhanguo Ce says: "Today one seeks bupleurum and finds it by the tomb of Liang's father in the shadow of Que, loading it by the cartful." [But] jiegeng found in marshy lowlands will not be obtained even after many generations. The Erya says: tulu, tulou. Guo Pu says: it resembles qi. According to the Mingyi [Records], this is an alternate name; below there is also a separate tulu entry — but this is not correct.

[Feihao zi (a plant):] Flavor bitter, cold. It governs toothache, expels worms, [treats] flesh sores and cramping, enables a person to walk vigorously, causes one to see ghosts; eating too much makes a person run wildly. Long-term use lightens the body, enables one to run as fast as a galloping horse, strengthens the will, increases strength, and penetrates the spirit. Another name is Hengtang. Grows in river valleys.

The physician's record says: another name is Cifei lan [orchid]. Tao Hongjing says that nowadays apothecaries mostly write it as henjì [thistle], the old form being song.

The Shuowen has no entry for the characters song or hui; the Shiji, in the biography of Chunyu Yi, says...

The Guangya says: Cipei lan orchid. Another name Cixing tang; grows on seashores and in Yongzhou; harvest the seeds in the fifth month.

[A story:] When a noblewoman of Chuanchuan carried a child but could not give birth, she drank [a preparation of] langdang [henbane]; one source in the Bencao Tujing quotes this as langdang.

[Caohao (Artemisia/wormwood):] Flavor bitter, cold. It governs mange and itching, malignant sores, kills insects, expels persistent heat lodged in the joints, and brightens the eyes. Another name is Qinghao; another name is Fangkui. Grows in rivers and marshes.

The physician's record says: grows at Huayin.

The Shuowen says: hao [wormwood], gu [drum]. Commentary and phonetic notes say hao may also be written as lian. The Erya says: hao, gu. Tao Hongjing says: this is today's qinghao; those in the middle of it used for moxibustion with a fragrant smell are gu. The Shiji, in the biography of Sima Xiangru...

[Xuanfu hua (inula flower):] Flavor salty, warm. It governs bound qi, fullness below [the heart], fright palpitations, removes water, opens the five viscera, resolves cold and heat, supplements the middle, and descends qi. Another name is Jinfeicao; another name is Shenghú. Grows in river valleys.

The physician's record says: another name Daihu; grows in flat marshes; harvest the flowers in the fifth month; dry in the sun for twenty days until done.

The Shuowen says: xuanfu is daogeng. The Erya says: xuanfu is daogeng. Guo Pu says: xuanfu resembles chrysanthemum.

Shennong Bencao Jing, Volume 3

[Page] 102

Rhubarb (Da Huang). Flavor: bitter; nature: cold. It principally treats blood stasis, blood blockage with alternating chills and fever, breaks up concretions, accumulations and gatherings, retained fluids and undigested food; it purges and cleanses the intestines and stomach, expels the old and brings forth the new, and frees the passage of water and grain. [The original has the character "Dao" (道).] Below this: regulates the center and promotes digestion. It is at peace with and harmonizes the five viscera. Grows in mountain valleys.

Wu Pu says: flavor bitter, non-toxic; Bian Que [says] bitter, non-toxic; Li's [school says] slightly cold — it is called "General-in-Chief." It grows either in Shu Commandery's northern district or in Long-xi. In the second month flowers appear; the leaves grow red, in sets of four opposite pairs, the yellow artemisia grows to a height of about three feet; in the third month the flowers are yellow, in the fifth month the fruit is black; roots are gathered in the third month — the roots have a yellow juice. Slice and dry in shade.

The Mingyi says: another name is Huang Liang; it grows in He-xi and Long-xi; roots are gathered in the second and eighth months and dried over fire.

Pharmaceutical [note]: The Guangya says "Huang Liang" means the same thing.
[Pharmaceutical note]: The Lanlan section formerly rendered Ting Ting Lan. [Imperial edition.]

Tingli (Lepidium/Descurainia seed). The Guangya says: [Imperial edition.]
The Mingyi says: another name is Xia Li; another name is Guang Hao; gather the fruit after the beginning of summer, dry in shade; it goes well with wine.

Tingli: the Shuowen says it is a grass called Xia Li; the Guangya says it is Gou Hao; it grows at Da Shi; Tingli is also [mentioned in the] Erya; Guo Pu says the fruit and leaves both resemble mustard; the Huainanzi, "Miaocheng Xun" chapter says [something about it].

Tingli cures puffiness/swelling [Zhang]; the Xijing Zaji says Tingli dies in the height of summer.

Balloon Flower root (Jie Geng). Flavor: acrid; nature: slightly warm. It principally treats pain in the chest and flanks as if stabbed by a knife, abdominal fullness, intestinal rumbling with a hollow sound, fright, fear, and palpitations. [Imperial Encyclopedia citation; original text printed in black characters.] Another name: Li Ru; another name: Fang Tu; another name: Bai Yao; another name: Geng Cao; another name: Qi Ju. Grows in tall artemisia thickets; roots are gathered in the second and eighth months and sun-dried.

Wu Pu says: sweet, non-toxic; Li's [school says] greatly cold; the leaves resemble those of Qi Ju, like the tube of a zheng [instrument], purplish-red; sprouts in the second month. [Imperial Encyclopedia edition.]

Lei Gong says: Jie Geng — another name Fu Di; another name Bai Yao; another name Li Ru; another name Lu Ru. Shennong [says] harmonizing, bitter, non-toxic; Bian Que, Huangdi [say] salty; Qi Bo [says] —

The Mingyi says: another name Li Ru; another name Fang Tu; another name Bai Yao; another name Geng Cao; another name Qi Ju. Grows in tall artemisia thickets; roots are gathered in the second and eighth months and sun-dried.
