translation:
The Guangya dictionary says: "Yuanwei" is the same as Shegan (Belamcanda chinensis). In the Xunzi's chapter "Encouraging Learning" it says: "In the west there is a tree called Shegan, its stem four inches long." Fan Zi Ji Ran says the root of Shegan is like [a snake].

Shé (Snake) — the combined character is the word "cāng." [Place: ] Anding.
[Two characters unclear] — Guangsha says: combined.
The Mingyi [Famous Physicians] records: grows in Yizhou; harvested in the eighth month; dried in shade.
According to the Bencao Tujing: some say this is Quepiào (sparrow gourd), which is actually another name for Luómo (Metaplexis japonica). According to Lu Ji, Yuanlan is another name for Luómo; people in Youzhou call it Quepiào, which is the same as the "lǐ" in the Erya. Yuanlan is also found in Tang Bencao, listed separately under Luómo; it is not the same as Nüqing.
Flavor: bitter; nature: cold. Main uses: cold damage with fever, malarial fever, ghost toxin, phlegm accumulation in the chest causing vomiting and reflux. Another name: Hucao. Grows in river valleys.

Hengshan (Dichroa febrifuga)
Wu Pu says: Hengshan is also called Qiye. Shennong and Qibo say it is bitter; Li's classification: greatly cold; Tongjun says it is acrid and toxic. Harvested in the second and eighth months.
The Mingyi records: grows in Yizhou and central Han; roots harvested in the eighth month; dried in shade.
Note: In the Hou Han Shu, the biography of Hua Tuo says Tuo transmitted the Qiye Qingzhan Powder (Lacquer-leaf and Qingzhan Powder): one dou of lacquer leaf shavings and fourteen liang of qingzhan — this is the standard formula. It is said that long-term use eliminates the three worms and benefits the five viscera.

Shu Qi (Dichroa febrifuga aerial parts)
Flavor: acrid; nature: balanced. Main uses: treating epilepsy, rebellious ascending qi, chills and fever, abdominal masses and accumulations, evil qi, qingzhan, ghost toxin. [Note: "zhù" is written as "dǎn" in some editions.] Grows in river valleys.
Wu Pu says: grows as the leaf of Shu Qi; another name is Hengshan. Shennong, Qibo, and Leigong say it is acrid and toxic; the Yellow Emperor says it is acrid; one tradition says it is sour, resembling lacquer leaves and blue-green菁, similar in appearance; harvested in the fifth month.
The Mingyi records: grows in the Jiangling mountains and in the Shu-Han region of central China; it is the sprout of Changshan; leaves harvested in the fifth month and dried in shade.
Note: the Guangya says Hengshan is Shu Qi. Fan Zi Ji Ran says Shu Qi comes from Shu commandery.

translation:
Veratrum album (Lilu)
[From the Shennong Bencao Jing, Volume 3]

Lilu (Veratrum / false hellebore): Taste: acrid, cold. Primary uses: gu-toxin, cough with counterflow qi, diarrhea and intestinal flux, head sores, scabies and itching, malignant sores; kills all gu-parasites and toxins; removes dead flesh. Another name: Cong Ran. Grows in mountain valleys.
It is salty and toxic. Wu Pu says: Lilu — another name is Cong Kui, another name is Feng Lu, another name is Hui Kui. [御覽 citation:] Also called Gong; also called Shan. Shennong and Leigong say it is acrid and toxic. Huangdi says it is toxic. [Qi Bo adds further notes.]
Wu Pu says: another name is Cong Kui; grows on Tai Shan. The Fan Zi Ji Ran says: Lilu comes from Hedong; the yellow-white variety is best. The Erya says: E — mountain onion — grows on Tai Shan. Roots harvested in the third month, dried in the shade. Small [rootlets] connect; roots harvested in the second month.

The Mingyi says: another name is Cong Kui; another name is Shan Cong, grows on Tai Shan. Bianque says it is bitter, toxic, and greatly cold. Leaf and root. [The Yulan] also gives names Gong and Shan.

Gou Wen (Gelsemium / heartbreak grass):
[The Yulan] records an alternate name.

Wu Pu says: Qin Gou Wen — another name is Du Gen (poison root). Taste: acrid, warm. Primary uses: metal-weapon wounds, breast abscesses, chest obstruction, malign wind, cough with counterflow qi, edema; kills ghost-infixation [parasitic spirits causing disease].

The Mingyi says: Grows on Fu Gao mountain and in Kuaiji; roots harvested in the first month.

[Case:] The Guangya says: Tu Si (dodder) is also called Cong Ji.

The Mingyi says: Grows on Fu Gao mountain, and according to the Huainan Zi commentary, if a viper bites a person and you apply this with water-shield (Brasenia), it will heal. People in Gaomen call it "Wen Zang"; it is also called Ye Ge (wild kudzu) from the Ling [mountains]. [Gou Wen is deadly.]

The root [section from] Guangya says: Grows on Fu Gao mountain; the Huainan Zi — Lin Xun chapter — says if a viper bites a person and you apply it with water-shield it heals. People in Gaomen call it "吻葬 (wen zang)" and also call it Wild Kudzu from the mountain range. Kougui (桂心) with onion leaves.

Southerners call it Hu Man; the common name is Duan Chang Cao (intestine-severing herb). This plant is extremely toxic; it is not used medicinally. It is feared that the one listed in the materia medica is a different substance — not this Gou Wen. Other names: Wu Shan (crow fan), Wu Pu (crow reed). Grows in river valleys.

She Gan (Belamcanda / blackberry lily):
Wu Pu says: She Gan — taste bitter, balanced. Primary uses: cough with counterflow qi, throat impediment (laryngitis/pharyngitis), throat pain preventing rest and breathing, disperses urgent qi, abdominal counterflow evil qi, great heat from food and drink. Another name: Wu Shan; another name: Wu Pu. Grows in river valleys.

The Mingyi says: another name is Wu Yu; another name is Wu Chui; another name is Cao Jiang. Grows in the open fields of Nanyang. The root is harvested on the third day of the third month and dried in the shade.

一〇七
translation:
Ruǔ (䕡茹): Flavor salty, neutral. Governs heart pain, warms the interior, eliminates chronic white-patch skin disease (vitiligo), pinworms, snake-bite venom, abdominal masses and various worms. An alternate name is Gǔlú; grows in ponds and marshes.

The Míng Physicians say: It grows in the Eastern Sea and in Bóhǎi, Zhāngwǔ county. Harvested in the eighth month and dried in the shade.

Commentary from the Ěryǎ states: [various philological notes on variant names and textual identifications with Jūlíng or Yīnzhī; the commentator notes uncertainty about which name is correct and declines to settle the question.]

Báijí and Lì: [the Yùlǎn version reads:] Flavor bitter, neutral. Governs swellings, festering sores, injuries to the yin regions, dead muscle tissue, evil qi in the stomach, robber-wind, ghost-strike, and lax, unresponsive impediment. Alternate names: Gāngēn, Liánjícǎo. Grows in river valleys.

Wú Pǔ says: Shennong [classifies it as] bitter; the Yellow Emperor [classifies it as] acrid; Shì [the Elder] as greatly cold; Léi Gōng as acrid and non-toxic. The leaves resemble ginger; the flower of the lí lú opens upward in the tenth month in purple-red color; the root is white. Harvested in the second, eighth, and ninth months.

The Míng Physicians say: It grows in Běishān, Yuānjù, and Yuèshān.

Annotation: The text on Lord Yáng Gōng's method of taking huángjīng says huángjīng is another name for báijí; it is also an alternate name for huángjīng. Today physicians list huángjīng separately.

The Míng Physicians say: Cháng Shān — roots harvested in the twelfth month and dried in the shade.

Dàjǐ (Euphorbia): Flavor bitter, cold. Governs gu toxin, twelve kinds of edema and fullness, acute pain, accumulations and gatherings, wind striking the skin with rash-pain, and vomiting counterflow. An alternate name is Qióngjù. [Textual note: the ancient commentary suggests this entry and the following "grows in river marshes" may originally have been one entry — three characters noted by the editor.]

Commentary from the Ěryǎ: [Guo Pu notes] this is today's medicinal herb Dàjǐ, which expels water. The Huáinánzǐ, "Miùchēng" chapter, also says: Dàjǐ expels water.

Zéqī (Euphorbia helioscopia): Flavor bitter, slightly cold. Governs skin heat, distension of the abdomen, water qi, puffy swelling of the four limbs and face, and insufficiency of male yin qi. Grows in river marshes.

The Míng Physicians say: An alternate name is Qījīng; it is the seedling of Dàjǐ. Grows on Tàishān. Stems and leaves harvested on the third day of the third month and the seventh day of the seventh month, and dried in the shade.

Commentary from the Guǎngyǎ: Tàijīng is Zéqī.

translation:
Shennong Bencao Jing, Volume 3

106

Gan Sui (Euphorbia kansui): Flavor bitter, cold. Governs large-abdomen hernia-masses, abdominal fullness, facial and ocular puffiness, retained fluids and undigested food; breaks up concretions, firm accumulations, and clumps; promotes passage through the water-grain pathway. Another name: Zhutian. Grows in river valleys.

Wu Pu says: Gan Sui is also called Zhutian, Ze, Chongze, Guichou, Linggao, Gangao, and Ganze. According to Shennong and Tongjun it is bitter and toxic; according to Qibo and Leigong it is toxic and requires collection of the root in the second and eighth months, then dried in the shade.

The Mingyi says: Also named Gangao, Lingze, and Chongze; grows in Zhongshan. Root collected in the second month, dried in the shade.

Examination: The Guangya says Lingze is Gan Sui. The Fanzi Jiran says Gan Sui comes from the Sanfu region.

Bai Lian (Ampelopsis japonica): Flavor bitter, neutral. Governs abscesses, swellings, ulcers, and sores; disperses bound qi; stops pain; eliminates heat; redness of the eyes; childhood fright-epilepsy; warm malaria; swelling and pain in women's genitalia. Another name: Mianhe. Another name: Baicao. Grows in mountain valleys.

The Mingyi says: Also named Baigen, also named Kunlun. Grows on Hengshan. Root collected in the second and eighth months, dried in the sun.

Examination: The Shuowen says tu is white and yellow, sometimes written as ji. The Maoshi says ji vine. Lu Ji's commentary says ji resembles the wuluan tree; its leaves are full and fine; its seeds are jet black like swallow droppings and cannot be eaten. People of the secluded regions call it wufu; its stems and leaves are fed to cattle to eliminate heat. The Erya says lu yao biao jiang. Guo Pu says this is uncertain. According to the Pian, yao is white ji. The classic gives "Mianhe" as another name, which sounds close to this and is likely the same plant.

Qing Xiang Zi (Celosia argentea seed): Flavor bitter, slightly cold. Governs pathogenic qi; heat in the skin; wind itching and body pruritus; kills the three worms. Another name: Cao Jueming; treats cracked or discolored lips and mouth. Another name: Caohao. Another name: Qihao. Grows in flat valleys.

The Mingyi says: Grows alongside roads. Leaves collected on the third day of the third month, dried in the shade. Seeds collected in the fifth and sixth months.

Examination: The Weilüe records that during the Chupingzhong period there was an Elder of the Green Ox who regularly took Qing Xiang Zi. The character xiang in the text should be written as xiang (箱).

名醫曰名嵇生陳留。

神農本草經卷三

一〇九
translation:
Master Wu Pu says: Wolf's Tooth (Langya) — also called Zhilan, also called Wolf's Teeth, also called Great Tooth, also called Baozi. According to Shennong and the Yellow Emperor: bitter, toxic. According to Tongjun: or salty. According to Qibo and Lei Gong and Bian Que: bitter. It has no [toxicity noted by some]. Grows in Wanju. Leaves green, roots red. Flowers in the sixth and seventh months, fruits in the eighth month; the fruit is black. Harvested in the first and eighth months; roots are dried in the sun.
The Mingyi records: also called Wolf's Teeth, also called Great Tooth. Grows in Huainan and Wanju. Roots collected in the eighth month, dried in the sun.

Annotation: Fan Zi's Jiran records: Wolf's Tooth comes from the Three Adjunct Regions; the white-colored specimens are the best.

Sheep's Sorrel (Yangti): flavor acrid, nature warm. Governs thieving wind lodged in the skin causing crawling pain, warm-type scabies, and malign toxins and various sores. Grows in valleys.
Master Wu Pu says: Sheep's Sorrel flowers — according to Shennong and Lei Gong: acrid, toxic. Grows in Huainan. Treats thieving wind, malign toxins, and various evil qi.
The Mingyi records: also called Yuzhi. Grows on Taihang Mountain and in Huainan. Flowers collected in the third month and dried in shade.

Guang Ya records: Sheep's Sorrel (Yangti) — its flower is beautiful and bright. The Gujin Zhu records: Sheep's Sorrel flowers are yellow; if sheep eat it they die; if sheep see it their hooves scatter — hence the name Yangti. Tao Hong[jing records]...

Phytolacca (Shanglu): flavor acrid, nature balanced. Governs water swelling, hernia pain, concretions and conglomerations; eliminates abscesses and swellings; kills ghost essences and malign entities. Also called Gegen (Kudzu Root). Also called Yehu (Night Caller). Grows in valleys.
The Mingyi records: The specimens shaped like a human form possess spiritual power. Grows in Xianyang.

Annotation: The Shuowen says Ge herb is called Danglu. In the Zhouyi, Dajun Yun calls it Gelu. Zheng Xuan says Gelu is Shanglu (Phytolacca). The character Ge is simply a borrowed form; its pronunciation is like Ge. Today in Guanzhong it is also called...

Jili (Tribulus) — in Jiangdong it is called Danglu grass; its branches and leaves correspond to each other in value. The Guang Ya records: the common Ge, Mawei Hao — this is also Shanglu. The rustic characters of the merchants use Ge as a loan character with the same pronunciation. Today in Guanzhong it is also called [the same].

Sheep's Sorrel (Yangti): flavor bitter, nature cold. Governs baldness of the head, scabies and itching; eliminates heat; treats female genital erosion. [Note: the following four characters appear without the character "Jue".] Also called Dongfang Su, also called Lian Chong Lu, also called Guimu. Grows in river marshes.
The Mingyi records: also known as Ji; grows in Chenliu.

translation:
Shennong Bencao Jing, Volume 3

Yinyu (Skimmia japonica): Flavor bitter, warm. Governs evil qi of the five viscera, cold and heat in the chest and abdomen, emaciation resembling malaria with episodes at fixed times, wind-damp impediment pain in all the joints. Grows in river valleys.

Wu Pu says: Yinyu — also called Wancao, also called Bigong. Slightly warm, toxic. Shaped like Mangcao but finer and softer.

The Mingyi record says: Also called Wancao, also called Bigong. Grows on Taishan. Leaves are gathered on the third day of the third month and dried in the shade.

Guanzhong (shield fern, Dryopteris crassirhizoma): Flavor bitter, slightly cold. Governs evil heat qi in the abdomen and various toxins; kills three kinds of worms. Also called Guanjie, also called Guanqu, also called Baitou. Also called Hujuan, also called Bianfu.

Wu Pu says: Guanzhong — also called Guanlai, also called Guanzhong, also called Qumu, also called Guanzhong, also called Boqin, also called Yaozao, also called Bianfu, also called Huangcan. According to Shennong.

Grows in mountain valleys.

Qibo: bitter, toxic. Tunjun and Bianque: bitter. One classic says: sweet, toxic. Huangdi: salty and sour. One classic says: bitter, non-toxic. Leaves are yellow, growing in opposite pairs; the black hairs cluster together; green in both winter and summer, never aging.

Flowers in the fourth month, fruit in the eighth month, black, clustered in rows. Roots are gathered in the third and eighth months, seeds gathered in the fifth month in Shao Shi Shan. Roots gathered in the second and eighth months and dried in the shade.

The Mingyi record says: Also called Boping, also called Yaozao. This herb is called Chitou; grows at Yuanshan and at Wanju and Shaoshi Mountain. Guo Pu says: leaves are round and pointed, stems hairy, spreading black along the ground, does not die in winter or summer. Also called Jue.

Commentary: the Shuowen says it is a kind of Mao grass. The Guangya says Guanjie is Guanzhong. Guo Pu in the Erya says Bianfu — stops diarrhea with Guanzhong. Guo Pu in the Erya also says Bianfu — this is the same plant.

Qu (another entry) further says above: Bianfu governs cold damage, warm malaria, the twelve waters, breaks up accumulations and masses, large wall-like abscesses and fistulas, flushes the intestines and stomach, removes lingering food stagnation, cold and heat evil qi, promotes water passages. Grows in river valleys.

Lianhua (Ampelopsis): Flavor bitter, balanced, cold. Governs cold damage and warm malaria.

The Mingyi record says: Grows in Xianyang and at Zhongmu in Henan. Flowers gathered in the sixth month and dried in the shade.

Yazi (wolf's tooth, Agrimonia): Flavor bitter, cold. Governs evil qi, heat qi, scabies and itching, malignant sores and wounds, scabies; expels white worms. Also called Langya. Grows in river valleys.

translation:
The Illustrious Physicians say: another name is "Nai He Cao" [Nahe Herb]. It grows on high mountains and in open fields. Collected in the fourth month.

Commentary: Tao Hongjing says that near the roots there is a white downy covering resembling the white head of a person, hence the name.

Ghost [Gui] Herb
Wu [Pu]: taste acrid, warm. Governs: killing gu-toxins, ghost-possession, spirit-creature infestations; dispels foul qi and inauspiciousness; expels evil and resolves the hundred poisons. One name: Juesi [Sparrow Rhinoceros]. One name: Mamu Dugong [Horse-Eye Poison Duke]. One name: Jiu Yue. Grows in mountain valleys.

The Illustrious Physicians say: another name Tian Yue; another name Jiu Yue; another name Tian Yue; another name Que Xi; another name Mamu Gong. One name: Jie Du [Antitoxin]. Grows in the mountain valleys of Jiuzhen and Yuanju. Collect the roots in the second and eighth months. [Imperial览]

Wu Pu says: one name Jiu Yue. Collect in the second and eighth months. [Imperial览]

Sheep Peach [Yang Tao]
The Illustrious Physicians say: one name Tian Yue; one name Jie Du. Grows in the mountain valleys of Jiuzhen and Yuanju. Collect roots in the second and eighth months.

Wu [Pu]: taste bitter, cold. Governs: sudden fever, body suddenly turning red, wind-water accumulations, malignant sores; eliminates children's fever. Collect in the second month. One name: Ghost Peach. One name: Sheep Intestine. Grows in river valleys.

Commentary: Shuowen says: "Chang Chang Chu, a type of blade-cutting plant." One name Yu Yi; one name Zhi Yi; one name Yang Tao. The Guangya says: grows in mountain forests and open fields, collected in the second month and dried in the shade. One name Ghost Peach. One name Sheep Intestine. Grows in river valleys.

Considered to be: Chu Pi; Zhang Guanya says Chang Chu is a blade-cutting plant; Lu Ji says it is now called Yang Tao [Sheep Peach], or called Ghost Peach. The leaves resemble peach leaves; the flowers are white; the seeds are like small wheat grains, reddish, resembling a peach; the Mao Shi [Book of Odes] says "In the lowlands grows Chang Chu." People today—

The Nong Chu tradition says Chang Chu is a blade-cutting plant. Lu Ji says: today's Yang Tao is this plant. The leaves are long and narrow, flowers purple-red in color; its branches and stems are slender, growing over one foot, trailing as a vine over other plants. People today—

Consider it: mud-irrigated, heavy, and not like a willow. Near the lower root, when cut with a knife, the bark and stem can be roasted in hot ash until they peel off, and can be used to wrap writing-brush tubes.

Female Verdure [Nü Qing]
Wu Pu says: Female Verdure, one name Huo. According to Shennong and Huangdi: warm; repels evil, kills gu-toxins, expels foul evil qi, dispels ghost-fever and malaria, wards off inauspiciousness. One name: Sparrow Gourd. [Imperial览, written as—]

Female Verdure: taste acrid, balanced [ping]. Governs: gu-toxins; expels evil malignant qi; kills ghost-fever and malarial disease; wards off inauspiciousness. One name: Sparrow Gourd. [Imperial览, written as—]

The Illustrious Physicians say: it is the root of She Han [Snake-Embrace herb]. Grows at Zhuyai. Collected in the eighth month, dried in the shade.

Commentary: the Guangya says Female Verdure is Wu Ge. The Erya says Cai Wan Lan is a branch. The tradition says Wan—

The Shuowen dictionary says: "Yu" is an aquatic grass, read like "xu"; xu is an aquatic grass; peng is a stem-type grass. The Guangya says: yu is the sheep's hoof plant (Rumex). The Mao Odes say: "We gather its xu." Commentary notes that the local name is "ox-feeding plant." According to Lu Ji, people today call it "sheep's hoof." Tao Hongjing says people today call it "bald-leaf plant," and it is also referred to in the Odes as "we gather its xu." Some suspect that Lu Ying is the flower of this plant (Sambucus). This herb is also called Lian Chong Lu; Lu Ying is also called Shuo Diao, also named Dong, and is likewise bitter and cold.

Polygonum aviculare (Qiao Xu): Flavor acrid, balanced. Its main uses: treats chronic skin conditions, scabies, itching, jaundice, and hemorrhoids; kills three types of worms. [Commentary citations omitted.] Also named Xu. Grows in mountain valleys.

Wu Pu says: Qiao Xu is also called Xu Bian; also called Qiao Man.

The Mingyi records: grows in Donglai; harvested in the fifth month and dried in shade; also called Qiao Jing.

Commentary notes the Shuowen says Qiao Xu is "yi," growing by water. According to the Erya it is "bamboo yi"; Guo Pu says it resembles small Chenopodium, with reddish stems and nodes, grows well along roadsides and is edible. It also kills worms. The Han Odes and Stone Classic agree.

Langdu (Wolf's Bane, Stellera chamaejasme): Flavor acrid, balanced. Its main uses: coughs with qi rising, breaks up accumulations, treats food stagnation, alternating cold and heat, water retention, malignant sores, rat-fistula, putrefying ulcers, ghost-toxin, gu-poison; kills birds and beasts. Also named Xu Du. Grows in mountain valleys.

The Mingyi records: grows in Qinting and Fenggao; roots harvested in the second and eighth months, dried in shade.

Commentary: The Guangya says Langdu—the word "xu du" appears to have been dropped above. The Zhongshan Jing says that on Mount Dabo there is a plant that resembles a taro but hairy, with green flowers and white fruit, called [Langdu]; if one takes it regularly one will not die young and can cure abdominal ailments.

Baitouweng (Pulsatilla chinensis): Flavor bitter, warm. Its main uses: intermittent fever with madness, alternating cold and heat, abdominal masses and accumulations, goiter-type swelling, drives out stagnant blood, stops pain, heals metal wounds. Grows in the mountain valleys of Song Mountain. Breaks up qi, treats manic cold-heat, stops pain.

Wu Pu says: Baitouweng is also called Wild Old Man and Huwang Shizhe; grows in mountain valleys.

translation:
The commentary states: "Lí" (蘺) means deer-bean plant (鹿藿); it is read like piāo. The Guangya says lí is deer-bean plant. The Erya says lí is deer-bean plant; its fruit and stem — Guo Pu says: this is today's deer-bean (鹿豆); the leaves resemble those of the soybean; the root is yellow and fragrant; it grows as a climbing vine.

Zaoxiu (蚤休): flavor bitter, slightly cold. It governs fright epilepsy with head-shaking and tongue-wagging, heat qi in the abdomen, welling-abscesses and flat-abscesses, sores, genital erosion, kills the three worms, and removes snake venom. Another name: zaoxiu. Grows in river valleys.

The medical commentary states: It grows in Shanyang and Yuanju.

Zheng Qiao notes: Zaoxiu is also called zhexiu, Chonglou Jinxian, Chongtai, and Cao Gansui; today people call it Purple River Chariot (紫河車). Those who take it as a dietary supplement use the stem and leaves, which are also attractive to look at. It is often planted in courtyards.

Shichang-sheng (石長生): flavor salty, slightly cold. It governs cold and heat, malignant sores, fire-heat, repelling ghost-qi and inauspicious influences. The Yulan version reads "dispelling ghost and demon toxic qi." Another name: Dan-cao. The Yulan citation says: grows in mountain valleys. The Yulan Dansha-cao citation says: grows in mountain valleys.

Wu Pu states: According to Shennong, Shichang-sheng is bitter and cold; according to Lei Gong, it is acrid. One classic says it is sweet; it grows in Xianyang.

The physicians state: It grows among the rocks of Chenggu, treating various welling-abscesses and spasms of the four limbs, aching cold pain, genital wilting, shortness of breath and weakness, and leg swelling. Grows in river valleys. The current edition mistakenly writes jiāng (薑). Another name: jí. Grows in fields and wilds; collect leaves in spring and summer, collect in autumn and winter.

Luying (陸英): flavor bitter, cold. It governs welling-abscesses among the bones, spasms of the four limbs, aching cold pain, genital wilting, shortness of breath, weakness, and leg swelling. Grows in river valleys. Current editions write jiāng. Another name: jí. Grows in fields and wilds; collect leaves in spring and summer, collect in autumn and winter.

The physicians state: it grows at Bear Ear Mountain and Yuanju. Collect at the beginning of autumn. They also note: Shuodiao (蒴藋) flavor sour, warm, toxic. Another name: Dancao. Current editions have an error. Another name: jí; grows in fields and wilds; collect leaves in spring and summer, collect in autumn and winter.

The commentary on the Shuowen says: Chén (莀) is a grass, read like hé. Jí is a shoot-grass. The Guangya says: biān and àng are the shoots of Luying. The Erya says jí is a creeping grass, read like jí; it is a kind of sprouting grass. The Guangya says biān and àng are shoots of Luying.

Collect the roots of jǐn (蓳).

It is difficult to call these one single species; they are most likely of the same category. Luying is described as something whose shoots, if one takes biān and àng as its seedlings, are what later people failed to recognize — and so Shuodiao was separately listed. The current commentary says Luying is bitter, cold, and non-toxic, while Shuodiao is sour, warm, and toxic — so the two are clearly not the same.

Lan Cao (orchid herb): Also known as: Lu Ji says it has another name, Mi Mi; people of Youzhou call it Que Piao. TheBie Lu (Supplementary Records) says Que Piao's white juice treats insect and snake bites. This is the juice of the seedling of Nü Qing; the Tang Materia Medica lists it separately.

Luo Mi Tiao: Not [the same].

Lian Qiao (forsythia): Flavor bitter, neutral. Mainly treats cold and heat, scrofula, neck lumps, swellings and malignant sores, goiter and tumors, heat accumulation, and gu toxin (parasitic poisoning). Also named Yi Qiao, also named Lan Hua, also named Yao, also named San Lian. Grows in mountain valleys.

translation:
The Shuowen Jiezi says: "yuan (芫) is a fish poison." The Erya says: "hang (杭) is a fish poison." Guo Pu explains: "Hang is a large tree, resembling chestnut, growing in the south; its bark is thick, its sap red, and it bears fruit enclosing seeds inside." The Fanzi Jiran says: "Guo. Yuan-hua (芫華) comes from the Sanfu region." The Shiji, in the biography of Chunyu Yi, records that a woman in Linzi suffering from worm disease was treated by drinking a preparation of yuan-hua, and worms numbering several sheng were expelled, and the illness was cured. Yan Shigu's commentary on the Jijiu pian says: "Yuan is purely said to refer to the ears." It grows in the south and uses its annual fruit separately. A single hang tree, as mentioned by Zuo Si, refers to the su-hang-lu trees — these are not the fish-poison hang.
The category "Lower-grade herbs" contains forty-nine items, formerly forty-eight. Under the wood section, yuan-hua (芫華) should be placed here.
Bā dòu (巴豆): flavor pungent, warm. It primarily treats cold damage, warm malaria, alternating chills and fever, breaks up concretions, accumulations, hard masses, and retained fluids, thin phlegm, and glomus; treats abdominal distension and water swelling; opens up blockages and obstructions; promotes the passage of water and grain; removes malignant flesh; eliminates ghost poisons, gu toxin, and evil things; kills worms and fish. An alternate name is Ba Shu (巴叔; the Yulan text writes this as jiao [椒]; another text writes it as jiu [救]). The Yulan citation adds: "It exercises the five viscera and six bowels, opens passages, and promotes the flow of water and grain through the body."
Wu Pu says: Bā dòu, another name Ba Shu Jun. Flavor pungent. Toxic according to the Yellow Emperor; sweet and toxic according to Master Li. It primarily warms and heats cold conditions. The leaves resemble those of the large bean; harvested in the eighth month and dried in shade.
The Mingyi says: it grows in Ba Commandery; harvested in the eighth month, dried in shade; remove the heart and skin before use.
The Guangya says: "Ba Shu is bā dòu." The Huainanzi, in the "Forest of Persuasions" chapter, says: "Fish eat bā dòu and die; people eat it and grow fat." The Fanzi Jiran likewise says: "Fish that eat bā dòu die; humans who eat it grow fat."
Shǔ jiè (蜀芥): flavor pungent, warm. It primarily treats pathogenic qi and coughing counterflow; warms the center; expels cold from the joints, skin, and dead muscle; relieves cold damp impediment pain; moves qi downward. Long-term use prevents the hair from turning white, lightens the body, and prolongs life. Grows in river valleys.
The Mingyi says: An alternate name is Mie Li (蔑藜). It grows in Qin (among the Qin pepper plants, as noted in the Erya). From Ba Commandery, harvested in the eighth month. Tao Hongjing's note says: locally it is called dried [product].
Shan Lu Ji says: The people of Shu use it to make tea. It is also found among the Qin pepper plants noted in the Erya. From Ba Commandery; Hongjing notes it is dried in shade locally.
Bēi cí (卑茨): flavor pungent and salty, warm. It primarily treats wind impediment, dead muscle, pathogenic qi, wind in the head with lacrimation; opens the nine orifices; kills malign spirits and tidings. Locally called nan (楠). Grows in river valleys.
The Mingyi says: it grows in Yong Province and in Zou County of Lu; specimens resembling pig's teeth are of superior quality; harvested in the ninth and tenth months, dried in shade.
Case note: The Shuowen says "ci (茨) is a fish poison." The Mingyi text says "ci grass fruit." The Fanzi Jiran says: "Bēi cí comes from the Sanfu region; the highest grade is priced at one qian per piece." The Guangzhi says: "Ji qi zi (雞栖子) is bēi cí." The yulan and御 texts note: bēi is an abbreviated form of the grass character.

Shennong Bencao Jing, Volume Three — 115

蘡䒷味苦平主久欬上氣喘逆久寒驚悸痂疥白禿瘍氣殺皮膚小蟲生川谷。

鈎也唐本注云蘡草也俗名棄薦草爾雅所謂王鈎。

牛扁味苦微寒主身皮創熱氣可作浴湯殺牛蟲小蟲又療牛病生川谷。

芫華味辛溫主欬逆上氣喉鳴咽腫短氣蠱毒鬼瘧疰痛癰腫殺蟲魚一名去水生川谷。蕭非
臭普日芫華一名去水一名兒草根一名黄大戟神農黄帝有毒扁鵲伯苦李氏大寒二

Shennong Bencao Jing, Volume Three

Ying Yu (Ampelopsis/wild grape): Flavor bitter, balanced. Primarily treats: prolonged coughing with qi rising upward, panting and counterflow, long-standing cold, fright palpitations, scabs and mange, white baldness sores, pathogenic qi, and kills small insects on the skin. Grows in river valleys.

Wu Pu states: Wang Chu — one name is Huang Cao (yellow grass). According to Shennong and Lei Gong: grows on Mount Tai in mountain valleys. Treats bodily heat, pathogenic qi, and fever in children. (Imperial review note.)

According to the Mingyi: can be used to dye things yellow, producing a golden color. Also grows in Qingyi. Harvested in the ninth and tenth months.

Investigation: The Shuowen says Ying grass is also Wang Chu. The Erya says Wang Chu; Guo Pu says it is today called Ya Jiao Sha (duck-foot sedge). The Shijing verse "Green bamboo, so graceful" — the commentary identifies it as Wang Chu.

Gou: also in the Tang Bencao annotation described as Ying grass, commonly called Qi Jian grass, which is what the Erya calls Wang Gou.

Niu Bian: Flavor bitter, slightly cold. Primarily treats: skin lesions, heat qi; can be used to make a bathing decoction, kills ox parasites and small insects, also treats ox diseases. Grows in river valleys.
According to the Mingyi: grows in Guiyang.

Investigation: Tao Hongjing says it is commonly stored under the name Bian Te or Bian Du.

Xia Ku Cao (Selfheal/Prunella): Flavor bitter and acrid, cold. Treats: heat, itching, carbuncles, scrofulous sores, head sores; breaks up concretions, disperses goiter, resolves bound qi, reduces foot swelling, dampness-impediment; lightens the body. One name is Xi Ju, another is Nai Dong. Grows in river valleys. (Xiao classifies it under the Wood section, not here.)

According to the Mingyi: one name is Yan Mian. Grows in Shu Commandery. Harvested in the fourth month.

Yuan Hua (Genkwa/Daphne genkwa): Flavor acrid, warm. Primarily treats: coughing with counterflow qi, throat rattling, throat swelling, shortness of breath, gu toxin, ghost malaria, fixed pain, carbuncle swelling; kills insects and fish. One name is Qu Shui. Grows in river valleys. (Xiao disagrees with this classification.)

Wu Pu states: Yuan Hua — one name Qu Shui, one name Er Cao Gen, one name Huang Da Ji. Shennong and the Yellow Emperor: toxic. Bian Que and Bo Ku: Li's classification — greatly cold.

According to the Mingyi: harvest flowers in the third and fifth months. The root of Yuan Hua — one name Chi Yuan Gen. (Shennong, Lei Gong)

The leaves emerge green in the first month, become dark when thick; the flowers are purple, red, or white. In the third month the fruit falls and the leaves then grow. Harvest flowers in the third and fifth months; harvest roots in the ninth or eighth month; dry in shade.

According to the Mingyi: one name Du Yu, one name Du Yuan. Its root is called Shu Sang and can be used to poison fish. Grows at Huai Yuan. Harvest flowers on the third day of the third month; dry in shade.

Gongku: toxic. Grows in Xie Commandery. Harvested in the ninth and eighth months. Long-term consumption causes diarrhea. Can be used to poison fish. Grows at Huai Yuan. Harvest on the third day of the third month; dry in shade.

(Imperial Overview text also appears in illustrated editions.)

味苦寒。主殺三蟲逐毒氣胃中熱利丈夫不利女子作摩膏除小兒百病。名雷矢。大。一。

案范子計然云雷矢出漢中色白者善及漢中土中八月朵根暴乾。

名醫曰一名雷矢。一名雷實。生石城及漢中士中八月采根暴乾。

桐葉味苦寒主惡蝕創著陰皮主五痔殺三蟲華主傳豬創飼豬肥大三倍生山谷。

名醫曰生桐柏山。

translation:
"They resemble plums and are edible. Shen Kuo's Supplement to the Brush Talks states: The inscription at the Palace Gate reads: In the Hualin Garden there are 314 trees of the Che-xia plum variety, and one Ao plum tree."

Mang Cao (Illicium lanceolatum): Flavor acrid, warm. It governs wind in the head, abscesses, breast abscesses, hernial lumps, eliminates bound qi, itching and scratching, and kills insects and fish. It grows in mountain valleys.
Wu Pu says: Mang Cao is also called Spring Grass. According to Shennong it is acrid; according to Lei Gong and Tong Jun it is bitter and toxic. It grows in Shang Valley mountain valleys, or in Wan Ju. Collected in the fifth month. Treats wind. [Two characters in the Imperial览edition show textual corruption.]

Commentary: The Zhongshan Jing, as commented upon by Guo Pu, states: It is also called Mang Cao. The Bencao says the Zhou Rites records that the Li clan officer was in charge of using Mang Cao fumigation to expel vermin. Fan Zi Ji Ran says: Mang Cao comes from the Sanfu region. Guo Pu says of Spring Grass: Today it is used to poison fish. The Erya records: On Chao Xie Mountain there is an herb called Mang Cao. In Shang Valley and Wan Ju, the leaves are collected in the fifth month and dried in the shade.

The Mingyi says: Another name is Shen; another name is Spring Grass. Grows in the mountain valleys of Shang Valley, or in Wan Ju. Collect leaves in the fifth month and dry in the shade.

Lei Jiu [Imperial览edition writes "Lei"]. Bencao writes "Gong御览陶景 says: Tao Hongjing says the character is also written as Jun. One name is Mang Cao. The Bencao says…

Flavor bitter, cold. It governs killing three types of worms, expelling toxic qi, stomach heat; benefits men but not women. Made into a rubbing paste, it eliminates the hundred ailments of children. It is named Lei Shi (Thunder Arrow). [Notes on characters follow.]

Wu Pu says: Lei Jiu — according to Shennong it is bitter; according to the Yellow Emperor and Qi Bo and Tong Jun it is sweet and toxic; according to Bian Que it is sweet and non-toxic; according to Li Shi it is greatly cold. [Alternate source notes: collected in the eighth month.] Also called Lei Shi (Thunder Fruit).

Commentary: Fan Zi Ji Ran says: Lei Shi comes from Hanzhong; white ones are the best. Collected from within the soil in Hanzhong in the eighth month, roots dug up and dried in the sun.

The Mingyi says: Another name is Lei Shi; another name is Lei Shi (Thunder Fruit). Grows in Shi Cheng and in Hanzhong, underground. Collect roots in the eighth month and dry in the sun.

Tong Ye (Paulownia leaf): Flavor bitter, cold. It governs malignant erosive sores, genital skin conditions, and five types of hemorrhoids; kills three worms. The flowers, when fed to pigs, make them grow three times as fat. Grows in mountain valleys.

The Mingyi says: Grows on Tongbai Mountain.
Commentary: The Shuowen says: Tong means "glory"; it is the Wutong tree (Firmiana simplex), also called Qiu. The Erya says: Qiu is Wu; Guo Pu comments: This is today's Wutong. Also called Rong Tong tree. Guo Pu says: This is the Wutong. The Mao Odes say: Wu [text continues on next page]…

Shennong Bencao Jing, Volume Three — 117

Willow Flower (Liu Hua): Flavor bitter, cold. Principal actions: wind-water [edema], jaundice, heat and blackness of the face. Also known as willow catkins (liu xu). The leaves principally treat horse scabies and sores. The fruit principally treats festering abscesses, expels pus and blood. The seed juice treats thirst. Grows in rivers and marshes.
Commentary from the Shuowen [Jiezi]: refers to "liu" [willow]. The Mingyi [ji] says: grows in Langye.
The middle variety is also called yang-pu-liu. Guo Pu says it can be used for arrows; it is what the Zuozhuan calls "the cattails of Dongze"; the Mao Shi says "do not break my qi tree," and the commentary says qi is a type of wood; Lu Ji says it grows in marshes.
Belongs to the willow family.

Willow: Flavor bitter, cold. Principal actions: warm diseases, cold damage, high fever, agitation and mania, kills three types of worms, treats scabies and sores, promotes urination and water passage. Grows in mountain valleys.
The Mingyi says: grows in Jing Mountain.

Melia Fruit (Lian Shi): Flavor bitter, cold. Principal actions: warm diseases, cold damage, high fever, agitation and mania, kills three types of worms, treats scabies and sores, promotes urination and water passage. Grows in mountain valleys.
The Mingyi says: grows in Jing Mountain.

Bush Cherry Kernel (Yuli Ren): Flavor sour, balanced. Principal actions: great abdominal water swelling, swelling of the face, eyes, and four limbs; promotes urination and water passage. The root principally treats dental decay and strengthens teeth. Also known as jue li. Grows in mountain valleys.
Commentary: The Shuowen says: in the seventh month, the melia tree [blossoms]. Gao You says the melia fruit resembles the melia; Guo Pu says the melia fruit is named for its seed resembling a fingertip, white and sticky, and can be used to wash clothes. The Huainanzi, Shize chapter records the same.
Wu Pu says: Yuli, also called che-xia-li, also called di-li, also called che-xia-li, also called di-kuan.
The Mingyi says: also called che-xia-li, also called que-li, also called di-li. Grows on high mountains and hillocks; harvest the root in the fifth and sixth months.
Commentary from the Shuowen: lian, white lian. The Guangya says: mountain plum. Its flavor is sour. The Erya says: chang-lian. Guo Pu says: in Guanxi today there is the lian tree, like a cherry tree and edible. The Mao Shi says: "in the sixth month eat the yu"; the commentary says yu belongs to the di family. Liu Ji's Notes on the Mao Shi says: the tree is five or six feet tall, its fruit is as large as a plum, bright red, sweet to eat. The Mao Shi also says: "the flowers of the chang-tang"; the commentary says chang-tang is a tang tree. Lu Ji says: wu-li, also called que-li, also called che-xia-li; found throughout mountain areas; its flowers are either white or red; ripens in the sixth month; the fruit is large.

The famous physicians say: another name is Ju Gu. It grows on Xiong'er Mountain and is harvested in the fourth month. According to Li Dangzhi, it is also called Shen Shu, Yang Lu, Mu Jing, Kong Shu. Its bark is white and hollow inside, with nodes at intervals; the berries resemble wolfberries, ripen red in winter, and taste sweet and bitter.

Mouse Plum (Shu Li): It governs cold-heat disorders and scrofula sores. It grows in fields and open country.
Wu Pu says: Mouse Plum is also called Niu Li, with the alternate name Lan Yu.
The famous physicians say: another name is Niu Li, another is Bi Ci; harvested at no fixed season.
According to the Shuowen: Yù is the mouse catalpa; the Erya also says Yù is the mouse catalpa. Guo Pu says it belongs to the sorghum family; today in Jiangdong there is the Tiger Catalpa. The Mao Shi says: on the northern hills there is Yù — the commentary says Yù is the mouse catalpa. The famous physicians call it Mouse Catalpa; it is uncertain whether this is the same plant. The Tang commentary notes: one name is Zhao Li, one name is Fu Li, one name is Wu Cha.

Yao Shi Gen (Drug-Fruit Root): Flavor acrid, warm. Governs miasmic qi, various fistulas, scabies, itching, acid vomiting, and broken injuries; tonifies the bone marrow. Another name is Lian Mu. Grows in mountain valleys.
The famous physicians say: grows in Shu Commandery; harvested at no fixed season.
According to the Guangya: Bei Fu is Yao Shi.

Luan Hua: Flavor bitter, cold. Governs eye pain with tearing, all injuries causing swelling of the eye. Grows in river valleys.
The famous physicians say: grows in Hanzhong; harvested in the fifth month.
According to the Shuowen: Luan wood resembles the Lan tree. The Shan Hai Jing says: on the Mountain of Clouds and Rain there is a tree called Luan with yellow wood, red branches, and green leaves; the silkworm emperor takes medicine from it. The Bai Hu Tong says: the grave trees of the feudal lords are cypress, those of great officers are Luan, those of officials are locust.
Shen Kuo's Mengqi Bitan (Supplementary Notes) says: there is a variety of Luan whose fruit can be made into prayer beads; it is called Mu Luan, which is the Luan Hua of this herbal.

梓
桐生矣傳云梧桐柔木也。

黃環
名醫曰生蜀主蠱毒鬼注鬼魅邪氣在藏中除欬逆寒熱。一名凌泉。一名大就生山谷。一名苦有毒二月生初出正亦高。味苦有毒二月生初出正亦高。

名醫曰。二尺葉黃員端大蔓葉有汗黃白五月實員三月采根根黃從理。
案蜀都賦有黃環劉逵云黃環出蜀郡沈括筆談云黃鑷即今朱藤也天下皆有葉如槐其花穗懸紫色如葛花可作菜食火不熟亦有小毒京師人家園圃中作大架種之謂之紫藤花者是也。
淺疏味辛寒主身皮膚中熱除邪氣止遺溺可作浴湯生山谷及田野故邱虛地。
translation:
Shennong Bencao Jing, Volume Three

Zi (Catalpa)
The Tong tree: tradition says the Chinese parasol tree is a soft wood.
The white bark: flavor bitter, cold; primarily treats fever, expels three kinds of worms; the leaves, when pounded and applied, can be used as a poultice for pig wounds, and feeding pigs with it makes them fatten to three times their normal size. Grows in mountain valleys.
The Mingyi (Supplementary Physicians' Records) says: grows in Henei.

Commentary: The Shuowen (dictionary) says zi is qiu (Catalpa); also written as the character 榟. Zi and qiu are the same. The Erya says: the locust tree with small leaves is called rui. The qiu tree with fine leaves is called rui. Guo Pu says: "locust" should read "qiu." The qiu with fine leaves is called rui. The Mao Shi (Book of Odes) says: yi, tong, zi, qi — the commentary says yi belongs to the zi family. Lu Ji: rui also; zi and qiu — Guo Pu says: the old ones with rough, scaly bark are qiu. Also, the zi tree with smooth-grained white wood that produces seed pods is called zi; the fruit covered in tong-like bark is called yi.
Rui: large with rough bark — Guo Pu says: this is the zi tree.
The one called zi: a qiu with loose grain, white flesh, bearing seed pods is called zi; its fruit, covered in tong-like bark, is called yi.

Shi Nan (Photinia / rock southern shrub)
The Mingyi says: it primarily nourishes kidney qi, treats internal injury and decline of yin qi, benefits the sinews, bones, skin, and hair; the fruit kills gu toxins and breaks up accumulations, disperses wind impediment. One name: Guimu (Ghost Eye). Grows in mountain valleys.

Huang Huan (Yellow Ring)
The Mingyi says: grows in Shu (Sichuan). Primarily treats gu toxins, ghost possession, ghost confusion, and evil qi lodged in the organs; eliminates coughing counterflow, cold, and heat. One name: Lingquan (Numinous Spring). One name: Dajiu. Grows in mountain valleys. One name: bitter; toxic; sprouts in the second month, the first growth comes up quite tall. Flavor bitter, toxic; sprouts in the second month, the first growth comes up quite tall.
Wu Pu says: Shu Huang Huan; one name Gui Dupou; one name root-leek. Shennong, the Yellow Emperor, Qibo, Tong Jun, and Bian Que all describe it as pungent. One tradition says the flavor is bitter and toxic; it sprouts in the second month and the first shoots come up quite tall — like the spokes of a cart wheel radiating out. Treats gu toxin and nightmare-suppression conditions.
The Mingyi says: two chi tall; leaves yellow, rounded at the tips; the large trailing leaves have a yellow-white sap; fruit rounded in the fifth month; roots harvested in the third month; roots yellow with longitudinal grain.
Commentary: The Ode to the Shu Capital mentions huang huan. Liu Kui says huang huan comes from Shu commandery. Shen Kuo's Brush Talks says huang nie is the same as what is now called zhu teng (wisteria); it is found everywhere under heaven. The leaves resemble those of the locust tree; the flower clusters hang down; the color is purple like the kudzu flower and the flowers can be eaten as a vegetable; if not cooked through they are mildly toxic. In the capital, people train it over large trellises in their gardens and call it "purple wisteria flower" — that is this plant.

Qian Shu (Shallow Dredge / Lespedeza or similar)
Flavor pungent, cold. Primarily treats fever in the skin and body surface, eliminates evil qi, stops urinary incontinence; can be used to prepare a medicinal bath. Grows in mountain valleys, open fields, old ruins, and waste ground.

六畜毛蹄甲。味鹹平。主鬼注。蠱毒。寒熱。癲癎狂。走駱駝毛。尤良。
案陶宏景云六畜謂馬牛羊豬狗雞也蹄卽蹄省文。
右獸下品四種舊同。
蝦蟆味辛寒主邪氣破癥堅。血癰腫。創服之不患熱病。生江湖池澤。取陰乾東行者良。
名醫曰。一名蟾蜍。一名去甫。一名苦蠪生江湖五月五日。取其皮蠪蠪其行兕兕。或作蠪蠪蠪蠪諸以服。
案說文云。蝦蟆也。蟆蝦蟆也。蠪兕蠪蠪諸也。其鳴蠪諸兕兕克兕。或作蠪蠪蠪蠪蟆以服。詩日得此蠪蠪言其行蠪蠪其行兕兕。
爾雅諸也。夏小正傳云。蝦域。者長股也。或日屈造之屬也。郭璞云。似蝦蟆居陸地淮南謂之去蚊。又螫郭。
鳴者廣雅云蝦蟆類。周禮云蠪氏。鄭司農云蠪蠪蠪。云術雅云竈蠪蟆諸。郭璞云。似蝦蟆居陸地淮南謂之去蚊。又螫郭。
璞云。蛙類周禮之謂蠪氏。鄭司農云。韓詩注云咸施蟆蝦蟆也。元謂蠪令御所食蛙也。月令云仲夏之月反舌。
無聲蔡邕云今謂之蝦蟆。群君韓詩注云咸施蟆蝦蟆也。元謂蠪令御所食蛙也。月令云仲夏之月反舌。
蝦蟆。又鼓造。一日蝦蟆。抱樸子曰以自解去父血。中二字。黑字。主漏下赤白寒熱破石淋殺禽獸賊鼠生池澤。
抱樸子曰以自解去父血。中二字。黑字。主漏下赤白寒熱破石淋殺禽獸賊鼠生池澤。
刀。味辛微寒大御覽本補。中二字。主漏下赤白寒熱破石淋殺禽獸賊鼠生池澤。魏武帝曾收左元放而桎梏之而得自然解脫以何法乎。寬御。
吳普曰馬刀。一名齊蛆神農岐伯桐君鹹有毒扁鵲小寒大毒生池澤江海采無時也。
名醫曰一名馬蛤生江湖及東海采無時。
神農本草經卷三　一二一
translation:
Six Domestic Animals' Hair, Hooves, and Shells. Flavor: salty, balanced. Governs: ghost-possession ailments, gu toxins, alternating chills and fever, epilepsy and mania. Camel hair is especially good.
Note: Tao Hongjing says the six domestic animals are horse, ox, sheep, pig, dog, and chicken. "Hoof" (蹄) is an abbreviated writing of the same character.
The above are the lower-grade animal items, four entries total, same as the old text.
Toad (蝦蟆). Flavor: acrid, cold. Governs: pathogenic qi, breaks up hard masses, blood abscesses and swellings, sores; taking it internally prevents heat illness. Grows in rivers, lakes, and marshes. Collect in the shade; those traveling eastward are best.
The Mingyi (Famous Physicians) says: also called chan chu (toad); also called qu fu; also called ku long. Lives in rivers and lakes. Collected on the fifth day of the fifth month. Take its skin...
The Shuowen (Dictionary) says: ha ma (toad). Mo is also ha ma. Long si is a type of creature. Its call resembles various sounds...
The Erya (encyclopedia) says it belongs to the "zhu" category. The Xia Xiaozheng commentary says "xia yu" (river toad).郭璞 says it resembles the toad but lives on land; in Huainan it is called "qu wen." It also stings.
The Mingya (Guang Ya dictionary) says the ha ma category. The Zhouli says the long clan. Zheng Sinong says...Guo Pu says it resembles the toad and lives on land; in the Huainan region it is called "qu wen."
Pu says frog is what the Zhouli's "long clan" refers to. Zheng Sinong says Han Shi annotation says "xian shi" means ha ma (toad). Yuan says the long order was food the emperor ate—frogs. The Yueling (Monthly Ordinances) says in mid-summer the "reversing tongue" (frogs) fall silent.
Cai Yong says what is now called ha ma. The group of gentlemen's Han Shi annotation says "xian shi" means ha ma. Yuan says the imperial food item was frogs. The Yueling says in mid-summer the reversing tongue falls silent.
Ha ma. Also called "drum creature." One name is ha ma. Baopuzi says using it one can free oneself from bonds and shed shackles; in the middle two characters written in black: governs flooding below with red and white discharge, alternating cold and heat, breaks up stone strangury, kills birds, beasts, and pest rats. Grows in pools and marshes.
Baopuzi says using it one can free oneself from bonds. Middle two characters in black: governs flooding below, alternating cold and heat, breaks up stone strangury, kills beasts and pest rats. Grows in pools and marshes.
Dao (razor clam). Flavor: acrid, slightly cold. The Imperial Overview supplement: governs flooding below with red and white, alternating cold and heat, breaks up stone strangury, kills beasts and pest rats. Grows in pools and marshes. Emperor Wei Wu once imprisoned Yuan Fang in fetters and the man shed them naturally—by what method? (Kuanyu commentary.)
Wu Pu says: Ma dao (razor clam). Also called qi ju. Shennong and Qibo and Tong Jun all say it is toxic; Bian Que says slightly cold, greatly toxic. Grows in pools, marshes, rivers, and seas; collected at any time.
The Mingyi says: also called ma ha. Grows in rivers, lakes, and the Eastern Sea; collected at any time.
Shennong Bencao Jing, Volume Three — 121

蔓椒．味苦溫．主風寒濕痺．癰節疥除四肢厥氣．邪痛．一名家椒．生川谷及邱家閑．
名醫曰．一名豬椒．一名彘椒．一名狗椒．生雲中朶蕈根袁釀酒．
案陶宏景云俗呼為樛以椒薔小不香爾．一名稀椒可以蒸病出汗也．
右木下品一十七種售以十八種今移芫華入草．
豚卵．味苦溫．主驚狐癲疾鬼注蠱毒除寒熱賁豚．五癃邪氣攣縮．一名豚顛懸蹄主五痔伏熱在腸．腸癰．
內蝕．
案說文云豨．間謂之豬子．从象省象形．从又持肉以給祭祀篆文作豚．方言云．豬其子或謂之豚．或謂之貑．
吳揚之間謂之豬子．豚脂味辛溫．主癰瘡惡創死肌寒風濕痺四肢拘縵不收風頭厲氣通湊理．一名官脂生山谷．
名醫曰．生南山及淮海邊冬至解其角漢書云劉向以為廦之為言迷也蓋牧獸之淫者也．
案說文云廦庭屬冬至解其角漢書云劉向以為廦之為言迷也蓋牧獸之淫者也．
廦鼠．主墮胎令人產易生平谷．
名醫曰．生山都．
案說文云廦鼠形飛走且乳之鳥也籀文作鼺廣雅云鷄惝飛鼺也陶宏景云是廦鼠一名飛生見爾雅云廦鼠夷由也舊作鼺非．

神農本草經卷三
一一〇
translation:
Manjiao (Zanthoxylum): Flavor bitter, warm. Governs wind-cold dampness impediment, carbuncles, joint scab, removes reversal qi from the four limbs, evil pain. Another name: Jiajiao. Grows in valleys and around hillside homesteads.
The Mingyi records: Also called Zhujiao, Zhijiao, Gougiao. Grows in Yunzhong. The root can be steeped in wine to treat disease by promoting sweating.
Tao Hongjing notes: Commonly called Jiu; the pepper is small and not very fragrant. Another name is Xijiao; it can be used in steam therapy to induce sweating in illness.
The above are the lower-grade wood items, seventeen kinds in total, now increased to eighteen with the addition of Yuanhua moved into the herb category.

Piglet Testicle (Tun Luan): Flavor bitter, warm. Governs fright, fox-madness, epilepsy, ghost-infestation, gu-poison; removes cold-heat, surging piglet qi, the five urinary blockages, evil qi, and cramping contraction. Another name: Tun Dian. Suspended hoof governs the five hemorrhoids, latent heat in the intestines, and intestinal carbuncle, internal erosion.
The Shuowen says: "Xi" is what people in between [certain regions] call a pig; the character is derived from the elephant radical, simplified in form, with a hand holding meat to offer at sacrifice; the seal-form writes it as "tun." Fangyan says: a pig's young may be called "tun" or "ji."
In the Wu-Yang region they are called "pig-children." Lard: flavor acrid, warm. Governs carbuncles, malignant sores, dead muscle, cold-wind dampness impediment, inability to flex the four limbs, wind-head li-qi, and promotes interstice-flow. Another name: Guanzhi. Grows in mountain valleys.
The Mingyi records: grows in the southern mountains and along the Huai Sea coast; at winter solstice it sheds its horns. The Han History records that Liu Xiang interpreted the word "pi" as meaning "lost/confused," referring to the licentiousness of grazing animals.
The Shuowen says: the pi-courtyard category; sheds its horns at winter solstice. The Han History records Liu Xiang said the word "pi" means "confused," referring to the lasciviousness of grazing animals.

Flying Squirrel (Pi Shu): Governs causing miscarriage, making childbirth easy. Grows in Pinggu.
The Mingyi records: grows in Shandu.
The Shuowen records: the pi-mouse has a form that both flies and walks, and also suckles young like a bird; the archaic script writes it as Lei. The Guangya says: jichangfei is the lei. Tao Hongjing says it is the pi-mouse, also called Feisheng. The Erya says: the pi-mouse is also called Yiyou. The old form writes it as Lei, which is incorrect.

名醫曰。一名土蜂。生熊耳及羊柯。或人屋閒。
棠說文云。蠮螉蒲盧細要土蜂也。或作蜾蠃。蠃也。廣雅云。土蜂蟷螂也。爾雅土蜂。毛詩云。蜾蠃有
子螺蠃負之傳云螺蠃也蒲盧也鄭云蒲盧果蠃。闢土蜂也方言云蟲其小者
謂之蠮螉。或謂之蚹蛻說文蟷字。或當為醫。夫政也者蒲盧也。
吳蛻味辛溫。主鬼注蠱毒嗽諸蛇蟲魚毒殺鬼物老精溫虐去三蠱。御寬引云。大觀本在。水蛭下。掌生川谷。
名醫曰。生大吳江南赤頭足者良。
案廣雅云。生蛒吳公也。
水蛭味鹹平。主逐惡血瘀血月閉。御寬作。破血痕積聚無子利水道生池澤。
名醫曰。一名蛭。一名至掌。生雷澤。五六月暴乾。
案說文云。郭璞云未詳据名醫即蛭至掌也蟲蛭至掌也爾雅云蛭蟲郭璞云今江東呼水中蛭蟲入人肉者為蜞又蛭蟺蚓
掌郭璞云未詳据名醫即蛭至掌也
斑苗味辛寒。主寒熱鬼注蠱毒。癰疽蝕。死肌破石癃。一名龍尾生川谷。
吳普曰斑猫。一名斑蛭。一名龍蛇。一名斑苗。一名勝髡。一名蟲蛩。一名晏青。神農辛岐伯鹹桐君有毒。
名醫曰生河東。八月取陰乾。
扁鵲曰生河內川谷。或生水石。

神農本草經卷三

一二三
translation:
The Mingyi (Eminent Physicians) says: Another name is earth-wasp (tu feng). It lives in Xiong'er and Yangke mountains, or in the spaces within human dwellings.

Notes: The Shuowen says: The yaying (mud-dauber wasp) is the pulu — a slender-waisted earth-wasp. It is also written as guoluo. Guoluo is a type of wasp. The Guangya says: the earth-wasp is the praying mantis. The Erya says earth-wasp. The Shijing says: the guoluo wasp has offspring — it carries them. Zheng (Xuan) says: pulu is the fruit-wasp. This refers to the earth-wasp. The Fangyan says: the small among such insects are called yaying. They are also called fudui. According to the Shuowen the character dang should perhaps be read as "physician." "Those who are administrators" refers to the pulu.

Wu She: Flavor is acrid, warm. It governs ghost-infliction (gui zhu), gu-poison, coughing, all manner of snake and insect and fish toxins; it kills ghost-things and old malevolent spirits; it warms malarial conditions and expels the three kinds of gu-worms. Yu Kuan cites: The Daguan bencao places this entry under "water leech." It grows in river valleys.

The Mingyi says: It grows in Greater Wu and Jiangnan. Those with red heads and feet are the best.

The Guangya says: the sheng-wu is the centipede (wugong).

Water Leech (shui zhi): Flavor is salty, neutral. It governs expelling malign blood and stagnant blood, and amenorrhea. (Yu Kuan's edition has "breaking up blood-masses, accumulations and gatherings, childlessness, promoting urination.") It grows in ponds and marshes.

The Mingyi says: Another name is zhi; another name is zhizhang. It grows in Leize. Collected in the fifth or sixth month and dried in the sun.

Notes: The Shuowen says — Guo Pu says he does not know the basis; according to the Mingyi this is the zhi-zhizhang, the leech. The Erya says: the zhi insect — Guo Pu says that in Jiangdong today, leeches that enter human flesh in the water are called qi; also zhi and shanyin (earthworms).

Blister Beetle (ban mao): Flavor is acrid, cold. It governs alternating chills and fevers, ghost-infliction, gu-poison, abscesses and ulcerations, eroding of dead flesh, and breaking up urinary stones and strangury. Another name is Long Wei (dragon's tail). Grows in river valleys.

Wu Pu says: Blister beetle, also called ban zhi, also called long she (dragon snake), also called ban mao, also called sheng kun, also called chong qiong, also called yan qing. According to Shennong it is acrid; according to Qibo it is salty; according to Tongjun it is toxic.

The Mingyi says: It grows in Hedong. Collected in the eighth month and dried in the shade.

Bian Que says: It grows in the river valleys of Henei, or on water-washed rocks.

Shennong Bencao Jing, Volume Three

神農本草經卷三

蛇蛻味鹹平主小兒百二十種驚癇瘈瘲疾寒熱腸痔蟲毒蛇癇火熬之良一名龍子衣一名蛇符一為一邪。

棠范子計然云馬刀出河東藪文類聚引本經云文蛤表有文又曰馬刀一曰名蛤則嘗古本與文蛤

名龍子單衣一名弓皮生川谷及田野。

吳普曰蛇蛻一名龍子皮一名龍子單衣一名弓皮一名蛇附一名蛇筋一名龍皮一名龍單衣。御覧

棠說文云它蟲也从虫而長象宛曲垂尾形或作蛇蛻蟬所解皮也廣雅云蛻蟠蛻也中山經云來

邱蜘味鹹寒主蠱疫去三蟲伏尸鬼注蠱毒殺長蟲仍自化作水生平土。

吳普曰一名白頸蟺一名附引御覧

名醫曰一名土龍二月取陰乾。

棠說文云螾側行者或作蚯蚓也廣雅云蚯蚓蜿蟺引無也爾雅云蟺蚯蟺蛆蟲郭璞云即蛆蟲也江

東呼寒蚓舊作蚯蚓非呂氏春秋淮南子邱蚓出不从蟲又說山訓云蠕無筋骨之強高誘注蠕一名蛇

蟠蟠味辛平主久聾欬逆毒氣出刺出汗生川谷。

蟠也舊又有白蟺二字据吳普古本當無也。
translation:
Shennong Bencao Jing, Volume Three

Snake Slough (shed snake skin): Flavor salty, nature balanced. Treats children's one hundred and twenty kinds of fright convulsions, spasms, diseases with chills and fever, intestinal hemorrhoids, worm toxins, and snake-induced convulsive disorders. Roasting over fire is best. Also named "Dragon Child's Garment," "Snake Talisman." Another name is "Yi Xie" (one evil).

Tang Fanzi's Jiran says: "Horse Clam comes from Hedong marshes." The Wenleiju cites the Bencao Jing as saying the Wen Clam has markings on its surface; another name is Horse Clam. In one text it is called Ge; the ancient edition equates it with Wen Clam.

Also named Dragon Child's Single Garment, Bow Skin. Found in river valleys and open fields.

Wu Pu says: Snake slough is also called Dragon Child Skin, Dragon Child Single Garment, Bow Skin, Snake Appendage, Snake Sinew, Dragon Skin, Dragon Single Garment. [Cited from Yulan]

Tang: Shuowen says it is a creature of the chong (reptile/insect) class, elongated in form, depicted with a curved, trailing tail; sometimes written with the snake-slough character. "Slough" refers to the shed skin of cicadas and snakes. The Guangya says: slough, coiled-slough. The Zhongshan Jing says it comes from...

Qiu earthworm: Flavor salty, cold. Treats gu-poison pestilence, eliminates the three worms and corpse-ghost possession, kills long worms. It spontaneously dissolves into water and lives in flat soil.

Wu Pu says: also named White-Necked Earthworm, and one other name. [Cited from Yulan]

Mingyi ji says: also named Earth Dragon. Collected in the second month, dried in shade.

Tang: Shuowen says it is a sideways-moving creature; also written as qiu-yin (earthworm). Guangya calls it qiu-yin, wan-shan. The Erya says it is the qiu-shan type, a kind of worm. Guo Pu says it is the same as the maggot-worm. In the Jiangdong region it is called Cold Earthworm. The old text writes it as qiu-yin, but this is wrong. In Lüshi Chunqiu and Huainanzi it is written qiu-yin without the insect radical. The Shunxun chapter says: "Ruan has no sinew or bone for strength," and Gao You in his commentary notes that ruan is another name for snake.

Spot-beetle: Flavor acrid, balanced. Treats long-standing deafness, coughing counterflow, toxic qi, removes thorns and splinters, induces sweating. Found in river valleys.

The character pan also appears; the old text added the two characters "white chan," but based on Wu Pu's ancient edition they should not be there.

蛞蝓味鹹寒。主小兒驚癇瘛瘲腹張寒熱大人痎疾狂易。一名蛞蚓。火熬之良。生池澤。
名醫曰。生長沙五月五日取蒸藏之。
案說文云蜒蚰渠蚰。一日天杜廣雅云。天杜蛞蝓也衛雅云蛞蛞蛞蛞郭璞云黑甲蟲噬螫土玉篇蛞蜊

蟶蛄咏鹹寒。主產難出肉中刺。在肉窟作刺。潰癰腫下哽噎嗌。寬作解毒除惡創。一名螻蛄御覽作。一名天
同說文無蛞字渠蚰。即蛄音之緩念。御覽作刺。

案說文云。生東城夏至取暴乾。
名醫曰。夜出者良生平澤。

一名殼。蛄也蛞蛄也廣雅云爻鼠津蛄蟀。蟀蛄也。夏小正云三月蟀蛄鳴高誘云蟀蛄也。

案說文云。生蠶蝶也衛雅云殼天蟀郭璞云蟀蛄也淮南子時則訓云孟夏之月蟀蟬鳴高誘云蟀蛄也。

謂蛄蛄為石鳳今無文。
方言云蛄蛄謂之杜格蟀蟀謂之蟀蛄。或謂之蟀蛄南楚謂之杜狗。或謂之蟀蟀陸璣詩疏云本草又

則鳴殼天蟀也衛雅云殼天蟀郭璞云蟀蛄也。

馬陸味辛溫主腹中大堅癥破積聚息肉惡創白禿一名百足生川谷。
名醫曰。一名馬軒生元菟。
吳普曰。一名馬軒御覽。
案說文云馬蚿馬蟓馬蚿也。又馬蝚蟫。

神農本草經卷三
一二五
translation:
Slug (Kuoyu): Flavor salty, cold. Governs fright epilepsy and convulsions in children, abdominal distension, chills and fever, and malaria and madness in adults. Another name: earthworm (Kuoyin). Best when roasted over fire. Grows in pools and marshes.
The Mingyi says: grows in Changsha; gather on the fifth day of the fifth month, steam and store.
Commentary from Shuowen and other sources: various alternate names and identifications are given, including Yanyou, Quyu, Tiandu, Kuoyu; Guo Pu says it has a black shell and bites; Yupian identifies it as Kuoli.

Mole Cricket (Louqu): Flavor salty, cold. Governs difficult childbirth, removal of thorns lodged in flesh, ulceration of swellings and tumors, choking in the throat. Resolves toxins and eliminates malignant sores. Another name: Louqu. Also called Tiangu.
From Shuowen and other sources: various character forms and pronunciations are noted; the Yulan text has variant readings.

Commentary from Shuowen: produced at Dongcheng; gather at the summer solstice and dry in the sun.
The Mingyi says: the ones that emerge at night are best; grows in flat marshes.
Another name: Ke. It is also called Gugu. The Guangya says it is called Yaoshu-Jingu. The Xia Xiaozheng says: in the third month the Shuaiju chirps. Gao You says it is the Shuaiju.

From Shuowen: it is the silkworm butterfly. Various classical sources give different names: Ke-Tian-Shuai, Shuaiju. The Huainanzi Shize Xun says: in the first month of summer the Shuaichan begins to call; Gao You identifies it as Shuaiju.

Various classical sources (Fangyan, Erya, Lu Ji's Shishu) note regional names for this creature: in different areas it is called Duge, Shuaishuai, Dugou, and various other names. The Bencao is also cited.

Millipede (Malu): Flavor acrid, warm. Governs large hard masses in the abdomen, breaks up accumulations, eliminates necrotic flesh, malignant sores, and favus (white baldness). Another name: Baizu (Hundred-Legs). Grows in river valleys.
The Mingyi says: another name Maxuan; grows in Yuantu.
Wu Pu says: another name Maxuan (per the Yulan).
Commentary from Shuowen: called Maxian, Maxiang, also Marou, Tan.

Commentary: The Shuowen [Jiezi] says that yingyuan [salamander] is a venomous creature like a lizard. The Guangya says yingyuan is the same as qunqing. The Mingyi [Bielu] lists it separately under the wuqing entry; the sounds of wu and qun are close. It was formerly written as "mao," a common character form. Wu [Pu]'s text says it is also called banmiao, which is correct.

Bei Zi [Cowrie Shell]: Flavor salty, nature balanced. Governs eye cloudiness, ghost-infestation, gu-toxin, abdominal pain, bleeding, the five types of urinary obstruction, and promotes urination. Burned [i.e., calcined] for use it is effective. Found in ponds and marshes.

The Mingyi says: Also called bei chi; found in the Eastern Sea.

Commentary: The Shuowen says bi is a sea shell creature. Guo Pu says it lives in water and is called pian; its form resembles [a cowrie]. The Erya says: small shells are called ji. Guo Pu says: today's fine shells, which also come in purple, are from Rinan.

Also, fan are small and oval, according to Guo Pu — these are the above-mentioned small shells.

Shi Can [Stone Silkworm]: Flavor salty, nature cold. Governs the five urinary obstructions, breaks stone strangury, causes abortion, internally resolves bound qi, promotes urination, and disperses heat. Also called sha chong [sand worm]. Found in ponds and marshes.

Wu Pu says: Shi Can is also called sha chong. According to Shennong and Leigong: sour, non-toxic; grows in Hanzhong; treats the five stranguries, breaks internal bound qi, promotes urination, and disperses heat. [Cited from the] Imperial Overview.

The Mingyi says: Grows in the Jiang and Han [river region].

Commentary: The Guangya says sha chong is the same as zhi zhu [spider]. The Huainan Wanbi Shu says sha chong is also called peng huo and also called di pi. The Imperial Overview's insect section, citing Li Dangzhi, says: a type of creature shaped like [something] that enters the skin from water and can kill people — this differs somewhat from Li's description.

Cui Bao says: [it] grows in Hanzhong; [treats] childhood fright epilepsy, alternating chills and fever, and bound qi; the creature is large and red; enters the skin from water and can kill people; called can she; harvested in the eighth month.

The Mingyi says: sweet, balanced; governs childhood fright epilepsy, alternating chills and fever, bound qi; the creature is large and red; enters the skin from water and can kill people; called can she; harvested in the eighth month.

Commentary: The Shuowen says ha li [clam] is the sile [a spiral shell creature]. The Erya says lulu is jiling. Guo Pu says it carries a round [shell] on its back. Today people in Qingzhou call those that carry [shells] ha li.

The sound of qi and hui are similar; because they resemble sparrow eggs and also resemble the pupae of lan-type insects, they are so called.

According to the Bencao jing, the name is que weng [sparrow pouch].

The Shijing says: "The silverfish (clothes moth) has a salty, warm flavor, non-toxic. It governs women's abdominal masses and difficult urination (the Yulan edition has 'promotes urination'). Flat marshes.

The Mingyi says: One name is li; it is produced at Xianyang.

The above insects and fish, lower class, eighteen varieties, same as the old edition.

Peach kernel (Prunus persica seed): flavor bitter, balanced. Governs blood stasis, amenorrhea, abdominal masses, and kills small worms. Peach blossom kills malevolent ghosts and improves facial complexion. Peach mummy-fruit (shrunken dried peach on the tree): slightly warm, governs killing of all ghost essences and malevolent spirits. (Cited from the Chuxue Ji.)

Peach fuzz kills hundreds of things; the kernel tastes bitter and balanced, and when the fruit does not fall, the peach fuzz governs bleeding downward, blood stasis, fever and cold accumulation, and barrenness. Peach grubs kill evil ghosts, dispel inauspicious influences; grows in river valleys.

The Mingyi says: Peach kernels are harvested in the seventh month; kernels are dried in the shade. Flowers are collected on the third day of the third month, dried in the shade. The peach mummy-fruit (tao xiao) is also named tao nu, or xiao jing, which is the fruit that remains clinging to the tree without falling, with its dried flesh inside.

In the first month the peach grub (tao du) is the insect that eats the peach tree; it lives on Mount Tai.

The Shuowen says: tao is a fruit. The Yupian says: tao is a hairy fruit. The Erya says: peach and plum belong to the category of stone fruits. Guo Pu says: inside the fruit there is a stone containing a kernel. Sun Yan says: peach and plum fruits all contain stones.

Qiu (earthworm-like creature): The Erya states: Ma Xian, Ma Juan, Gou. Commonly called Ma Quan. The Huainanzi, "Seasonal Regulations" chapter, states: In the last month of summer, rotting creatures transform into Ran. Gao You comments: Ran is the Ma Juan. The Fangyan states: Ran has many legs but cannot move as fast as a snake. The "Military Strategy" chapter also states: like the feet of Ran. Gao You comments: Ran is the Ma Juan. The Bowuzhi states: Ma Li, also called Bai Zu (centipede). When cut in two, each half goes its own way.

Wu Pu states: Also called Yuan Qing, Du Long, Qing Hong.

Case note from the Guangya: Also called Qing Meng. Collected at Ru Mountain in the eighth month. Tao Hongjing states: It resembles a large flying ant. Counterfeits are transformations of ban mao (blister beetles), shaped like large beans.

Shu Fu (wood louse/pill bug): Flavor: sour, warm. Governs: qi blockage with inability to urinate, amenorrhea in women, abdominal masses, fever and chills, and promoting urination. Alternative name: Fu Pan. Alternative name: Ran Wei. Found in level valleys.

The Mingyi records: Also called Wei Fei. Found in Wei Commandery and on the ground of households. Collected on the fifth day of the fifth month.

Alternative name: written in black characters. Alternative name: Sheng Chi.

Yi Huo (firefly): Flavor: acrid, slightly warm. Governs: brightening the eyes, children's fire sores, heat qi, gu-poison, ghost-possession, and connecting with the spirit. Alternative names: Ye Zhao, Yi Yao, Jiu Huo, Jing Tian, Lan Huo, Xie Huo. (Collected in the Ju Wenlei.)

Marsh (Ze): [section heading]

一二一九
translation:
Roots can be used for containers. It is also said to be called "han cai" (a water cress-like plant), resembling garlic and growing in water.
The above are vegetables, lower-grade products, two kinds, same as the old edition.
Pi Zi: flavor sweet and warm. It governs evil qi in the abdomen, eliminates the three worms, snake-gu toxins, ghost-possession, and corpse-fixation. Grows in mountain valleys. The cavity entry is in the Tang edition.
The Mingyi [Supplement] says: grows in Yongchang.
Commentary: Tao Hongjing says: doctors from ancient times have never used this herb. Physicians and pharmacists of all eras no longer recognize it. Another name is Ji Zi. Its form and category are unknown. Zhang Yuxi [notes]:
The tree resembles a fir, its seeds resemble areca nuts. The Bencao Jing insect section says "Pi Zi"; Su's commentary says the character "Pi" should use the wood radical. The Erya calls it "Pai." Combined: seven [entries].
The three compilations together have 365 kinds. The method [covers] 365 degrees. One degree corresponds to one day, forming one year. One hundred and thirty items; doubling that number gives 730 names.
Zhang Yuxi says: In the Bencao examples, the Shennong Bencao Jing entries are written in red, while the Mingyi Bielu entries are written in black. The Shennong drugs number 365 kinds. Now here it says doubling the number gives 730 names. This means the secondary entries of the Mingyi Bielu are being included in the count. Therefore the text below this point belongs to the Bielu and should be written in black ink. The confusion between red and black is due to errors accumulated over long years of copying.
Conclusion: Zhang Yuxi's explanation is correct. [These entries] are changed to small characters.
Drugs have the roles of sovereign, minister, assistant, and envoy, to be combined harmoniously in proper proportion: one sovereign, two ministers, three assistants, five envoys; or alternatively one sovereign, three ministers, nine assistants and envoys.
Drugs have yin-yang pairing relationships: mother-child, sibling, root-stem, flower-fruit, herb-mineral, bone-flesh. Some work alone; some are mutually reinforcing; some assist each other; some are mutually restraining; some are antagonistic; some are incompatible; some counteract each other's toxicity. Of these seven relationships, when combining drugs one should use those that are mutually reinforcing or assisting; do not use those that are antagonistic or incompatible. If there is toxicity that must be controlled, one may use those in a restraining or counteracting relationship. Otherwise, do not combine them.

Shennong Bencao Jing, Volume 3

一二八
translation:
Apricot Kernel (Xingren): Flavor sweet, warm. Governs coughing with counterflow qi, rumbling in the throat, throat obstruction, descending qi, promoting lactation after birth, metal wounds, cold running-piglet syndrome. Grows in river valleys.

The Shuowen states: grows in Jin (Shanxi) mountains.
The Mingyi records: grows in Jin mountains.
Commentary: The Shuowen states apricot is a fruit. The Guanzi "Di Yuan" chapter says: in the five fertile soils the appropriate tree is the apricot. The commentary citing Huainanzi says the apricot has a kernel inside.

The above are two items in the lower grade of Fruits, same as the old edition.

Fu Pi (Fermented Shroud): Flavor acrid, neutral. Governs epidemic malaria with chills and fever, pathogenic qi, diarrhea, impotence, headache from drinking, grows in Han Zhong.
Wu Pu states: it is the flower of the small red bean. Also called Fu Pi. Harvested in the seventh month, dried in the shade for forty days, treats headache, stops thirst, and calms urgency.
The Mingyi records: grows in Han Zhong. It is the flower of the small red bean. Harvested in the seventh month, dried in shade. Shennong: bitter, toxic; harvested seventh month, dried in shade forty days, treats headache, stops thirst, calms urgency.

The above is one item in the lower grade of Grains, same as the old edition.

Bitter Bottle Gourd (Ku Hu): Flavor bitter, cold. Governs great water-swelling of the face and four limbs, drains water, causes vomiting. Grows in river marshes.

The Mingyi records: grows in Jin region. The Guangya states it is the hu gourd. The Erya states hu and qi are varieties. The Mao Shi states the hu has bitter leaves; the commentary says the hu is called hu; also in the ninth month one cuts the bottle gourd.

Commentary: The Shuowen states qin is the Chu mallow, a plant related to the aquatic plants. The Zhouli mentions celery in marshy ground. The Erya states: qin is the Chu mallow. Guo Pu says: it is the water celery of today. The Zilin says: it grows in water.

Shennong Bencao Jing, Volume Three

130

Medicinal substances have five flavors — sour, salty, sweet, bitter, and acrid — and four qi: cold, hot, warm, and cool. They may be toxic or non-toxic. They are dried in the shade or dried in the sun. There are proper methods for the time and season of collection and preparation, and for distinguishing raw from processed, and genuine from spurious, old stock from fresh.

The nature of medicines determines their appropriate form: some are best as pills, some as powders, some boiled in water, some steeped in wine, some as simmered pastes. Some substances suit several forms. Some cannot be used in decoctions or wine. One should always follow the nature of the medicine.

When wishing to treat illness, first examine its origin. If the five viscera are not yet depleted, the six bowels not yet exhausted, the blood and vessels not yet disordered, and the spirit not yet scattered, taking medicine will certainly restore life. But if the illness has already taken hold, only half a cure may be achieved.

Once the fever has passed its peak, life will be difficult to preserve entirely.

When using toxic medicines to treat disease, begin with an amount the size of a millet grain. When the illness departs, stop immediately. If it does not depart, double the dose. If it still does not depart, increase it tenfold. Use the departure of the illness as the measure.

Treat cold with hot medicines, heat with cold medicines, indigestion with emetics or purgatives, ghost possession and gu toxin with toxic medicines, abscesses and tumors with medicines for sores, wind-damp with wind-damp medicines — always match the treatment to what is appropriate.

For illness above the chest and diaphragm, eat first then take the medicine. For illness below the heart and abdomen, take the medicine first then eat. For illness in the four limbs and blood vessels, take medicine on an empty stomach in the morning. For illness deep in the marrow and bones, take medicine on a full stomach at night.

The chief categories of serious illness are: wind stroke, cold damage, alternating cold and heat, warm malaria, sudden turmoil illness, severe abdominal swelling and edema, intestinal dysentery, diarrhea, obstruction of urination and defecation, rushing-piglet disorder, counterflow qi, retching and vomiting, jaundice, wasting thirst, retained fluids, food accumulation, hard lumps, masses and conglomerations, fright and possession, epilepsy, ghost possession, throat obstruction, tooth pain, deafness, blindness, metal-weapon wounds, sprains and fractures, abscesses, malignant sores, hemorrhoids and fistulas, goiter and tumors, and in men: the five taxations and seven injuries with vacuity and emaciation; in women: vaginal discharge, flooding and spotting, blood block, genital erosion, and injury from worms, snakes, and gu toxin. These are the broad categories and chief indications. The variations and subsidiary conditions that arise from them should each be addressed by tracing back to their root threads.

Postscript to the Revised Edition

This book was originally typeset from a printed edition of the Shennong Bencao Jing (Divine Farmer's Classic of Materia Medica), compiled by Sun Xingyan and others of the Qing dynasty, incorporating records by Wu Pu and others. Before this reprint, the Sun edition was collated and compared against the edition of the Shennong Bencao Jing compiled by Sun and published by Zhou Xuehai. The above 231 varieties have mutual restraint and facilitation relationships; the remainder have no counterparts. It is said that 33 or 34 varieties were added subsequently. [Annotation:] Note —

On the day of Lidong (Start of Winter), chrysanthemum and juniper are the first to grow, serving as the leaders for Yangqi Stone, mantis egg-case, and ten other substances, and are the chiefs over two hundred herbs.

On the day of Lichun (Start of Spring), magnolia bark and blackberry lily are the first to grow, serving as facilitators for bupleurum and pinellia, governing headache and forty-five joints.

On the day of Lixia (Start of Summer), the cockroach is the first to emerge, serving as facilitator for ginseng and poria, governing the seven regions of the abdomen and preserving the spirit at the center.

On the day of Xiazhi (Summer Solstice), zhuyu (evodia) is the first to grow, serving as facilitator for oyster shell and aconite accessory root, governing the four limbs and thirty-two joints.

On the day of Liqiu (Start of Autumn), angelica and siler are the first to grow, serving as facilitators for asarum and dichondra, governing the twenty-four joints of the chest and back.

[Marginal note:] These five entries are not original annotations; they are not what common scholars investigate. The five items, though annotated, may be put to use at the margins. They come from the Yaodui [Herb Counterparts text]; their meaning and purport are confused and turbid — therefore they are here set aside.

Furthermore, Sun's edition, basing itself on character dictionaries to annotate the herbal classic, corrected some vulgar-form characters.
